1. Aadhaar establishes identity.
2. Aadhaar is conclusive proof of citizenship.
3. Aadhaar is not, by itself, proof of citizenship under Section 9 of the Aadhaar Act.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
7.x: Aadhaar proves identity but not citizenship. Therefore, statements 1 and 3 are correct, while statement 2 is false.
7.tq: Trap the common confusion between identity proof and citizenship proof.
7.sec: Universal angles

7.s: Which of the following pairs is correctly matched?
o: NPR — persons granted citizenship under the CAA alone
7.x: The National Register of Citizens concerns citizens only, whereas the National Population Register covers all usual residents. Thus, NRC—citizens only is correctly matched.
7.tq: Separate the narrower citizenship register from the broader residents’ register.
7.sec: Universal angles

7.s:
Consider the following statements:
1. The CAA has been challenged under Article 14 because it uses religion and country of origin in deciding eligibility.
2. The debate concerning the CAA includes the relationship between a religion-based test and the equality guarantee under Article 14.
3. The CAA challenge is based exclusively on the constitutional validity of Article 239.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
7.x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct. The challenge concerns the use of religion and country of origin in relation to Article 14; Article 239 is unrelated to this issue.
7.tq: Find the unrelated constitutional provision in a set of closely connected statements.
7.sec: Universal angles

7.s: Which one of the following reflects the change in the broad basis of Indian citizenship mentioned in contemporary debates?
o: From territorial citizenship to provincial citizenship
From jus sanguinis to jus soli
From jus soli to jus sanguinis
From single citizenship to dual citizenship
7.x: India has shifted from jus soli, citizenship based primarily on place of birth, towards jus sanguinis, citizenship based primarily on descent or blood relationship.
7.tq: Discriminate between the two Latin expressions by their underlying basis of citizenship.
7.sec: Universal angles

7.s: In the context of recent administrative developments, citizenship-related work under the CAA was moved to which authority?
7.x: Citizenship-related work under the CAA was moved to District Collectors. This is an administrative development concerning the processing of citizenship matters.
7.tq: Identify the authority assigned the function rather than the body that legislated on the subject.
7.sec: Universal angles

7.s:
With reference to citizenship verification during electoral roll revision, consider the following statements:
1. The Election Commission of India may check citizenship during roll revision.
2. Doubtful cases may be referred to the Central Government.
3. The Election Commission alone finally determines every doubtful citizenship case.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
7.x: The Election Commission may check citizenship during revision of electoral rolls, while doubtful cases may go to the Central Government. It is incorrect to state that the Election Commission alone finally determines every doubtful case.
7.tq: Distinguish an initial checking role from the authority handling doubtful cases.
7.sec: Universal angles

7.s: Which of the following is correctly matched with Andhra Pradesh’s constitutional and political development?
o: Andhra State — first linguistic State; bifurcation of Andhra Pradesh — 2014
Andhra State — first Union Territory; bifurcation of Andhra Pradesh — 2000
Andhra State — first linguistic State; bifurcation of Andhra Pradesh — 1953
Andhra State — first State formed under Article 239; bifurcation of Andhra Pradesh — 2019
7.x: Andhra State, formed in 1953, was the first linguistic State. Andhra Pradesh was bifurcated in 2014.
7.tq: Check both parts of a paired historical statement instead of accepting a partially familiar match.
7.sec: Universal angles

8.s:
Consider the following statements regarding the applicability of Fundamental Rights:
1. Articles 23 and 24 are denied to all foreigners.
2. Enemy aliens do not enjoy the safeguards under Article 22 in the circumstances specified in Article 22(3).
3. Companies can claim rights available to all persons, but cannot claim the rights under Article 19.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
8.x: Statement 1 is false because Articles 23 and 24 are not denied to aliens. Statements 2 and 3 are correct: Article 22(3) excludes enemy aliens from specified safeguards, and companies may claim all-persons rights but not Article 19 rights.
8.tq: Find the swapped pair: Articles 23 and 24 are not among the rights denied to aliens.
8.sec: Rights available only to citizens vs to all persons (Articles 14-30)

8.s: A foreign national ordinarily residing in India seeks protection against discrimination based solely on place of birth under Article 15. Which of the following is the most appropriate constitutional position?
o: The protection is available because Article 15 is available to every person.
The protection under Article 15 is available only to citizens.
The protection is available only if the person is an enemy alien.
The protection is available only through Article 23.
8.x: Article 15 is among the Fundamental Rights available only to citizens. It is not an all-persons right available to foreign nationals merely because they reside in India.
8.tq: Apply the citizen-only list to a short factual situation rather than recalling the list mechanically.
8.sec: Rights available only to citizens vs to all persons (Articles 14-30)

8.s: Which one of the following Articles is available to both citizens and foreigners, subject to constitutional exceptions?
8.x: Article 21 is available to all persons. Articles 19, 16 and 29 are included among the rights available only to citizens.
8.tq: Discriminate between the closely placed citizen-only Articles 16, 19 and 29 and the all-persons Article 21.
8.sec: Rights available only to citizens vs to all persons (Articles 14-30)

8.s:
Match List-I with List-II and select the correct answer using the code given below:

List-I (Article)
a. Article 15
b. Article 20
c. Article 29
d. Article 27

List-II (Availability)
i. Only citizens
ii. All persons
iii. Only citizens
iv. All persons

option codes:
8.x: Articles 15 and 29 are available only to citizens, while Articles 20 and 27 are available to all persons. Therefore, the matching is a–i, b–ii, c–iii and d–iv.
8.tq: Start from the sure pairs: Article 15 is citizen-only and Article 20 is an all-persons right.
8.sec: Rights available only to citizens vs to all persons (Articles 14-30)

8.s: Which one of the following pairs is NOT correctly matched?
o: Article 23 — Right to freedom of religion
Article 14 — Equality before law and equal protection of laws
8.x: Article 23 deals with the right against exploitation, including prohibition of traffic in human beings and forced labour. The right to freedom of religion is covered by Articles 25 to 28.
8.tq: Find the wrong group–article association by checking the standard six-group classification.
8.sec: Fundamental Rights - six groups, article range, original vs present number, claimed rights not in Part III

8.s: Part III of the Constitution of India extends from:
8.x: Part III contains Fundamental Rights and extends from Article 12 to Article 35.
8.tq: Test the exact constitutional range directly, with neighbouring Parts as plausible distractors.
8.sec: Fundamental Rights - six groups, article range, original vs present number, claimed rights not in Part III

8.s:
Arrange the following groups of Fundamental Rights in the order in which their article ranges occur in Part III, beginning with the earliest:
A. Right against exploitation
B. Right to equality
C. Cultural and educational rights
D. Right to freedom of religion
8.x: The sequence is right to equality (Articles 14–18), right against exploitation (23–24), right to freedom of religion (25–28), and cultural and educational rights (29–30).
8.tq: Use the first and last article ranges to place the groups in sequence.
8.sec: Fundamental Rights - six groups, article range, original vs present number, claimed rights not in Part III

8.s: Which one of the following correctly represents the present number and original number of groups of Fundamental Rights?
8.x: The Constitution originally contained seven groups of Fundamental Rights. The right to property was removed from Part III by the 44th Amendment, leaving six groups at present.
8.tq: Separate the original and present figures before examining the options.
8.sec: Fundamental Rights - six groups, article range, original vs present number, claimed rights not in Part III

8.s: The right to property was removed from the list of Fundamental Rights by the 44th Amendment Act of 1978 and is presently protected as a legal or constitutional right under:
8.x: The 44th Amendment Act, 1978 removed Article 31 from the Fundamental Rights chapter. Property is now protected under Article 300A in Part XII as a constitutional/legal right.
8.tq: Use the amendment–article–Part chain instead of confusing the former Article 31 with the present provision.
8.sec: Fundamental Rights - six groups, article range, original vs present number, claimed rights not in Part III

8.s: Which one of the following is NOT a Fundamental Right expressly included in Part III?
o: Right to education for children aged six to fourteen years
8.x: The right to employment is a Directive Principle under Article 41, not a Fundamental Right. Education for children aged six to fourteen is a Fundamental Right under Article 21A.
8.tq: Distinguish claimed socio-economic rights from rights expressly placed in Part III.
8.sec: Fundamental Rights - six groups, article range, original vs present number, claimed rights not in Part III

8.s:
Consider the following pairs:
1. Equal pay for equal work — Article 39(d)
2. Right to vote — Article 326 and election laws
3. Right to shelter — Express Fundamental Right in Part III
4. Right to property — Article 300A
Which of the pairs given above are correctly matched?
8.x: Pairs 1, 2 and 4 are correct. Equal pay for equal work is a constitutional goal under Article 39(d), voting is a statutory right connected with Article 326 and election laws, and property is protected under Article 300A. Right to shelter is not an express Fundamental Right, though courts have read it into Article 21.
8.tq: Check whether each claimed right is express, derivative, statutory or a Directive Principle.
8.sec: Fundamental Rights - six groups, article range, original vs present number, claimed rights not in Part III

8.s: The right to education for children between six and fourteen years is a Fundamental Right under:
o: Article 30, inserted by the 73rd Amendment Act
Article 19, inserted by the 42nd Amendment Act
Article 24, inserted by the 44th Amendment Act
Article 21A, inserted by the 86th Amendment Act, 2002
8.x: Article 21A was inserted by the 86th Amendment Act, 2002, making education for children aged six to fourteen a Fundamental Right. The Right of Children to Free and Compulsory Education Act, 2009 gives effect to it.
8.tq: Link the age range, Article 21A and the 86th Amendment without confusing them with child-labour provisions.
8.sec: Fundamental Rights - six groups, article range, original vs present number, claimed rights not in Part III

8.s: Which of the following statements regarding Fundamental Rights is correct?
o: They can be enforced only after Parliament passes a law under Article 35.
They are enforceable only by the High Courts.
They are non-justiciable because they are political principles.
An aggrieved person may directly approach the Supreme Court under Article 32.
8.x: Fundamental Rights are justiciable, and Article 32 permits an aggrieved person to move the Supreme Court directly for their enforcement. High Courts can also enforce them under Article 226, along with other legal rights.
8.tq: Identify the constitutional remedy that directly establishes justiciability: Article 32.
8.sec: Features of Part III - justiciable, not absolute, reasonable restrictions, positive vs negative, foreign model

8.s:
Consider the following statements:
1. Fundamental Rights are subject to reasonable restrictions where the Constitution permits such restrictions.
2. Courts examine the reasonableness of restrictions through judicial review.
3. Every Fundamental Right is absolute and cannot be regulated by law.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
8.x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct. Fundamental Rights are qualified rather than absolute, and courts review restrictions for constitutional validity and reasonableness. Statement 3 is false.
8.tq: Reject the absolute claim and retain the two statements describing the restriction-and-review framework.
8.sec: Features of Part III - justiciable, not absolute, reasonable restrictions, positive vs negative, foreign model

8.s: How many grounds of reasonable restriction are listed in Article 19 in all?
8.x: Article 19 contains eleven grounds of reasonable restriction in all. These restrictions must be imposed by law and must fall within constitutionally recognised grounds.
8.tq: Test the precise numerical detail with nearby figures as distractors.
8.sec: Features of Part III - justiciable, not absolute, reasonable restrictions, positive vs negative, foreign model

8.s: Which one of the following is a negative right, in the sense that it primarily limits State action?
8.x: Article 20 is a negative right that limits State action in relation to conviction for offences. Articles 21A, 29 and 30 are examples of positive rights conferring particular privileges or protections.
8.tq: Distinguish negative restraints on the State from positive rights that confer privileges.
8.sec: Features of Part III - justiciable, not absolute, reasonable restrictions, positive vs negative, foreign model

8.s: Which one of the following sets consists only of examples of positive Fundamental Rights?
8.x: Articles 21A, 29 and 30 confer educational or cultural privileges and are treated as examples of positive rights. The other sets contain negative rights that primarily restrict State action.
8.tq: Classify each option by the direction of the right rather than by its subject title.
8.sec: Features of Part III - justiciable, not absolute, reasonable restrictions, positive vs negative, foreign model

8.s: Which one of the following Articles is NOT included among the provisions imposing near-absolute limits on legislative power?
8.x: Articles 15, 17, 18, 20 and 24 are identified as provisions imposing near-absolute limits on legislative power. Article 19 permits reasonable restrictions on specified grounds and is therefore not in that group.
8.tq: Find the exception within a closely related Article list.
8.sec: Features of Part III - justiciable, not absolute, reasonable restrictions, positive vs negative, foreign model

8.s: Fundamental Rights are primarily enforceable against the State, but which of the following Articles also operate against private persons in the situations covered by them?
8.x: Although most Fundamental Rights operate against State action, Articles 15(2), 17, 23 and 24 also impose obligations relevant to private persons. The other combinations do not represent the specified group.
8.tq: Use the exception-to-the-general-rule method: identify the Articles that can bind private persons.
8.sec: Features of Part III - justiciable, not absolute, reasonable restrictions, positive vs negative, foreign model

8.s: The model for the Fundamental Rights chapter of the Indian Constitution was principally drawn from the:
8.x: The Fundamental Rights chapter of the Indian Constitution was modelled principally on the United States Bill of Rights.
8.tq: Test the foreign constitutional source directly, using other constitutional models as distractors.
8.sec: Features of Part III - justiciable, not absolute, reasonable restrictions, positive vs negative, foreign model

8.s: Which one of the following correctly describes Fundamental Rights?
o: They are both natural and legal rights and protect individuals as well as minorities.
They are only legal rights and have no natural-rights character.
They protect only minorities and not individuals.
They are exclusively political rights available only during elections.
8.x: Fundamental Rights have both natural and legal dimensions and are intended to protect individuals and minorities. They are not confined to electoral or exclusively political rights.
8.tq: Choose the comprehensive description and reject options that use exclusive language.
8.sec: Features of Part III - justiciable, not absolute, reasonable restrictions, positive vs negative, foreign model

8.s: Which authority alone is empowered under Article 33 to restrict the application of Fundamental Rights to members of the armed forces and specified security services?
o: The Supreme Court by judicial order
8.x: Article 33 empowers Parliament alone to restrict or abrogate the application of Fundamental Rights for members of the armed forces, paramilitary forces, police, intelligence organisations and related staff, including specified non-combatants.
8.tq: Ask who would do this job: Article 33 expressly assigns the power to Parliament, not the executive or States.
8.sec: Who can limit Fundamental Rights - Parliament vs courts, Articles 33-35

8.s:
Consider the following statements regarding Article 33:
1. Parliament may restrict Fundamental Rights of members of the armed forces.
2. The power may extend to specified non-combatant employees such as cooks and barbers.
3. State Legislatures may exercise the same power independently for maintaining public order.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
8.x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct. Article 33 gives the power exclusively to Parliament, so Statement 3 is false.
8.tq: Spot the wrong authority in Statement 3 while retaining the specific scope of Article 33.
8.sec: Who can limit Fundamental Rights - Parliament vs courts, Articles 33-35

8.s: Which one of the following statements regarding Article 34 is correct?
o: It automatically suspends Articles 20 and 21 whenever martial law is declared.
It deals with preventive detention during a National Emergency only.
It empowers State Legislatures to declare martial law throughout India.
It permits restriction of Fundamental Rights while martial law is in force and allows Parliament to indemnify officials; martial law is not defined in the Constitution.
8.x: Article 34 concerns restrictions on Fundamental Rights while martial law is in force and permits Parliament to indemnify officials for acts connected with it. The Constitution does not define martial law.
8.tq: Combine the Article 34 subject, Parliament’s indemnity power and the constitutional omission on definition.
8.sec: Who can limit Fundamental Rights - Parliament vs courts, Articles 33-35

8.s: Under Article 35, which body has exclusive legislative competence to make laws on the matters specified in that Article?
8.x: Article 35 assigns legislative power exclusively to Parliament for matters including Articles 16(3), 32(3), 33 and 34, and for prescribing punishments for offences under Part III. The purpose is uniformity throughout India.
8.tq: Apply the exclusive-authority trap to distinguish Parliament from State Legislatures.
8.sec: Who can limit Fundamental Rights - Parliament vs courts, Articles 33-35

8.s:
Match List-I with List-II and select the correct answer using the code given below:

List-I (Article)
a. Article 33
b. Article 34
c. Article 35
d. Article 359

List-II (Provision)
i. Restriction during martial law and indemnity by Parliament
ii. President’s order suspending enforcement of specified Fundamental Rights
iii. Parliament’s exclusive power to legislate on specified Part III matters
iv. Restriction of Fundamental Rights of specified forces and security services

option codes:
8.x: Article 33 concerns specified forces and security services, Article 34 concerns martial law, Article 35 gives Parliament exclusive legislative power on specified matters, and Article 359 concerns the President’s order suspending enforcement of named rights.
8.tq: Start with the distinctive pairs Article 33–forces and Article 34–martial law, then complete the remaining matches.
8.sec: Who can limit Fundamental Rights - Parliament vs courts, Articles 33-35

8.s: Which one of the following correctly distinguishes Articles 358 and 359?
o: Article 358 operates only during armed rebellion, whereas Article 359 operates only during financial emergency.
Article 358 concerns automatic suspension of Article 19 during war or external aggression, whereas Article 359 concerns a Presidential order suspending enforcement of named Fundamental Rights.
Article 358 is a power of the Supreme Court, whereas Article 359 is a power of Parliament.
Article 358 suspends enforcement of all Fundamental Rights, whereas Article 359 suspends only Article 19.
8.x: Article 358 automatically suspends Article 19 only when the Emergency is based on war or external aggression, not armed rebellion. Article 359 enables the President to suspend enforcement of named Fundamental Rights by order, but not Articles 20 and 21.
8.tq: Split the two similar provisions by authority, trigger and scope instead of treating both as identical emergency powers.
8.sec: Who can limit Fundamental Rights - Parliament vs courts, Articles 33-35

8.s: A constitutional amendment affecting a Fundamental Right is challenged before the Supreme Court. Which of the following principles is applicable?
o: Fundamental Rights cannot be amended under any circumstances.
Parliament may amend Fundamental Rights only through a constitutional amendment, subject to the basic-structure limitation.
Parliament may amend Fundamental Rights through an ordinary statute without limitation.
Only State Legislatures may amend Fundamental Rights.
8.x: Fundamental Rights may be altered through the constitutional amendment procedure, but the amendment is subject to the basic-structure doctrine laid down in Kesavananda Bharati (1973). An ordinary law cannot amend the Constitution.
8.tq: Distinguish constitutional amendment from ordinary legislation and apply the basic-structure limitation.
8.sec: Who can limit Fundamental Rights - Parliament vs courts, Articles 33-35

8.s: The basic-structure limitation on Parliament’s amending power is associated with which case and year?
8.x: The basic-structure doctrine was laid down in Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala in 1973. It limits Parliament’s power to amend the Constitution, including provisions relating to Fundamental Rights.
8.tq: Link the doctrine with its leading case and year, while avoiding nearby constitutional cases.
8.sec: Who can limit Fundamental Rights - Parliament vs courts, Articles 33-35

8.s: Which doctrine states that a law is void only to the extent of its inconsistency with Fundamental Rights, while the separable valid portion continues to operate?
8.x: The doctrine of severability invalidates only the inconsistent portion of a law, provided that portion can be separated from the valid remainder.
8.tq: Use the exact meaning of the doctrine rather than the associated case.
8.sec: Doctrines - meaning and case where applied (eclipse, severability, waiver)

8.s: The doctrine of Eclipse primarily applies to a law which is:
o: A pre-Constitution law inconsistent with Fundamental Rights
A post-Constitution law violating the rights of non-citizens only
A constitutional amendment violating the basic structure
A contractual provision waived by a citizen
8.x: The doctrine of eclipse mainly applies to pre-Constitution laws inconsistent with Fundamental Rights. Such laws become dormant rather than completely dead.
8.tq: Discriminate between the scope of Eclipse and the other doctrines.
8.sec: Doctrines - meaning and case where applied (eclipse, severability, waiver)

8.s:
Consider the following statements about the doctrine of Eclipse:
1. An inconsistent pre-Constitution law becomes dormant rather than being completely wiped out.
2. The law may revive when the constitutional conflict is removed.
3. The doctrine was applied in Bhikaji Narain Dhakras v. State of Madhya Pradesh.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
8.x: All three statements are correct. In Bhikaji Narain Dhakras, the inconsistent law was treated as eclipsed and capable of revival after removal of the conflict through the First Amendment.
8.tq: Test the meaning, consequence and leading case together.
8.sec: Doctrines - meaning and case where applied (eclipse, severability, waiver)

8.s: Which case is associated with the application of the doctrine of Waiver in relation to Fundamental Rights?
o: Bhikaji Narain Dhakras v. State of MP
Motor General Traders v. State of AP
8.x: In Basheshar Nath v. CIT (1959), it was held that a person cannot waive a Fundamental Right.
8.tq: Match the doctrine with its leading case.
8.sec: Doctrines - meaning and case where applied (eclipse, severability, waiver)

8.s: With reference to the doctrine of Waiver, which one of the following statements is correct?
o: A person cannot waive a Fundamental Right, though statutory or contractual rights may be given up.
Only constitutional rights may be voluntarily given up.
Waiver applies only to rights available to non-citizens.
A citizen may permanently waive any Fundamental Right by contract.
8.x: Fundamental Rights cannot be waived by an individual. Statutory and contractual rights, unlike Fundamental Rights, may be relinquished.
8.tq: Apply the distinction between Fundamental Rights and ordinary legal rights.
8.sec: Doctrines - meaning and case where applied (eclipse, severability, waiver)

8.s:
Match List-I with List-II:

List-I (Doctrine)
(a) Eclipse
(b) Severability
(c) Waiver
(d) Prospective overruling

List-II (Meaning)
(i) Ruling operates only for the future
(ii) A person cannot give up a Fundamental Right
(iii) Inconsistent law remains dormant and may revive
(iv) Only the inconsistent portion of a law is void

Select the correct answer using the code given below:
8.x: Eclipse means dormancy and possible revival; Severability preserves the separable valid part; Waiver cannot operate against Fundamental Rights; Prospective overruling operates only in the future.
8.tq: Start from the sure pair and eliminate codes.
8.sec: Doctrines - meaning and case where applied (eclipse, severability, waiver)

8.s: Which one of the following pairs is NOT correctly matched?
o: Severability — State of Gujarat v. Ambica Mills
8.x: State of Gujarat v. Ambica Mills is associated with the extension of the doctrine of Eclipse to post-Constitution laws affecting non-citizens. Severability is associated with cases such as A.K. Gopalan, R.M.D.C. and Motor General Traders.
8.tq: Find the wrongly assigned case rather than recalling the doctrine alone.
8.sec: Doctrines - meaning and case where applied (eclipse, severability, waiver)

8.s: The decision in State of Gujarat v. Ambica Mills is significant because it:
o: Introduced the doctrine of prospective overruling
Applied Eclipse to a post-Constitution law in relation to non-citizens
Established that a person may waive Fundamental Rights
Held that Fundamental Rights can never be amended
8.x: Ambica Mills (1974) extended the doctrine of Eclipse to post-Constitution laws operating against non-citizens.
8.tq: Use the distinctive qualification attached to a famous case.
8.sec: Doctrines - meaning and case where applied (eclipse, severability, waiver)

8.s: The doctrine of Progressive Interpretation treats the Constitution as:
o: A rigid document confined to the original understanding of its framers
A document subordinate to ordinary legislation
A document applicable only to disputes involving citizens
A living document to be read in accordance with present needs
8.x: Progressive Interpretation reads the Constitution as a living document capable of responding to present social and constitutional needs.
8.tq: Identify the central idea of the doctrine from its constitutional application.
8.sec: Doctrines - meaning and case where applied (eclipse, severability, waiver)

8.s: Which case is associated with the widening of Article 21 through progressive interpretation?
o: Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India
Shankari Prasad v. Union of India
Bhikaji Narain Dhakras v. State of MP
8.x: Maneka Gandhi (1978) widened the interpretation of Article 21 and is an important example of progressive constitutional interpretation.
8.tq: Link the interpretive doctrine with its constitutional example.
8.sec: Doctrines - meaning and case where applied (eclipse, severability, waiver)

8.s: Payment of wages below the minimum wage to labourers, in the circumstances recognised by the Supreme Court, amounts to:
o: A restriction on freedom of association under Article 19(4)
8.x: Payment below the minimum wage may amount to forced labour under Article 23, as recognised in the PUDR/Asiad case of 1982.
8.tq: Translate a factual situation into the applicable Fundamental Right.
8.sec: Violation of Fundamental Rights - statement-based scenarios

8.s: A person employing a child below fourteen years in a factory or mine would violate:
8.x: Article 24 prohibits the employment of children below fourteen years in factories, mines and other hazardous employment.
8.tq: Separate the child-exploitation provision from forced labour and discrimination provisions.
8.sec: Violation of Fundamental Rights - statement-based scenarios

8.s: Denial of admission to a State-aided educational institution solely on the ground of religion, race, caste or language is prohibited by:
8.x: Article 29(2) prohibits denial of admission to a State-maintained or State-aided educational institution on these grounds.
8.tq: Identify the specific clause governing admission to State-aided institutions.
8.sec: Violation of Fundamental Rights - statement-based scenarios

8.s:
Consider the following statements:
1. Excluding Dalits from a public well may violate Article 15(2).
2. Excluding Dalits from a public shop may violate Article 17.
3. The protections under Articles 15(2) and 17 may operate against private persons in such situations.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
8.x: Exclusion of Dalits from public facilities can attract Articles 15(2) and 17, and these protections are not confined to State action in such cases.
8.tq: Combine the prohibited conduct, constitutional provisions and horizontal application.
8.sec: Violation of Fundamental Rights - statement-based scenarios

8.s: A prohibition imposed on an association can be treated as a restriction under Article 19(4) only when it is based on:
o: The grounds constitutionally permitted under Article 19(4)
Any reason considered desirable by the executive
An ordinance that is immune from judicial review
8.x: Restrictions on freedom of association under Article 19(4) must be based on the constitutionally specified grounds and remain subject to constitutional scrutiny.
8.tq: Ask whether the restriction fits the constitutional grounds rather than accepting executive discretion.
8.sec: Violation of Fundamental Rights - statement-based scenarios

8.s: A violation of Articles 19 or 21 by a purely private individual ordinarily gives rise to:
o: An ordinary legal remedy rather than a writ remedy against the private individual
A remedy exclusively before the Election Commission
An automatic writ petition under Article 32 against that individual
8.x: Where the alleged violation is by a private individual and does not involve enforceable public-law action, the ordinary legal remedy is generally available rather than a writ.
8.tq: Distinguish enforceable public-law rights from an ordinary private-law remedy.
8.sec: Violation of Fundamental Rights - statement-based scenarios

8.s: Under Article 13(1), laws in force before the commencement of the Constitution which are inconsistent with Fundamental Rights are:
o: Void only to the extent of inconsistency
Valid even to the extent of inconsistency
Void in their entirety in every case
8.x: Article 13(1) renders a pre-Constitution law void only to the extent that it conflicts with Fundamental Rights. It does not refer to laws existing before Independence as such.
8.tq: Watch the precise constitutional time reference and the words ‘to the extent’.
8.sec: Article 13 - meaning of law, precedence of the Constitution, amendments as law

8.s: Which of the following is included within the expression ‘law’ under Article 13(3)?
o: Ordinance, order, bye-law, rule, regulation, notification, custom or usage
Only a constitutional amendment made under Article 368
Only a judicial decision of the Supreme Court
Only an Act passed by Parliament
8.x: Article 13(3) gives a broad meaning to law, including ordinances, orders, bye-laws, rules, regulations, notifications, customs and usages having the force of law.
8.tq: Test the complete statutory list rather than one familiar item.
8.sec: Article 13 - meaning of law, precedence of the Constitution, amendments as law

8.s: Article 13(2) prohibits the State from making a law which:
o: Changes the distribution of legislative powers only
Regulates contractual rights between private parties alone
Creates a new district within a State
Abridges or takes away the rights conferred by Part III
8.x: Article 13(2) declares that the State shall not make any law which takes away or abridges the Fundamental Rights conferred by Part III; such a law is void to that extent.
8.tq: Match the constitutional clause with the prohibited legislative action.
8.sec: Article 13 - meaning of law, precedence of the Constitution, amendments as law

8.s: Which constitutional amendment inserted Article 13(4), excluding constitutional amendments made under Article 368 from the operation of Article 13?
8.x: The Twenty-fourth Amendment Act, 1971 inserted Article 13(4), providing that Article 13 would not apply to constitutional amendments made under Article 368.
8.tq: Pair the specific clause with the correct amendment year.
8.sec: Article 13 - meaning of law, precedence of the Constitution, amendments as law

8.s:
Consider the following statements regarding constitutional amendments and Article 13:
1. In Shankari Prasad, the Supreme Court held that Parliament could amend Fundamental Rights.
2. In Golaknath, Fundamental Rights were given a transcendental position and Parliament was held unable to abridge them.
3. Kesavananda Bharati held that Fundamental Rights could be amended subject to the basic structure limitation.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
8.x: All three statements correctly describe the holdings associated with Shankari Prasad, Golaknath and Kesavananda Bharati.
8.tq: Track the constitutional position across successive landmark decisions.
8.sec: Article 13 - meaning of law, precedence of the Constitution, amendments as law

8.s: Which one of the following best describes the constitutional significance of Article 13?
o: It prevents courts from examining delegated legislation.
It applies only to laws enacted before the Constitution.
It makes Fundamental Rights subordinate to ordinary legislation.
It provides the basis for judicial review and gives Fundamental Rights precedence over ordinary law.
8.x: Article 13 is the constitutional basis of judicial review of laws inconsistent with Fundamental Rights and establishes the supremacy of Fundamental Rights over ordinary law.
8.tq: Choose the option capturing both the function and effect of Article 13.
8.sec: Article 13 - meaning of law, precedence of the Constitution, amendments as law

8.s:
Arrange the following decisions and amendments in chronological order:
A. Kesavananda Bharati case
B. Shankari Prasad case
C. Twenty-fourth Constitutional Amendment
D. Golaknath case
8.x: The correct order is Shankari Prasad (1951), Golaknath (1967), Twenty-fourth Amendment (1971), and Kesavananda Bharati (1973).
8.tq: Fix the earliest and latest events first, then place the middle developments.
8.sec: Article 13 - meaning of law, precedence of the Constitution, amendments as law

8.s: Dr. B. R. Ambedkar described which constitutional provision as the ‘heart and soul’ of the Constitution?
8.x: Dr. Ambedkar described Article 32 as the heart and soul of the Constitution because it provides the right to move the Supreme Court for enforcement of Fundamental Rights.
8.tq: Associate the famous description with the exact Article, not merely with Part III generally.
8.sec: Descriptions of Fundamental Rights - who said

8.s:
Which of the following is included within the expression ‘State’ under Article 12 of the Constitution of India?
1. The Government and Parliament of India
2. The Government and Legislature of each State
3. All local authorities
4. Other authorities in India or under the control of the Government of India
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
8.x: Article 12 includes the Union Government and Parliament, State Governments and Legislatures, local authorities, and other authorities in India or under the control of the Government of India.
8.tq: Use complete constitutional enumeration and check whether any category has been omitted.
8.sec: Article 12 - meaning of State, other authorities, instrumentality cases

8.s: Which one of the following cases laid down the tests for determining whether a body is an instrumentality or agency of the State?
o: R.D. Shetty v. International Airport Authority
8.x: R.D. Shetty v. International Airport Authority (1979) laid down the tests for identifying an instrumentality or agency of the State.
8.tq: Match the case with its distinctive constitutional holding rather than its year alone.
8.sec: Article 12 - meaning of State, other authorities, instrumentality cases

8.s:
Consider the following statements regarding the decision in Ajay Hasia v. Khalid Mujib:
1. A society running a Regional Engineering College was treated as ‘State’.
2. The constitutional test depends on how the body was created and controlled, not merely on its legal form.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
8.x: In Ajay Hasia v. Khalid Mujib (1981), the society running a Regional Engineering College was held to be ‘State’. The Court emphasised creation and control rather than the formal legal form of the body.
8.tq: Separate the substance of governmental control from the formal label of an institution.
8.sec: Article 12 - meaning of State, other authorities, instrumentality cases

8.s: In which of the following cases was it held that a body may be regarded as ‘State’ when it is financially, functionally and administratively dominated by the Government?
o: R.D. Shetty v. International Airport Authority
8.x: Pradeep Kumar Biswas (2002) held that financial, functional and administrative domination by the Government is a significant basis for treating a body as ‘State’.
8.tq: Use the three-part domination test as the identifying phrase for the correct case.
8.sec: Article 12 - meaning of State, other authorities, instrumentality cases

8.s: Which one of the following was the principal holding in Rajasthan SEB v. Mohan Lal (1967)?
o: Private bodies are always subject to writ jurisdiction
A society running a Regional Engineering College is not a public authority
Only bodies incorporated directly by Parliament can be ‘State’
Statutory bodies are included within ‘other authorities’
8.x: Rajasthan SEB v. Mohan Lal (1967) recognised statutory bodies as ‘other authorities’ for the purposes of Article 12.
8.tq: Distinguish the statutory-body principle from the later instrumentality tests.
8.sec: Article 12 - meaning of State, other authorities, instrumentality cases

8.s:
Consider the following statements:
1. A body’s formal legal form is by itself decisive in determining whether it is ‘State’ under Article 12.
2. Government share capital may be relevant in applying instrumentality or agency tests.
3. Deep and pervasive governmental control may be relevant in determining whether a body is ‘State’.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
8.x: Statements 2 and 3 are correct because government share capital and deep and pervasive control are relevant factors. Statement 1 is false because Ajay Hasia held that creation and control, rather than form alone, are material.
8.tq: Spot the absolute formulation that wrongly makes legal form conclusive.
8.sec: Article 12 - meaning of State, other authorities, instrumentality cases

8.s: Which of the following is NOT ordinarily correct regarding writ petitions against private bodies?
o: The ordinary rule is subject to the circumstance of State collusion
Writs ordinarily lie against every private body because Article 12 includes all institutions
A writ may become maintainable where the State acts in collusion with a private body
Writs do not ordinarily lie against private bodies
8.x: Writs do not ordinarily lie against private bodies merely because they perform an activity. An exception may arise where the State acts in collusion with the private body.
8.tq: Reject the option that uses an overbroad ‘every’ formulation and ignores the ordinary rule.
8.sec: Article 12 - meaning of State, other authorities, instrumentality cases

8.s: A private organisation performs a public activity, but no governmental authority is shown to be involved in the alleged violation. Which position is most consistent with the general rule concerning writs?
o: A writ can never lie against a private organisation under any circumstances
A writ ordinarily lies because every public activity makes the organisation ‘State’
A writ does not ordinarily lie merely because the organisation performs a public activity
A writ lies only when Parliament specifically authorises the organisation
8.x: Writs do not ordinarily lie against private bodies merely on the basis of their public activity. The rule is not absolute, since State collusion can alter the position.
8.tq: Apply the ordinary rule while avoiding the absolute trap in the words ‘every’ and ‘never’.
8.sec: Article 12 - meaning of State, other authorities, instrumentality cases

8.s: The demand to make the right to vote a Fundamental Right concerns a right which is presently regarded as:
o: A legal right derived exclusively from Article 21
A statutory right under Section 62 of the Representation of the People Act, 1951, with a constitutional basis under Article 326
A constitutional right enforceable only under Article 32
8.x: The right to vote is presently treated as statutory under Section 62 of the Representation of the People Act, 1951, and is constitutionally connected with Article 326. It is not presently a Fundamental Right.
8.tq: Separate a statutory electoral right from a Fundamental Right and identify both cited provisions.
8.sec: Universal angles

8.s: The Supreme Court has reaffirmed that the rights to vote and contest elections are:
o: Natural rights outside the constitutional framework
Fundamental Rights available under Part III
8.x: The rights to vote and contest elections have been reaffirmed as statutory rights, rather than Fundamental Rights under Part III.
8.tq: Discriminate between the related but distinct rights to vote and contest and their legal status.
8.sec: Universal angles

8.s: Which one of the following groups of provisions is commonly described as the ‘golden triangle’ of the Constitution?
8.x: Articles 14, 19 and 21 are collectively described as the golden triangle because of their interrelationship in protecting liberty and individual rights.
8.tq: Recall the standard constitutional grouping rather than selecting adjacent Fundamental Rights articles.
8.sec: Universal angles

8.s:
Which of the following statements regarding Fundamental Rights is correct?
1. They operate as a check on governmental power.
2. They protect minorities.
3. They limit Parliament through Article 13.
4. They are regarded as a bulwark of liberty and the rule of law.
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
8.x: Fundamental Rights check governmental power, protect minorities, support liberty and the rule of law, and limit Parliament through Article 13.
8.tq: Test several connected constitutional purposes and choose the complete combination.
8.sec: Universal angles

8.s: Which one of the following correctly distinguishes the constitutional position in Britain from that in India regarding Fundamental Rights?
o: Britain has no codified Fundamental Rights; its rights rest on conventions and the rule of law
India, unlike Britain, protects rights only through conventions
Britain has a single written code of Fundamental Rights identical to Part III of India
Britain has no protection of rights because it follows neither conventions nor the rule of law
8.x: Britain does not have codified Fundamental Rights in the Indian constitutional sense; protection rests largely on conventions and the rule of law.
8.tq: Compare the source and form of rights protection instead of confusing absence of codification with absence of rights.
8.sec: Universal angles

8.s:
Which of the following Articles and provisions were inserted by the First Amendment Act, 1951?
1. Article 31A
2. Article 31B
3. The Ninth Schedule
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
8.x: The First Amendment Act, 1951 added Articles 31A and 31B and introduced the Ninth Schedule. The amendment is associated with the constitutional protection of certain land reform laws.
8.tq: Treat the amendment, its two Articles and the Schedule as one connected constitutional package.
8.sec: Universal angles

8.s: With reference to the Ninth Schedule, which statement is correct?
o: All laws placed in it are permanently immune from every form of judicial review
It contains only provisions relating to elections
Its protective effect has been subjected to limitations by the decision in I.R. Coelho (2007)
It was created by the Forty-Fourth Amendment Act, 1978
8.x: I.R. Coelho (2007) limited the absolute character of Ninth Schedule protection by permitting judicial scrutiny where basic-structure principles are affected.
8.tq: Use the later judicial limitation to reject the extreme claim of complete and permanent immunity.
8.sec: Universal angles

8.s:
Arrange the following developments in chronological order:
A. Decision in Rajasthan SEB v. Mohan Lal
B. Decision in R.D. Shetty v. International Airport Authority
C. Decision in Ajay Hasia v. Khalid Mujib
D. Decision in Pradeep Kumar Biswas
8.x: The cases were decided in 1967, 1979, 1981 and 2002 respectively: Rajasthan SEB, R.D. Shetty, Ajay Hasia and Pradeep Kumar Biswas.
8.tq: Fix the earliest and latest cases first, then place the two closely related instrumentality decisions.
8.sec: Article 12 - meaning of State, other authorities, instrumentality cases

9.s:
Which of the following grounds are expressly mentioned in Article 15(1) as prohibited grounds of discrimination?
1. Religion
2. Race
3. Caste
4. Sex
5. Place of birth
6. Descent
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
9.x: Article 15(1) prohibits discrimination only on the grounds of religion, race, caste, sex and place of birth. Descent is specifically added in Article 16(2), not Article 15(1).
9.tq: Separate the closely related grounds in Articles 15 and 16 instead of treating their lists as identical.
9.sec: Articles 14-18 - content and clause text  [APPSC]

9.s:
Article 15(2) prohibits denial of access, on the specified grounds of discrimination, to which of the following?
1. Shops and public restaurants
2. Hotels
3. Wells, tanks and bathing ghats
4. Places of public entertainment
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
9.x: The listed places under Article 15(2) are shops, restaurants, hotels, wells, tanks and bathing ghats. Places of public entertainment are not included in the specified list given here.
9.tq: Test the exact statutory list and reject an attractive but unlisted addition.
9.sec: Articles 14-18 - content and clause text  [APPSC]

9.s: A private hotel refuses entry to a person solely on the ground of caste. Which constitutional provision is most directly attracted?
9.x: Article 15(2) applies to access to places such as hotels and binds private persons as well as the State. It prohibits discrimination on the specified grounds in such access.
9.tq: Apply the clause to a private-person situation rather than assuming that equality provisions bind only the State.
9.sec: Articles 14-18 - content and clause text  [APPSC]

9.s: Which one of the following correctly distinguishes Articles 14 and 15?
o: Article 14 applies to all persons, whereas Article 15 is available only to citizens.
Article 14 applies only to citizens, whereas Article 15 applies to all persons.
Both Articles 14 and 15 are available only to citizens.
Both Articles 14 and 15 apply only to foreigners residing in India.
9.x: Article 14 applies to any person within the territory of India. Article 15 is a right available only to citizens.
9.tq: Discriminate between the beneficiaries of two neighbouring constitutional provisions.
9.sec: Articles 14-18 - content and clause text  [APPSC]

9.s:
With reference to Article 16, consider the following statements:
1. It guarantees equality of opportunity in matters of public employment.
2. Descent and residence are among the grounds added to the prohibited list under Article 16(2).
3. Parliament alone may prescribe residence requirements for certain public employment.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
9.x: Article 16 concerns equality of opportunity in public employment. Article 16(2) includes descent and residence, while Article 16(3) permits Parliament to prescribe residence requirements for certain jobs.
9.tq: Combine the general guarantee with the specific clauses and the authority competent to act.
9.sec: Articles 14-18 - content and clause text  [APPSC]

9.s: Under Article 16(3), which body is competent to prescribe a residence requirement for certain public employment?
o: The Governor of the concerned State
9.x: Article 16(3) specifically empowers Parliament to prescribe residence requirements for certain classes of employment or appointment under a State or Union territory.
9.tq: Use the ‘who would do this job?’ method to identify the constitutionally specified authority.
9.sec: Articles 14-18 - content and clause text  [APPSC]

9.s: Which of the following statements regarding Article 17 is correct?
o: It abolishes titles conferred by the State.
It abolishes untouchability and makes the enforcement of any disability arising from it an offence.
It prohibits discrimination only on grounds of religion and race.
It abolishes untouchability only in government offices.
9.x: Article 17 abolishes untouchability, forbids its practice and treats enforcement of any disability arising from it as an offence.
9.tq: Match the constitutional article with both its prohibition and its legal consequence.
9.sec: Articles 14-18 - content and clause text  [APPSC]

9.s: Which one of the following is correctly matched?
o: Article 18 — Equality of opportunity in public employment
9.x: Article 17 deals with the abolition of untouchability. Article 14 concerns equality before law, Article 15 discrimination, and Article 18 titles.
9.tq: Use article-subject matching and eliminate provisions assigned to neighbouring articles.
9.sec: Articles 14-18 - content and clause text  [APPSC]

9.s: Which of the following pairs is NOT correctly matched?
9.x: Articles 39(b), 39(c) and 39(d), which are Directive Principles, are associated with economic equality. Social equality is associated with Articles 15, 17 and 18.
9.tq: Identify the reversed comparison in a classification table.
9.sec: Types of equality - article securing each  [APPSC]

9.s: The constitutional provisions relating to no exclusion from electoral rolls on specified grounds and adult suffrage primarily secure which type of equality?
9.x: Articles 325 and 326 are associated with political equality through non-exclusion from electoral rolls and adult suffrage.
9.tq: Connect a constitutional mechanism with the type of equality it advances.
9.sec: Types of equality - article securing each  [APPSC]

9.s: According to B. R. Ambedkar, liberty, equality and fraternity are best understood as:
o: Economic objectives confined to the Directive Principles
Three independent ideals applicable to separate institutions
Duties imposed only on public servants
9.x: Ambedkar described liberty, equality and fraternity as an inseparable trinity.
9.tq: Recall the precise formulation associated with the constitutional thinker.
9.sec: Types of equality - article securing each  [APPSC]

9.s: Which of the following special provisions is correctly matched with its beneficiary group?
o: Article 16(4) — Foreign citizens inadequately represented in services
Article 16(5) — All religious minorities in public employment
9.x: Article 15(3), part of the original Constitution, permits special provisions for women and children. The other pairings misstate the beneficiary groups or scope of the relevant clauses.
9.tq: Start from the sure beneficiary-clause pair and reject swapped groups.
9.sec: Articles 15 and 16 special provisions - beneficiaries, groups not covered  [APPSC]

9.s: Article 15(4), inserted by the First Constitutional Amendment, 1951, provides for special provisions for:
o: Socially and educationally backward classes, Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes
9.x: Article 15(4) covers socially and educationally backward classes, Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes. It was inserted by the First Amendment in 1951.
9.tq: Link an amendment number and year with the precise beneficiary group.
9.sec: Articles 15 and 16 special provisions - beneficiaries, groups not covered  [APPSC]

9.s: Which statement regarding Article 15(5) is correct?
o: It applies to public employment and excludes all educational institutions.
It applies only to government educational institutions.
It permits special provisions for SEBCs, SCs and STs in admissions to private aided or unaided institutions, except minority institutions.
It covers only women and children in private institutions.
9.x: Article 15(5), inserted by the 93rd Amendment, 2005, covers admissions in private aided or unaided educational institutions for SEBCs, SCs and STs, but excludes minority institutions under Article 30.
9.tq: Use the scope trap involving private institutions and the minority-institution exception.
9.sec: Articles 15 and 16 special provisions - beneficiaries, groups not covered  [APPSC]

9.s: Which of the following groups is NOT covered by the special provisions specifically described under Article 15?
9.x: The listed Article 15 special provisions cover women, children, SEBCs, SCs, STs and, under Article 15(6), EWS. Aged persons are not included in this list.
9.tq: Find the excluded group rather than selecting a group expressly named in the provision.
9.sec: Articles 15 and 16 special provisions - beneficiaries, groups not covered  [APPSC]

9.s: The reservation contemplated by Article 16(4) relates to backward classes which:
o: Are identified solely on the basis of age
Are represented only in private employment
Are not adequately represented in the services under the State
9.x: Article 16(4) permits reservation for backward classes that, in the opinion of the State, are not adequately represented in the services under it.
9.tq: Read the qualifying condition carefully: the constitutional test is inadequate representation in services.
9.sec: Articles 15 and 16 special provisions - beneficiaries, groups not covered  [APPSC]

9.s: Which provision permits reservation in promotion for members of the Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes?
9.x: Article 16(4A) concerns reservation in promotion for SCs and STs, along with consequential seniority as reflected in the relevant amendments.
9.tq: Distinguish the promotion clause from the clauses dealing with admissions, religion or foreign titles.
9.sec: Articles 15 and 16 special provisions - beneficiaries, groups not covered  [APPSC]

9.s:
Consider the following statements:
1. The 77th Amendment inserted Article 16(4A).
2. The 81st Amendment dealt with carry-forward of unfilled reserved vacancies.
3. The 85th Amendment is associated with consequential seniority in promotion.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
9.x: The 77th Amendment, 1995, inserted Article 16(4A); the 81st Amendment, 2000, addressed carry-forward vacancies; and the 85th Amendment, 2001, provided promotion with consequential seniority.
9.tq: Build the answer by mapping each amendment to its distinct reservation effect.
9.sec: Articles 15 and 16 special provisions - beneficiaries, groups not covered  [APPSC]

9.s: Article 16(4B), inserted by the 81st Constitutional Amendment, deals with:
o: Reservation for women in educational institutions
Reservation for EWS up to 10 per cent
Carry-forward of unfilled reserved vacancies as a separate class outside the 50 per cent ceiling
9.x: Article 16(4B) treats carried-forward unfilled reserved vacancies as a separate class and places them outside the 50 per cent ceiling referred to in the provision.
9.tq: Use the amendment-effect pairing and retain the specific ceiling-related detail.
9.sec: Articles 15 and 16 special provisions - beneficiaries, groups not covered  [APPSC]

9.s: The 103rd Constitutional Amendment, 2019, inserted Articles 15(6) and 16(6) relating to:
o: Reservation for SCs and STs in promotions only
Reservation for EWS up to 10 per cent
9.x: The 103rd Amendment inserted Articles 15(6) and 16(6), providing for reservation for Economically Weaker Sections up to 10 per cent. It was passed as the 124th Amendment Bill in the Lok Sabha.
9.tq: Match the amendment year and clause numbers with the percentage and beneficiary group.
9.sec: Articles 15 and 16 special provisions - beneficiaries, groups not covered  [APPSC]

9.s:
Arrange the following amendments in chronological order:
A. 103rd Constitutional Amendment
B. 77th Constitutional Amendment
C. 93rd Constitutional Amendment
D. 81st Constitutional Amendment
9.x: The amendments were enacted in the order 77th (1995), 81st (2000), 93rd (2005) and 103rd (2019).
9.tq: Anchor the earliest and latest amendments first, then place the intermediate years.
9.sec: Articles 15 and 16 special provisions - beneficiaries, groups not covered  [APPSC]

9.s: Article 16(5) permits a qualification relating to religion or denomination in respect of an office connected with:
o: Every public employment under a State
9.x: Article 16(5) permits offices connected with religious or denominational institutions to be kept for persons professing that particular religion or belonging to that denomination.
9.tq: Identify the institutional exception rather than applying the religious qualification to all public employment.
9.sec: Articles 15 and 16 special provisions - beneficiaries, groups not covered  [APPSC]

9.s: Which of the following statements about Article 18(1) is correct?
o: The State may confer any hereditary title with the President’s consent.
The State shall confer no title except military or academic distinctions.
Only foreign titles are prohibited under Article 18(1).
National awards are expressly declared to be titles under Article 18(1).
9.x: Article 18(1) prohibits the State from conferring titles, except military and academic distinctions. The provision does not prohibit those two categories.
9.tq: Use the stated exception to avoid the extreme claim that every distinction is prohibited.
9.sec: Article 18 - titles abolished, foreign titles, consent, national awards  [APPSC]

9.s: Under Article 18(2), a citizen of India:
o: May accept a foreign title with the consent of the Governor
May accept only an academic title from a foreign State
Shall not accept any title from a foreign State
May accept a foreign title without restriction
9.x: Article 18(2) provides that no citizen of India shall accept any title from a foreign State.
9.tq: Distinguish the absolute constitutional bar on citizens from the consent-based rule for certain non-citizens.
9.sec: Article 18 - titles abolished, foreign titles, consent, national awards

9.s: A non-citizen holding an office of profit or trust under the State seeks to accept a title from a foreign State. Whose consent is constitutionally required?
9.x: Under Article 18(3), a non-citizen holding an office of profit or trust under the State requires the President’s consent to accept a foreign title.
9.tq: Apply the authority trap by identifying the office-holder whose consent is expressly named.
9.sec: Article 18 - titles abolished, foreign titles, consent, national awards

9.s:
No person holding an office of profit or trust under the State may accept, without the President’s consent, which of the following from a foreign State?
1. Any present
2. Any emolument
3. Any office
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
9.x: Article 18(4) requires the President’s consent for a person holding an office of profit or trust under the State to accept any present, emolument or office from a foreign State.
9.tq: Test the complete three-part list and avoid dropping the final item.
9.sec: Article 18 - titles abolished, foreign titles, consent, national awards

9.s: Which one of the following correctly describes the effect of the decision in Balaji Raghavan v. Union of India (1996)?
o: The decision authorised award-holders to use the awards as hereditary titles.
Bharat Ratna and Padma awards were held not to be titles under Article 18, but they must not be used as prefixes or suffixes.
All national awards were held to be military distinctions only.
Bharat Ratna and Padma awards were held to be titles and were abolished.
9.x: The Supreme Court held that Bharat Ratna and Padma awards are not titles under Article 18. However, they cannot be used as prefixes or suffixes to a person’s name.
9.tq: Separate the legal status of an award from the prohibited manner of using it.
9.sec: Article 18 - titles abolished, foreign titles, consent, national awards

9.s: Bharat Ratna and Padma awards were stopped in 1977 and revived in:
9.x: The Bharat Ratna and Padma awards were discontinued in 1977 and revived in 1980.
9.tq: Use the two-event timeline and select the later revival year rather than the interruption year.
9.sec: Article 18 - titles abolished, foreign titles, consent, national awards

9.s:
Assertion (A): Article 18 is associated with social equality.
Reason (R): It seeks to end artificial distinctions created through State-conferred titles.
o: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
9.x: Both statements are true. Article 18 advances social equality by abolishing artificial distinctions arising from State-conferred titles, subject to the stated exceptions.
9.tq: Check whether the reason directly explains why the provision advances the stated type of equality.
9.sec: Article 18 - titles abolished, foreign titles, consent, national awards

9.s: Which one of the following correctly distinguishes equality before law from equal protection of laws?
o: Equality before law is a positive concept of classification, whereas equal protection is a negative concept of uniformity
Equality before law is a negative concept denying special privilege, whereas equal protection is a positive concept permitting reasonable classification
Equality before law applies only to citizens, whereas equal protection applies only to foreigners
Both are negative concepts derived exclusively from the Indian Constitution
9.x: Equality before law is a negative concept associated with absence of special privilege and subjection of all persons to ordinary law. Equal protection of laws is a positive concept requiring like treatment in like circumstances and permitting reasonable classification.
9.tq: Split the options by comparing the origin, character and legal effect of the two expressions.
9.sec: Article 14 - equality before law vs equal protection, rule of law, arbitrariness, classification  [APPSC]

9.s: The expression ‘equality before law’ is primarily associated with which of the following?
o: The British doctrine of Dicey's rule of law
The Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms
The French Declaration of the Rights of Man
The American doctrine under the Fourteenth Amendment
9.x: Equality before law has British origins and is associated with Dicey's rule of law. Equal protection of laws is associated with the American Fourteenth Amendment.
9.tq: Use the origin-based distinction to separate two constitutionally similar expressions.
9.sec: Article 14 - equality before law vs equal protection, rule of law, arbitrariness, classification  [APPSC]

9.s:
With reference to the rule of law as explained by A.V. Dicey, consider the following statements:
1. It involves the absence of arbitrary power.
2. It requires equality before law.
3. It means that rights flow from the Constitution rather than being declared by courts.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
9.x: Dicey's elements include absence of arbitrary power, equality before law and the predominance of legal spirit. India accepts the first two elements, but in India rights flow from the Constitution rather than being the result of rights declared by courts.
9.tq: Find the statement that reverses the Indian position on the source of rights.
9.sec: Article 14 - equality before law vs equal protection, rule of law, arbitrariness, classification  [APPSC]

9.s: The rule of law is regarded as which of the following in the Indian constitutional system?
o: A power available only to the executive
A directive applicable only during an Emergency
A basic feature of the Constitution
9.x: The rule of law is recognised as a basic feature of the Constitution and cannot be destroyed by constitutional amendment.
9.tq: Identify the constitutional status of the doctrine rather than its individual components.
9.sec: Article 14 - equality before law vs equal protection, rule of law, arbitrariness, classification  [APPSC]

9.s:
Which of the following are recognised exceptions to the ordinary operation of equality before law?
1. Immunity of the President and Governors from criminal proceedings during their term of office
2. Special position of foreign diplomats
3. Immunities of United Nations agencies
4. Immunity of every public servant from civil proceedings
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
9.x: The recognised exceptions include constitutional immunity of the President and Governors during their term, diplomatic immunity and immunities of UN agencies. There is no general immunity for every public servant from civil proceedings.
9.tq: Eliminate the overbroad statement extending an exception to every public servant.
9.sec: Article 14 - equality before law vs equal protection, rule of law, arbitrariness, classification  [APPSC]

9.s: Under Article 361, a civil proceeding against the President or a Governor during the term of office can be instituted only after—
9.x: Article 361 protects the President and Governors from civil proceedings during their term unless the prescribed two months' notice has been given.
9.tq: Focus on the precise notice period instead of the broader immunity principle.
9.sec: Article 14 - equality before law vs equal protection, rule of law, arbitrariness, classification  [APPSC]

9.s: In which case did the Supreme Court state that ‘equality is antithetic to arbitrariness’ or that equality and arbitrariness are sworn enemies?
o: M.R. Balaji v. State of Mysore
Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India
Indra Sawhney v. Union of India
E.P. Royappa v. State of Tamil Nadu
9.x: E.P. Royappa v. State of Tamil Nadu (1974) established the close constitutional relationship between equality and non-arbitrariness.
9.tq: Match the distinctive judicial formulation with the case in which it was stated.
9.sec: Article 14 - equality before law vs equal protection, rule of law, arbitrariness, classification  [APPSC]

9.s: Which one of the following propositions is associated with Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India (1978) in the context of Article 14?
o: Class legislation is always valid if enacted by Parliament
Any arbitrary State action violates Article 14
Article 14 applies only to taxation laws
9.x: Maneka Gandhi reinforced the principle that arbitrary State action is inconsistent with Article 14. Unguided discretionary power may therefore be struck down.
9.tq: Use the case-law principle rather than confusing it with the classification test.
9.sec: Article 14 - equality before law vs equal protection, rule of law, arbitrariness, classification  [APPSC]

9.s: A law creates two groups for different treatment. For the classification to be valid under Article 14, which combination is required?
o: Intelligible differentia and rational nexus with the object of the law
9.x: The twin test of reasonable classification is an intelligible differentia distinguishing the grouped persons or things and a rational nexus between the differentia and the object sought to be achieved.
9.tq: Apply the twin test to distinguish reasonable classification from class legislation.
9.sec: Article 14 - equality before law vs equal protection, rule of law, arbitrariness, classification  [APPSC]

9.s: Article 14 forbids—
o: class legislation, while permitting reasonable classification
reasonable classification based on intelligible differentia
9.x: Article 14 does not prohibit classification as such. It prohibits class legislation and permits classification satisfying intelligible differentia and rational nexus.
9.tq: Watch for the extreme word ‘all’ and distinguish class legislation from reasonable classification.
9.sec: Article 14 - equality before law vs equal protection, rule of law, arbitrariness, classification  [APPSC]

9.s: The Supreme Court’s April 2026 ruling concerning pensioners and serving employees reaffirmed that the State—
o: must abolish dearness allowance for pensioners
cannot treat pensioners differently from serving employees on dearness allowance without constitutionally valid justification
may always treat pensioners differently from serving employees on dearness allowance
can classify employees only on the basis of residence
9.x: The ruling held that the State cannot arbitrarily treat pensioners differently from serving employees in relation to dearness allowance. The classification must satisfy Article 14 requirements.
9.tq: Apply non-arbitrariness and rational classification to a concrete administrative distinction.
9.sec: Article 14 - equality before law vs equal protection, rule of law, arbitrariness, classification  [APPSC]

9.s:
Consider the following statements regarding Article 17:
1. Untouchability is expressly defined in the Constitution.
2. Article 17 operates against private persons also.
3. Article 17 belongs to the Right to Equality group.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
9.x: The Constitution does not define ‘untouchability’. Article 17 is a Fundamental Right within the Right to Equality group and can operate against private persons as well.
9.tq: Reject the precise-sounding but false claim that the Constitution defines untouchability.
9.sec: Article 17 - untouchability, category, enforcing laws  [other exams]

9.s: Which one of the following Acts specifically addresses atrocities against members of the Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes?
o: SC and ST (Prevention of Atrocities) Act, 1989
National Commission for Backward Classes Act, 1993
9.x: The SC and ST (Prevention of Atrocities) Act, 1989 addresses atrocities against members of Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes. The Protection of Civil Rights Act, 1955 primarily concerns enforcement against untouchability.
9.tq: Discriminate between two related laws by matching each law with its specific subject.
9.sec: Article 17 - untouchability, category, enforcing laws  [other exams]

9.s: The Protection of Civil Rights Act, 1955 and the SC and ST (Prevention of Atrocities) Act, 1989 are overseen by which department?
9.x: Both Acts are overseen by the Department of Social Justice.
9.tq: Use the responsible administrative department as the identifying fact.
9.sec: Article 17 - untouchability, category, enforcing laws  [other exams]

9.s: Who is associated with ensuring that Article 17 made untouchability a punishable offence?
9.x: B.R. Ambedkar ensured that Article 17 constitutionally treated untouchability as a punishable offence.
9.tq: Match the constitutional contribution with the principal figure associated with it.
9.sec: Article 17 - untouchability, category, enforcing laws  [other exams]

9.s:
Arrange the following cases in chronological order:
A. M.R. Balaji
B. Champakam Dorairajan
C. Indra Sawhney
D. M. Nagaraj
9.x: The cases were decided in the order Champakam Dorairajan (1951), M.R. Balaji (1963), Indra Sawhney (1992) and M. Nagaraj (2006).
9.tq: Fix the earliest and latest cases first, then place the two intermediate rulings.
9.sec: Reservation cases - ruling issue, creamy layer and 50% ceiling origin

9.s: The Supreme Court struck down the Communal Government Order in Champakam Dorairajan primarily under—
9.x: In Champakam Dorairajan (1951), the Communal G.O. was struck down under Article 29(2). The case also established the then-prevailing position that Directive Principles were subordinate to Fundamental Rights, leading to the First Amendment and Article 15(4).
9.tq: Match the case with the specific constitutional provision involved in its ruling.
9.sec: Reservation cases - ruling issue, creamy layer and 50% ceiling origin

9.s: Which case is associated with the proposition that reservation should generally remain below 50 per cent?
9.x: M.R. Balaji (1963) stated that reservation should generally remain below 50 per cent.
9.tq: Associate the numerical ceiling principle with the case that first articulated it.
9.sec: Reservation cases - ruling issue, creamy layer and 50% ceiling origin

9.s:
With reference to Indra Sawhney (1992), consider the following statements:
1. It upheld 27 per cent reservation for Other Backward Classes.
2. It introduced the exclusion of the creamy layer.
3. It upheld reservation in promotions as a general rule.
4. It recognised a 50 per cent ceiling, subject to extraordinary situations.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
9.x: Indra Sawhney upheld the 27 per cent OBC quota, introduced the creamy-layer exclusion and recognised the 50 per cent ceiling subject to extraordinary situations. It did not uphold reservation in promotions as a general rule.
9.tq: Identify the single reversed proposition concerning reservation in promotions.
9.sec: Reservation cases - ruling issue, creamy layer and 50% ceiling origin

9.s: The constitutional principle of excluding the creamy layer from reservation for Other Backward Classes originated in—
9.x: The creamy-layer principle originated in Indra Sawhney (1992).
9.tq: Distinguish the origin of a doctrine from later cases dealing with its application.
9.sec: Reservation cases - ruling issue, creamy layer and 50% ceiling origin

9.s: Which one of the following is the income limit for the OBC creamy layer mentioned in the 2017 notification?
9.x: The OBC creamy-layer income limit mentioned in the 2017 notification is ₹8 lakh a year. Andhra Pradesh aligned its definitions with the central thresholds.
9.tq: Read the figure precisely and distinguish it from nearby income thresholds.
9.sec: Reservation cases - ruling issue, creamy layer and 50% ceiling origin

9.s: Which of the following correctly describes the ruling in M. Nagaraj (2006)?
o: It introduced the 27 per cent OBC quota
It permitted sub-classification among Scheduled Castes
It upheld the 77th, 81st and 85th Amendments and required quantifiable data regarding backwardness, inadequate representation and efficiency
It struck down all amendments relating to reservation in promotions
9.x: M. Nagaraj upheld the 77th, 81st and 85th Amendments and required the State to show quantifiable data concerning backwardness, inadequacy of representation and administrative efficiency under Article 335.
9.tq: Use the case’s distinctive combination of upheld amendments and evidentiary requirements.
9.sec: Reservation cases - ruling issue, creamy layer and 50% ceiling origin

9.s: Which one of the following statements about Jarnail Singh (2018) is correct?
o: It required fresh data proving the backwardness of SCs and STs in every case
It upheld the EWS reservation under the 103rd Amendment
It abolished the creamy-layer principle for OBCs
It held that no data on SC/ST backwardness was needed and applied the creamy-layer principle to SC/ST promotions
9.x: Jarnail Singh (2018) held that separate data establishing backwardness of SCs and STs was not necessary, while applying the creamy-layer principle to SC/ST promotions.
9.tq: Separate the backwardness-data requirement from the creamy-layer requirement in promotions.
9.sec: Reservation cases - ruling issue, creamy layer and 50% ceiling origin

9.s: The 103rd Constitutional Amendment providing reservation for Economically Weaker Sections was upheld by the Supreme Court in—
9.x: In Janhit Abhiyan (2022), the Supreme Court upheld the 103rd Amendment providing 10 per cent EWS reservation by a 3:2 majority.
9.tq: Combine the case name, amendment, percentage and majority to identify the precise ruling.
9.sec: Reservation cases - ruling issue, creamy layer and 50% ceiling origin

9.s: State of Punjab v. Davinder Singh (2024) is associated with which proposition?
o: The 50 per cent ceiling is completely abolished
The creamy layer applies only to economically weaker sections
Reservation in promotions is unconstitutional in every circumstance
Sub-classification of Scheduled Castes is permitted
9.x: State of Punjab v. Davinder Singh (2024) permitted sub-classification of Scheduled Castes.
9.tq: Match the recent case with its specific reservation jurisprudence issue.
9.sec: Reservation cases - ruling issue, creamy layer and 50% ceiling origin

9.s:
Which of the following are recognised exceptions or qualifications to the 50 per cent reservation ceiling?
1. Extraordinary situations such as remote areas
2. Carry-forward of backlog vacancies under the 81st Amendment
3. EWS reservation upheld in Janhit Abhiyan
4. Every reservation made by a State legislature without limitation
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
9.x: Extraordinary situations, carry-forward vacancies under the 81st Amendment and the EWS reservation recognised in Janhit Abhiyan are stated qualifications or exceptions. There is no unrestricted power for every State legislature to exceed the ceiling.
9.tq: Reject the absolute statement that removes all constitutional limits on reservation.
9.sec: Reservation cases - ruling issue, creamy layer and 50% ceiling origin

9.s: The National Commission for Backward Classes has constitutional status under—
9.x: The National Commission for Backward Classes is a constitutional body under Article 338B.
9.tq: Distinguish closely numbered constitutional provisions relating to commissions.
9.sec: Reservation cases - ruling issue, creamy layer and 50% ceiling origin

9.s: Which amendment-clause pair is correctly matched?
9.x: The First Amendment, 1951 inserted Article 15(4). Article 16(4A) was inserted by the 77th Amendment, Article 16(4B) by the 81st, Article 15(5) by the 93rd and Article 16(6) by the 103rd Amendment.
9.tq: Start with the sure amendment-clause pair and eliminate the swapped clauses.
9.sec: Amendments changing Articles 15-16 (1st, 77th, 81st, 85th, 93rd, 103rd)

9.s: The provision concerning carry-forward of backlog vacancies was introduced through—
o: Article 15(4), inserted by the First Amendment
