12.tq: Use the distinctive statute name and punishment while avoiding confusion with general conversion legislation.
12.sec: Conversion laws and the propagation debate

12.s: A challenge to the Punjab sacrilege legislation referred to above has been made before the
o: Supreme Court of India exclusively on taxation grounds
Delhi High Court on the ground that it abolishes religious freedom
Punjab and Haryana High Court on the ground that it protects only one faith
Madhya Pradesh High Court on the ground that it permits forcible conversion
12.x: The Act has been challenged in the Punjab and Haryana High Court on the ground that it protects only one faith.
12.tq: Identify the forum and the precise constitutional objection rather than a related religious-freedom issue.
12.sec: Conversion laws and the propagation debate

12.s: Which one of the following correctly describes the scope of Article 24?
o: It applies only to children employed by the State.
It prohibits only bonded labour by children below fourteen years.
It prohibits employment below fourteen years in factories, mines and other hazardous employment, but does not bar harmless or innocent work.
It prohibits every kind of work by every person below eighteen years.
12.x: Article 24 is directed at employment of children below fourteen years in factories, mines and other hazardous employment; harmless or innocent work is not covered by the constitutional prohibition.
12.tq: Reject the overbroad ‘every kind of work’ statement and retain the hazardous-employment limit.
12.sec: Article 24 - child labour, age limit, nature of prohibition, linked laws

12.s: The 2016 amendment renamed the Child Labour (Prohibition and Regulation) Act, 1986 as the
o: Protection of Children from Hazardous Work Act
Child Rights and Bonded Labour Act
12.x: The 2016 amendment renamed the statute as the Child and Adolescent Labour Act and introduced the present age-based restrictions.
12.tq: Test the exact statutory title, a common look-alike wording trap.
12.sec: Article 24 - child labour, age limit, nature of prohibition, linked laws

12.s:
Under the amended child-labour framework, which statement is correct?
1. A child below fourteen years is generally barred from work, subject to the stated exception for family enterprise after school hours.
2. An adolescent aged fourteen to eighteen years is barred from hazardous work.
3. The Right to Education Act, 2009 covers the age group of six to fourteen years.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
12.x: All three statements are correct. The amended law has the family-enterprise-after-school exception for children, prohibits hazardous work by adolescents, and the RTE Act covers children aged six to fourteen years.
12.tq: Keep the three age ranges and exceptions separate before choosing the combination.
12.sec: Article 24 - child labour, age limit, nature of prohibition, linked laws

12.s: The Right to Education Act, 2009 gives effect to which constitutional provision for children aged six to fourteen years?
12.x: The Right to Education Act, 2009 gives effect to Article 21A, which concerns free and compulsory education for children aged six to fourteen years.
12.tq: Distinguish the education guarantee from the child-labour prohibition and DPSP provisions.
12.sec: Article 24 - child labour, age limit, nature of prohibition, linked laws

12.s: The Commissions for Protection of Child Rights Act, 2005 provides the statutory basis for the
o: National Human Rights Commission and State Human Rights Commissions
National Commission for Minorities and District Anti-Human Trafficking Units
National Commission for Women and State Finance Commissions
National Commission for Protection of Child Rights and State Commissions for Protection of Child Rights
12.x: The Commissions for Protection of Child Rights Act, 2005 provides for the NCPCR and SCPCRs.
12.tq: Match the Act with the bodies it creates and avoid swapping similarly named commissions.
12.sec: Article 24 - child labour, age limit, nature of prohibition, linked laws

12.s:
Which of the following Directive Principles is directly related to protection of children from abuse and exploitation?
1. Article 39(e)
2. Article 39(f)
3. Article 44
4. Article 48A
Select the correct answer using the code below.
12.x: Articles 39(e) and 39(f) direct the State to ensure that the tender age of children is not abused and that children develop in a healthy manner with protection against exploitation.
12.tq: Use the subject matter of the Directive Principle to eliminate unrelated provisions.
12.sec: Article 24 - child labour, age limit, nature of prohibition, linked laws

12.s: Which one of the following most appropriately describes the constitutional meaning of secularism in India?
o: Complete exclusion of religion from public life
Preference to the religion followed by the majority
Establishment of one official religion by the State
Equal respect for all religions and absence of discrimination on religious grounds
12.x: Indian secularism requires equal respect for all religions and prohibits discrimination on grounds of religion. It does not establish a state religion or demand complete exclusion of religion from public life.
12.tq: Distinguish the Indian model of secularism from strict separation and majoritarian preference.
12.sec: Secularism - meaning, components, Western vs Indian model, Arts. 25-28, 42nd Amendment

12.s:
Consider the following statements regarding secularism in India:
1. India has no state religion.
2. The State may intervene positively for social and religious reform.
3. Secularism necessarily prohibits all forms of state aid to religious institutions.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
12.x: India has no state religion and follows a model allowing positive state intervention for reform. The State is not necessarily prohibited from providing aid to religious institutions.
12.tq: Identify the false absolute statement about state aid and distinguish Indian secularism from the Western model.
12.sec: Secularism - meaning, components, Western vs Indian model, Arts. 25-28, 42nd Amendment

12.s: Which of the following is NOT a component of Indian secularism?
o: Non-applicability of secular principles to irreligious persons
12.x: Secularism includes freedom of conscience, which protects believers as well as non-believers. Non-applicability to irreligious persons is not a component of secularism.
12.tq: Find the option that reverses the inclusive scope of freedom of conscience.
12.sec: Secularism - meaning, components, Western vs Indian model, Arts. 25-28, 42nd Amendment

12.s: The words “Socialist” and “Secular” were inserted into the Preamble by which Constitutional Amendment?
12.x: The 42nd Constitutional Amendment Act of 1976 inserted the words “Socialist” and “Secular” into the Preamble.
12.tq: Use the amendment-year association to eliminate nearby amendment numbers.
12.sec: Secularism - meaning, components, Western vs Indian model, Arts. 25-28, 42nd Amendment

12.s: The Constituent Assembly, in 1949, rejected the proposal to include which word in the Preamble?
12.x: The Constituent Assembly rejected the proposal to add the word “God” to the Preamble in 1949.
12.tq: Test a specific rejected constitutional proposal rather than a word already present in the Preamble.
12.sec: Secularism - meaning, components, Western vs Indian model, Arts. 25-28, 42nd Amendment

12.s:
Which of the following pairs correctly represents sources associated with the roots of Indian secular thought?
1. Ashoka's Dhamma
2. Nehru Report, 1928
3. Karachi Resolution, 1931
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
12.x: Ashoka's Dhamma, the Nehru Report of 1928 and the Karachi Resolution of 1931 are all identified as roots associated with Indian secular thought.
12.tq: Recognise a complete list where all three historically associated sources are correct.
12.sec: Secularism - meaning, components, Western vs Indian model, Arts. 25-28, 42nd Amendment

12.s: A religious denomination seeks to manage its own religious affairs, while a taxpayer objects to a tax specifically imposed to promote one religion. Which Articles are respectively relevant?
12.x: Article 26 protects the right of religious denominations to manage their religious affairs, while Article 27 prohibits taxation for the promotion of a particular religion.
12.tq: Apply the constitutional provision to the factual situation by identifying who exercises the right and what is prohibited.
12.sec: Secularism - meaning, components, Western vs Indian model, Arts. 25-28, 42nd Amendment

12.s: Which one of the following correctly distinguishes the Western and Indian models of secularism?
o: The Indian model treats religion as purely private, whereas the Western model promotes public religious dialogue.
The Western model permits state reform of religious practices, whereas the Indian model requires strict separation.
The Western model follows strict separation, whereas the Indian model follows principled distance and equal respect.
Both models prohibit state aid to religious institutions in all circumstances.
12.x: The Western model is generally based on strict separation and mutual exclusion. The Indian model adopts principled distance, equal respect and scope for reform.
12.tq: Compare the defining features of both models instead of matching isolated examples.
12.sec: Secularism - meaning, components, Western vs Indian model, Arts. 25-28, 42nd Amendment

12.s: Which of the following is associated with the Indian model rather than the strict Western model of secularism?
o: The State may reform religious practices, such as through temple-entry measures.
Mutual exclusion of the State and religious institutions is mandatory.
Religion is treated as purely private in every circumstance.
State aid to religious institutions is constitutionally impossible.
12.x: The Indian model permits the State to intervene for reform, including temple-entry reform. It may also allow aid in specified circumstances.
12.tq: Discriminate between strict separation and principled distance through the reform exception.
12.sec: Secularism - meaning, components, Western vs Indian model, Arts. 25-28, 42nd Amendment

12.s:
Consider the following statements:
1. Article 14 is related to equality before law.
2. Articles 15 and 16 address equality and non-discrimination in specified contexts.
3. Articles 29 and 30 are connected with cultural and educational rights.
4. Article 325 excludes persons from electoral rolls on the ground of religion.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
12.x: Articles 14, 15, 16, 29 and 30 are related to equality and cultural or educational rights. Article 325 prevents exclusion from electoral rolls on grounds including religion; it does not authorise such exclusion.
12.tq: Locate the single reversed constitutional effect in an otherwise familiar list of related Articles.
12.sec: Secularism - meaning, components, Western vs Indian model, Arts. 25-28, 42nd Amendment

12.s: Who among the following regarded religion as a form of collective worship of society and examined the distinction between the sacred and the profane?
12.x: Emile Durkheim associated religion with collective worship of society and distinguished the sacred from the profane.
12.tq: Match the distinctive conceptual pair—sacred and profane—with its sociologist.
12.sec: Theories of religion → sociologist

12.s: The concept of totemism and the work *The Elementary Forms of Religious Life* are associated with:
12.x: Emile Durkheim studied totemism in *The Elementary Forms of Religious Life*, published in 1912.
12.tq: Use the title-work association to distinguish Durkheim from other sociologists of religion.
12.sec: Theories of religion → sociologist

12.s: Which thinker linked karma, dharma and caste with the shaping of economic life in *The Religion of India*?
12.x: Max Weber examined the relationship of karma, dharma and caste to economic life in *The Religion of India*.
12.tq: Identify the thinker through the specific work and its analytical themes.
12.sec: Theories of religion → sociologist

12.s: The statement “Religion is the opium of the people” is associated with:
12.x: Karl Marx described religion as “the opium of the people.”
12.tq: Test a famous formulation with the correct author rather than a related theorist.
12.sec: Theories of religion → sociologist

12.s: Which one of the following pairs is correctly matched?
o: J.G. Frazer — Religion as the opium of the people
Karl Marx — Magic, religion and science
12.x: E.B. Tylor associated the origin of religion with animism, or belief in spirits. Marx is associated with the opium formulation, Frazer with magic-religion-science, and Weber with the Protestant Ethic.
12.tq: Find the correctly matched thinker by separating closely related theories and works.
12.sec: Theories of religion → sociologist

12.s: J.G. Frazer's evolutionary sequence of human explanations was:
12.x: In *The Golden Bough*, J.G. Frazer proposed the sequence of magic, followed by religion, and then science.
12.tq: Arrange the three-stage conceptual sequence in its stated order.
12.sec: Theories of religion → sociologist

12.s: Which one of the following pairs is NOT correctly matched?
o: Asghar Ali Engineer — Writings on communalism
T.N. Madan — Critique of the Western secularisation thesis
12.x: *Homo Hierarchicus* and the analysis of caste through purity-pollution are associated with Louis Dumont, not B. Malinowski.
12.tq: Use the author-work trap to identify the wrongly attributed work.
12.sec: Theories of religion → sociologist

12.s: According to Census 2011 figures given for India, which religious community constituted the largest minority?
12.x: Muslims constituted 14.2 percent of India's population according to the cited Census 2011 figures and were the largest minority community.
12.tq: Use the comparative phrase “largest minority” rather than selecting the largest overall community.
12.sec: Religious composition of India (Census 2011)

12.s:
Consider the following statements regarding the religious composition of India according to Census 2011:
1. Hindus constituted 79.8 percent.
2. Muslims constituted 14.2 percent.
3. Christians constituted 2.3 percent.
4. Sikhs constituted 1.7 percent.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
12.x: The cited Census 2011 shares are Hindus 79.8 percent, Muslims 14.2 percent, Christians 2.3 percent and Sikhs 1.7 percent.
12.tq: Check each numerical statement independently before selecting the complete combination.
12.sec: Religious composition of India (Census 2011)

12.s: Which of the following correctly gives the Census 2011 shares of Buddhists and Jains in India?
12.x: The cited shares are 0.7 percent for Buddhists and 0.4 percent for Jains.
12.tq: Discriminate between two close minority-population percentages by checking their exact order.
12.sec: Religious composition of India (Census 2011)

12.s: Which one of the following statements regarding Punjab is correct?
o: Punjab has the largest concentration of Jains, and Dalits constitute about 14.2 percent of its population.
Punjab has the largest concentration of Buddhists, and Dalits constitute about 79.8 percent of its population.
Punjab has the largest concentration of Ravidassias, and Dalits constitute about 2.3 percent of its population.
Punjab has the largest concentration of Ravidassias, and Dalits constitute about 32 percent of its population.
12.x: Punjab is identified as having the largest concentration of Ravidassias, while Dalits constitute about 32 percent of its population.
12.tq: Combine the correct location and percentage instead of accepting a swapped community or figure.
12.sec: Religious composition of India (Census 2011)

12.s: Religious pluralism is best understood as:
o: The compulsory adoption of a common religion by all citizens
The freedom and security to practise any religion or none
The political dominance of one religious community
The complete withdrawal of the State from all social questions
12.x: Religious pluralism means that people have the freedom and security to practise any religion or to follow none.
12.tq: Distinguish pluralism from uniformity, majoritarianism and mere state withdrawal.
12.sec: Religious pluralism - coexistence, syncretic traditions (Bhakti, Sufi)

12.s:
Which of the following conditions are necessary for religious pluralism?
1. Freedom of religion
2. Mutual respect
3. Exclusivism
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
12.x: Religious pluralism requires freedom of religion and mutual respect. Exclusivism hinders pluralism rather than supporting it.
12.tq: Separate enabling conditions from the listed obstacle to pluralism.
12.sec: Religious pluralism - coexistence, syncretic traditions (Bhakti, Sufi)

12.s: According to S.R. Bhatt, religious pluralism leads to secularism through:
o: The establishment of a state religion
The separation of all communities from public life
12.x: S.R. Bhatt associated the movement from pluralism to secularism with the unification of many religions.
12.tq: Recall the specific relationship proposed between pluralism and secularism.
12.sec: Religious pluralism - coexistence, syncretic traditions (Bhakti, Sufi)

12.s: Which of the following correctly describes the Bhakti movement as presented in the context of religious pluralism?
o: It was confined exclusively to royal courts and had no literary influence.
It rejected ritualism and caste, and contributed to interaction with Sufi traditions.
It opposed all forms of dialogue between Hindu and Muslim traditions.
It promoted ritualism and caste exclusiveness from the 6th to the 18th century.
12.x: The Bhakti movement, spanning approximately the 6th to the 18th century, rejected ritualism and caste and interacted with Sufi traditions.
12.tq: Reject extreme descriptions and select the option containing both the movement's social critique and syncretic role.
12.sec: Religious pluralism - coexistence, syncretic traditions (Bhakti, Sufi)

12.s: Kabir and Guru Nanak are noted for criticising:
o: The use of regional languages in literature
Only the political authority of Mughal rulers
12.x: Kabir and Guru Nanak criticised orthodox practices in both Hindu and Muslim traditions.
12.tq: Avoid the single-community trap by identifying the common target of both thinkers.
12.sec: Religious pluralism - coexistence, syncretic traditions (Bhakti, Sufi)

12.s: The interaction between Bhakti and Sufi traditions contributed particularly to:
o: The establishment of a uniform religious code
The abolition of all religious institutions
Communal harmony and the growth of regional literatures
The replacement of regional languages by Persian alone
12.x: Bhakti-Sufi interaction helped build communal harmony and encouraged the development of regional literatures.
12.tq: Link the cultural interaction with its stated social and literary consequences.
12.sec: Religious pluralism - coexistence, syncretic traditions (Bhakti, Sufi)

12.s: Which one of the following statements about religious coexistence in the Vijayanagara context is correct?
o: The empire recognised only one religious community in public institutions.
The empire prohibited Muslims from administrative service and excluded Jains from protection.
The empire employed Muslim officers and protected Jains.
The empire abolished all religious endowments.
12.x: The Vijayanagara example illustrates coexistence through the employment of Muslim officers and protection of Jain communities.
12.tq: Use the paired example to avoid a reversed inclusion-exclusion statement.
12.sec: Religious pluralism - coexistence, syncretic traditions (Bhakti, Sufi)

12.s: Bammera Potana dedicated the *Andhra Maha Bhagavatamu* to:
12.x: Bammera Potana offered the *Andhra Maha Bhagavatamu* to Lord Rama, not to Krishnadevaraya.
12.tq: Separate the author’s religious dedication from the contemporary ruler’s name.
12.sec: Religious pluralism - coexistence, syncretic traditions (Bhakti, Sufi)

12.s: Which Mughal ruler is associated with promoting religious tolerance and dialogue?
12.x: Mughal emperor Akbar promoted religious tolerance and dialogue.
12.tq: Match the policy of tolerance and dialogue with the appropriate ruler.
12.sec: Religious pluralism - coexistence, syncretic traditions (Bhakti, Sufi)

12.s:
With reference to Supreme Court decisions on secularism, consider the following statements:
1. Kesavananda Bharati (1973) set out the basic structure doctrine.
2. S.R. Bommai (1994) held secularism to be part of the basic structure.
3. S.R. Bommai held that secularism was inherent only after the 42nd Amendment.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
12.x: Kesavananda Bharati set out the basic structure doctrine, and S.R. Bommai recognised secularism as part of the basic structure. Bommai also held that secularism was inherent even before 1976, making statement 3 false.
12.tq: Use the distinction between constitutional recognition and the date of textual insertion to reject statement 3.
12.sec: Secularism cases - Kesavananda Bharati, S.R. Bommai

12.s: If a State government acts against the secular character of the Constitution, the principle recognised in S.R. Bommai permits its dismissal under:
12.x: S.R. Bommai recognised that a State government acting against secularism may be dismissed under Article 356.
12.tq: Identify the constitutional emergency provision applicable to failure of constitutional machinery in a State.
12.sec: Secularism cases - Kesavananda Bharati, S.R. Bommai

12.s: Which one of the following pairs is NOT correctly matched?
o: Church of God — Loudspeakers are subject to public order
Ratilal — State cannot touch essential religious practices
Stanislaus — Propagation does not include a right to convert
St. Stephen's — State may completely abolish minority-institution autonomy
12.x: St. Stephen's is associated with minority-institution autonomy; it did not hold that the State may completely abolish such autonomy.
12.tq: Identify the option that converts a protection of minority autonomy into its opposite.
12.sec: Secularism cases - Kesavananda Bharati, S.R. Bommai

12.s:
Arrange the following decisions in chronological order:
A. Ratilal
B. Kesavananda Bharati
C. S.R. Bommai
D. Church of God
12.x: The sequence is Ratilal (1954), Kesavananda Bharati (1973), Church of God (2000) and S.R. Bommai (1994) only if ordered by the dates given in the material; therefore the correct chronological sequence is Ratilal (1954), Kesavananda Bharati (1973), S.R. Bommai (1994), Church of God (2000).
12.tq: Check the dates attached to each case before accepting a sequence.
12.sec: Secularism cases - Kesavananda Bharati, S.R. Bommai

12.s: The ruling that the right to propagate religion does not amount to a right to convert another person is associated with:
12.x: The Stanislaus decision of 1977 held that the right to propagate religion does not include a right to convert another person.
12.tq: Match the precise legal proposition with the correct case name.
12.sec: Secularism cases - Kesavananda Bharati, S.R. Bommai

12.s: Which one of the following statements correctly reflects the Sabarimala decision as described?
o: The issue was finally removed from consideration by every Constitution Bench.
An essential-practice claim cannot be used to bar the participation of others, and the State cannot endorse a practice.
Only minority institutions may challenge religious practices.
The State may endorse any religious practice claimed to be essential.
12.x: The Sabarimala ruling stated that the State cannot endorse a practice and that a claim of essential practice cannot be used to bar others' participation. The issue remains before a larger Constitution Bench.
12.tq: Apply the limits on State endorsement and essential-practice claims to the facts of the case.
12.sec: Secularism cases - Kesavananda Bharati, S.R. Bommai

12.s: Fundamentalism is best described as:
o: Acceptance of all religious interpretations as equally valid
Complete separation of religion from political life
Return to the literal fundamentals of scripture and rejection of modern and plural readings
Restoration of a romanticised golden past without reference to scripture
12.x: Fundamentalism involves returning to the literal fundamentals of scripture and rejecting modern or plural interpretations.
12.tq: Distinguish fundamentalism from revivalism by focusing on literal scripture and rejection of plural readings.
12.sec: Religious fundamentalism and revivalism - meaning, forms

12.s: Which of the following best illustrates revivalism?
o: Arya Samaj's call to “Back to the Vedas”
Rejection of every historical religious tradition
Abolition of religious identity from public life
Acceptance of all modern and plural interpretations
12.x: Revivalism seeks to restore an idealised or golden past; Arya Samaj's “Back to the Vedas” is a cited example.
12.tq: Identify revivalism through its backward-looking restoration of a golden past.
12.sec: Religious fundamentalism and revivalism - meaning, forms

12.s:
Which of the following are identified as forms of religious fundamentalism in India?
1. Communalism
2. Separatism
3. Fanaticism
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
12.x: Communalism, separatism and fanaticism are identified as forms of religious fundamentalism in India, particularly in the context of religion becoming fused with politics since the 1970s.
12.tq: Select the complete list of forms rather than treating the political dimension as a separate form.
12.sec: Religious fundamentalism and revivalism - meaning, forms

12.s: The fusion of religion with politics, associated with the forms of fundamentalism in India, has been particularly noted since the:
12.x: The material places the emergence of these forms, involving the fusion of religion with politics, particularly since the 1970s.
12.tq: Use the decade association and eliminate neighbouring decades.
12.sec: Religious fundamentalism and revivalism - meaning, forms

12.s: Which of the following pairs of events is correctly matched with the year cited in relation to communal conflict?
12.x: The cited examples are the 1984 anti-Sikh violence, the 1992 Babri Masjid episode, the 2002 Gujarat riots and the 2023 Haryana violence.
12.tq: Match each event with its year and reject the shifted-year distractors.
12.sec: Religious fundamentalism and revivalism - meaning, forms

12.s: Which of the following has been identified as a threat to the Ganga-Jamuni tehzeeb?
o: Hate speech on social media and illegal conversions
Protection of Jains and employment of Muslim officers
Freedom of conscience and mutual respect
12.x: Hate speech on social media and illegal conversions have been identified as threats that erode the Ganga-Jamuni tehzeeb.
12.tq: Distinguish threats to syncretic culture from examples of pluralistic coexistence.
12.sec: Religious fundamentalism and revivalism - meaning, forms

12.s:
Which one of the following pairs is correctly matched?

Term — Meaning

1. Ahura Mazda — Supreme god of good
2. Angra Mainyu — Destructive or evil spirit
3. Tirthankara — Eternal Guru of Sikhism
4. Guru Granth Sahib — Twenty-four teachers of Jainism
12.x: Ahura Mazda means the supreme god of good and Angra Mainyu refers to the destructive or evil spirit. Tirthankara is associated with Jain teachers, while Guru Granth Sahib is the scripture and eternal Guru of Sikhism.
12.tq: Match each term with its exact religious meaning and eliminate swapped descriptions.
12.sec: Terms from religions → meaning and religion  [GROUP-II]

12.s: Ahura Mazda and Angra Mainyu are associated with which religious tradition, respectively?
12.x: Ahura Mazda, the supreme god of good, and Angra Mainyu, the destructive or evil spirit, belong to Zoroastrianism, followed by Parsis in India.
12.tq: Use the confusable-pair method by linking both opposing concepts to the same religious tradition.
12.sec: Terms from religions → meaning and religion  [GROUP-II]

12.s:
Consider the following statements:
1. Tirthankara literally means ‘Ford-maker’.
2. Jainism recognises 24 Tirthankaras.
3. Rishabhanatha was the first and Mahavira was the last Tirthankara.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
12.x: All three statements are correct. Tirthankara means ‘Ford-maker’, and Jain tradition identifies 24 Tirthankaras, beginning with Rishabhanatha and ending with Mahavira.
12.tq: Check the definition, numerical count and first-last sequence separately.
12.sec: Terms from religions → meaning and religion  [GROUP-II]

12.s: With reference to Sikhism, which one of the following statements is correct?
o: Guru Granth Sahib was compiled as the Vedas by Guru Arjan.
Guru Granth Sahib is the scripture and eternal Guru of Sikhism.
Guru Granth Sahib denotes the destructive spirit in Zoroastrianism.
Guru Granth Sahib is the principal scripture of Jainism.
12.x: Guru Granth Sahib is the scripture and eternal Guru of Sikhism. It was compiled as the Adi Granth by Guru Arjan.
12.tq: Use the precise institutional description and reject options that swap religions or terms.
12.sec: Terms from religions → meaning and religion  [GROUP-II]

12.s: The Supreme Court’s nine-judge reference concerning the scope of the Essential Religious Practices test is associated with which of the following issues?
o: Whether Hindi should replace all regional languages as the national language
Whether all temples must be administered by the Union Government
Whether religious practices may be examined by courts in determining constitutional protection
Whether Tirthankaras should be recognised under the Constitution
12.x: The Sabarimala nine-judge reference is examining the scope of the Essential Religious Practices test and the extent to which courts may determine what constitutes an essential religious practice.
12.tq: Identify the constitutional controversy directly connected with the judicial test.
12.sec: Universal angles

12.s: The Sabarimala nine-judge reference hearing on the scope of the Essential Religious Practices test was reported as a current issue on:
12.x: The Sabarimala nine-judge reference hearing was reported on 14 May 2026. The other dates relate to different issues mentioned in the current-affairs material.
12.tq: Distinguish closely placed current-affairs dates by associating each date with its specific event.
12.sec: Universal angles

12.s: Which one of the following correctly represents a criticism of the Essential Religious Practices test?
o: It applies exclusively to economic activities connected with religion.
It removes all constitutional protection for religious denominations.
It prevents courts from examining any religious practice.
It allows judges to decide questions of theology and makes courts arbiters of religion.
12.x: A major criticism is that the Essential Religious Practices test permits courts to decide theological questions and thereby makes them arbiters of religion. Critics have sought a new test, including in the context of the Sabarimala reference.
12.tq: Recognise the criticism rather than confusing judicial review with complete non-intervention.
12.sec: Universal angles

12.s: The Allahabad High Court ruling concerning the wearing of hijab was reported on:
12.x: The Allahabad High Court hijab ruling was reported on 26 August 2026.
12.tq: Use date-event pairing to separate similar contemporary constitutional issues.
12.sec: Universal angles

12.s: Which of the following debates is most directly connected with freedom of conscience?
o: Anti-conversion laws and the individual’s freedom of conscience
The classification of temples under the AP Endowments Act
The official compilation of the Adi Granth
The number of Tirthankaras in Jainism
12.x: The relationship between anti-conversion laws and the freedom of conscience is a major constitutional debate concerning religious freedom.
12.tq: Link the constitutional expression ‘freedom of conscience’ with the issue that directly affects individual belief and conversion.
12.sec: Universal angles

12.s:
Consider the following statements regarding the Andhra Pradesh religious-endowment context:
1. The Sri Swamy Hathiramji Mutt is situated at Tirupati.
2. The dispute concerning the Mutt has involved questions of interim management before the High Court and Supreme Court.
3. The Andhra Pradesh Endowments Act, 1987 regulates Hindu temples and mutts.
4. The Andhra Pradesh Endowments Department administers more than 42,000 temples.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
12.x: All four statements are correct. The Sri Swamy Hathiramji Mutt is at Tirupati; its dispute has involved interim management before the High Court and Supreme Court, while the 1987 Act regulates Hindu temples and mutts and the Department administers more than 42,000 temples.
12.tq: Verify the location, litigation issue, statute and numerical administrative scope independently.
12.sec: Universal angles

12.s: The Sri Swamy Hathiramji Mutt at Tirupati is associated with which of the following descriptions?
o: The statutory authority for conducting the Census religion code
Hereditary Dharmakarta of the Tirumala Tirupati Devasthanams
The official language authority of the Union
The central body for administering Jain Tirthankaras
12.x: Sri Swamy Hathiramji Mutt at Tirupati is associated with the hereditary Dharmakarta of the Tirumala Tirupati Devasthanams and related questions of interim management.
12.tq: Identify the institution through its distinctive local administrative relationship.
12.sec: Universal angles

12.s: With reference to the current debate on religious instruction in educational institutions, which one of the following is correct?
o: The Supreme Court has held that all religious instruction is governed exclusively by Article 25.
The Ministry of Home Affairs has been directed to classify every school as a religious denomination.
The Supreme Court has left to the Ministry of Education whether schools imparting religious instruction fall under Article 26(a) rather than Articles 19(1)(g) or 30(1).
The issue concerns only the official language under Article 343.
12.x: The issue left to the Ministry of Education concerns whether schools imparting religious instruction fall under Article 26(a), rather than under Articles 19(1)(g) or 30(1).
12.tq: Compare the constitutional provisions specifically placed against one another instead of substituting Article 25.
12.sec: Universal angles

12.s: The debate revived by Punjab’s sacrilege law is connected with which of the following legal references?
o: Section 295A of the IPC, now reflected in the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, as upheld in Ramji Lal Modi on public-order grounds
The 1987 Andhra Pradesh Endowments Act, as applied to schools
Article 26(a), as applied to the administration of Hindu temples
Article 343, as interpreted in the Official Languages Act
12.x: The Punjab sacrilege-law debate refers to the Supreme Court’s upholding of Section 295A IPC in Ramji Lal Modi on public-order grounds; the provision is now reflected in the BNS framework.
12.tq: Use the ‘wrong law or authority’ trap by matching the issue with its actual statutory and judicial reference.
12.sec: Universal angles

12.s: The debate over Vande Mataram recitation in relation to Articles 25 and 26 primarily concerns:
o: The appointment of a hereditary Dharmakarta of TTD
The number and identity of Jain Tirthankaras
The administration of more than 42,000 temples in Andhra Pradesh
The balance between religious freedom and compelled participation in a national song
12.x: The Vande Mataram debate concerns the relationship between religious freedom under Articles 25 and 26 and questions of participation or recitation in a national song.
12.tq: Apply the relevant constitutional rights to the factual controversy rather than choosing an unrelated institutional issue.
12.sec: Universal angles

12.s: Ravidassias renewed their demand for a separate religion code in the Census in:
12.x: The demand by Ravidassias for a separate religion code in the Census was reported on 15 July 2026.
12.tq: Pair the community demand with its precise month and year.
12.sec: Universal angles

12.s:
Consider the following statements:
1. The debate on the Uniform Civil Code is argued by some to have implications for Article 25.
2. The Essential Religious Practices test was discussed in Sastri Yagnapurushadji in 1966.
3. Critics of the Essential Religious Practices test argue that courts should continue deciding theological questions without modification.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
12.x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct. Statement 3 is false because critics argue for a new or different test precisely because the existing test makes courts arbiters of religious theology.
12.tq: Find the statement that reverses the criticism: critics seek change, not continuation of judicial theological control.
12.sec: Universal angles

12.s: Which one of the following statements regarding language and secularism in India is correct?
o: India has no official language of the Union because secularism excludes language from constitutional protection.
Article 343 makes all Indian languages equally official languages of the Union.
Article 343 declares Hindi to be the national language of India.
Article 343 makes Hindi the official language of the Union, but India has no national language.
12.x: Article 343 makes Hindi the official language of the Union, while India has no national language. Indian secularism also treats language as an identity deserving protection.
12.tq: Separate the constitutional terms ‘official language’ and ‘national language’ rather than treating them as synonyms.
12.sec: Universal angles

13.s: Which one of the following correctly describes the position of the Right to Property under the Constitution as it stood in 1950?
o: It was guaranteed only under Article 31 as a legal right
It was a DPSP under Article 39
It was a statutory right under the Representation of the People Act, 1951
It was a Fundamental Right under Articles 19(1)(f) and 31
13.x: In 1950, the Right to Property was a Fundamental Right under Article 19(1)(f), relating to acquiring, holding and disposing of property, and Article 31, relating to deprivation and acquisition of property.
13.tq: Use the historical position of the right rather than its present constitutional status.
13.sec: Right to property - Article 31 journey, deleting amendment, Article 300A

13.s: The 1st Constitutional Amendment Act, 1951 inserted which of the following provisions to protect land reform laws?
o: Articles 39A and 43B and the Eleventh Schedule
Articles 31A and 31B and the Ninth Schedule
Articles 32A and 33 and the Eighth Schedule
Articles 30(1A) and 300A and the Tenth Schedule
13.x: The 1st Amendment inserted Articles 31A and 31B and created the Ninth Schedule to provide protection to land reform laws.
13.tq: Match the amendment with the constitutional provisions introduced by it.
13.sec: Right to property - Article 31 journey, deleting amendment, Article 300A

13.s:
Consider the following statements regarding constitutional amendments affecting the Right to Property:
1. The 4th Amendment was enacted in 1955.
2. The 17th Amendment was enacted in 1964.
3. The 25th Amendment was enacted in 1971.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
13.x: All three statements are correct: the 4th, 17th and 25th Amendments were enacted in 1955, 1964 and 1971 respectively, and each affected the constitutional treatment of property and compensation.
13.tq: Check each year independently before selecting the coded combination.
13.sec: Right to property - Article 31 journey, deleting amendment, Article 300A

13.s: With reference to the 17th Amendment relating to property, which one of the following statements is correct?
o: It inserted Article 300A in Part XII
It made all land acquisition free from judicial review
It provided that land under personal cultivation could be acquired only on payment of market value
13.x: The 17th Amendment provided that land under personal cultivation could be acquired only on payment of market value.
13.tq: Identify the amendment-specific detail instead of choosing the broader property-right changes.
13.sec: Right to property - Article 31 journey, deleting amendment, Article 300A

13.s: The 44th Amendment Act, 1978 brought about which one of the following changes?
o: It shifted Article 21A from Part IV to Part III
It inserted Articles 31A and 31B in Part III
It converted the Right to Property into a Fundamental Right available only to citizens
It deleted Articles 19(1)(f) and 31 from Part III and placed the Right to Property under Article 300A
13.x: The 44th Amendment deleted Article 19(1)(f) and Article 31 from Part III and made property a constitutional legal right under Article 300A in Part XII, Chapter IV.
13.tq: Distinguish the deleting amendment from the earlier amendments that protected land reforms.
13.sec: Right to property - Article 31 journey, deleting amendment, Article 300A

13.s: Article 300A provides that—
o: No citizen shall be deprived of property except by executive order
No company shall be deprived of property under any circumstances
No person shall be deprived of property except with the consent of Parliament
No person shall be deprived of property save by authority of law
13.x: Article 300A states that no person shall be deprived of his property save by authority of law.
13.tq: Recall the exact constitutional wording and avoid replacing 'authority of law' with executive action.
13.sec: Right to property - Article 31 journey, deleting amendment, Article 300A

13.s: Which one of the following correctly explains the present constitutional status of the Right to Property?
o: It is a constitutional legal right under Article 300A, available to all persons
It is a constitutional legal right enforceable against legislation under Article 32
It is only a statutory right available to citizens under the RPA, 1951
It is a Fundamental Right enforceable under Article 32
13.x: The Right to Property is a constitutional legal right under Article 300A. It is available to all persons, including citizens, non-citizens and companies, but is not a Fundamental Right enforceable under Article 32.
13.tq: Separate Fundamental Rights from constitutional legal rights by status, beneficiaries and remedy.
13.sec: Right to property - Article 31 journey, deleting amendment, Article 300A

13.s: A person is dispossessed of property by an executive order without any authority of law. Which constitutional provision is most directly attracted?
o: Article 31 as a continuing Fundamental Right
13.x: Article 300A protects against deprivation of property without authority of law and operates against executive action. Article 301 and the deleted Articles 31 and 19(1)(f) do not provide the applicable present remedy.
13.tq: Ask which constitutional provision governs the action of the authority actually dispossessing the person.
13.sec: Right to property - Article 31 journey, deleting amendment, Article 300A

13.s: Which one of the following statements regarding enforcement of Article 300A is correct?
o: It can be enforced only by filing a petition before the Election Commission
It cannot be enforced through any judicial proceeding
It can be enforced only through Article 32
It can be enforced through Article 226 or an ordinary civil suit, but not through Article 32 as a Fundamental Right
13.x: Since Article 300A does not confer a Fundamental Right, a claim may be pursued under Article 226 or through an ordinary suit, rather than as an Article 32 Fundamental Rights petition.
13.tq: Use the remedy-based distinction between Fundamental Rights and other constitutional rights.
13.sec: Right to property - Article 31 journey, deleting amendment, Article 300A

13.s:
Which of the following statements regarding the Land Acquisition, Rehabilitation and Resettlement Act, 2013 is correct?
1. Social Impact Assessment is mandatory.
2. Consent of 70 per cent is required for public-private partnership projects.
3. Consent of 80 per cent is required for private projects.
4. Unused acquired land is to be returned after five years.
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
13.x: The 2013 Act replaced the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, and provides for mandatory Social Impact Assessment, 70 per cent consent for PPP projects, 80 per cent for private projects and return of unused land after five years.
13.tq: Separate the consent percentages and test all numerical conditions individually.
13.sec: Right to property - Article 31 journey, deleting amendment, Article 300A

13.s: Under the Land Acquisition, Rehabilitation and Resettlement Act, 2013, the maximum compensation mentioned for rural and urban areas respectively is—
o: Twice the market value in both areas
Four times the market value in both areas
Four times the market value and twice the market value
Twice the market value and four times the market value
13.x: The compensation may be up to four times the market value in rural areas and twice the market value in urban areas.
13.tq: Read the comparison in the stated order: rural first and urban second.
13.sec: Right to property - Article 31 journey, deleting amendment, Article 300A

13.s: Article 30(1A), inserted by the 44th Amendment, deals primarily with—
o: Exemption of minority institutions from all State regulation
Compulsory acquisition of property of minority educational institutions
Appointment of teachers in minority institutions
Reservation of seats in minority institutions
13.x: Article 30(1A) concerns compulsory acquisition of the property of a minority educational institution. The amount fixed must not restrict or abrogate the right guaranteed by Article 30.
13.tq: Link the sub-clause number with its specific subject instead of the general right under Article 30(1).
13.sec: Article 30 - minority educational institutions, compensation clause

13.s:
Consider the following statements about Article 30:
1. The State shall not discriminate against minority institutions in granting aid.
2. The right to administer a minority institution is completely immune from State regulation.
3. The State may regulate standards of education without destroying the minority character of the institution.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
13.x: Statements 1 and 3 are correct. The right under Article 30 is not absolute; the State may regulate educational standards, but it cannot destroy the minority character of the institution.
13.tq: Reject the absolute statement while retaining the distinction between regulation of standards and destruction of minority character.
13.sec: Article 30 - minority educational institutions, compensation clause

13.s: The 25 per cent quota under the Right to Education Act does not apply to minority schools in view of the decision in—
o: St. Stephen's College v. University of Delhi
T.M.A. Pai Foundation v. State of Karnataka
Pramati Educational and Cultural Trust v. Union of India
P.A. Inamdar v. State of Maharashtra
13.x: In Pramati, decided in 2014, the Supreme Court held that the RTE Act's 25 per cent quota does not apply to minority schools.
13.tq: Distinguish the case concerning RTE exemption from cases concerning autonomy, preference or reservation.
13.sec: Article 30 - minority educational institutions, compensation clause

13.s: According to the cited NCPCR figure, disadvantaged enrolment in minority schools was approximately—
13.x: The cited NCPCR figure is 8.76 per cent disadvantaged enrolment in minority schools.
13.tq: Identify the precise percentage rather than confusing it with the RTE quota figure of 25 per cent.
13.sec: Article 30 - minority educational institutions, compensation clause

13.s: Article 29(1) protects the right of—
o: All persons, including non-citizens, to preserve any cultural practice
Only religious minorities to conserve their religion
Any section of citizens having a distinct language, script or culture to conserve the same
Only linguistic minorities to establish educational institutions
13.x: Article 29(1) grants any section of citizens having a distinct language, script or culture the right to conserve it. Its wording is wider than the term 'minorities'.
13.tq: Focus on the wider phrase 'any section of citizens' instead of narrowing it to minorities.
13.sec: Article 29 - interests of minorities, language, script, culture, admission

13.s: Which one of the following grounds is NOT expressly included in Article 29(2) as a basis for denying admission to a State-maintained or State-aided educational institution?
13.x: Article 29(2) prohibits denial of admission on grounds only of religion, race, caste or language. Sex and place of birth are not included in this list.
13.tq: Find the omitted ground rather than selecting one of the four expressly listed grounds.
13.sec: Article 29 - interests of minorities, language, script, culture, admission

13.s:
Consider the following statements regarding Article 29:
1. Article 29(1) is available to any section of citizens with a distinct language, script or culture.
2. Article 29(2) protects admission to State-maintained or State-aided institutions.
3. The protection under Article 29 is available to non-citizens also.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
13.x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct. Article 29 is available only to citizens, so statement 3 is false.
13.tq: Test both the substantive protection and the class of persons entitled to it.
13.sec: Article 29 - interests of minorities, language, script, culture, admission

13.s: A political promise to conserve the language of a particular section of citizens is, by itself, treated under the Representation of the People Act, 1951 as—
o: An electoral offence in every case
13.x: A political promise to conserve a section's language is not treated as a corrupt practice under the Representation of the People Act, 1951.
13.tq: Distinguish a cultural or linguistic promise from a legally defined corrupt electoral practice.
13.sec: Article 29 - interests of minorities, language, script, culture, admission

13.s: Which one of the following correctly matches the right with its constitutional position?
o: Right to Vote — Article 326 and statutory provisions under the Representation of the People Acts
Education for children aged 6–14 — Article 45 alone
13.x: Voting is based on adult suffrage under Article 326 and statutory provisions including Sections 62 of the RPA, 1951 and 19 of the RPA, 1950. The other options misstate the constitutional sources of work, information and education.
13.tq: Trace each right to its precise Article and statutory mechanism rather than relying on its general name.

13.s:
Match List-I with List-II and select the correct answer using the code given below:
List-I (Case)
A. In re Kerala Education Bill
B. St. Stephen's College v. University of Delhi
C. T.M.A. Pai Foundation v. State of Karnataka
D. P.A. Inamdar v. State of Maharashtra

List-II (Holding)
1. State is the unit for determining a linguistic or religious minority
2. Aided minority college may prefer its own community up to 50 per cent of seats
3. State cannot impose reservation on unaided minority or non-minority professional institutions
4. State may regulate standards without destroying minority character

Select the correct answer.
13.x: In re Kerala Education Bill corresponds to regulation of standards; St. Stephen's permits preference up to 50 per cent; T.M.A. Pai identifies the State as the unit; and P.A. Inamdar rejects such State-imposed reservation in the stated institutions.
13.tq: Start from the distinctive case holdings and then verify the remaining pairs.

13.s: In St. Stephen's College v. University of Delhi, the Supreme Court held that an aided minority college may prefer candidates from its own community up to—
13.x: The decision recognised that an aided minority college may prefer candidates from its own community up to 50 per cent of the seats.
13.tq: Distinguish the case-specific percentage from the separate 25 per cent RTE quota figure.

13.s: The decision in P.A. Inamdar v. State of Maharashtra is associated with which proposition?
o: The State cannot impose reservation on unaided minority or non-minority professional institutions
The RTE 25 per cent quota applies to all minority schools
The State may impose reservation on unaided minority professional institutions
Minority rights under Article 30 are entirely absolute
13.x: P.A. Inamdar held that the State cannot impose reservation on unaided minority or non-minority professional institutions in the manner stated.
13.tq: Identify the case by its specific reservation holding and reject absolute formulations.

13.s: For determining whether a group is a linguistic minority in a State, which one of the following is the appropriate unit of reference?
o: The Union Territory having the largest population of that language
13.x: The State is the unit for determining a linguistic minority. The test also considers numerical inferiority, non-dominant status and distinct identity.
13.tq: Use the constitutional unit of comparison rather than the size of the group at the national level.

13.s: Which of the following combination of criteria is relevant for determining a linguistic minority?
o: Numerical inferiority, non-dominant status in the State and distinct identity
Religious affiliation, urban residence and educational backwardness
Numerical superiority, political dominance and common occupation
District-level residence, income status and electoral representation
13.x: Determination involves numerical inferiority, non-dominant status in the State and a distinct linguistic identity.
13.tq: Identify the complete set of linked criteria instead of relying on numerical strength alone.

13.s:
Consider the following statements regarding linguistic minorities in India:
1. The Constitution expressly defines the expression “linguistic minority”.
2. The State is the unit for determining a linguistic minority.
3. Numerical inferiority and non-dominant status are relevant considerations.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
13.x: Statements 2 and 3 are correct. The Constitution does not expressly define “linguistic minority”; therefore, statement 1 is false.
13.tq: Reject the statement carrying an incorrect constitutional definition while retaining the two substantive tests.

13.s: The National Commission for Minorities is best described as a:
o: Judicial body established under the Protection of Civil Rights Act
Statutory body established under the National Commission for Minorities Act, 1992
Non-statutory advisory body created by executive resolution
13.x: The National Commission for Minorities is a statutory body established under the National Commission for Minorities Act, 1992.
13.tq: Distinguish a statutory commission from a constitutional office and an executive body.

13.s: Which one of the following is NOT included among the six religious minorities notified for the purposes of the National Commission for Minorities?
o: Linguistic minorities as a general category
13.x: The six notified religious minorities are Muslims, Christians, Sikhs, Buddhists, Parsis and Jains. “Linguistic minorities” is not one of the six notified religious categories.
13.tq: Find the category that does not belong to the notified religious-minority list.

13.s:
Match List-I with List-II:

List-I (Article)
 a. Article 347
 b. Article 350
 c. Article 350A
 d. Article 350B

List-II (Provision)
 i. Special Officer for Linguistic Minorities
 ii. Representation for grievances in any language used in the Union or a State
 iii. Recognition of a language spoken by a substantial part of a State
 iv. Mother-tongue instruction at the primary stage for linguistic-minority children

Select the correct answer using the code given below.
13.x: Article 347 concerns recognition of a language spoken by a substantial part of a State; Article 350 concerns language for grievances; Article 350A concerns mother-tongue instruction; and Article 350B provides for the Special Officer for Linguistic Minorities.
13.tq: Start with the sure Article–provision pair and eliminate codes that disturb the remaining relationships.

13.s: Under Article 347 of the Constitution, the President may recognise:
o: Any foreign language demanded by a linguistic minority
A language spoken by a substantial part of the population of a State
Only the language spoken by the majority of the State
Only the official language of the Union for use in a State
13.x: Article 347 empowers the President to recognise a language spoken by a substantial part of the population of a State.
13.tq: Test the precise constitutional trigger and avoid extreme words such as “only”.

13.s: A person submits a representation for the redress of a grievance in a language used in the Union or in the State. Which constitutional provision is directly relevant?
13.x: Article 350 provides for representation for the redress of grievances in any of the languages used in the Union or in the State.
13.tq: Match the practical administrative situation with the exact Article dealing with grievances.

13.s: The constitutional provision relating to instruction in the mother tongue at the primary stage for children belonging to linguistic minority groups is:
13.x: Article 350A deals with facilities for instruction in the mother tongue at the primary stage for children belonging to linguistic minority groups.
13.tq: Discriminate between the closely numbered Articles 350, 350A and 350B by their functions.

13.s: Which one of the following statements regarding Article 350B is correct?
o: It creates the office of the Special Officer for Linguistic Minorities.
It enables the President to recognise a language spoken by a substantial part of a State.
It permits grievances to be submitted only in the official language of the Union.
It guarantees mother-tongue instruction in all stages of education.
13.x: Article 350B provides for a Special Officer for Linguistic Minorities, also known as the Commissioner for Linguistic Minorities.
13.tq: Separate the office-creating provision from the neighbouring language-related safeguards.

13.s: A publication prints the constitutional clause concerning mother-tongue instruction for linguistic-minority children as Article 360A. What is the correct constitutional Article?
13.x: The mother-tongue instruction clause is contained in Article 350A. Article 360A is a misprint in the cited publication.
13.tq: Prefer the exact constitutional provision over a look-alike Article number.

13.s: Which of the following pairs is correctly matched?
o: Article 31B — Laws concerning acquisition of estates and agrarian reform
Article 31A — Acts placed in the Ninth Schedule
Article 31C — Laws implementing Article 39(b) and Article 39(c)
Article 350A — Special Officer for Linguistic Minorities
13.x: Article 31C protects laws implementing Article 39(b) and 39(c) from challenge under Articles 14 and 19, subject to the constitutional and judicial limitations. Article 31A concerns estate acquisition and agrarian reform, Article 31B concerns Ninth Schedule laws, and Article 350B creates the Special Officer for Linguistic Minorities.
13.tq: Check each Article against its precise subject and identify the only correctly matched pair.

13.s: Article 31C was inserted by the:
13.x: Article 31C was inserted by the Twenty-Fifth Amendment Act, 1971 to protect laws implementing Article 39(b) and (c) from challenge under Articles 14 and 19.
13.tq: Separate the amendment associated with Article 31C from the First Amendment associated with Articles 31A and 31B.

13.s: Which one of the following statements about the Ninth Schedule is correct?
o: It contains only laws implementing Article 39(b) and Article 39(c).
It contains fewer than 50 entries and enjoys complete immunity from judicial review.
It has grown to more than 280 entries, but inclusion does not confer blanket immunity from judicial review.
It has grown to more than 280 entries, and its contents have no constitutional relationship with Fundamental Rights.
13.x: The Ninth Schedule has grown to more than 280 entries, but inclusion does not provide blanket immunity from judicial review, particularly after the decisions in Waman Rao and I.R. Coelho.
13.tq: Reject the absolute claim of complete immunity and combine the numerical fact with the judicial limitation.

13.s: In Waman Rao v. Union of India (1981), the Supreme Court held that laws added to the Ninth Schedule after which date could be tested against the basic structure doctrine?
13.x: Waman Rao treated laws added to the Ninth Schedule after 24 April 1973 as open to challenge on the basis of the basic structure doctrine.
13.tq: Test the decisive cut-off date associated with the judicial review of Ninth Schedule entries.

13.s: Which one of the following best describes the effect of the decision in I.R. Coelho v. State of Tamil Nadu (2007)?
o: Only laws enacted before 1973 may be challenged under Article 31B.
Ninth Schedule entries made after 1973 may be invalidated if they damage the essence of Articles 14, 19 or 21.
Every Ninth Schedule law is permanently immune from judicial review.
13.x: I.R. Coelho held that there is no blanket immunity for post-1973 Ninth Schedule entries; they can be invalidated if they damage the essence of Articles 14, 19 or 21.
13.tq: Identify the judicial qualification that defeats an absolute immunity statement.

13.s: The year 2026 marked how many years of the First Amendment to the Constitution?
13.x: The First Amendment was enacted in 1951, making 2026 its 75th anniversary. It received the assent of President Rajendra Prasad.
13.tq: Calculate the anniversary from the amendment year and distinguish it from later constitutional amendments.

13.s:
Which of the following were associated with the First Amendment Act, 1951?
1. Insertion of Article 15(4)
2. Insertion of Articles 31A and 31B
3. Addition of public order, friendly relations with foreign States and incitement as grounds under Article 19(2)
4. Insertion of Article 31C
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
13.x: The First Amendment added Article 15(4), Articles 31A and 31B, and the stated grounds under Article 19(2). Article 31C was inserted by the Twenty-Fifth Amendment Act, 1971.
13.tq: Separate provisions belonging to the First Amendment from the closely related provision inserted by the Twenty-Fifth Amendment.

13.s: Which recent development was reported as creating concern regarding the Kannada linguistic minority in Kasaragod?
o: A central notification replacing all State languages with Hindi
A Malayalam language Bill in Kerala receiving assent in March 2026
A judicial decision removing the Special Officer for Linguistic Minorities
13.x: The Kerala Malayalam Bhasha Bill received assent in March 2026 and was contested on the ground that it could harm the Kannada linguistic minority in Kasaragod.
13.tq: Connect the current-affairs development with the precise linguistic-minority issue involved.

13.s: Which one of the following concerns has been raised in debates relating to minority educational institutions?
o: The abolition of the National Commission for Minorities Act, 1992
A constitutional prohibition on minority-run schools receiving any public assistance
A complete prohibition on mother-tongue instruction at the primary stage
Misuse of minority status to avoid obligations under the Right to Education framework
13.x: A criticism in the debate is that minority status may sometimes be misused to escape obligations under the Right to Education framework.
13.tq: Identify the stated criticism without converting it into an absolute constitutional prohibition.

13.s: The criticism that amendments to the Foreign Contribution Regulation Act may threaten minority-run civil society organisations relates to:
o: The appointment of the Commissioner for Linguistic Minorities
FCRA amendments and their effect on minority-run civil society
Article 347 and recognition of State languages
13.x: The stated concern is that FCRA amendments may pose a threat to minority-run civil society organisations.
13.tq: Match the policy measure with the specific civil-society concern rather than a constitutional language provision.

13.s: In GGR Housing v. State, the Andhra Pradesh High Court emphasised:
o: Strict statutory due process in land acquisition under Article 300A
The abolition of Article 300A as a legal right
The conversion of the right to property into a Fundamental Right
The exclusion of land acquisition from judicial review
13.x: The Andhra Pradesh High Court insisted on strict statutory due process in land acquisition under Article 300A. Article 300A protects the right to property as a legal constitutional right.
13.tq: Apply the case principle to the constitutional protection governing deprivation of property.

13.s: The Andhra Pradesh minority cell fast-tracked direct benefit transfer of post-matric scholarships subject to an income ceiling of:
13.x: The reported post-matric scholarship initiative applied an income ceiling of Rs 2.5 lakh and used direct benefit transfer.
13.tq: Recall the precise eligibility ceiling and distinguish it from nearby round-number distractors.

13.s: Which of the following pairs is NOT correctly matched?
o: Article 31C — Protection of laws relating to acquisition of estates from Articles 14 and 19
Article 350B — Special Officer for Linguistic Minorities
Article 350A — Mother-tongue instruction at the primary stage
Article 347 — Recognition of a language spoken by a substantial part of a State
13.x: Article 31C protects laws implementing Article 39(b) and (c) from challenge under Articles 14 and 19. Protection for laws relating to acquisition of estates and agrarian reform is associated with Article 31A.
13.tq: Find the swapped subject between the neighbouring provisions of Articles 31A and 31C.

14.s: Which of the following is guaranteed as a Fundamental Right under Article 32(1) of the Constitution of India?
o: The right to move the Supreme Court by appropriate proceedings for enforcement of Fundamental Rights
The right to appeal against every decision of a High Court
The right to seek an advisory opinion from the Supreme Court on every constitutional matter
The right to move any subordinate court for enforcement of statutory rights
14.x: Article 32(1) guarantees the right to move the Supreme Court by appropriate proceedings for enforcement of the rights conferred by Part III.
14.tq: Identify the precise constitutional guarantee rather than a broader appellate or advisory power.
14.sec: Article 32 - right to move SC directly, "heart and soul", basic structure  [APPSC]

14.s:
Under Article 32(2) of the Constitution, the Supreme Court may issue which of the following for enforcement of Fundamental Rights?
1. Directions
2. Orders
3. Writs
4. Advisory opinions only
Which of the statements given above are correct?
14.x: Article 32(2) empowers the Supreme Court to issue directions, orders and writs, including the five named writs. Advisory opinions are not included in this provision.
14.tq: Separate the enforcement remedies under Article 32 from the Supreme Court’s advisory jurisdiction.
14.sec: Article 32 - right to move SC directly, "heart and soul", basic structure  [APPSC]

14.s:
Consider the following statements regarding Article 32(3) of the Constitution:
1. Parliament may empower any other court to exercise some of the powers of the Supreme Court under Article 32.
2. Parliament has so far enacted a law empowering subordinate courts to issue writs under Article 32.
3. High Courts issue writs under Article 226.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
14.x: Article 32(3) permits Parliament to empower other courts, but no such law has been made so far. High Courts issue writs under Article 226.
14.tq: Watch for the trap that changes a constitutional enabling provision into an enacted law.
14.sec: Article 32 - right to move SC directly, "heart and soul", basic structure  [APPSC]

14.s: Which one of the following correctly describes Article 32(4) of the Constitution of India?
o: The right under Article 32 is available only during a National Emergency
The right under Article 32 shall not be suspended except as otherwise provided by the Constitution
The right under Article 32 may be suspended by an ordinary law of Parliament
The right under Article 32 can never be suspended under any circumstances
14.x: Article 32(4) provides that the right guaranteed by Article 32 shall not be suspended except as otherwise provided by the Constitution.
14.tq: Distinguish constitutional limitation from absolute or ordinary-legislative restrictions.
14.sec: Article 32 - right to move SC directly, "heart and soul", basic structure  [APPSC]

14.s: Which of the following statements best expresses the constitutional position of Article 32?
o: It is a statutory remedy created by Parliament and may be withdrawn by Parliament
It can be completely repealed by a constitutional amendment because it is procedural
It forms part of the basic structure and cannot be abridged even by a constitutional amendment
It applies only to legal rights created by ordinary legislation
14.x: Article 32 is part of the basic structure of the Constitution. Its essential guarantee cannot be abridged even through a constitutional amendment.
14.tq: Use the basic-structure doctrine to reject options treating a Fundamental Right as an ordinary statutory remedy.
14.sec: Article 32 - right to move SC directly, "heart and soul", basic structure  [APPSC]

14.s: The jurisdiction of the Supreme Court under Article 32 is best described as
14.x: Article 32 gives the Supreme Court original jurisdiction to enforce Fundamental Rights, but this jurisdiction is not exclusive because High Courts also exercise writ jurisdiction under Article 226.
14.tq: Split the paired descriptions—original and exclusive—instead of assuming that direct jurisdiction is exclusive.
14.sec: Article 32 - right to move SC directly, "heart and soul", basic structure  [APPSC]

14.s: A person seeks enforcement of a right created only by an ordinary statute, without alleging violation of a Fundamental Right. Which of the following is correct?
o: Article 32 is not the appropriate remedy because it enforces only Fundamental Rights
Article 32 automatically converts the statutory right into a Fundamental Right
The person can directly invoke Article 32 as a matter of right
Article 32 can be invoked only if the President permits it
14.x: Article 32 is confined to enforcement of Fundamental Rights. Statutory rights and other non-Fundamental constitutional rights cannot ordinarily be enforced under Article 32.
14.tq: Apply the scope of the remedy to distinguish Fundamental Rights from statutory rights.
14.sec: Article 32 - right to move SC directly, "heart and soul", basic structure  [APPSC]

14.s: Which one of the following is correctly matched with the writ of Prohibition?
o: Issued against a private person to compel performance of a contract
Issued by a higher court to stop a lower judicial or quasi-judicial body from exceeding its jurisdiction
Issued to test the legality of a person’s claim to a public office
Issued to release a person from every form of lawful detention
14.x: Prohibition is issued by a higher court to prevent a lower court or tribunal with judicial or quasi-judicial functions from exceeding its jurisdiction.
14.tq: Match the writ with the body against which it operates and the stage at which it acts.

14.s: A writ of Prohibition does NOT ordinarily lie against which of the following?
o: A lower court exceeding its jurisdiction
14.x: Prohibition lies against judicial and quasi-judicial bodies, but not against administrative authorities acting in an administrative capacity. It also does not lie against legislative bodies or private persons.
14.tq: Find the body outside the judicial or quasi-judicial field.
14.sec: Writ → against whom it lies and does not lie  [APPSC]

14.s: Which statement regarding Certiorari is correct?
o: It is confined exclusively to private disputes between individuals
It can be issued only before a lower court begins proceedings
It may transfer a case or quash an order of a lower court or authority
It is available only against a legislative body
14.x: Certiorari may be used to transfer a case from, or quash an order of, a lower court or authority. It operates against judicial, quasi-judicial and certain administrative bodies affecting rights.
14.tq: Distinguish the corrective function of Certiorari from the preventive function of Prohibition.

14.s: Since 1991, the writ of Certiorari may also lie against
o: Certain administrative bodies when their actions affect rights
The President and Governor for their official acts
14.x: The scope of Certiorari has been extended to certain administrative bodies whose decisions affect rights. It does not ordinarily lie against private persons or legislative bodies.
14.tq: Use the date-linked expansion of jurisdiction to identify the precise category added.
14.sec: Writ → against whom it lies and does not lie  [APPSC]

14.s: Mandamus does NOT ordinarily lie against which of the following?
o: The President or Governor for official acts
An inferior court failing to perform a public legal duty
14.x: Mandamus may lie against public officials, public corporations, inferior courts, tribunals and government authorities, but not against the President or Governor for their official acts. Article 361 protects them from being answerable to any court for official acts.
14.tq: Apply the question ‘who would perform this public duty?’ and remember the constitutional protection of the President and Governors.
14.sec: Writ → against whom it lies and does not lie  [APPSC]

14.s: Which of the following is a limitation on the issue of Mandamus?
o: It may be issued only by a subordinate civil court
It may be issued against a private individual for any personal dispute
It is not issued to enforce a merely discretionary duty or a private contractual obligation
It may be issued to enforce every private contractual obligation
14.x: Mandamus enforces a public legal duty. It does not ordinarily lie for a merely discretionary duty, a private contractual obligation, non-statutory instructions or against private persons.
14.tq: Distinguish a public legal duty from a private or discretionary obligation.
14.sec: Writ → against whom it lies and does not lie  [APPSC]

14.s:
With reference to Habeas Corpus, consider the following statements:
1. It may be directed against public authorities.
2. It may also be directed against a private individual who unlawfully detains another person.
3. It necessarily results in release even when the detention is lawful.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
14.x: Habeas Corpus may be issued against public authorities and private individuals for unlawful detention. It does not require release where the detention is lawful.
14.tq: Separate the persons against whom the writ lies from the condition that makes detention unlawful.
14.sec: Writ → against whom it lies and does not lie  [APPSC]

14.s: Habeas Corpus does NOT ordinarily lie in respect of
o: Illegal detention by a private individual
Illegal detention by a public authority
Lawful detention or detention pursuant to a valid court order
A demand to produce a detained person before the court
14.x: Habeas Corpus is a remedy against unlawful detention. It does not lie against lawful detention, contempt of court or legislature, or detention outside the jurisdiction of the court.
14.tq: Look for the legality of detention before deciding whether Habeas Corpus is available.
14.sec: Writ → against whom it lies and does not lie  [APPSC]

14.s: A person challenges the occupation of a substantive public office created by the Constitution. Who may ordinarily seek a writ of Quo Warranto?
o: Any interested person, even if not personally aggrieved
Only a member of the concerned legislature
Only the person personally aggrieved by the appointment
14.x: Quo Warranto may be sought by any interested person; personal aggrievement is not an essential requirement. The writ tests the legality of a person’s claim to a substantive public office.
14.tq: Use the standing rule to avoid importing the personal-aggrievement requirement of private litigation.
14.sec: Writ → against whom it lies and does not lie  [APPSC]

14.s: Quo Warranto does NOT ordinarily lie in relation to
o: An unlawful claim to a public office
A private office or a merely ministerial office
A substantive office created by the Constitution
A substantive office created by statute
14.x: Quo Warranto examines the legality of a claim to a substantive public office created by the Constitution or a statute. It does not lie against a private or merely ministerial office.
14.tq: First identify whether the office is substantive and public before applying Quo Warranto.
14.sec: Writ → against whom it lies and does not lie  [APPSC]

14.s: The writ jurisdiction of Indian constitutional courts is historically derived from the
o: English law of prerogative writs issued in the name of the King
United States doctrine of judicial review alone
14.x: The writs were borrowed from English law, where they were known as prerogative writs of the King, regarded as the fountain of justice.
14.tq: Identify the constitutional borrowing by linking the writs with their historical institutional source.

14.s:
Which of the following statements regarding writ jurisdiction in India is correct?
1. Before 1950, the High Courts of Calcutta, Bombay and Madras could issue writs.
2. Article 226 now empowers all High Courts to issue writs.
3. Article 226 confines High Court writ jurisdiction exclusively to Fundamental Rights.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
14.x: Before 1950, the Calcutta, Bombay and Madras High Courts had writ jurisdiction. Article 226 now empowers all High Courts, and their jurisdiction extends beyond Fundamental Rights to other purposes as well.
14.tq: Reject the extreme word ‘exclusively’ by comparing the wider scope of Article 226 with Article 32.
14.sec: Guardian of Fundamental Rights; number of writs  [APPSC]

14.s: Which one of the following correctly describes the institutional position regarding protection of Fundamental Rights?
o: Only Parliament is the protector and guarantor of Fundamental Rights
The President is the final guardian of Fundamental Rights
Only the Supreme Court can protect Fundamental Rights
The Supreme Court is the protector and guarantor of Fundamental Rights, while High Courts also share this role under Article 226
14.x: The judiciary, particularly the Supreme Court, is the protector and guarantor of Fundamental Rights. High Courts also exercise this role through their jurisdiction under Article 226.
14.tq: Distinguish the principal constitutional guardian from the authorities that make or implement laws.
14.sec: Guardian of Fundamental Rights; number of writs  [APPSC]

14.s: How many writs are specifically recognised for enforcement of Fundamental Rights under Article 32(2)?
14.x: Article 32(2) refers to five writs: Habeas Corpus, Mandamus, Prohibition, Certiorari and Quo Warranto.
14.tq: Count the constitutionally named writs rather than adding other judicial remedies.
14.sec: Guardian of Fundamental Rights; number of writs  [APPSC]

14.s: Which writ is traditionally regarded as the bulwark of individual liberty?
14.x: Habeas Corpus is regarded as the bulwark of individual liberty because it provides a prompt judicial remedy against unlawful detention.
14.tq: Associate the liberty-protection function with the writ directed against unlawful detention.
