20.x: Local bodies have had one-third reservation for women since 1992. Articles 243D and 243T deal with reservation in Panchayats and Municipalities, respectively.
20.tq: Distinguish the existing local-body reservation framework from the separate and still-unimplemented reservation for Parliament and Assemblies.
20.sec: Universal angles

21.s: Which one of the following most accurately describes the basic structure doctrine?
o: The Supreme Court alone may amend the Constitution when required
Only the Preamble can be amended subject to judicial approval
Parliament may amend every constitutional provision without limitation
Parliament may amend the Constitution, but cannot damage or destroy its core features
21.x: The doctrine permits amendment of any part of the Constitution under Article 368, but prohibits alteration, damage or destruction of features that give the Constitution its identity.
21.tq: Choose the precise statement distinguishing the amending power from its constitutional limitation.
21.sec: Basic structure doctrine - meaning, absence of definition, judicial review and supremacy debate

21.s:
Consider the following statements regarding the basic structure doctrine:
1. It is expressly defined in a separate provision of the Constitution.
2. It was developed by the Supreme Court through judicial decisions.
3. Its content has evolved case by case.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
21.x: The doctrine is not expressly defined in the Constitution. It is judge-made and its elements have emerged progressively through case law.
21.tq: Identify the false statement carrying the textual-definition trap.
21.sec: Basic structure doctrine - meaning, absence of definition, judicial review and supremacy debate

21.s: With reference to the present position on constitutional amendments, which one of the following is correct?
o: Fundamental Rights may be amended only by an executive order
Fundamental Rights may be amended, provided the basic structure is not damaged
Fundamental Rights cannot be amended under any circumstances
Fundamental Rights are outside the scope of Article 368
21.x: Parliament can amend Fundamental Rights under Article 368, but the amendment remains subject to the basic structure limitation.
21.tq: Apply the rule to a specific constitutional component rather than recalling an isolated case name.
21.sec: Basic structure doctrine - meaning, absence of definition, judicial review and supremacy debate

21.s:
Consider the following statements:
1. The Preamble is a part of the Constitution.
2. The Preamble may be amended, subject to the basic structure limitation.
3. The basic structure doctrine means that only the Preamble cannot be amended.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
21.x: The Preamble is part of the Constitution and is amendable subject to the basic structure doctrine. Basic structure is not confined to the Preamble alone.
21.tq: Separate the true constitutional position from the restrictive ‘only’ formulation.
21.sec: Basic structure doctrine - meaning, absence of definition, judicial review and supremacy debate

21.s: The basic structure doctrine primarily rests on which constitutional principle?
o: Supremacy of Parliament over the Constitution
Supremacy of the executive over the legislature
Supremacy of conventions over written provisions
Supremacy of the Constitution and judicial review by the courts
21.x: The doctrine rests on the supremacy of the Constitution and the power of courts to review constitutional amendments against its basic features.
21.tq: Test the underlying constitutional principle rather than the name of the doctrine.
21.sec: Basic structure doctrine - meaning, absence of definition, judicial review and supremacy debate

21.s: Which of the following is NOT a reason why the Indian Parliament is not sovereign in the British sense?
o: Parliament possesses an unlimited amending power
The Constitution is written and supreme
21.x: Parliament does not possess an unlimited amending power. The written Constitution, Fundamental Rights, judicial review, federal division of powers and limited amending power restrict parliamentary sovereignty.
21.tq: Find the option that reverses a feature of the limited constitutional system.
21.sec: Basic structure doctrine - meaning, absence of definition, judicial review and supremacy debate

21.s:
Assertion (A): The basic structure doctrine has been criticised as judicial rewriting of the Constitution.
Reason (R): The doctrine has no explicit textual definition and its content is developed by unelected judges case by case.
o: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
21.x: Both statements are true. The absence of a textual definition and the open-ended judicial development of the doctrine form the basis of this criticism.
21.tq: Check whether the reason directly explains the criticism stated in the assertion.
21.sec: Basic structure doctrine - meaning, absence of definition, judicial review and supremacy debate

21.s: Which of the following is regarded as a defence of the basic structure doctrine?
o: It checks majoritarian misuse of Article 368 and strengthens constitutionalism
It makes Parliament sovereign in the British sense
It permits majoritarian misuse of Article 368
21.x: The doctrine is defended as a major contribution of the judiciary to constitutionalism because it checks the misuse of the amending power by a temporary majority.
21.tq: Distinguish the stated defence of a doctrine from its criticisms and legal effects.
21.sec: Basic structure doctrine - meaning, absence of definition, judicial review and supremacy debate

21.s: The Supreme Court held in Shankari Prasad (1951) that:
o: The basic structure doctrine applies to all Ninth Schedule laws
Article 368 includes the power to amend Fundamental Rights and an amendment is not law under Article 13
An amendment is law under Article 13 and cannot abridge Fundamental Rights
21.x: Shankari Prasad held that Article 368 covers amendments to Fundamental Rights and that a constitutional amendment is not ‘law’ within the meaning of Article 13.
21.tq: Match the earliest case with its specific holding and avoid later-case attributes.
21.sec: Case → contribution and chronological order

21.s: Which one of the following is correctly matched?
o: Sajjan Singh — first application of the basic structure doctrine
Golaknath — Fundamental Rights are transcendental and immutable
Shankari Prasad — 42nd Amendment provisions struck down
21.x: Golaknath held that Fundamental Rights were transcendental and immutable, treated an amendment as law under Article 13, and held that Parliament could not abridge Fundamental Rights.
21.tq: Use the case-contribution pair and reject achievements belonging to later or different cases.
21.sec: Case → contribution and chronological order

21.s: The dissent of Justice Mudholkar in which case first referred to the idea of ‘basic features’ of the Constitution?
21.x: Justice Mudholkar’s dissent in Sajjan Singh (1965) is noted as the first judicial reference to the idea of basic features.
21.tq: Test the precursor observation rather than the later case that formally propounded the doctrine.
21.sec: Case → contribution and chronological order

21.s:
With reference to the Golaknath case, consider the following statements:
1. It overruled the earlier position in Shankari Prasad and Sajjan Singh.
2. It held that an amendment is ‘law’ under Article 13.
3. It was decided by an 11-judge bench by a 6:5 majority.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
21.x: All three statements are correct. Golaknath overruled the earlier position, treated an amendment as law under Article 13, and was decided by 11 judges with a 6:5 majority.
21.tq: Verify the case’s holding, effect on precedent and numerical bench details together.
21.sec: Case → contribution and chronological order

21.s: The constitutional response to the Golaknath judgment was provided through which amendment, which amended Articles 13 and 368?
21.x: The 24th Constitutional Amendment Act of 1971 was Parliament’s response to Golaknath and amended Articles 13 and 368.
21.tq: Match the amendment number and year with the constitutional response to the judgment.
21.sec: Case → contribution and chronological order

21.s: Which one of the following statements about Kesavananda Bharati is correct?
o: It was decided on 26 January 1975 by a 13-judge bench by a 6:7 majority
It was decided by a 7-judge bench by a 6:5 majority in 1971
It was decided on 24 April 1973 by a 13-judge bench by a 7:6 majority
It was decided by an 11-judge bench by a unanimous decision in 1973
21.x: Kesavananda Bharati was decided on 24 April 1973 by a 13-judge bench with a 7:6 majority.
21.tq: Discriminate among closely related dates, bench sizes and majority figures.
21.sec: Case → contribution and chronological order

21.s:
Consider the following statements regarding Kesavananda Bharati:
1. It first propounded the basic structure doctrine.
2. It overruled Golaknath.
3. It upheld the 24th Constitutional Amendment.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
21.x: All three statements are correct. The judgment propounded the basic structure doctrine, overruled Golaknath and upheld the 24th Amendment.
21.tq: Combine the case’s principal doctrinal contribution with its treatment of the earlier judgment and amendment.
21.sec: Case → contribution and chronological order

21.s:
Match List-I with List-II and select the correct answer using the code given below:

List-I (Case)
a. Indira Gandhi v. Raj Narain
a. Minerva Mills
c. Waman Rao
d. I.R. Coelho

List-II (Contribution)
i. Ninth Schedule laws after 1973 became subject to testing
ii. Doctrine applies from 24 April 1973
 iii. First application of the doctrine and protection of free and fair elections
iv. Struck down clauses (4) and (5) of Article 368 inserted by the 42nd Amendment
21.x: Indira Gandhi v. Raj Narain was the first application; Minerva Mills invalidated clauses (4) and (5) of Article 368; Waman Rao fixed 24 April 1973; I.R. Coelho made post-1973 Ninth Schedule laws testable.
21.tq: Start with the sure case-contribution pairs and eliminate codes that conflict with them.
21.sec: Case → contribution and chronological order

21.s: In which case was the basic structure doctrine applied for the first time, with free and fair elections treated as a basic feature?
21.x: Indira Gandhi v. Raj Narain (1975) marked the first application of the basic structure doctrine, and the relevant clause of the 39th Amendment was struck down; free and fair elections were recognised as a basic feature.
21.tq: Distinguish the formal propounding of a doctrine from its first subsequent application.
21.sec: Case → contribution and chronological order

21.s: The Supreme Court struck down clauses (4) and (5) of Article 368, inserted by the 42nd Amendment, in:
21.x: In Minerva Mills (1980), the Court struck down clauses (4) and (5) of Article 368 and reaffirmed judicial review, limited amending power and harmony between Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles.
21.tq: Match the challenged constitutional provision with the case that invalidated it.
21.sec: Case → contribution and chronological order

21.s: Which case held that the basic structure doctrine applies to constitutional amendments made on or after 24 April 1973?
21.x: Waman Rao (1981) held that the basic structure doctrine applies from 24 April 1973, the date of the Kesavananda Bharati judgment.
21.tq: Use the distinctive cut-off date to identify the relevant case.
21.sec: Case → contribution and chronological order

21.s: What was the principal significance of I.R. Coelho (2007) in the development of the basic structure doctrine?
o: It declared all Ninth Schedule laws immune from review
It upheld the 17th Amendment without qualification
It made Ninth Schedule laws placed there after 1973 subject to basic structure review
It first recognised the Preamble as part of the Constitution
21.x: I.R. Coelho held that laws inserted into the Ninth Schedule after 1973 could be tested against the basic structure of the Constitution.
21.tq: Distinguish later application to the Ninth Schedule from the original articulation of the doctrine.
21.sec: Case → contribution and chronological order

21.s: Golaknath challenged which constitutional amendment concerning State land laws placed in the Ninth Schedule?
21.x: The Golaknath case challenged the Seventeenth Constitutional Amendment, which concerned State land reform laws placed in the Ninth Schedule.
21.tq: Identify the amendment directly associated with the litigation instead of the later amendment enacted in response.
21.sec: Case → contribution and chronological order

21.s: The Ninth Schedule was introduced into the Constitution by which Amendment and along with which Article?
o: The First Amendment Act, 1951 and Article 31B
The Twenty-Fourth Amendment Act, 1971 and Article 31C
The Seventh Amendment Act, 1956 and Article 31A
The Forty-Second Amendment Act, 1976 and Article 32
21.x: The Ninth Schedule was created by the First Constitutional Amendment Act, 1951, along with Article 31B. Article 31A was also inserted by the same Amendment, but Article 31B specifically provides protection to laws placed in the Ninth Schedule.
21.tq: Use the amendment–Article pair rather than identifying the amendment alone.
21.sec: Ninth Schedule and basic structure - purpose, laws placed, Waman Rao cut-off, I.R. Coelho test  [APPSC]

21.s: The original purpose of inserting laws in the Ninth Schedule was to protect which of the following from challenge for violation of Fundamental Rights?
o: Laws relating exclusively to preventive detention
Laws concerning the appointment of judges
21.x: The Ninth Schedule was initially intended to protect land-reform and zamindari-abolition laws from challenges based on violation of Fundamental Rights.
21.tq: Identify the original purpose by distinguishing land-reform laws from later additions.
21.sec: Ninth Schedule and basic structure - purpose, laws placed, Waman Rao cut-off, I.R. Coelho test  [APPSC]

21.s:
Consider the following statements regarding the Ninth Schedule:
1. It protects both Central and State laws.
2. A law can be placed in it only by Parliament through a constitutional amendment.
3. It was originally created mainly to protect laws relating to land reforms.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
21.x: All three statements are correct. The Ninth Schedule covers Central and State laws, inclusion requires a constitutional amendment by Parliament, and its original focus was land-reform legislation.
21.tq: Check the institutional requirement and the original purpose before selecting the combined option.
21.sec: Ninth Schedule and basic structure - purpose, laws placed, Waman Rao cut-off, I.R. Coelho test  [APPSC]

21.s: The Ninth Schedule initially contained how many Acts?
21.x: The Ninth Schedule began with 13 Acts, primarily relating to land reforms.
21.tq: Retain the initial numerical value separately from the present number of entries.
21.sec: Ninth Schedule and basic structure - purpose, laws placed, Waman Rao cut-off, I.R. Coelho test  [APPSC]

21.s: The number of entries in the Ninth Schedule is stated to have increased to approximately:
21.x: The Ninth Schedule, which began with 13 Acts, is stated to contain 282 entries at present.
21.tq: Distinguish the present figure from the original count of 13 Acts.
21.sec: Ninth Schedule and basic structure - purpose, laws placed, Waman Rao cut-off, I.R. Coelho test  [APPSC]

21.s: Tamil Nadu's law providing 69 per cent reservation was placed in the Ninth Schedule by which Constitutional Amendment?
21.x: The Tamil Nadu 69 per cent reservation law was placed in the Ninth Schedule through the 76th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1994.
21.tq: Link the famous law with its specific amendment number and year.
21.sec: Ninth Schedule and basic structure - purpose, laws placed, Waman Rao cut-off, I.R. Coelho test  [APPSC]

21.s: Which one of the following correctly describes the ruling in Waman Rao v. Union of India?
o: Only laws added after 26 January 1950 could be reviewed.
All Ninth Schedule laws were declared automatically void.
The Ninth Schedule was held immune from judicial review in all circumstances.
Laws added to the Ninth Schedule after 24 April 1973 were made open to basic-structure review.
21.x: Waman Rao fixed 24 April 1973 as the cut-off date. Ninth Schedule entries added after that date could be examined on the touchstone of the basic structure doctrine.
21.tq: Focus on the cut-off date and the consequence attached to post-cut-off entries.
21.sec: Ninth Schedule and basic structure - purpose, laws placed, Waman Rao cut-off, I.R. Coelho test  [APPSC]

21.s:
Consider the following statements:
1. Waman Rao treated 24 April 1973 as a significant cut-off date.
2. Ninth Schedule laws added after the cut-off date are completely immune from judicial review.
3. The basic-structure doctrine is relevant to examining post-cut-off Ninth Schedule entries.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
21.x: Statements 1 and 3 are correct. Statement 2 is false because post-24 April 1973 entries are open to basic-structure review rather than enjoying complete immunity.
21.tq: Reject the absolute expression “completely immune” and apply the cut-off rule.
21.sec: Ninth Schedule and basic structure - purpose, laws placed, Waman Rao cut-off, I.R. Coelho test  [APPSC]

21.s: The decision in I.R. Coelho v. State of Tamil Nadu is associated with which of the following propositions?
o: Post-1973 Ninth Schedule laws may be invalidated if they damage the basic structure.
Only pre-1973 laws can be tested for violation of Fundamental Rights.
Parliament may place laws in the Ninth Schedule without a constitutional amendment.
Ninth Schedule laws have blanket immunity from judicial review.
21.x: I.R. Coelho rejected blanket immunity and held that post-1973 Ninth Schedule laws can be examined to determine whether they damage the basic structure.
21.tq: Identify the case by its rejection of blanket immunity.
21.sec: Ninth Schedule and basic structure - purpose, laws placed, Waman Rao cut-off, I.R. Coelho test  [APPSC]

21.s: The I.R. Coelho case applied the ‘rights test’ or ‘direct impact test’ primarily with reference to the essence of which Articles?
21.x: Under the rights or direct-impact test, a post-1973 Ninth Schedule law may be invalid if it abrogates the essence of the rights protected under Articles 14, 19 and 21.
21.tq: Separate the three Articles in the direct-impact test from other Fundamental Rights provisions.
21.sec: Ninth Schedule and basic structure - purpose, laws placed, Waman Rao cut-off, I.R. Coelho test  [APPSC]

21.s: I.R. Coelho v. State of Tamil Nadu was decided by a bench comprising:
21.x: I.R. Coelho was decided by a nine-judge Bench of the Supreme Court.
21.tq: Associate the case with its bench strength, a frequently tested numerical detail.
21.sec: Ninth Schedule and basic structure - purpose, laws placed, Waman Rao cut-off, I.R. Coelho test  [APPSC]

21.s: Which of the following pairs is NOT correctly matched?
21.x: I.R. Coelho was decided in 2007, not 1997. The other three case-year pairs are correctly matched.
21.tq: Find the wrong case-year pair rather than relying on the sequence alone.
21.sec: Ninth Schedule and basic structure - purpose, laws placed, Waman Rao cut-off, I.R. Coelho test  [APPSC]

21.s: Which case held that constitutional amendments, including those inserting laws into the Ninth Schedule, cannot destroy the basic structure of the Constitution?
o: Waman Rao v. Union of India
I.R. Coelho v. State of Tamil Nadu
Minerva Mills v. Union of India
Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala
21.x: Kesavananda Bharati (1973) established that the amending power cannot be used to destroy the basic structure, including through Ninth Schedule insertions.
21.tq: Match the foundational basic-structure rule with the case that first propounded it.
21.sec: Ninth Schedule and basic structure - purpose, laws placed, Waman Rao cut-off, I.R. Coelho test  [APPSC]

21.s:
Match List-I with List-II:
List-I (Case)
a. Kesavananda Bharati
b. Waman Rao
c. I.R. Coelho

List-II (Rule)
i. Rights or direct-impact test
 ii. Basic-structure limitation on amendments
 iii. Cut-off date of 24 April 1973

Select the correct answer using the code given below:
21.x: Kesavananda Bharati established the basic-structure limitation, Waman Rao prescribed the 24 April 1973 cut-off, and I.R. Coelho applied the rights or direct-impact test.
21.tq: Start from the sure pair: Waman Rao corresponds to the 24 April 1973 cut-off.
21.sec: Ninth Schedule and basic structure - purpose, laws placed, Waman Rao cut-off, I.R. Coelho test  [APPSC]

21.s: Which of the following was declared or affirmed as an element of the basic structure in Kesavananda Bharati?
o: Complete immunity of the Ninth Schedule
Right to property as an absolute Fundamental Right
21.x: Kesavananda Bharati recognised, among other elements, the supremacy of the Constitution as part of the basic structure. Unlimited amending power and complete Ninth Schedule immunity are contrary to the doctrine.
21.tq: Select a recognised basic-structure element and reject propositions that negate constitutional limitations.
21.sec: Elements declared basic structure → case  [APPSC]

21.s: Which one of the following sets was associated with the basic structure in Kesavananda Bharati?
o: Secularism, federalism and separation of powers
Preventive detention, reservation and emergency powers
Property taxation, trade regulation and local government
Official language, citizenship and electoral rolls
21.x: Kesavananda Bharati associated secularism, federalism and separation of powers, among other constitutional principles, with the basic structure.
21.tq: Recognise the cluster of foundational constitutional principles rather than isolated ordinary provisions.
21.sec: Elements declared basic structure → case  [APPSC]

21.s: Free and fair elections were recognised as part of the basic structure in which case?
o: L. Chandra Kumar v. Union of India
S.R. Bommai v. Union of India
Minerva Mills v. Union of India
21.x: Indira Gandhi v. Raj Narain (1975) recognised free and fair elections as a basic-structure element and represented the first application of the doctrine.
21.tq: Distinguish the first application of the doctrine from the case that first propounded it.
21.sec: Elements declared basic structure → case  [APPSC]

21.s: Which of the following was held to be part of the basic structure in Minerva Mills?
o: Judicial review, limited amending power and harmony between Fundamental Rights and DPSP
Only the power of judicial review of High Courts
The absolute supremacy of Parliament over the Constitution
21.x: Minerva Mills (1980) affirmed judicial review, the limited nature of the amending power, and the balance or harmony between Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles.
21.tq: Use the three-part association of Minerva Mills instead of confusing it with Kesavananda or Golaknath.
21.sec: Elements declared basic structure → case  [APPSC]

21.s:
Consider the following pairs:
1. Welfare state — Bhim Singhji case
2. Rule of law — P. Sambamurthy case
3. Arts. 32, 136, 141 and 142 — Delhi Judicial Service Association case
4. Independence of judiciary — NJAC case
Which of the pairs given above are correctly matched?
21.x: All four pairs are correctly matched. Bhim Singhji is associated with the welfare state, P. Sambamurthy with rule of law, Delhi Judicial Service Association with the specified Supreme Court powers, and the NJAC case with judicial independence.
21.tq: Verify each case against its specific basic-structure element before choosing the cumulative option.
21.sec: Elements declared basic structure → case  [APPSC]

21.s: The principle of secularism was reaffirmed as part of the basic structure in which case?
o: Kuldip Nayar v. Union of India
S.R. Bommai v. Union of India
Indira Sawhney v. Union of India
21.x: S.R. Bommai v. Union of India (1994), decided by a nine-judge Bench, reaffirmed secularism and federalism as basic-structure principles.
21.tq: Link secularism and federalism with S.R. Bommai rather than with the earlier Kesavananda ruling.
21.sec: Elements declared basic structure → case  [APPSC]

21.s: Which case is associated with the basic-structure status of the powers of the High Courts under Articles 226 and 227?
o: L. Chandra Kumar v. Union of India
Indra Sawhney v. Union of India
P. Sambamurthy v. Union of India
Bhim Singhji v. Union of India
21.x: L. Chandra Kumar (1997) is associated with the basic-structure status of the High Courts’ powers under Articles 226 and 227.
21.tq: Match the specific constitutional Articles with the case dealing with judicial review powers.
21.sec: Elements declared basic structure → case  [APPSC]

21.s: Which of the following pairs is correctly matched?
o: Free and fair elections — Minerva Mills
High Court powers under Articles 226 and 227 — S.R. Bommai
21.x: Indra Sawhney is associated with the principle of equality as a basic-structure element. The other pairs assign the principles to incorrect cases.
21.tq: Use the case-specific association and watch for swapped case names.
21.sec: Elements declared basic structure → case  [APPSC]

21.s: The expression that the Preamble’s objectives embody the basic structure implies that those objectives:
o: May be altered without constitutional limitation by Parliament
Can be removed by an ordinary parliamentary law
Cannot be amended in a manner that destroys the basic structure under Article 368
Have no relevance to constitutional interpretation
21.x: The objectives embodied in the Preamble form part of the Constitution’s basic structure. They cannot be amended under Article 368 in a manner that destroys that structure.
21.tq: Apply the basic-structure limitation to a proposed constitutional amendment rather than treating amendment power as unlimited.
21.sec: Elements declared basic structure → case  [APPSC]

21.s:
Consider the following statements:
1. Secularism was recognised as a basic feature even before the word was inserted into the Preamble.
2. The word ‘secular’ was inserted into the Preamble by the 42nd Amendment Act, 1976.
3. Secularism became a basic feature only because of its textual insertion in 1976.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
21.x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct. Statement 3 is false because secularism was treated as a basic feature even before the word ‘secular’ was added to the Preamble by the 42nd Amendment.
21.tq: Separate constitutional text from the underlying basic-structure principle.
21.sec: Elements declared basic structure → case  [APPSC]

21.s: Which case first limited Parliament’s power to amend Fundamental Rights?
21.x: Golaknath (1967) was the first case listed as limiting Parliament’s amending power over Fundamental Rights. Kesavananda Bharati subsequently propounded the broader basic-structure doctrine.
21.tq: Discriminate between the earlier limitation in Golaknath and the later doctrine in Kesavananda Bharati.
21.sec: Case that FIRST propounded the doctrine vs case that FIRST limited the amending power  [other exams]

21.s:
Match List-I with List-II:
List-I (Milestone)
a. First limitation of Parliament’s amending power over Fundamental Rights
b. First propounding of the basic-structure doctrine
c. First application of the doctrine

List-II (Case)
i. Indira Gandhi v. Raj Narain
 ii. Golaknath
 iii. Kesavananda Bharati

Select the correct answer using the code given below:
21.x: Golaknath was the first limitation of the amending power over Fundamental Rights; Kesavananda Bharati first propounded the basic-structure doctrine; and Indira Gandhi v. Raj Narain first applied it.
21.tq: Build the answer from the three distinct milestone–case pairs.
21.sec: Case that FIRST propounded the doctrine vs case that FIRST limited the amending power  [other exams]

21.s:
Which of the following statements correctly describes the relationship between Golaknath and Kesavananda Bharati?
1. Golaknath preceded Kesavananda Bharati.
2. Golaknath first limited Parliament’s power to amend Fundamental Rights.
3. Kesavananda Bharati first propounded the basic-structure doctrine.
4. Both cases are identified as the first application of the doctrine.
Select the correct answer using the code given below:
21.x: Statements 1, 2 and 3 are correct. Statement 4 is false because the first application is associated with Indira Gandhi v. Raj Narain, not both Golaknath and Kesavananda Bharati.
21.tq: Eliminate the overbroad final statement by distinguishing doctrinal milestones.
21.sec: Case that FIRST propounded the doctrine vs case that FIRST limited the amending power  [other exams]

21.s: The 39th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1975, was challenged in which case?
o: I.R. Coelho v. State of Tamil Nadu
Waman Rao v. Union of India
Minerva Mills v. Union of India
Indira Nehru Gandhi v. Raj Narain
21.x: The 39th Amendment was challenged in Indira Nehru Gandhi v. Raj Narain (1975), in which the provision placing the election of the Prime Minister beyond judicial scrutiny was struck down.
21.tq: Match the amendment with the case in which it was challenged.
21.sec: Amendments challenged or struck down on basic structure (39th, 42nd, 99th) → case

21.s: Which of the following provisions introduced or widened by the 42nd Constitutional Amendment was struck down in Minerva Mills?
o: Articles 368(4) and 368(5), and the widened Article 31C
21.x: Minerva Mills struck down Articles 368(4) and 368(5), which sought to make Parliament's amending power unlimited and amendments non-justiciable, along with the widened form of Article 31C.
21.tq: Use the specific amendment-provision pairing rather than identifying the case by name alone.
21.sec: Amendments challenged or struck down on basic structure (39th, 42nd, 99th) → case

21.s:
Consider the following statements regarding the NJAC case:
1. The 99th Constitutional Amendment was challenged in the case.
2. The National Judicial Appointments Commission Act was struck down.
3. The decision was delivered by a majority of 4:1.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
21.x: All three statements are correct. The Supreme Court struck down the 99th Amendment and the NJAC Act in 2015 by a 4:1 majority, treating judicial independence as part of the basic structure.
21.tq: Check the amendment, the associated law and the numerical majority together.
21.sec: Amendments challenged or struck down on basic structure (39th, 42nd, 99th) → case

21.s:
With reference to important basic-structure cases, consider the following pairs:
1. Waman Rao — Cut-off date of 24 April 1973 for Ninth Schedule protection
2. S.R. Bommai — Secularism and federalism as basic features
3. I.R. Coelho — Reviewability of Ninth Schedule laws inserted after 24 April 1973
Which of the pairs given above are correctly matched?
21.x: All three pairs are correctly matched. Waman Rao fixed 24 April 1973 as the relevant cut-off, S.R. Bommai recognised secularism and federalism as basic features, and I.R. Coelho held that later Ninth Schedule laws remain subject to review.
21.tq: Start with the distinctive date and then verify the two case-doctrine associations.
21.sec: Amendments challenged or struck down on basic structure (39th, 42nd, 99th) → case

21.s:
Arrange the following cases in chronological order:
A. I.R. Coelho
B. Waman Rao
C. S.R. Bommai
D. Minerva Mills
21.x: The correct chronological order is Waman Rao (1981), Minerva Mills (1980), S.R. Bommai (1994), and I.R. Coelho (2007). Therefore, after correcting the sequence by year, the order is Minerva Mills, Waman Rao, S.R. Bommai and I.R. Coelho: D, B, C, A.
21.tq: Fix the earliest and latest cases first, then distinguish the two middle cases by year.
21.sec: Amendments challenged or struck down on basic structure (39th, 42nd, 99th) → case

21.s: Which one of the following statements about Waman Rao is NOT correct?
o: It held that all Ninth Schedule laws were permanently immune from judicial review.
It concerned the Ninth Schedule and laws protected under Article 31A.
It fixed 24 April 1973 as an important cut-off date.
21.x: Waman Rao did not grant permanent immunity to all Ninth Schedule laws. It distinguished laws placed in the Ninth Schedule before and after 24 April 1973.
21.tq: Find the absolute claim that reverses the limited protection recognised by the case.
21.sec: Amendments challenged or struck down on basic structure (39th, 42nd, 99th) → case

21.s: The Constitution Bench decision in Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala was delivered by a bench of:
21.x: Kesavananda Bharati was decided by a 13-judge Constitution Bench, the largest bench constituted by the Supreme Court for this case.
21.tq: Identify the exact bench-strength figure, a common numerical discriminator.
21.sec: Kesavananda Bharati - bench strength, majority, overruled case

21.s: Which of the following correctly states the outcome of Kesavananda Bharati?
o: The decision was by 7:6 majority and overruled Golaknath.
The decision was by 9:4 majority and declared the Preamble unamendable.
The decision was unanimous and overruled Golaknath.
The decision was by 6:7 majority and upheld Golaknath without modification.
21.x: The basic-structure doctrine was propounded in Kesavananda Bharati by a 7:6 majority. The judgment overruled Golaknath on the scope of Parliament's amending power.
21.tq: Separate the bench strength from the decision majority and identify the overruled precedent.
21.sec: Kesavananda Bharati - bench strength, majority, overruled case

21.s: Kesavananda Bharati was decided on which date, under the Chief Justiceship of S.M. Sikri?
21.x: The judgment in Kesavananda Bharati was delivered on 24 April 1973, when S.M. Sikri was the Chief Justice of India.
21.tq: Distinguish the exact day and year from nearby constitutional dates.
21.sec: Kesavananda Bharati - bench strength, majority, overruled case

21.s: Which of the following propositions was held in Kesavananda Bharati?
o: The Preamble is outside the Constitution and cannot be amended.
The Preamble can be amended without any constitutional limitation.
The Preamble has overriding force over every constitutional provision.
The Preamble is part of the Constitution but can be amended subject to the basic-structure limitation.
21.x: Kesavananda Bharati held that the Preamble is part of the Constitution and amendable, but an amendment cannot destroy the Constitution's basic structure.
21.tq: Discriminate between the Preamble being part of the Constitution and the limits on amending it.
21.sec: Kesavananda Bharati - bench strength, majority, overruled case

21.s: Who argued in India in 1965 that the amending power has implied limitations, drawing upon Germany's Basic Law?
21.x: German jurist Dietrich Conrad argued in India in 1965 that constitutional amending power is subject to implied limitations, drawing on the experience of Germany's Basic Law.
21.tq: Pair the jurist with both the year and the country from which the idea was drawn.
21.sec: Origin of the doctrine idea - jurist and country

21.s: The idea of implied limitations on constitutional amendment, which influenced the basic-structure doctrine, was associated with the constitutional experience of:
21.x: The idea was drawn from Germany's Basic Law, as explained by Dietrich Conrad in India in 1965.
21.tq: Test the country associated with the origin of the doctrinal idea rather than the Indian case that adopted it.
21.sec: Origin of the doctrine idea - jurist and country

21.s: Which one of the following is a Supreme Court-evolved interpretive doctrine?
o: Unlimited amending power under Article 368(4) and (5)
DPSP primacy over Articles 14 and 19 under Article 31C
21.x: Pith and substance is a judge-made interpretive doctrine evolved by the Supreme Court. The other listed propositions were associated with constitutional amendments enacted by Parliament.
21.tq: Separate judge-made interpretive doctrines from rules created through constitutional amendment.
21.sec: Doctrines evolved by the Supreme Court vs by Parliament  [APPSC, GROUP-II]

21.s: Which of the following sets consists entirely of doctrines evolved by the Supreme Court?
o: Eclipse, severability and pith and substance
Article 31C primacy, prospective overruling and colourable legislation
Unlimited amending power, territorial nexus and harmonious construction
21.x: Eclipse, severability and pith and substance are all Supreme Court-evolved interpretive doctrines. Article 31C primacy, Article 13(4) and unlimited amending power were created through constitutional amendments, while prospective overruling originated in Golaknath.
21.tq: Eliminate sets containing a Parliament-created amendment rule or a separately identified doctrine.
21.sec: Doctrines evolved by the Supreme Court vs by Parliament  [APPSC, GROUP-II]

21.s: Prospective overruling was evolved by the Supreme Court in which case?
21.x: The doctrine of prospective overruling was adopted by the Supreme Court in Golaknath (1967).
21.tq: Match the distinctive judicial doctrine with the case in which it originated.
21.sec: Doctrines evolved by the Supreme Court vs by Parliament  [APPSC, GROUP-II]

21.s: The proposition that a constitutional amendment is not ‘law’ for the purpose of Article 13(4), and that Parliament may amend Fundamental Rights, was introduced by the:
21.x: The 24th Amendment inserted Article 13(4) and affirmed Parliament's power to amend Fundamental Rights through the constitutional amendment procedure.
21.tq: Distinguish neighbouring amendments by their specific constitutional consequence.
21.sec: Doctrines evolved by the Supreme Court vs by Parliament  [APPSC, GROUP-II]

21.s:
Consider the following statements:
1. The 25th Amendment gave primacy to the Directive Principles over Articles 14 and 19 through Article 31C.
2. The 42nd Amendment widened the scope of Article 31C.
3. The widened form of Article 31C was fully upheld in Minerva Mills.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
21.x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct. The widened Article 31C was struck down in Minerva Mills; therefore, statement 3 is false.
21.tq: Use the amendment sequence and the later judicial response to identify the false concluding statement.
21.sec: Doctrines evolved by the Supreme Court vs by Parliament  [APPSC, GROUP-II]

21.s: Parliament's attempt to make its amending power unlimited and amendments non-justiciable was made through:
o: The 25th Amendment and the original Article 31C
The 99th Amendment and the NJAC Act
21.x: The 42nd Amendment inserted Articles 368(4) and 368(5) to declare amendments non-justiciable and the amending power unlimited. These provisions were struck down in Minerva Mills.
21.tq: Ask who created the power and which exact provisions expressed it.
21.sec: Doctrines evolved by the Supreme Court vs by Parliament  [APPSC, GROUP-II]

21.s: In Kesavananda Bharati, which part of Article 31C was struck down as violating the basic structure?
o: The provision giving effect to any Directive Principle an absolute priority over the Constitution
The provision creating the Ninth Schedule
The provision enabling Parliament to amend Fundamental Rights
The provision barring courts from questioning whether a law gives effect to the Directive Principles
21.x: Kesavananda Bharati struck down the part of Article 31C that barred courts from examining whether a law actually gave effect to a Directive Principle. Judicial review was held to be part of the basic structure.
21.tq: Identify the precise judicial-review restriction rather than confusing it with the general objective of Article 31C.
21.sec: Doctrines evolved by the Supreme Court vs by Parliament  [APPSC, GROUP-II]

21.s: Which of the following best expresses the constitutional significance of judicial review under the basic-structure doctrine?
o: Judicial review is available only when the President refers a question to the Supreme Court.
Judicial review may be removed by an ordinary law of Parliament.
Judicial review applies only to Fundamental Rights and never to amendments.
Judicial review is basic and cannot be removed even by a constitutional amendment.
21.x: Judicial review is itself regarded as a basic feature of the Constitution. Consequently, even a constitutional amendment cannot abolish it.
21.tq: Test the consequence of recognising a constitutional feature as part of the basic structure.
21.sec: Universal angles

21.s: The Supreme Court's recent position concerning the words ‘Socialist’ and ‘Secular’ in the Preamble is that they:
o: Were declared unconstitutional because they were inserted by the 42nd Amendment.
Were held to be enforceable Fundamental Rights in themselves.
Were removed from the Preamble by judicial direction.
Were upheld, and challenges to their insertion by the 42nd Amendment were rejected.
21.x: The Supreme Court upheld the words ‘Socialist’ and ‘Secular’ in the Preamble and rejected challenges to their insertion through the 42nd Amendment.
21.tq: Distinguish judicial validation of an amendment from striking down the amendment.
21.sec: Universal angles

21.s: The 75th anniversary of the First Constitutional Amendment, which created the Ninth Schedule, fell on:
21.x: The First Constitutional Amendment completed 75 years on 18 June 2026. It was the amendment that created the Ninth Schedule.
21.tq: Combine the anniversary figure with the exact date and identify the relevant amendment.
21.sec: Universal angles

21.s: The argument that voting should be elevated beyond a statutory right is linked in the contemporary basic-structure debate primarily with:
o: Democracy and free and fair elections as basic features
The primacy of Directive Principles over Fundamental Rights
The basic feature of judicial independence alone
The immunity of all election disputes from judicial review
21.x: The argument is based on the view that democracy and free and fair elections are basic features of the Constitution, and therefore voting deserves stronger constitutional protection.
21.tq: Connect the proposed legal change with the basic constitutional features invoked to support it.
21.sec: Universal angles

21.s: Which of the following is a criticism of the basic-structure doctrine?
o: It is fully codified in an exhaustive constitutional list.
It is criticised as vague and unlisted, and as reflecting judicial supremacy.
It prevents every constitutional amendment without exception.
It was created directly by Parliament through Article 368(4).
21.x: Critics argue that the doctrine is vague, lacks an exhaustive constitutional list and may result in judicial supremacy. Supporters regard it as a shield protecting the Constitution from majoritarian excesses.
21.tq: Distinguish the criticism of indeterminacy from the supporters’ justification of constitutional protection.
21.sec: Universal angles

21.s: Which of the following statements regarding the debate on the 129th Amendment Bill, 2024, is correct?
o: The Supreme Court struck down the Bill for violating judicial independence.
Former CJI B.R. Gavai stated before the JPC that the Bill did not violate the basic structure, while U.U. Lalit and Sanjiv Khanna raised doubts.
Former CJI B.R. Gavai stated that simultaneous polls necessarily violate the basic structure.
Former CJIs U.U. Lalit and Sanjiv Khanna rejected all basic-structure concerns about simultaneous polls.
21.x: B.R. Gavai told the Joint Parliamentary Committee that the 129th Amendment Bill, 2024, did not violate the basic structure, whereas former Chief Justices U.U. Lalit and Sanjiv Khanna raised basic-structure doubts.
21.tq: Match each public position with the correct constitutional office-holder.
21.sec: Universal angles

21.s: Which case is regarded as the first application of the basic-structure doctrine by the Supreme Court?
o: Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala
Minerva Mills v. Union of India
Indira Nehru Gandhi v. Raj Narain
I.R. Coelho v. State of Tamil Nadu
21.x: The first application of the doctrine is identified with Indira Nehru Gandhi v. Raj Narain (1975), where the relevant part of the 39th Amendment was struck down.
21.tq: Distinguish the case that formulated the doctrine from the later case that first applied it.
21.sec: Universal angles

22.s: The Supreme Court judgment in Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India (1978) primarily concerned which of the following?
o: Recognition of privacy as a fundamental right
Imposition of President's Rule in a State
22.x: The Maneka Gandhi case concerned the impounding of her passport. It also expanded the interpretation of Article 21 by requiring procedure to be fair, just and reasonable.
22.tq: Identify the specific issue associated with the landmark case.
22.sec: Case → issue decided (Maneka Gandhi, S.R. Bommai, Vishaka, Puttaswamy, Shreya Singhal, Navtej Johar, Shayara Bano)

22.s: Which one of the following propositions was laid down in Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India?
o: Procedure established by law need not satisfy standards of fairness.
The right to life includes a life with dignity and the procedure under Article 21 must be just, fair and reasonable.
The right to travel abroad is exclusively a statutory right.
22.x: Maneka Gandhi held that Article 21 protects more than mere existence, includes dignity and travel abroad, and requires a procedure that is just, fair and reasonable. This interpretation also binds the legislature.
22.tq: Distinguish the expanded constitutional meaning from the narrow pre-Maneka interpretation of Article 21.
22.sec: Case → issue decided (Maneka Gandhi, S.R. Bommai, Vishaka, Puttaswamy, Shreya Singhal, Navtej Johar, Shayara Bano)

22.s:
With reference to S.R. Bommai v. Union of India, consider the following statements:
1. The exercise of power under Article 356 is subject to judicial review.
2. A floor test is relevant for determining whether a government enjoys majority support.
3. Secularism was recognised as a basic feature of the Constitution.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
22.x: All three statements are correct. The nine-judge S.R. Bommai judgment made President's Rule reviewable, emphasised the floor test and recognised secularism as part of the basic structure.
22.tq: Use the three linked holdings of a single landmark constitutional judgment.
22.sec: Case → issue decided (Maneka Gandhi, S.R. Bommai, Vishaka, Puttaswamy, Shreya Singhal, Shayara Bano)

22.s: The Vishaka judgment of 1997 is associated with which of the following?
o: Guidelines for conducting a floor test
Guidelines for the use of preventive detention
Guidelines against sexual harassment at the workplace
22.x: Vishaka v. State of Rajasthan recognised workplace sexual harassment as violating equality and life, and laid down binding Vishaka Guidelines until Parliament enacted legislation.
22.tq: Match the landmark case with the specific constitutional or institutional problem it addressed.
22.sec: Case → issue decided (Maneka Gandhi, S.R. Bommai, Vishaka, Puttaswamy, Shreya Singhal, Navtej Johar, Shayara Bano)

22.s: The Vishaka Guidelines were issued primarily because workplace sexual harassment was held to violate which combination of constitutional guarantees?
o: Freedom of religion and cultural rights
Rights against exploitation and freedom of conscience
22.x: The Vishaka judgment treated workplace sexual harassment as a violation of the constitutional guarantees of equality and life. The Guidelines operated until Parliament enacted a law on the subject.
22.tq: Test the rights affected rather than merely recalling the name of the case.
22.sec: Case → issue decided (Maneka Gandhi, S.R. Bommai, Vishaka, Puttaswamy, Shreya Singhal, Shayara Bano)

22.s: In K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India (2017), the Supreme Court held that:
o: Privacy is a fundamental right under Article 21.
Article 21 does not include decisional autonomy.
Privacy is a statutory right but not a fundamental right.
Privacy is available only to citizens during an Emergency.
22.x: The Puttaswamy judgment recognised the right to privacy as a fundamental right under Article 21. It also rejected the reasoning adopted in ADM Jabalpur.
22.tq: Test the exact constitutional status and Article attached to the right.
22.sec: Case → issue decided (Maneka Gandhi, S.R. Bommai, Vishaka, Puttaswamy, Shreya Singhal, Navtej Johar, Shayara Bano)

22.s: Which one of the following judgments rejected the reasoning of ADM Jabalpur regarding fundamental rights during Emergency?
22.x: K.S. Puttaswamy expressly rejected the reasoning of ADM Jabalpur. ADM Jabalpur had held that fundamental rights, including Article 21, were unenforceable during the Emergency.
22.tq: Discriminate between closely associated constitutional judgments by their distinctive holding.
22.sec: Case → issue decided (Maneka Gandhi, S.R. Bommai, Vishaka, Puttaswamy, Shreya Singhal, Navtej Johar, Shayara Bano)

22.s:
Consider the following statements:
1. Navtej Singh Johar (2018) read down Section 377 of the Indian Penal Code.
2. Consensual same-sex acts between adults were decriminalised by the judgment.
3. The judgment was delivered by a five-judge Bench.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
22.x: All three statements are correct. The five-judge Bench in Navtej Singh Johar read down Section 377 and decriminalised consensual same-sex acts between adults.
22.tq: Combine the case year, statutory provision, legal effect and Bench strength.
22.sec: Case → issue decided (Maneka Gandhi, S.R. Bommai, Vishaka, Puttaswamy, Shreya Singhal, Navtej Johar, Shayara Bano)

22.s: Which case was the first to read down Section 377 of the Indian Penal Code?
22.x: The Naz Foundation case before the Delhi High Court in 2009 was the first to read down Section 377. Navtej Singh Johar subsequently gave the Supreme Court ruling in 2018.
22.tq: Separate the earlier initiating judgment from the later Supreme Court judgment.
22.sec: Case → issue decided (Maneka Gandhi, S.R. Bommai, Vishaka, Puttaswamy, Shreya Singhal, Shayara Bano)

22.s: The Supreme Court in Shayara Bano v. Union of India held that:
o: Instant triple talaq was valid as an essential religious practice.
Article 25 completely excludes personal law from judicial review.
Polygamy and halala were both declared unconstitutional in the same judgment.
Instant triple talaq was invalid and was not an essential religious practice.
22.x: Shayara Bano declared instant triple talaq invalid and held that it was not an essential religious practice under Articles 25 and 26. The questions of polygamy and halala were left open.
22.tq: Find the precisely limited holding and reject the overbroad extension of the judgment.
22.sec: Case → issue decided (Maneka Gandhi, S.R. Bommai, Vishaka, Puttaswamy, Shreya Singhal, Navtej Johar, Shayara Bano)

22.s:
Arrange the following judgments in chronological order:
A. Vishaka
B. Shreya Singhal
C. S.R. Bommai
D. K.S. Puttaswamy
22.x: S.R. Bommai was decided in 1994, Vishaka in 1997, Shreya Singhal in 2015 and K.S. Puttaswamy in 2017.
22.tq: Anchor the earliest and latest years, then arrange the middle judgments.
22.sec: Case → issue decided (Maneka Gandhi, S.R. Bommai, Vishaka, Puttaswamy, Shreya Singhal, Navtej Johar, Shayara Bano)

22.s: Which one of the following pairs is NOT correctly matched?
o: Indra Sawhney — 50 per cent ceiling and creamy layer exclusion
Minerva Mills — Fundamental Rights and DPSP are complementary
22.x: S.R. Bommai concerned Article 356, judicial review, floor tests and secularism as a basic feature; it did not concern abolition of untouchability. The other three pairs are correctly matched.
22.tq: Find the judgment whose subject is unrelated to the constitutional principle in the pair.
22.sec: Case → issue decided (Maneka Gandhi, S.R. Bommai, Vishaka, Puttaswamy, Shreya Singhal, Navtej Johar, Shayara Bano)

22.s:
Which of the following statements regarding Kesavananda Bharati and Minerva Mills is correct?
1. Kesavananda Bharati recognised the basic structure doctrine.
2. Kesavananda Bharati held that the Preamble is part of the Constitution.
3. Minerva Mills held that Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles are complementary.
4. Minerva Mills struck down the unlimited-power clauses introduced by the 42nd Amendment.
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
22.x: All four statements are correct. Kesavananda Bharati established the basic structure doctrine and recognised the Preamble as part of the Constitution, while Minerva Mills protected the balance between Fundamental Rights and DPSP.
22.tq: Test multiple holdings across two foundational basic-structure judgments.
22.sec: Case → issue decided (Maneka Gandhi, S.R. Bommai, Vishaka, Puttaswamy, Shreya Singhal, Shayara Bano)

22.s: Which one of the following was NOT a holding associated with Indra Sawhney?
o: A 50 per cent ceiling on reservation in ordinary circumstances
No reservation in promotion under Article 16(4)
Recognition of secularism as a basic feature
22.x: Recognition of secularism as a basic feature was associated with S.R. Bommai, not Indra Sawhney. Indra Sawhney dealt with the reservation ceiling, creamy layer exclusion and reservation in promotion under Article 16(4).
22.tq: Use a nearby landmark judgment as the distractor while isolating the actual subject of the case.
22.sec: Case → issue decided (Maneka Gandhi, S.R. Bommai, Vishaka, Puttaswamy, Shreya Singhal, Navtej Johar, Shayara Bano)

22.s: Which statement correctly describes ADM Jabalpur (1976)?
o: It struck down Section 66A of the Information Technology Act.
It held that Fundamental Rights, including Article 21, were unenforceable during Emergency.
It held that Article 21 remained fully enforceable during Emergency.
It established privacy as a fundamental right.
22.x: ADM Jabalpur held that Fundamental Rights, including Article 21, could not be enforced during the Emergency. The reasoning was later effectively overruled and rejected in Puttaswamy.
22.tq: Discriminate between a discredited earlier ruling and the later judgment that rejected it.
22.sec: Case → issue decided (Maneka Gandhi, S.R. Bommai, Vishaka, Puttaswamy, Shreya Singhal, Navtej Johar, Shayara Bano)

22.s:
Which of the following pairs is correctly matched?
1. M.C. Mehta v. Kamal Nath — Public Trust Doctrine
2. M.C. Mehta v. Union of India, oleum gas case — Absolute liability
3. Vellore Citizens Welfare Forum — Precautionary Principle and Polluter Pays Principle
4. Ratlam Municipality — Municipal duty concerning public nuisance
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
22.x: All four pairs are correct. These judgments established or applied important environmental principles including public trust, absolute liability, precautionary action, polluter pays and municipal responsibility for public nuisance.
22.tq: Start from the sure doctrine–case pairs and verify the remaining environmental principles.
22.sec: Environmental judgments → doctrine laid down

22.s: The Public Trust Doctrine in Indian environmental law is particularly associated with which case?
22.x: M.C. Mehta v. Kamal Nath (1997) is associated with the Public Trust Doctrine. The doctrine was also introduced into Indian environmental law through the M.C. Mehta cases.
22.tq: Recall the distinctive doctrine attached to the leading environmental case.
22.sec: Environmental judgments → doctrine laid down

22.s: The principle of absolute liability was laid down in which environmental case?
o: M.C. Mehta v. Union of India, oleum gas case (1987)
22.x: The oleum gas case, M.C. Mehta v. Union of India (1987), established the principle of absolute liability for hazardous or inherently dangerous activities.
22.tq: Match the liability doctrine with the case and year in which it was laid down.
22.sec: Environmental judgments → doctrine laid down

22.s: Which one of the following cases recognised the Precautionary Principle and Polluter Pays Principle as part of Indian law?
o: T.N. Godavarman v. Union of India
Vellore Citizens Welfare Forum v. Union of India
22.x: Vellore Citizens Welfare Forum (1996) recognised the Precautionary Principle and Polluter Pays Principle as part of Indian environmental law.
22.tq: Distinguish two environmental principles from the other case-specific doctrines.
22.sec: Environmental judgments → doctrine laid down

22.s: In T.N. Godavarman, the expression 'forest' was interpreted to include:
o: All land recorded as forest in government records, irrespective of ownership
Only forests owned by the Union Government
Only areas containing commercially valuable timber
Only reserved forests notified under forest laws
22.x: T.N. Godavarman (1995) interpreted forest broadly to include all areas recorded as forest in government records, regardless of ownership.
22.tq: Reject the ownership and notification qualifiers that narrow the legal definition.
22.sec: Environmental judgments → doctrine laid down

22.s: The Ratlam Municipality judgment is associated with which of the following?
o: Municipal duty to address public nuisance
Mandatory use of CNG in Delhi
22.x: Ratlam Municipality (1980) recognised the municipal duty to deal with public nuisance and protect public health and sanitation.
22.tq: Identify the local-governance duty rather than an environmental liability doctrine.
22.sec: Environmental judgments → doctrine laid down

22.s:
Consider the following statements regarding the M.C. Mehta environmental cases:
1. The Taj Trapezium case involved closure or relocation of polluting industries.
2. Use of CNG in Delhi was associated with the M.C. Mehta series.
3. The M.C. Mehta cases had no connection with the Public Trust Doctrine.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
22.x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct. Statement 3 is false because the M.C. Mehta cases also introduced the Public Trust Doctrine into Indian environmental law.
22.tq: Locate the single reversed statement among several case-series applications.
22.sec: Environmental judgments → doctrine laid down

22.s: The Aadhaar judgment of 2018 was delivered by a Bench of:
22.x: The Aadhaar judgment, also called Puttaswamy II, was delivered in 2018 by a five-judge Bench, which upheld the Aadhaar Act with limitations by a 4:1 majority.
22.tq: Test the exact Bench strength and numerical division in a constitutional judgment.
22.sec: Puttaswamy Aadhaar judgment - data retention, private entities, services where Aadhaar is mandatory

22.s: Under the Aadhaar judgment, authentication records could be retained for a maximum period of:
22.x: The Aadhaar ruling limited retention of authentication records to a maximum of six months. A three-month retention period was not the applicable ruling.
22.tq: Distinguish the correct retention period from the close numerical distractor.
22.sec: Puttaswamy Aadhaar judgment - data retention, private entities, services where Aadhaar is mandatory

22.s: Which one of the following correctly describes the effect of striking down Section 57 of the Aadhaar Act?
o: Private entities could not demand Aadhaar merely under the authority of Section 57.
Aadhaar became unavailable for all government subsidies.
Private entities could freely demand Aadhaar for every contract.
Aadhaar was declared invalid for income-tax purposes.
22.x: The Supreme Court struck down Section 57, preventing private entities from demanding or using Aadhaar on that statutory basis. Aadhaar remained relevant for specified public purposes.
22.tq: Ask which authority or legal provision can support the claimed demand for identification.
22.sec: Puttaswamy Aadhaar judgment - data retention, private entities, services where Aadhaar is mandatory

22.s: Aadhaar was held mandatory for which of the following purposes?
o: Subsidies or benefits charged to the Consolidated Fund and PAN or income-tax returns
Private insurance contracts and employment applications
Opening every bank account and obtaining every SIM card
22.x: Aadhaar was held mandatory for specified subsidies and benefits funded from the Consolidated Fund, and for PAN and income-tax return requirements. It was not made mandatory for bank accounts, SIMs, school admissions or examinations.
22.tq: Separate constitutionally permitted mandatory uses from services for which Aadhaar was not compulsory.
22.sec: Puttaswamy Aadhaar judgment - data retention, private entities, services where Aadhaar is mandatory

22.s:
With reference to the Aadhaar judgment, consider the following statements:
1. Aadhaar was not mandatory for bank accounts.
2. Aadhaar was not mandatory for SIM cards.
3. Aadhaar was not mandatory for school admissions or examinations.
4. The judgment authorised contracts with private corporations to share Aadhaar data without restriction.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
22.x: Statements 1, 2 and 3 are correct. Statement 4 is false because the judgment did not permit unrestricted contracts with private corporations for sharing Aadhaar data.
22.tq: Use the service-by-service distinction and reject the overbroad data-sharing claim.
22.sec: Puttaswamy Aadhaar judgment - data retention, private entities, services where Aadhaar is mandatory

22.s: Aadhaar, by itself, does NOT establish which of the following?
o: Eligibility for a specified benefit when legally required
Citizenship, domicile or date of birth
22.x: Section 9 of the Aadhaar Act provides that Aadhaar does not by itself prove citizenship, domicile or date of birth.
22.tq: Identify the legal limitation that prevents an identity document from becoming proof of unrelated status.
22.sec: Puttaswamy Aadhaar judgment - data retention, private entities, services where Aadhaar is mandatory

22.s:
Which one of the following pairs is correctly matched?
1. Aadhaar judgment — Five judges, 4:1 majority
2. In re Article 370 — Five judges, unanimous
3. State of Punjab v. Davinder Singh — Seven judges, 6:1 majority
4. In re Article 370 — States may sub-classify Scheduled Castes
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
22.x: Pairs 1, 2 and 3 are correct. Pair 4 is false because sub-classification of Scheduled Castes was held in State of Punjab v. Davinder Singh, not in the Article 370 case.
22.tq: Start with Bench-strength pairs and identify the swapped holding in the final pair.
22.sec: Puttaswamy Aadhaar judgment - data retention, private entities, services where Aadhaar is mandatory

22.s:
Consider the following statements regarding In re Article 370:
1. The judgment was delivered in December 2023.
2. It was delivered unanimously by a five-judge Bench.
3. It upheld the abrogation and directed restoration of Jammu and Kashmir statehood.
4. It directed Assembly elections to be held by 30 September 2024.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
22.x: All four statements are correct. The five-judge Bench unanimously upheld the abrogation, directed restoration of statehood and specified the deadline of 30 September 2024 for Assembly polls.
22.tq: Combine date, Bench composition, outcome and deadline in a current constitutional ruling.
22.sec: Puttaswamy Aadhaar judgment - data retention, private entities, services where Aadhaar is mandatory

22.s: The judgment in State of Punjab v. Davinder Singh (August 2024) held that:
o: States cannot classify Scheduled Castes internally under any circumstances.
Sub-classification applies only to Other Backward Classes.
Only Parliament may sub-classify Scheduled Castes, and E.V. Chinnaiah was reaffirmed.
States may sub-classify Scheduled Castes, and it overruled E.V. Chinnaiah (2004).
22.x: The seven-judge Bench in State of Punjab v. Davinder Singh, by a 6:1 majority, held that States may sub-classify Scheduled Castes and overruled E.V. Chinnaiah (2004).
22.tq: Test the precise direction of the later judgment and the precedent it overruled.
22.sec: Puttaswamy Aadhaar judgment - data retention, private entities, services where Aadhaar is mandatory

22.s: Which legislation was enacted in response to the Vishaka judgment of 1997?
o: Sexual Harassment of Women at Workplace (Prevention, Prohibition and Redressal) Act, 2013
Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act, 2005
Muslim Women (Protection of Rights on Divorce) Act, 1986
Muslim Women (Protection of Rights on Marriage) Act, 2019
22.x: The Vishaka judgment led to the enactment of the Sexual Harassment of Women at Workplace Act, 2013, commonly called the POSH Act.
22.tq: Link the landmark judgment to the legislation enacted in response.
22.sec: Case → law enacted in response (POSH Act 2013, Muslim Women Act 2019), earlier HC rulings on triple talaq

22.s: The Muslim Women (Protection of Rights on Marriage) Act, 2019 was enacted in response to which judgment?
22.x: The Shayara Bano judgment was followed by the Muslim Women (Protection of Rights on Marriage) Act, 2019, which made instant triple talaq punishable.
22.tq: Use the case-to-statute association to distinguish closely related Muslim personal law cases.
22.sec: Case → law enacted in response (POSH Act 2013, Muslim Women Act 2019), earlier HC rulings on triple talaq

22.s: The Muslim Women (Protection of Rights on Divorce) Act, 1986 was enacted following which case?
22.x: The 1986 Act followed the Shah Bano judgment of 1985.
22.tq: Discriminate between similarly named Shah Bano and Shayara Bano cases.
22.sec: Case → law enacted in response (POSH Act 2013, Muslim Women Act 2019), earlier HC rulings on triple talaq

22.s:
Consider the following statements regarding earlier judicial rulings on triple talaq:
1. The Allahabad High Court held triple talaq illegal.
2. The Supreme Court dealt with triple talaq in Shamim Ara in 2002.
3. The Allahabad High Court ruling referred to in this context was delivered in 1985.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
22.x: The Allahabad High Court held triple talaq illegal, and the Supreme Court considered the issue in Shamim Ara in 2002. The cited Allahabad High Court ruling dates to 1994, not 1985.
22.tq: Check the precise year while retaining the correct court-case associations.
22.sec: Case → law enacted in response (POSH Act 2013, Muslim Women Act 2019), earlier HC rulings on triple talaq

22.s: Which of the following was struck down in the Joseph Shine judgment?
o: Section 66A of the Information Technology Act
22.x: Joseph Shine struck down Section 497 IPC, which dealt with adultery.
22.tq: Associate the judgment with the exact statutory provision rather than the broad subject.
22.sec: Case → law or section struck down or read down

22.s: Talaq-e-biddat was set aside by the Supreme Court in which case?
22.x: The Shayara Bano judgment of 2017 set aside talaq-e-biddat, commonly known as instant triple talaq.
22.tq: Use the specific form of talaq as the clue for the correct case.
22.sec: Case → law or section struck down or read down

22.s: With effect from 1 July 2024, which of the following correctly describes the position under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita?
o: The IPC continues unchanged and adultery remains an offence under Section 497.
The BNS replaced the IPC, contains no adultery offence and has no equivalent of Section 377 IPC.
The BNS replaced the IPC but retains Section 377 as a separate provision.
The BNS replaced the IPC and abolished the offence of bigamy.
22.x: The Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita replaced the IPC from 1 July 2024. It contains no adultery offence and has no equivalent of Section 377 IPC; bigamy is dealt with under Section 82 BNS.
22.tq: Separate the current statutory position from the earlier IPC provisions.
22.sec: Case → law or section struck down or read down

22.s: The Vishaka guidelines primarily dealt with which matter?
o: Registration of FIRs for cognizable offences
22.x: The Vishaka guidelines provided for workplace harassment committees and operated until the 2013 legislation was enacted.
22.tq: Match the subject matter of the guidelines with the originating case.
22.sec: Case → guidelines laid down (Vishaka, D.K. Basu, Prakash Singh, Lalita Kumari)

22.s: Which of the following was NOT associated with the guidelines in D.K. Basu v. State of West Bengal?
o: Informing a relative or friend of the arrested person
Constitution of a State Security Commission
22.x: D.K. Basu dealt with safeguards relating to arrest and custody, including an arrest memo, informing kin and medical checks. A State Security Commission was associated with police reforms in Prakash Singh.
22.tq: Find the guideline belonging to a neighbouring case rather than the arrest-and-custody case.
22.sec: Case → guidelines laid down (Vishaka, D.K. Basu, Prakash Singh, Lalita Kumari)

22.s: Which of the following pairs is correctly matched?
o: Vishaka — mandatory FIR for cognizable offences
22.x: Prakash Singh laid down police reform measures. Lalita Kumari concerned mandatory FIR registration, D.K. Basu concerned arrest and custody safeguards, and Vishaka concerned workplace harassment.
22.tq: Use subject-based elimination among four landmark guideline cases.
22.sec: Case → guidelines laid down (Vishaka, D.K. Basu, Prakash Singh, Lalita Kumari)

22.s: Which of the following was NOT one of the police reform measures associated with Prakash Singh?
o: Security of tenure for the Director General of Police
Mandatory registration of every cognizable offence as an FIR under Section 154 CrPC
22.x: Prakash Singh concerned police reforms including the State Security Commission, DGP tenure, Police Establishment Board and Complaints Authority. Mandatory FIR registration was laid down in Lalita Kumari.
22.tq: Identify the one guideline shifted from police reform to FIR registration.
22.sec: Case → guidelines laid down (Vishaka, D.K. Basu, Prakash Singh, Lalita Kumari)

22.s: The Lalita Kumari judgment held that registration of an FIR is mandatory in relation to which category of offences?
o: Only offences punishable with life imprisonment
22.x: Lalita Kumari made registration of an FIR mandatory for cognizable offences under Section 154 CrPC, now corresponding to Section 173 of the BNSS.
22.tq: Apply the exact legal classification instead of the broader term ‘all offences’.
22.sec: Case → guidelines laid down (Vishaka, D.K. Basu, Prakash Singh, Lalita Kumari)

22.s: Which provision of the BNSS corresponds to Section 154 of the CrPC in the context of FIR registration?
22.x: The FIR-registration provision corresponding to Section 154 CrPC is Section 173 of the BNSS.
22.tq: Test the transition from the old criminal procedure provision to the new provision.
22.sec: Case → guidelines laid down (Vishaka, D.K. Basu, Prakash Singh, Lalita Kumari)

22.s:
Consider the following statements regarding the Constitution Bench decision on Article 370:
1. The Court held that Article 370 was temporary.
2. The Court held that the President could make Article 370 inoperative.
3. The Court directed that elections be held.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
22.x: The December 2023 Article 370 judgment treated Article 370 as temporary, upheld the power of the President to make it inoperative and directed elections.
22.tq: Retain all three holdings of a Constitution Bench decision rather than selecting only the headline issue.
22.sec: Recent Constitution Bench cases (electoral bonds, Article 370, SC sub-classification, demonetisation)

22.s: The Supreme Court upheld demonetisation in January 2023 by what majority and under which provision?
o: 3:2 under Section 26(2) of the RBI Act
4:1 under Section 26(2) of the RBI Act
22.x: The demonetisation decision was upheld by a 4:1 majority under Section 26(2) of the RBI Act.
22.tq: Combine the majority figure with the exact statutory provision.
22.sec: Recent Constitution Bench cases (electoral bonds, Article 370, SC sub-classification, demonetisation)

22.s: The Supreme Court struck down the electoral bonds scheme primarily in relation to which constitutional right?
22.x: In February 2024, the Court unanimously struck down the electoral bonds scheme in the context of voters’ right to information.
22.tq: Connect the scheme with the constitutional transparency right identified in the judgment.
22.sec: Recent Constitution Bench cases (electoral bonds, Article 370, SC sub-classification, demonetisation)

22.s: Which one of the following statements about Davinder Singh is correct?
o: A five-judge Bench unanimously prohibited sub-classification of Scheduled Castes.
A three-judge Bench permitted sub-classification only for Scheduled Tribes.
A nine-judge Bench by 4:1 upheld demonetisation.
A seven-judge Bench by 6:1 allowed sub-classification of Scheduled Castes and overruled Chinnaiah.
22.x: In August 2024, a seven-judge Bench in Davinder Singh, by 6:1, allowed sub-classification of Scheduled Castes and overruled E.V. Chinnaiah.
22.tq: Use bench size, majority and legal consequence together to reject mixed-up case descriptions.
22.sec: Recent Constitution Bench cases (electoral bonds, Article 370, SC sub-classification, demonetisation)

22.s: Which of the following pairs is correctly matched with the bench size and Chief Justice associated with the case?
o: Vishaka — three judges, CJI J.S. Verma
Maneka Gandhi — five judges, CJI D.Y. Chandrachud
Electoral Bonds — nine judges, CJI J.S. Khehar
Shayara Bano — seven judges, CJI Dipak Misra
22.x: Vishaka was decided by a three-judge Bench headed by CJI J.S. Verma. Maneka Gandhi had seven judges, Electoral Bonds had five judges headed by CJI D.Y. Chandrachud, and Shayara Bano had five judges headed by CJI Dipak Misra.
22.tq: Start with the distinctive three-judge Vishaka combination and eliminate swapped bench details.
22.sec: Case → bench size and chief justice

22.s:
Consider the following pairs:
1. Bommai — nine judges
2. Puttaswamy — nine judges, CJI J.S. Khehar
3. Maneka Gandhi — seven judges
4. Davinder Singh — seven judges
Which of the pairs given above are correctly matched?
22.x: Bommai and Puttaswamy were nine-judge cases; Puttaswamy was associated with CJI J.S. Khehar. Maneka Gandhi and Davinder Singh were decided by seven-judge Benches.
22.tq: Verify bench-size clusters before considering the Chief Justice detail.
22.sec: Case → bench size and chief justice

22.s: Which group of cases was associated with a five-judge Bench headed by CJI Dipak Misra?
o: Navtej Johar, Joseph Shine and Aadhaar
Bommai, Maneka Gandhi and Davinder Singh
Vishaka, Shayara Bano and D.K. Basu
22.x: Navtej Johar, Joseph Shine and Aadhaar were five-judge Bench cases associated with CJI Dipak Misra.
22.tq: Recognise the correct case cluster instead of matching a single isolated case.
22.sec: Case → bench size and chief justice

22.s: The judgment in E.V. Chinnaiah v. State of Andhra Pradesh (2004) dealt with which issue?
o: It struck down Andhra Pradesh’s SC sub-categorisation Act, 2000.
It struck down Section 66A of the Information Technology Act.
It upheld 100% reservation for teachers in Scheduled Areas.
It upheld the electoral bonds scheme.
22.x: E.V. Chinnaiah struck down the Andhra Pradesh SC sub-categorisation Act, 2000. The decision was overruled by Davinder Singh in 2024.
22.tq: Associate the AP judgment with its precise reservation issue and outcome.
22.sec: Judgments on AP matters (AP capital cases, AP reservation cases)

22.s: Which case struck down the 100% reservation of posts for teachers in Scheduled Areas?
o: State of Bombay v. F.N. Balsara
22.x: Chebrolu Leela Prasad Rao (2020) struck down the 100% ST quota for teachers in Scheduled Areas.
22.tq: Distinguish the two AP reservation cases by the reservation measure challenged.
22.sec: Judgments on AP matters (AP capital cases, AP reservation cases)

22.s: Which of the following correctly describes the recent legal position regarding the capital of Andhra Pradesh?
o: Kurnool became the sole capital under the 2022 Andhra Pradesh High Court judgment.
Visakhapatnam became the sole capital with effect from 2 June 2024, and the Supreme Court approved three capitals.
Amaravati became the sole capital with effect from 2 June 2024, and Parliament passed the AP Reorganisation (Amendment) Bill, 2026.
The Andhra Pradesh High Court upheld the three-capital proposal in 2022 without legislative action thereafter.
22.x: After the Andhra Pradesh High Court’s 2022 ruling against three capitals, Amaravati became the sole capital from 2 June 2024. Parliament passed the AP Reorganisation (Amendment) Bill, 2026, in April 2026.
22.tq: Track the sequence of court ruling, effective date and subsequent parliamentary action.
22.sec: Judgments on AP matters (AP capital cases, AP reservation cases)

22.s:
Arrange the following events in chronological order:
A. E.V. Chinnaiah judgment
B. Chebrolu Leela Prasad Rao judgment
C. Davinder Singh judgment
D. AP Reorganisation (Amendment) Bill, 2026
22.x: E.V. Chinnaiah was decided in 2004, Chebrolu Leela Prasad Rao in 2020, Davinder Singh in 2024 and the amendment Bill in 2026.
22.tq: Use the years as the first filter and then check the sequence of the AP developments.
22.sec: Judgments on AP matters (AP capital cases, AP reservation cases)

22.s: The public trust doctrine, as associated with M.C. Mehta v. Kamal Nath, means that:
o: Only Parliament can regulate private contracts.
The State holds natural resources in trust for the public.
The State may transfer all natural resources exclusively to private entities.
A law inconsistent with Fundamental Rights is permanently void in every situation.
22.x: Under the public trust doctrine, the State is treated as a trustee of natural resources for the benefit of the public.
22.tq: Apply the core meaning of the doctrine to the State’s relationship with natural resources.
22.sec: Doctrines → originating case

22.s: Which doctrine was laid down in Bhikaji Narain Dhakras (1955)?
22.x: The eclipse doctrine holds that a pre-Constitution law inconsistent with Fundamental Rights becomes dormant rather than dead and may revive if the constitutional impediment is removed.
22.tq: Match the distinctive ‘dormant, not dead’ idea with its originating case.
22.sec: Doctrines → originating case

22.s: The doctrine of pith and substance is particularly relevant when determining whether:
o: A law’s true nature falls within the legislative competence of a particular List.
An invalid statutory provision can be separated from the rest of an Act.
A hazardous industry is liable without exceptions.
22.x: The doctrine of pith and substance examines the true nature and character of a law to determine its appropriate legislative List. It is associated with State of Bombay v. F.N. Balsara (1951).
22.tq: Apply the doctrine to a Union-State legislative competence dispute.
22.sec: Doctrines → originating case

22.s: Which one of the following pairs is correctly matched?
o: Colourable legislation — K.C. Gajapati Narayan Deo
Prospective overruling — R.M.D.C. v. Union of India
Absolute liability — State of Bombay v. R.M.D.C.
22.x: The doctrine of colourable legislation is associated with K.C. Gajapati Narayan Deo (1953). Prospective overruling is associated with Golaknath, severability with R.M.D.C. v. Union of India, and absolute liability with M.C. Mehta’s Oleum gas leak case.
22.tq: Use the originating case rather than the definition alone to identify the correct pair.
22.sec: Doctrines → originating case

22.s: The principle that ‘what cannot be done directly cannot be done indirectly’ refers to which doctrine?
22.x: The doctrine of colourable legislation prevents a legislature from achieving indirectly what it lacks power to do directly. It is associated with K.C. Gajapati Narayan Deo (1953).
22.tq: Recognise the standard formulation of the doctrine.
22.sec: Doctrines → originating case
