22.s: Which case is associated with the doctrine of absolute liability for hazardous industries?
o: Motor General Traders v. State of Andhra Pradesh
M.C. Mehta, Oleum gas leak case
22.x: The absolute liability principle was evolved in M.C. Mehta’s 1987 Oleum gas leak case. It imposes liability on hazardous industries without the exceptions available under strict liability.
22.tq: Distinguish absolute liability from public trust and severability by the underlying subject.
22.sec: Doctrines → originating case

22.s: What is the essential meaning of prospective overruling?
o: A new judicial ruling operates only for the future.
A pre-Constitution law is dormant but not dead.
The invalid portion of a statute is removed while the remainder survives.
The true nature of a law determines its legislative List.
22.x: Prospective overruling means that the new judicial ruling operates prospectively rather than disturbing all past transactions. It is associated with Golaknath (1967).
22.tq: Match the temporal effect of the judgment with the doctrine’s exact meaning.
22.sec: Doctrines → originating case

22.s: Under the doctrine of severability, what is the effect of an invalid part of a statute?
o: The entire statute is automatically repealed.
The statute becomes dormant and automatically revives.
The invalid part is struck down while the remainder may survive.
The State legislature loses all legislative competence.
22.x: The doctrine of severability permits the invalid portion of a law to be struck down while the valid remainder survives, where separation is possible. It is associated with R.M.D.C. v. Union of India (1957).
22.tq: Test the practical consequence of severing an unconstitutional provision.
22.sec: Doctrines → originating case

22.s: The doctrine of territorial nexus permits a State law to operate outside the State when:
o: The law concerns only Union subjects.
The law has been approved by every State legislature.
The law is immune from judicial review.
There is a sufficient connection between the State and the subject of the law.
22.x: A State law may have extra-territorial operation when a sufficient territorial nexus exists between the State and the subject matter. The doctrine is associated with State of Bombay v. R.M.D.C. (1957).
22.tq: Apply the nexus requirement to an extra-territorial State law.
22.sec: Doctrines → originating case

22.s: Which doctrine is most directly applicable when a law enacted by one legislature appears to encroach upon a subject in another legislative List?
22.x: Pith and substance is the relevant doctrine for examining Union-State List encroachment by looking at the true nature and character of the law.
22.tq: Identify the doctrine from the federal legislative competence scenario.
22.sec: Doctrines → originating case

22.s: Which one of the following cases is associated with the compulsory registration of marriages?
o: Shayara Bano v. Union of India
Prem Shankar Shukla v. Delhi Administration
22.x: In Seema v. Ashwani Kumar (2006), the Supreme Court directed compulsory registration of marriages.
22.tq: Match the social reform direction with the correct judgment.
22.sec: Social-reform directions → case

22.s: The guidelines relating to sexual harassment of women at the workplace were laid down in which case?
o: Lily Thomas v. Union of India
Shah Bano v. Union of India
Sarla Mudgal v. Union of India
22.x: Vishaka v. State of Rajasthan (1997) laid down workplace sexual harassment guidelines, which were later replaced by the POSH Act, 2013.
22.tq: Identify the landmark case from its specific judicial guideline.
22.sec: Social-reform directions → case

22.s:
Consider the following statements regarding the Vishaka judgment:
1. It concerned sexual harassment at the workplace.
2. Its guidelines were later replaced by the POSH Act, 2013.
3. It declared instant triple talaq invalid.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
22.x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct. Statement 3 relates to Shayara Bano, not Vishaka.
22.tq: Separate closely related social-reform judgments by their subject matter.
22.sec: Social-reform directions → case

22.s: The Supreme Court judgment concerning handcuffing only in exceptional cases is associated with:
o: Prem Shankar Shukla v. Delhi Administration
Shamsher Singh v. State of Punjab
Rameshwar Prasad v. Union of India
22.x: Prem Shankar Shukla v. Delhi Administration (1980) held that handcuffing should be confined to exceptional cases.
22.tq: Recall the specific liberty-related holding attached to the case.
22.sec: Social-reform directions → case

22.s: Which one of the following correctly describes the decision in Shah Bano (1985)?
o: It held that instant triple talaq was constitutionally valid.
It struck down Section 8(4) of the Representation of the People Act.
It prescribed the composition of the Election Commission.
It concerned maintenance under Section 125 of the CrPC and called for a Uniform Civil Code.
22.x: The Shah Bano case concerned maintenance under Section 125 of the CrPC and called for a Uniform Civil Code. Section 125 CrPC is now reflected in Section 144 of the BNSS, 2023.
22.tq: Use the provision-and-principle combination to identify the correct case.
22.sec: Social-reform directions → case

22.s: Section 144 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 is mentioned in connection with which earlier legal provision?
o: Section 8(4) of the Representation of the People Act
Section 125 of the Code of Criminal Procedure
Section 82 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita
22.x: The maintenance provision associated with Shah Bano was Section 125 of the CrPC; the corresponding provision is now referred to as Section 144 of the BNSS, 2023.
22.tq: Discriminate between similarly numbered statutory provisions and their subjects.
22.sec: Social-reform directions → case

22.s:
Consider the following pairs:
1. Sarla Mudgal — Conversion to Islam cannot be used to evade bigamy law
2. Lily Thomas (2000) — Conversion to Islam cannot be used to evade bigamy law
3. Lily Thomas (2013) — Section 8(4) of the Representation of the People Act struck down
Which of the pairs given above are correctly matched?
22.x: All three pairs are correct. Sarla Mudgal (1995) and Lily Thomas (2000) addressed conversion and bigamy, while Lily Thomas (2013) concerned disqualification of convicted legislators.
22.tq: Separate judgments with the same litigant name by year and legal subject.
22.sec: Social-reform directions → case

22.s:
In Union of India v. Association for Democratic Reforms (2002), the Supreme Court held that election candidates must disclose which of the following?
1. Criminal record
2. Assets
3. Educational qualifications
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
22.x: The ADR judgment required candidates to disclose their criminal record, assets and educational qualifications.
22.tq: Identify the complete set of disclosure requirements rather than a partial list.
22.sec: Electoral and governance judgments

22.s: The introduction of the NOTA option on Electronic Voting Machines was associated with which judgment?
22.x: The PUCL judgment of 2013 directed the provision of the None of the Above option on EVMs.
22.tq: Recall the electoral reform linked to the named judgment.
22.sec: Electoral and governance judgments

22.s: Which one of the following was the effect of Lily Thomas v. Union of India (2013)?
o: Candidates were exempted from disclosing their assets.
Convicted MPs and MLAs could continue in office until their appeals were finally decided.
Section 8(4) of the Representation of the People Act was struck down and convicted MPs and MLAs were disqualified at once.
22.x: The Supreme Court struck down Section 8(4) of the RPA, resulting in immediate disqualification of convicted MPs and MLAs, subject to the applicable legal position.
22.tq: Reject the reversed consequence and identify the precise effect of striking down a provision.
22.sec: Electoral and governance judgments

22.s:
Consider the following statements about the electoral bonds judgment:
1. The scheme was struck down in February 2024.
2. The judgment was unanimous.
3. The decision was rendered by a five-judge Bench.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
22.x: The electoral bonds scheme was struck down in February 2024 by a unanimous five-judge Bench.
22.tq: Test date, unanimity and Bench strength together through a complete statement set.
22.sec: Electoral and governance judgments

22.s: According to the Anoop Baranwal judgment, the Chief Election Commissioner and Election Commissioners were to be selected by a committee comprising the:
o: Prime Minister, Union Home Minister and Chief Justice of India
President, Leader of Opposition and Chief Election Commissioner
Prime Minister, Leader of Opposition and Chief Justice of India
President, Prime Minister and Speaker of the Lok Sabha
22.x: Anoop Baranwal (2023) provided for selection by the Prime Minister, the Leader of Opposition and the Chief Justice of India until Parliament made a law.
22.tq: Use the composition of the appointing committee as the decisive clue.
22.sec: Electoral and governance judgments

22.s: Which one of the following changes was made by Parliament's 2023 law in relation to the selection committee for the Election Commission?
o: The Prime Minister was replaced by the President.
The Chief Justice of India was replaced by a Union Minister.
The Leader of Opposition was replaced by the Speaker of the Lok Sabha.
The Election Commissioner was replaced by the Governor.
22.x: Parliament's 2023 Act replaced the Chief Justice of India with a Union Minister in the selection arrangement.
22.tq: Focus on the single altered member instead of confusing the entire committee.
22.sec: Electoral and governance judgments

22.s: In Shamsher Singh (1974), the Supreme Court held that the Governor is generally bound by:
o: The directions of the Election Commission
The personal discretion of the President in every matter
The advice of the Chief Justice of the High Court
The aid and advice of the Council of Ministers
22.x: Shamsher Singh (1974), decided by a seven-judge Bench, affirmed that the Governor ordinarily acts on the aid and advice of the Council of Ministers.
22.tq: Apply the constitutional executive principle to the correct authority.
22.sec: Federalism and Governor cases

22.s: Which one of the following statements regarding Rameshwar Prasad (2006) is correct?
o: The dissolution of the Bihar Assembly was struck down and the Governor's report was held reviewable.
The judgment upheld instant triple talaq.
The judgment introduced NOTA in elections.
The Governor was held free to withhold Bills indefinitely.
22.x: Rameshwar Prasad (2006) struck down the dissolution of the Bihar Assembly and held that the Governor's report was subject to judicial review.
22.tq: Match the case with its constitutional event and review principle.
22.sec: Federalism and Governor cases

22.s: The decision in Nabam Rebia (2016) is associated with which proposition?
o: The Governor can replace the Council of Ministers without a floor test.
The Governor has no general discretion in matters such as summoning the House.
The Governor has unrestricted discretion in summoning the House.
The Governor may permanently suspend the functioning of the Assembly.
22.x: Nabam Rebia (2016) rejected a general discretionary power of the Governor, including in relation to summoning the House.
22.tq: Identify the constitutional limit by rejecting an extreme claim of unrestricted discretion.
22.sec: Federalism and Governor cases

22.s:
Consider the following statements:
1. In State of Punjab v. Principal Secretary to Governor (2023), the Governor was held unable to keep Bills pending indefinitely.
2. The case concerned the Governor's power to delay legislative Bills without constitutional limitation.
3. The decision is relevant to the relationship between the Governor and the elected government.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
22.x: Statements 1 and 3 are correct. Statement 2 reverses the holding: the Governor cannot keep Bills pending indefinitely.
22.tq: Find the reversed proposition hidden within a largely related set of statements.
22.sec: Federalism and Governor cases

22.s: Which one of the following correctly states the significance of State of Tamil Nadu v. Governor of Tamil Nadu?
o: The Governor is not bound by constitutional conventions in any circumstance.
The case abolished the office of the Governor.
The Governor's discretion cannot negate responsible government, and timelines were addressed for Bills.
The Governor may indefinitely postpone all Bills passed by the State Legislature.
22.x: The case held that the Governor's discretion cannot undermine responsible government and addressed timelines concerning Bills.
22.tq: Choose the option that states both linked elements of the holding without an extreme conclusion.
22.sec: Federalism and Governor cases

22.s:
The judgment in State of Tamil Nadu v. Governor of Tamil Nadu is described as follows:
1. It is dated 2023 in one official examination-related reference.
2. It was delivered in April 2025.
Which of the statements given above is correct?
22.x: The case is dated 2023 in the cited examination reference, while the judgment was delivered in April 2025.
22.tq: Keep the case-date reference distinct from the date of delivery.
22.sec: Federalism and Governor cases

22.s: In the later Presidential Reference opinion concerning the Governor, the Governor was described as a:
o: Permanent representative of the Union Executive
22.x: The later Presidential Reference opinion described the Governor as a “guide, philosopher and friend.”
22.tq: Recall the distinctive constitutional phrase associated with the opinion.
22.sec: Federalism and Governor cases

22.s:
Which of the following developments has been identified as a current relevance of the Shayara Bano and related personal-law debate?
1. The Supreme Court issued notice on a PIL seeking a ban on polygamy.
2. Javed (2003) held that polygamy is not an essential religious practice.
3. Bigamy is an offence under Section 82 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita.
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
22.x: All three statements are correct: notice was issued on the PIL, Javed (2003) addressed polygamy as an essential religious practice, and Section 82 of the BNS concerns bigamy.
22.tq: Combine the judicial precedent, current development and statutory provision without confusing their roles.
22.sec: Universal angles

22.s: Which one of the following developments is associated with the application of the privacy principle in Puttaswamy?
o: Selection of Election Commissioners by a committee
22.x: Puttaswamy's privacy principle was reported as having been applied to DNA paternity tests.
22.tq: Apply a broad constitutional right to the specific modern factual context.
22.sec: Universal angles

22.s: The proposition that “bail is the rule even under the UAPA” was associated with:
o: S.R. Bommai v. Union of India
Shamsher Singh v. State of Punjab
22.x: Andrabi v. NIA, reported on 18 May 2026, was associated with the proposition that bail is the rule even under the UAPA.
22.tq: Identify the case from the precise bail principle attributed to it.
22.sec: Universal angles

22.s: Which one of the following statements correctly reflects the current position mentioned regarding the creamy layer issue for Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes?
o: The issue concerns only economically weaker sections outside the reservation system.
The Supreme Court has abolished reservations for SCs and STs.
The Centre opposes an income-based creamy layer for SCs and STs.
The Centre supports an income-based creamy layer without qualification.
22.x: The stated current position is that the Centre opposes an income-based creamy layer for SCs and STs.
22.tq: Distinguish the stated governmental position from broader reservation-related claims.
22.sec: Universal angles

22.s: Which one of the following is cited as a criticism of the Vishaka and Prakash Singh judgments?
o: They avoided issuing any guidelines in the absence of legislation.
Their guideline-making has been criticised as judicial legislation, and police reforms remain poorly implemented.
They transferred all legislative power to the Governors.
They invalidated the power of judicial review.
22.x: Guideline-making in Vishaka and Prakash Singh has been criticised as judicial legislation, while implementation of police reforms remains poor.
22.tq: Identify the criticism rather than confusing judicial guidelines with legislative enactment.
22.sec: Universal angles

22.s: The contemporary political relevance of S.R. Bommai was revived by the Tamil Nadu government formation in 2026 because the case emphasises that:
o: The President's Rule is beyond judicial review.
A government's majority should ordinarily be tested on the floor of the House.
The Governor may decide the majority without an Assembly test.
A floor test is required only for local bodies.
22.x: S.R. Bommai is associated with the principle that a disputed legislative majority should be tested on the floor of the House.
22.tq: Apply a landmark federalism principle to a contemporary government-formation scenario.
22.sec: Universal angles

22.s: The Supreme Court's proposed guidelines on the use of artificial intelligence concerned the conduct of:
22.x: The proposed guidelines concerned the use of artificial intelligence by the bar and the bench.
22.tq: Identify the professional institutions directly covered by the proposed guidelines.
22.sec: Universal angles

22.s: Which one of the following concerns has been expressed regarding environmental jurisprudence?
o: Environmental clearances are becoming impossible in every case.
Environmental jurisprudence is “fading” as clearances pass easily.
Environmental regulation has been replaced entirely by personal-law judgments.
The judiciary has withdrawn from all environmental matters by constitutional mandate.
22.x: A concern has been expressed that environmental jurisprudence is fading because environmental clearances are passing easily.
22.tq: Recognise the stated criticism without reversing its direction.
22.sec: Universal angles

22.s: Articles 32, 141 and 142 are significant in the context of Vishaka and Seema because they enable the Supreme Court to:
o: Fill legislative gaps temporarily until Parliament acts
Dissolve State Legislatures whenever legislation is absent
Exercise only advisory jurisdiction in social matters
22.x: Articles 32, 141 and 142 provide the constitutional basis through which judicial decisions can fill legislative gaps until Parliament acts, as illustrated by Vishaka and Seema.
22.tq: Connect constitutional provisions with the institutional function they collectively support.
22.sec: Universal angles

23.s: The doctrine of parens patriae is primarily associated with which of the following?
o: The State acting as guardian of persons unable to protect themselves
The Union’s power over residuary subjects
The reconciliation of conflicting constitutional provisions
The invalidation of laws enacted by a State legislature
23.x: Parens patriae means that the State acts as guardian of persons who cannot protect themselves. It is generally invoked in welfare and rights cases.
23.tq: Identify the doctrine from its precise meaning and field of application.
23.sec: ■ Doctrine → meaning in one line and field of application  [APPSC]

23.s: The doctrine of pith and substance is applied mainly to determine which of the following?
o: Whether a law has received the President’s assent
The true nature of a law in relation to Union-State legislative lists
Whether a constitutional amendment violates the basic structure
Whether a fundamental right has been waived
23.x: Pith and substance examines the true nature and character of a law to determine legislative competence under the Union, State and Concurrent Lists.
23.tq: Match the doctrine with its principal constitutional field.
23.sec: ■ Doctrine → meaning in one line and field of application  [APPSC]

23.s: Which one of the following best describes the doctrine of colourable legislation?
o: A law operating outside a State is always unconstitutional
A State law automatically prevails over a Parliamentary law
A law may be invalidated because its political motive is improper
A legislature cannot do indirectly what it cannot do directly
23.x: Colourable legislation embodies the principle that what cannot be done directly cannot be done indirectly. It is concerned with legislative competence, not with the motive of the legislature.
23.tq: Distinguish legislative competence from legislative motive.
23.sec: ■ Doctrine → meaning in one line and field of application  [APPSC]

23.s: A State law having operation outside the State may nevertheless be valid when there is a sufficient connection between the State and the subject matter. This principle is known as:
23.x: The doctrine of territorial nexus permits a State law to operate beyond the State when a sufficient nexus exists between the State and the subject matter of the law.
23.tq: Apply the doctrine to an extra-territorial operation scenario.
23.sec: ■ Doctrine → meaning in one line and field of application  [APPSC]

23.s: The doctrine of harmonious construction requires courts to:
o: Prefer Fundamental Rights over every Directive Principle in all cases
Read apparently conflicting provisions so that both can operate
Treat all constitutional provisions as legally unenforceable
23.x: Harmonious construction seeks an interpretation under which apparently conflicting provisions, including Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles, can operate together.
23.tq: Select the interpretation that preserves both apparently conflicting provisions.
23.sec: ■ Doctrine → meaning in one line and field of application  [APPSC]

23.s: Which doctrine was identified in an APPSC question as reconciling Central and Provincial laws?
23.x: The doctrine of pith and substance is used to reconcile Central and Provincial, or Union and State, legislative powers by examining the true nature of the law.
23.tq: Recall the doctrine associated with Union-State legislative reconciliation.
23.sec: ■ Doctrine → meaning in one line and field of application  [APPSC]

23.s: With reference to colourable legislation, which one of the following statements is correct?
o: It primarily examines the personal motive of the legislators
It concerns the competence of the legislature to enact the law
It applies only to laws affecting Fundamental Rights
It permits indirect exercise of a prohibited legislative power
23.x: Colourable legislation concerns legislative competence. It does not principally examine motive, and it prohibits indirect exercise of a power that cannot be exercised directly.
23.tq: Use the competence-versus-motive distinction to eliminate the traps.
23.sec: ■ Doctrine → meaning in one line and field of application  [APPSC]

23.s: State of Bombay v. F.N. Balsara (1951) is associated with which doctrine?
23.x: In State of Bombay v. F.N. Balsara, the Prohibition Act was upheld as a public-health measure even though it incidentally touched imports. The case illustrates pith and substance.
23.tq: Link the leading case to the doctrine rather than to the incidental subject involved.
23.sec: ■ Doctrine → leading case (State of Bombay v Balsara, K.C. Gajapati Narayan Deo, Venkataramana Devaru)

23.s: In State of Bombay v. F.N. Balsara, the Prohibition Act was upheld primarily because its true character related to:
23.x: The Prohibition Act was treated according to its true character as a public-health measure, although it incidentally touched the subject of imports.
23.tq: Separate the true nature of the law from its incidental effect.
23.sec: ■ Doctrine → leading case (State of Bombay v Balsara, K.C. Gajapati Narayan Deo, Venkataramana Devaru)

23.s: Which case is associated with the doctrine of territorial nexus in relation to tax on prize competitions conducted from outside the State?
o: State of Bombay v. F.N. Balsara (1951)
23.x: State of Bombay v. R.M.D.C. (1957) concerned taxation of prize competitions run from outside the State and is associated with territorial nexus.
23.tq: Distinguish similarly named cases by the doctrine and factual setting.
23.sec: ■ Doctrine → leading case (State of Bombay v Balsara, K.C. Gajapati Narayan Deo, Venkataramana Devaru)

23.s: Sri Venkataramana Devaru (1958) is associated with harmonious construction in the context of reconciling:
23.x: Sri Venkataramana Devaru (1958) reconciled temple-entry provisions under Article 25(2)(b) with the rights of religious denominations under Article 26(b).
23.tq: Start from the sure case-article pairing.
23.sec: ■ Doctrine → leading case (State of Bombay v Balsara, K.C. Gajapati Narayan Deo, Venkataramana Devaru)

23.s:
Consider the following statements:
1. The true character of a law is determined by examining the whole Act, its object and its effect.
2. A.S. Krishna (1957) is associated with this approach.
3. The doctrine examines only the title given to the legislation.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
23.x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct. Statement 3 is false because the true character is not determined merely by the title; the whole Act, its object and its effect are considered.
23.tq: Reject the narrow title-only formulation and retain the whole-Act test.
23.sec: ■ Doctrine → leading case (State of Bombay v Balsara, K.C. Gajapati Narayan Deo, Venkataramana Devaru)

23.s: The doctrine of eclipse provides that a pre-Constitution law inconsistent with Fundamental Rights is:
o: Dormant and capable of revival when the constitutional bar is removed
Valid only after approval by the President
Automatically converted into a Directive Principle
23.x: Under the doctrine of eclipse, an inconsistent pre-Constitution law becomes dormant rather than completely extinct and may revive when the Fundamental Rights bar is removed.
23.tq: Distinguish dormancy from permanent invalidity.
23.sec: ■ Doctrines of FR interpretation (eclipse, severability, waiver) vs federal interpretation doctrines

23.s: Which one of the following correctly states the limitation clarified in Ambica Mills (1974) regarding the doctrine of eclipse?
o: It applies exclusively to constitutional amendments
It applies only to pre-Constitution laws
It applies only to post-Constitution laws
It applies only to State laws concerning taxation
23.x: Ambica Mills (1974) clarified that the doctrine of eclipse applies to pre-Constitution laws, not generally to post-Constitution laws enacted in violation of Fundamental Rights.
23.tq: Use the pre-Constitution versus post-Constitution distinction.
23.sec: ■ Doctrines of FR interpretation (eclipse, severability, waiver) vs federal interpretation doctrines

23.s: The doctrine of severability means that when only a part of a law violates Fundamental Rights:
o: Only the offending part is declared void, if it can be separated
The entire law must always be struck down
The offending part is waived by the affected citizen
The law becomes dormant until Parliament re-enacts it
23.x: Severability permits the valid portion of a law to remain operative when the unconstitutional portion can be separated. R.M.D.C. v. Union of India (1957) is associated with this doctrine.
23.tq: Apply the separability test instead of assuming total invalidity.
23.sec: ■ Doctrines of FR interpretation (eclipse, severability, waiver) vs federal interpretation doctrines

23.s: Which case is associated with the principle that Fundamental Rights cannot be waived?
23.x: In Basheshar Nath (1959), the principle was recognised that Fundamental Rights cannot be waived by an individual.
23.tq: Associate the non-waiver rule with its leading case.
23.sec: ■ Doctrines of FR interpretation (eclipse, severability, waiver) vs federal interpretation doctrines

23.s: Which of the following is NOT a federal interpretation doctrine?
23.x: Waiver is a doctrine concerning the interpretation of Fundamental Rights. Pith and substance, colourable legislation and territorial nexus are federal interpretation doctrines.
23.tq: Separate Fundamental Rights doctrines from Union-State competence doctrines.
23.sec: ■ Doctrines of FR interpretation (eclipse, severability, waiver) vs federal interpretation doctrines

23.s:
Consider the following doctrines:
1. Pith and substance
2. Colourable legislation
3. Territorial nexus
4. Incidental and ancillary powers
Which of the above belong to the group of federal interpretation doctrines?
23.x: All four are federal interpretation doctrines. Repugnancy is also included among the doctrines used in resolving legislative relations between the Union and the States.
23.tq: Recognise the complete doctrinal group rather than selecting only the familiar pairs.
23.sec: ■ Doctrines of FR interpretation (eclipse, severability, waiver) vs federal interpretation doctrines

23.s: The doctrine of incidental and ancillary powers implies that:
o: An incidental matter must always be placed in the Residuary List
Parliament has no power over matters not expressly listed
A legislative entry covers matters incidental to the subject expressly assigned to it
A State legislature can legislate on every subject connected with public order
23.x: A legislative power over a subject includes powers over matters incidental and ancillary to that subject. Legislative entries are given a wide meaning for this purpose.
23.tq: Apply the main-entry rule to an ancillary matter.
23.sec: ■ Doctrine of incidental and ancillary powers, repugnancy - Article 254

23.s: Which cases are associated with the doctrine of incidental and ancillary powers?
o: R.D. Joshi v. Ajit Mills and Calcutta Gas
23.x: R.D. Joshi v. Ajit Mills and the Calcutta Gas case are associated with the principle that an entry includes matters incidental and ancillary to it.
23.tq: Identify the cases by the doctrine they illustrate, not by their subject alone.
23.sec: ■ Doctrine of incidental and ancillary powers, repugnancy - Article 254

23.s: Under Article 254, in the event of repugnancy between a Parliamentary law and a State law on a Concurrent List subject, the general rule is that:
o: The Governor decides which law will operate
The State law prevails throughout India
The Parliamentary law prevails over the repugnant State law
23.x: Article 254 provides that, in case of repugnancy in the Concurrent List, the Parliamentary law prevails over the inconsistent State law.
23.tq: Ask which law prevails in a direct repugnancy conflict.
23.sec: ■ Doctrine of incidental and ancillary powers, repugnancy - Article 254

23.s:
Consider the following statements regarding Article 254(2):
1. A State law on a Concurrent List matter may prevail in that State if it has received the President’s assent.
2. Parliament may subsequently override such a State law.
3. President’s assent makes the State law permanently immune from Parliamentary legislation.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
23.x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct. Statement 3 is false because Parliament may later override a State law that has received the President’s assent.
23.tq: Watch for the absolute word “permanently” in the false statement.
23.sec: ■ Doctrine of incidental and ancillary powers, repugnancy - Article 254

23.s: Which one of the following correctly represents the order of legislative fields from the Union to the State level, followed by the residuary position?
o: Union, State, Concurrent; residuary power with the Supreme Court
Concurrent, Union, State; residuary power with the President
Union, Concurrent, State; residuary power with Parliament
State, Concurrent, Union; residuary power with States
23.x: The order is Union List, Concurrent List and State List. Residuary legislative power belongs to Parliament under Article 248.
23.tq: Recall both the list hierarchy and the authority holding residuary power.
23.sec: ■ Doctrine of incidental and ancillary powers, repugnancy - Article 254

23.s: Article 248 of the Constitution is associated with:
o: The binding force of Supreme Court decisions
The residuary legislative power of Parliament
The President’s assent to State laws
23.x: Article 248 vests residuary legislative power in Parliament.
23.tq: Match the Article number with its constitutional subject.
23.sec: ■ Doctrine of incidental and ancillary powers, repugnancy - Article 254

23.s: The doctrine of prospective overruling was first applied in India in:
23.x: The doctrine of prospective overruling was first applied by the Supreme Court in Golaknath (1967).
23.tq: Use the chronology of leading constitutional cases to identify the anchor case.
23.sec: ■ Doctrines from judiciary and executive (prospective overruling, stare decisis, pleasure, separation of powers)

23.s: Article 141 embodies the principle of stare decisis by providing that:
o: The law declared by every High Court binds all courts in India
Only advisory opinions of the Supreme Court are binding
Parliament must approve every Supreme Court judgment
The law declared by the Supreme Court is binding on all courts within India
23.x: Article 141 makes the law declared by the Supreme Court binding on all courts within India, reflecting the principle of stare decisis.
23.tq: Link the doctrine to the exact constitutional effect of Article 141.
23.sec: ■ Doctrines from judiciary and executive (prospective overruling, stare decisis, pleasure, separation of powers)

23.s: The doctrine of pleasure in relation to civil services is primarily contained in:
o: Article 310, subject to safeguards under Article 311
23.x: Article 310 embodies the pleasure doctrine, while Article 311 provides safeguards for civil servants against arbitrary dismissal, removal or reduction in rank.
23.tq: Pair the principal Article with its constitutional safeguard.
23.sec: ■ Doctrines from judiciary and executive (prospective overruling, stare decisis, pleasure, separation of powers)

23.s: Which statement correctly describes the doctrine of separation of powers as understood in Indian constitutional law?
o: It is completely rigid and excludes all overlap among organs
It is functional rather than rigid
It applies only to the executive and judiciary
It is not connected with the basic structure doctrine
23.x: Indian separation of powers is functional rather than rigid. Ram Jawaya Kapur (1955) illustrates this approach, while separation of powers is also regarded as part of the basic structure in Kesavananda Bharati.
23.tq: Reject the absolute “rigid” formulation and identify the Indian adaptation.
23.sec: ■ Doctrines from judiciary and executive (prospective overruling, stare decisis, pleasure, separation of powers)

23.s:
Arrange the following in chronological order:
A. Ram Jawaya Kapur
B. State of Bombay v. R.M.D.C.
C. Golaknath
D. Kesavananda Bharati
23.x: Ram Jawaya Kapur was decided in 1955, State of Bombay v. R.M.D.C. in 1957, Golaknath in 1967 and Kesavananda Bharati in 1973.
23.tq: Place the dated cases first and then verify the sequence.
23.sec: ■ Doctrines from judiciary and executive (prospective overruling, stare decisis, pleasure, separation of powers)

23.s: Which of the following doctrines is correctly matched with its foreign origin?
23.x: The doctrine of pith and substance was borrowed from Canada. Prospective overruling is associated with the United States, pleasure with England, and public trust with Roman law.
23.tq: Start with the sure foreign-origin pairing and eliminate the swapped origins.
23.sec: ■ Doctrines borrowed from foreign law and origin country

23.s:
Consider the following pairs:
1. Pith and substance — Canada
2. Prospective overruling — United States of America
3. Pleasure — England
4. Separation of powers — France
Which of the pairs given above are correctly matched?
23.x: All four pairs are correct. Separation of powers is associated with Montesquieu of France, while the other three origins are Canada, the United States and England respectively.
23.tq: Check each origin individually, especially the thinker-country association.
23.sec: ■ Doctrines borrowed from foreign law and origin country

23.s: The doctrine of public trust is stated to have its origin in:
23.x: The doctrine of public trust has its origin in Roman law.
23.tq: Directly identify the origin of the less commonly tested doctrine.
23.sec: ■ Doctrines borrowed from foreign law and origin country

23.s: The basic structure doctrine is identified in the material with which foreign origin?
23.x: The basic structure doctrine is identified with Germany as its foreign origin in the given constitutional comparison.
23.tq: Distinguish the origin of basic structure from the origin of separation of powers.
23.sec: ■ Doctrines borrowed from foreign law and origin country

23.s: Constitutional morality is best understood as:
o: Following the opinion of the numerical majority in every case
Giving priority to customary morality over constitutional text
Fidelity to constitutional values over popular morality
Applying only the personal morality of judges
23.x: Constitutional morality requires fidelity to constitutional values, even where those values conflict with prevailing or popular morality. The phrase is associated with Ambedkar, drawing on Grote.
23.tq: Distinguish constitutional values from popular or customary morality.
23.sec: ■ Constitutional morality and transformative constitutionalism as interpretive tools - case

23.s: The phrase “constitutional morality” is associated with B.R. Ambedkar’s reference to:
23.x: Ambedkar used the phrase constitutional morality after Grote.
23.tq: Recall the thinker linked to the phrase through Ambedkar.
23.sec: ■ Constitutional morality and transformative constitutionalism as interpretive tools - case

23.s: Which of the following cases is associated with the application of constitutional morality?
23.x: Constitutional morality was applied in Navtej Johar (2018), Sabarimala (2018) and NCT Delhi (2018).
23.tq: Identify the case from the interpretive tool it applied.
23.sec: ■ Constitutional morality and transformative constitutionalism as interpretive tools - case

23.s: Transformative constitutionalism views the Constitution primarily as:
o: A document concerned only with administrative procedure
A tool for changing an unequal society
A mechanism for preserving all pre-Constitution social practices
A code that excludes judicial interpretation
23.x: Transformative constitutionalism treats the Constitution as an instrument for transforming an unequal society and advancing substantive constitutional values.
23.tq: Identify the purpose-based meaning of the doctrine.
23.sec: ■ Constitutional morality and transformative constitutionalism as interpretive tools - case

23.s:
Which of the following cases are associated with transformative constitutionalism?
1. Navtej Johar
2. Joseph Shine
3. Sabarimala
23.x: Transformative constitutionalism was applied in Navtej Johar, Joseph Shine and Sabarimala.
23.tq: Treat the named-case list as a complete set and test every item.
23.sec: ■ Constitutional morality and transformative constitutionalism as interpretive tools - case

23.s: After Minerva Mills, the relationship between Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles was understood as:
o: Directive Principles being enforceable in preference to Fundamental Rights
Fundamental Rights being wholly superior and Directive Principles being irrelevant
Both being read harmoniously, with Fundamental Rights as means and Directive Principles as ends
Both being excluded from constitutional interpretation
23.x: After Minerva Mills, Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles are read harmoniously. Fundamental Rights are described as the means and Directive Principles as the ends.
23.tq: Use the means-versus-ends comparison to identify the integrated interpretation.
23.sec: ■ Constitutional morality and transformative constitutionalism as interpretive tools - case

23.s: Which one of the following is a criticism of constitutional morality?
o: It is considered subjective and a possible route to judicial overreach
It makes all Directive Principles directly enforceable
It gives unlimited legislative power to State governments
It prevents courts from referring to constitutional values
23.x: Critics argue that constitutional morality may be subjective and may provide a route to judicial overreach.
23.tq: Identify the recognised criticism rather than a consequence not stated.
23.sec: ■ Universal angles

23.s: The broader significance of constitutional interpretation doctrines is that they:
o: Replace the Constitution with conventions of foreign countries
Make every legislative dispute a matter of executive privilege
Keep federal lawmaking workable and determine how Fundamental Rights operate against laws
Remove the distinction between Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles
23.x: These doctrines make federal lawmaking workable and establish the manner in which Fundamental Rights operate in relation to legislation.
23.tq: Select the option covering both stated dimensions of significance.
23.sec: ■ Universal angles

23.s: Which statement correctly describes the current position regarding a 2025–26 ruling applying these doctrines by name?
o: There is a current 2025–26 ruling applying all these doctrines by name
There is no current 2025–26 ruling applying these doctrines by name
Only the doctrine of territorial nexus has been applied in a 2025–26 ruling
Only the doctrine of waiver has been applied in a 2025–26 ruling
23.x: The current relevance assessment states that there is no 2025–26 ruling applying these doctrines by name.
23.tq: Test the precise current-affairs status without extending it beyond the stated position.
23.sec: ■ Universal angles

24.s: Which constitutional amendment changed the constitutional basis of the Supreme Court's ruling in the Champakam Dorairajan case by introducing Article 15(4)?
24.x: The First Amendment introduced Article 15(4), following the Champakam Dorairajan ruling.
24.tq: Use the amendment-case association rather than relying on chronological guessing.
24.sec: Options against a judgment - override methods and their limits

24.s: The Twenty-fourth Constitutional Amendment was enacted in response to which judgment?
o: Madhav Rao v. Union of India
Indira Nehru Gandhi v. Raj Narain
Indra Sawhney v. Union of India
24.x: The Twenty-fourth Amendment followed the Golaknath judgment and concerned Parliament's power to amend the Constitution.
24.tq: Match the amendment with the correct judgment; nearby cases are used as distractors.
24.sec: Options against a judgment - override methods and their limits

24.s: The Twenty-fifth Constitutional Amendment was enacted in the context of the judicial decision concerning
24.x: The Twenty-fifth Amendment followed the litigation relating to bank nationalisation.
24.tq: Discriminate between closely associated amendment-case pairs.
24.sec: Options against a judgment - override methods and their limits

24.s: The abolition of privy purses was constitutionally addressed through the amendment enacted after which case?
24.x: The Twenty-sixth Amendment followed the Madhav Rao case concerning privy purses.
24.tq: Test the person-case and amendment-subject association directly.
24.sec: Options against a judgment - override methods and their limits

24.s: The Seventy-seventh Constitutional Amendment was enacted following the judgment in
24.x: The Seventy-seventh Amendment followed Indra Sawhney and dealt with reservation in promotions.
24.tq: Identify the correct amendment-case pair from similar constitutional disputes.
24.sec: Options against a judgment - override methods and their limits

24.s: Which of the following correctly describes a validating or amending law enacted to overcome a judicial judgment?
o: It merely declares the judgment void without altering the law.
It enables the legislature to decide the dispute itself as a court.
It changes the legal basis on which the judgment was founded.
It prevents all subsequent judicial review of the amended law.
24.x: A validating or amending law removes the basis of a judgment by changing the law. The legislature cannot simply declare a judgment void or adjudicate the dispute itself.
24.tq: Separate a genuine change in legal basis from an impermissible legislative declaration.
24.sec: Options against a judgment - override methods and their limits

24.s:
Consider the following statements regarding the Ninth Schedule:
1. A law may be placed in the Ninth Schedule through a constitutional amendment.
2. The Seventy-sixth Amendment placed Tamil Nadu's 69 per cent reservation law in the Ninth Schedule.
3. Entries inserted after 24 April 1973 are completely immune from judicial review.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
24.x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct. After I.R. Coelho, Ninth Schedule entries inserted after 24 April 1973 may be reviewed if they damage the basic structure.
24.tq: Find the absolute wording in the statement claiming complete immunity from review.
24.sec: Options against a judgment - override methods and their limits

24.s:
An ordinance used to alter the legal basis of a judicial decision is subject to which of the following requirements?
1. It is issued when the legislature is not in session.
2. It is subject to judicial review.
3. It must be laid before the House.
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
24.x: An ordinance is an executive law-making measure used when the legislature is not in session; it remains subject to judicial review and must be laid before the House.
24.tq: Check all three procedural conditions before selecting the inclusive code.
24.sec: Options against a judgment - override methods and their limits

24.s: Under which Article can the Supreme Court undertake a review of its own judgment?
24.x: Article 137 provides the Supreme Court's power to review its judgments.
24.tq: Distinguish the review provision from the ordinance, reference and writ provisions.
24.sec: Options against a judgment - override methods and their limits

24.s: Which one of the following statements regarding a Presidential reference under Article 143 is correct?
o: The President can ask the Supreme Court for its advisory opinion.
Only a State Governor can make such a reference.
The advice given by the Supreme Court is binding on the President.
A reference under Article 143 is a form of curative petition.
24.x: Article 143 enables the President to seek the Supreme Court's advice. That advice is not binding on the President.
24.tq: Discriminate between advisory jurisdiction and binding adjudication.
24.sec: Options against a judgment - override methods and their limits

24.s:
Consider the following statements:
1. Parliament can overrule a judicial judgment by passing a simple resolution.
2. Parliament may change the law or the constitutional basis underlying a judgment, subject to constitutional limits.
3. Every legislative override is subject to the basic structure limitation.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
24.x: Statement 1 is false because a simple resolution cannot overrule a judgment. Statements 2 and 3 are correct, but any amendment or law must respect the basic structure.
24.tq: Reject the simple-resolution trap and retain the two constitutionally qualified propositions.
24.sec: Options against a judgment - override methods and their limits

24.s: Which case invalidated the Thirty-ninth Amendment's validation of the election of the Prime Minister?
o: Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala
Indira Nehru Gandhi v. Raj Narain
Minerva Mills v. Union of India
I.R. Coelho v. State of Tamil Nadu
24.x: In Indira Nehru Gandhi v. Raj Narain, the validation of the Prime Minister's election through the Thirty-ninth Amendment was struck down.

24.s: The Supreme Court struck down the Forty-second Amendment's attempt to bar judicial review in
24.x: The limitation on judicial review introduced by the Forty-second Amendment was struck down in Minerva Mills.

24.s: A constitutional government is best described as a government that
o: places no restriction on executive discretion
is limited by the terms of the Constitution
is controlled exclusively by the judiciary
allows the legislature to exercise unlimited power
24.x: Constitutional government is limited government: governmental power operates within the terms and limits of the Constitution.
24.tq: Select the definition that states the governing principle without an absolute institutional claim.
24.sec: Constitutional government - definition and safeguards of liberty

24.s: Montesquieu regarded which arrangement as the most effective means of protecting liberty?
24.x: Montesquieu held that division of powers was the most effective way to protect liberty.
24.tq: Test the thinker-principle association directly.
24.sec: Constitutional government - definition and safeguards of liberty

24.s:
Which of the following are elements of constitutionalism?
1. Operation of powers within constitutional limits
2. Rule of law
3. Checks and balances
4. Judicial review and protection of Fundamental Rights
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
24.x: Constitutionalism includes constitutional limits on power, rule of law, checks and balances, judicial review and protection of Fundamental Rights.
24.tq: Use the inclusive option when every listed safeguard forms part of the concept.
24.sec: Constitutional government - definition and safeguards of liberty

24.s: In India, the Council of Ministers continues in office only so long as it enjoys the confidence of the
24.x: The Council of Ministers is subordinate to the legislature and remains in office only while it enjoys the confidence of the Lok Sabha.

24.sec: Legislative checks on executive - subordination, responsibility, motions

24.s: Collective responsibility of the Union Council of Ministers to the Lok Sabha is provided under
24.x: Article 75(3) provides for the collective responsibility of the Union Council of Ministers to the Lok Sabha.
24.tq: Match the constitutional provision with the Union-level responsibility rule.
24.sec: Legislative checks on executive - subordination, responsibility, motions

24.s: Which parliamentary devices primarily provide day-to-day watch over administration?
o: Question Hour, Zero Hour and discussions
24.x: Question Hour, Zero Hour and discussions enable day-to-day parliamentary scrutiny of administration.
24.tq: Match the device cluster with its precise purpose rather than a broader control function.

24.s: Adjournment motions, calling-attention motions and censure motions are principally used to

24.x: These motions draw attention to lapses in administration and government conduct.
24.tq: Identify the purpose of the motion instead of confusing it with removal or financial control.
24.sec: Legislative checks on executive - subordination, responsibility, motions

24.x: A no-confidence motion concerns the Council of Ministers' collective responsibility and is moved only in the Lok Sabha.
24.tq: Apply the confidence principle to identify the competent House.
24.sec: Legislative checks on executive - subordination, responsibility, motions

24.s:
Which of the following instruments are associated with parliamentary financial control over the executive?
1. Budget
2. Cut motions
3. Public Accounts Committee
4. Estimates Committee
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
24.x: The Budget, cut motions, Public Accounts Committee and Estimates Committee are instruments of financial control over the executive.
24.tq: Recognise the complete financial-control cluster and avoid omitting committee mechanisms.
24.sec: Legislative checks on executive - subordination, responsibility, motions

24.s: Impeachment under Article 61 is a parliamentary mechanism for the removal of the
24.x: Article 61 provides the procedure for impeachment of the President.
24.tq: Match the Article with the office it specifically governs.
24.sec: Legislative checks on executive - subordination, responsibility, motions

24.s: Article 50 of the Constitution directs the State to separate the judiciary from the executive in
o: the public services of the State
24.x: Article 50, a Directive Principle, directs separation of the judiciary from the executive in the public services of the State.
24.tq: Read the exact constitutional scope of Article 50 instead of expanding it to all institutions.
24.sec: Separation of powers - Article 50 and the degree adopted

24.s:
Consider the following statements about separation of powers in India:
1. India follows a completely rigid separation of powers.
2. Separation of powers is implicit rather than absolute.
3. Functions of organs overlap to create checks and balances.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
24.x: India does not follow a completely rigid separation. Separation is implicit, and overlapping functions help create checks and balances.
24.tq: Reject the absolute formulation and retain the two qualified statements.
24.sec: Separation of powers - Article 50 and the degree adopted

24.s: Which one of the following best describes the institutional arrangement adopted in India?
o: Rigid separation between legislature and executive with no overlap
Executive supremacy over the legislature and judiciary
Judicial supremacy over every legislative and executive function
Legislature-executive fusion under a parliamentary system, with an insulated judiciary
24.x: India has legislature-executive fusion in the parliamentary system, while the judiciary is insulated through constitutional safeguards.
24.tq: Compare the parliamentary fusion of legislature and executive with judicial insulation.
24.sec: Separation of powers - Article 50 and the degree adopted

24.s:
Which of the following provisions contribute to the insulation of the judiciary or the control of subordinate courts?
1. Article 50
2. Article 121
3. Article 211
4. Article 235
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
24.x: Articles 50, 121, 211 and 235 collectively reflect safeguards relating to judicial separation, discussion of judges and control of subordinate courts.
24.tq: Use the complete Article cluster rather than treating judicial insulation as a single-provision rule.
24.sec: Separation of powers - Article 50 and the degree adopted

24.s: The Supreme Court recognised separation of powers as a basic feature of the Constitution in
24.x: The basic-feature status of separation of powers is associated with the Kesavananda Bharati judgment of 1973.
24.tq: Use the landmark case-year association for the basic-structure doctrine.
24.sec: Separation of powers - Article 50 and the degree adopted

24.s: The President's power to summon and prorogue Parliament is primarily provided under
24.x: Article 85 deals with the summoning and prorogation of Parliament and the interval between its sessions.
24.tq: Distinguish summoning from presidential address, assent and ordinance powers.
24.sec: Executive checks on legislature - summoning, dissolution, ordinances, veto

24.s: Which one of the following correctly matches the authority and constitutional provision concerning the summoning of the State Legislature?
24.x: The Governor summons and prorogues the State Legislature under Article 174.
24.tq: Start with the sure authority-Article pair and eliminate the swapped Union provisions.

24.s: The maximum permissible gap between two sessions of Parliament or a State Legislature is
24.x: The Constitution requires that the interval between sessions must not exceed six months.
24.tq: Identify the constitutional time limit while rejecting shorter and longer distractors.

24.s:
Which of the following statements is correct regarding dissolution of the lower House?
1. The President may dissolve the Lok Sabha under Article 85(2).
2. The Governor may dissolve the State Legislative Assembly.
3. The Rajya Sabha is dissolved along with the Lok Sabha.
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
24.x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct. The Rajya Sabha is a continuing House and is not dissolved with the Lok Sabha.
24.tq: Use the lower-House versus continuing-House distinction to reject statement 3.
24.sec: Executive checks on legislature - summoning, dissolution, ordinances, veto

24.s:
Which pair is correctly matched?

List-I (Function)
 a. Address and messages of the President
 b. Address and messages of the Governor
 c. Union ordinance-making power
 d. State ordinance-making power

List-II (Article)
 i. Article 123
 ii. Article 175
 iii. Article 86
 iv. Article 213

Select the correct answer using the code given below.
24.x: Articles 86 and 87 concern presidential addresses and messages, Article 175 concerns the Governor's addresses and messages, Article 123 concerns Union ordinances, and Article 213 concerns State ordinances.
24.tq: Start from the ordinance pair and then verify the Union-State address provisions.
24.sec: Executive checks on legislature - summoning, dissolution, ordinances, veto

24.s: Which one of the following correctly states the constitutional provisions relating to assent and reservation of Bills?
24.x: Article 111 concerns presidential assent, Article 200 concerns the Governor's assent, and Article 201 concerns Bills reserved for the President.
24.tq: Separate the Union and State assent provisions from ordinance and reference Articles.

24.s:
Which of the following statements regarding judicial review is correct?
1. It extends to laws and executive action.
2. Articles 13, 32 and 226 are associated with judicial review.
3. A law declared ultra vires is void.
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
24.x: Judicial review covers laws and executive action; Articles 13, 32 and 226 provide important constitutional bases, and an ultra vires law is void.
24.tq: Confirm the three connected consequences of judicial review before selecting the complete code.
24.sec: Judicial checks - review, bar on discussing judges (Arts. 121, 211)

24.s: Under Article 121, discussion in Parliament on the conduct of a Supreme Court or High Court judge in the discharge of duties is permitted only when it is connected with
o: a resolution of the Rajya Sabha alone
a motion for removal of the judge
24.x: Article 121 bars such discussion except when it takes place on a motion for the judge's removal.
24.tq: Identify the constitutional exception to the bar rather than a general parliamentary device.
24.sec: Judicial checks - review, bar on discussing judges (Arts. 121, 211)

24.s: Article 211 prohibits discussion in a State Legislature on the conduct of
o: any member of the Union Council of Ministers
the Speaker of the Legislative Assembly only
a Supreme Court or High Court judge in the discharge of duties
24.x: Article 211 bars discussion in a State Legislature on the conduct of a Supreme Court or High Court judge in the discharge of duties.
24.tq: Distinguish the judicial conduct bar from other legislative office-holders.
24.sec: Judicial checks - review, bar on discussing judges (Arts. 121, 211)

24.s: Which constitutional provisions embody the reverse bar preventing courts from questioning legislative proceedings merely on the ground of irregular procedure?
24.x: Articles 122 and 212 prevent courts from inquiring into the validity of proceedings of Parliament or State Legislatures on the ground of irregular procedure.
24.tq: Match the reverse-bar principle with the correct Article pair.
24.sec: Judicial checks - review, bar on discussing judges (Arts. 121, 211)

24.s: Article 142 enables the Supreme Court to do which of the following?
o: Prevent all legislative proceedings from judicial scrutiny
Issue ordinances when Parliament is not in session
Remove a High Court judge without parliamentary procedure
Do complete justice and fill legal gaps in appropriate cases
24.x: Article 142 empowers the Supreme Court to do complete justice and may allow it to fill legal gaps. Its use can raise concerns about judicial overreach, and its scope is not precisely defined.
24.tq: Apply the constitutional power to a legal-gap situation rather than confusing it with ordinance or removal powers.
24.sec: Judicial checks - review, bar on discussing judges (Arts. 121, 211)

24.s: The guidelines issued before the enactment of the POSH Act, 2013 are an example of the Supreme Court using
o: Article 143 to issue binding advice to the President
Article 211 to remove a constitutional officer
Article 142 to fill a legal gap in pursuit of complete justice
24.x: The Vishaka guidelines, issued before the POSH Act, 2013, illustrate the use of Article 142 to fill a legal gap while pursuing complete justice.
24.tq: Recognise the constitutional power from its practical judicial application.
24.sec: Judicial checks - review, bar on discussing judges (Arts. 121, 211)

24.s: Which one of the following correctly reflects the ruling in Ram Jawaya Kapur v. State of Punjab (1955)?
o: The executive can exercise power only after receiving prior approval from the judiciary.
The Indian Constitution does not recognise a rigid separation of powers, and executive power extends to matters on which the legislature can make laws.
The Indian Constitution establishes a rigid separation of powers among the three organs of government.
The legislature may decide disputes arising from judicial proceedings.
24.x: In Ram Jawaya Kapur v. State of Punjab, the Supreme Court held that the Indian Constitution does not provide for a rigid separation of powers. It also recognised that executive power extends to matters on which the legislature can make laws.
24.tq: Test the precise holding of a constitutional case rather than accepting the extreme phrase ‘rigid separation’.
24.sec: Separation of powers → case

24.s:
Consider the following statements regarding the doctrine of separation of powers in India:
1. In Kesavananda Bharati, separation of powers was recognised as one of the basic features of the Constitution.
2. In Indira Nehru Gandhi v. Raj Narain, the Supreme Court held that the legislature could finally decide an election dispute.
3. The decision in Indira Nehru Gandhi v. Raj Narain was connected with the constitutional challenge to the 39th Amendment.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
24.x: Statements 1 and 3 are correct. Statement 2 is false: the Court held that the legislature cannot decide an election dispute because it is a judicial function; the case also struck down the relevant provision of the 39th Amendment.
24.tq: Identify the statement that reverses the judicial holding and then use the case context to select the code.

 c. Kesavananda Bharati

List-II (Principle)
 i. Separation of powers forms part of the basic features
 ii. Executive power extends to matters on which the legislature can make laws
 iii. Legislature cannot decide an election dispute

Select the correct answer using the code given below.
24.x: Ram Jawaya Kapur dealt with the scope of executive power; Indira Nehru Gandhi v. Raj Narain protected the judicial character of election disputes; Kesavananda Bharati recognised separation of powers among the basic features.
24.tq: Start from the sure case–holding pair and eliminate codes containing a swapped constitutional principle.

24.s: Montesquieu’s discussion of the separation of powers is principally associated with which work and year?
24.x: Montesquieu discussed the separation of powers in The Spirit of Laws, published in 1748. His analysis drew substantially on the British Constitution.
24.tq: Discriminate between a thinker’s exact work and nearby political-philosophy titles by checking both the work and year.
24.sec: Montesquieu - fusion vs separation in parliamentary and presidential systems

24.s: Which one of the following pairs is correctly matched?
o: Parliamentary system — fusion accompanied by cooperation and coordination
Parliamentary system — complete institutional separation between executive and legislature
Presidential system — executive drawn from and accountable to the legislature
Presidential system — nominal head and real Council of Ministers
24.x: The parliamentary system is characterised by fusion of powers, cooperation and coordination between the executive and legislature. In a presidential system, the executive is institutionally separate from the legislature.
24.tq: Use the reversed-comparison trap by distinguishing fusion in parliamentary government from separation in presidential government.
24.sec: Montesquieu - fusion vs separation in parliamentary and presidential systems

24.s: Which one of the following best describes the principal checks in the United States presidential system, in contrast to the parliamentary system?
o: Questions and confidence or no-confidence votes in the legislature
Fusion of the executive and legislative powers
Collective responsibility of the Council of Ministers to the lower house
Checks and balances among the three organs of government
24.x: The presidential system is based on separation of powers and checks and balances among the three organs. Questions and confidence or no-confidence votes are characteristic parliamentary mechanisms.
24.tq: Separate the two systems by matching each system with its characteristic accountability mechanism.
24.sec: Montesquieu - fusion vs separation in parliamentary and presidential systems

24.s:
The choice of the parliamentary system by the framers of the Indian Constitution was influenced by which of the following considerations?
1. Familiarity with parliamentary institutions under the Acts of 1919 and 1935
2. The need to accommodate India’s diversity
3. The desire to avoid American-style conflict between the executive and legislature
4. The constitutional preference for stability over responsibility expressed by Ambedkar
Which of the statements given above are correct?
24.x: Statements 1, 2 and 3 are correct reasons for choosing the parliamentary system. Statement 4 is false: Ambedkar preferred responsibility over stability.
24.tq: Spot the reversed constitutional preference in the final statement while retaining the three stated reasons for the framers’ choice.
24.sec: Montesquieu - fusion vs separation in parliamentary and presidential systems

24.s: Dr B.R. Ambedkar’s preference in the choice between responsibility and stability was in favour of
24.x: Ambedkar preferred responsibility over stability. This preference supported the parliamentary model, in which the executive remains accountable to the legislature.
24.tq: Test a closely confusable conceptual pair by asking for the exact order of preference.
24.sec: Montesquieu - fusion vs separation in parliamentary and presidential systems

24.s: Which one of the following statements is correct in relation to constitutionalism and majoritarianism?
o: Constitutionalism requires the judiciary to exercise all legislative powers.
Majoritarianism may override constitutionalism whenever a legislative majority is secured.
A majoritarian position cannot override constitutionalism.
Constitutionalism has no application to decisions supported by an elected majority.
24.x: A legislative or political majority cannot override constitutionalism. Constitutional limitations remain binding even when a decision is supported by a majority.
24.tq: Reject the extreme claim that electoral majority automatically removes constitutional limitations.
24.sec: Universal angles

24.s: The One Nation One Election Bill, as described in the context of electoral synchronisation, proposes amendments to which of the following Articles?
24.x: The One Nation One Election Bill is associated with amendments to Articles 83, 172 and 327. Critics argue that fixed tenure may weaken collective responsibility under Articles 75 and 164.
24.tq: Use article-number discrimination and avoid substituting the related collective-responsibility provisions.
24.sec: Universal angles

24.s:
Consider the following statements regarding the constitutional debate on simultaneous elections:
1. Critics argue that fixed tenure may weaken collective responsibility.
2. Articles 75 and 164 are associated with the collective responsibility concern.
3. The proposed amendments include Articles 83, 172 and 327.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
24.x: All three statements are correct. The proposed amendments concern Articles 83, 172 and 327, while the criticism relates to the possible weakening of collective responsibility under Articles 75 and 164.
24.tq: Keep the amendment articles distinct from the separate articles governing collective responsibility.
24.sec: Universal angles

24.s:
Which of the following developments has been criticised as potentially eroding the separation of powers?
1. Judicial overreach
2. Frequent use of Article 142
3. The ordinance route
4. Judicial activism as a constitutional concept in every circumstance
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
24.x: Judicial overreach, frequent use of Article 142 and the ordinance route have been criticised as capable of eroding separation of powers. Statement 4 is too broad: judicial activism is a matter of debate and is not stated as an unconditional cause in every circumstance.
24.tq: Find the overbroad statement and distinguish criticism of judicial overreach from the broader debate on judicial activism.
24.sec: Universal angles

24.s: In which year were the Collector’s judicial powers separated in the Madras Presidency, marking an early instance of separation of powers in the Andhra districts?
24.x: The Collector’s judicial powers were separated in the Madras Presidency in 1816. This is regarded as an early instance of separation of powers in the Andhra districts.
24.tq: Test the exact year by distinguishing an early administrative reform from the later constitutional developments of 1858 and 1919.
24.sec: Universal angles

24.s:
Arrange the following developments in chronological order:
A. Publication of Montesquieu’s The Spirit of Laws
B. Separation of the Collector’s judicial powers in the Madras Presidency
C. Kesavananda Bharati judgment
D. Indira Nehru Gandhi v. Raj Narain judgment

Select the correct sequence.
24.x: The correct order is 1748, 1816, 1973 and 1975: The Spirit of Laws, separation of the Collector’s judicial powers, Kesavananda Bharati, and Indira Nehru Gandhi v. Raj Narain.
24.tq: Fix the earliest intellectual reference first, then place the administrative reform and the two judgments by their years.
24.sec: Universal angles

25.s: Under Article 54 of the Constitution of India, which one of the following is included in the electoral college for the election of the President?
o: Nominated members of the Legislative Assemblies of Delhi and Puducherry
Elected members of the Legislative Assemblies of Delhi and Puducherry
Nominated members of both Houses of Parliament
Elected members of the Legislative Councils of the States
25.x: The electoral college includes elected MPs and elected MLAs of the States, Delhi and Puducherry. Nominated members and members of Legislative Councils are excluded.
25.tq: Distinguish elected members of eligible Houses from nominated members and Legislative Council members.
25.sec: Electoral college - who votes, who does not, value of vote

25.s: A Chief Minister who is a member of the Legislative Council of a State, rather than its Legislative Assembly, is entitled to
o: not vote in the election of the President
vote only if nominated by the Governor
vote in the election of the President by virtue of being the Chief Minister
vote only in the election of the Vice-President
25.x: Only elected members of State Legislative Assemblies form part of the Presidential electoral college. Membership of a Legislative Council does not confer this right, even on a Chief Minister.
25.tq: Apply the precise constitutional distinction between the Legislative Assembly and Legislative Council.
25.sec: Electoral college - who votes, who does not, value of vote

25.s:
Consider the following statements regarding the electoral college for the election of the President:
1. Nominated members of both Houses of Parliament are excluded.
2. Members of State Legislative Councils are excluded.
3. Elected members of the Legislative Assemblies of Delhi and Puducherry are included.
4. Elected members of all Union Territory Legislative Assemblies are included.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
25.x: Statements 1, 2 and 3 are correct. Statement 4 is false because the Constitution specifically includes Delhi and Puducherry, while Union Territories without Assemblies do not participate.
25.tq: Find the overbroad statement by separating the named Union Territories from all other Union Territories.
25.sec: Electoral college - who votes, who does not, value of vote

25.s: The election of the President of India is held by
o: direct voting through universal adult franchise and open ballot
simple majority voting by elected MPs and MLAs
proportional representation by means of the single transferable vote and open ballot
proportional representation by means of the single transferable vote and secret ballot
25.x: Article 55(3) prescribes proportional representation by means of the single transferable vote and voting by secret ballot.
25.tq: Test the paired constitutional features together: STV and secret ballot.
25.sec: Electoral college - who votes, who does not, value of vote

25.s: The system of proportional representation by means of the single transferable vote used in the election of the President was borrowed from the Constitution of
25.x: The Presidential election method of proportional representation by single transferable vote was borrowed from Ireland.
25.tq: Use the source-country association for a distinctive constitutional device.
25.sec: Electoral college - who votes, who does not, value of vote

25.s: The constitutional objective of maintaining uniformity among the States and parity between the States as a whole and the Union in the Presidential election is secured through
o: direct election by the people of India
equal vote value for every elector irrespective of the House represented
nomination of an equal number of electors by every State
differential value assigned to MLA and MP votes
25.x: Article 55(1) achieves these principles by assigning vote values to MLAs based on State population and distributing the aggregate MLA vote value among elected MPs.
25.tq: Connect the constitutional objective with the mechanism that gives effect to it.
25.sec: Electoral college - who votes, who does not, value of vote

25.s: The value of the vote of an elected member of a State Legislative Assembly is calculated by the formula:
o: Number of elected MLAs divided by State population, multiplied by 1,000
State population divided by the number of elected MLAs, multiplied by 1/1,000
State population divided by the number of elected MLAs, multiplied by 1,000
State population divided by the total number of members of both Houses of Parliament
25.x: The value of an MLA's vote is calculated as (population of the State divided by the number of elected MLAs) multiplied by 1/1000.
25.tq: Read the formula carefully and distinguish multiplication by 1/1000 from multiplication by 1000.
25.sec: Electoral college - who votes, who does not, value of vote

25.s: The value of the vote of an elected Member of Parliament in the election of the President is determined by
o: multiplying the value of the highest-valued MLA vote by the number of States
dividing the total value of all MLA votes by the total number of elected MPs
dividing the total number of elected MPs by the total value of all MLA votes
assigning an identical value fixed by Parliament to every MP
25.x: The value of an MP's vote equals the total value of all votes of elected MLAs divided by the total number of elected MPs.
25.tq: Identify the correct numerator and denominator in the constitutional calculation.
25.sec: Electoral college - who votes, who does not, value of vote

25.s: For determining the value of votes in the Presidential election, the population of the States is presently taken on the basis of the
25.x: The population base for calculating the value of votes is the 1971 Census, which has been frozen for this purpose.
25.tq: Test the frozen census base rather than the latest available census.
25.sec: Electoral college - who votes, who does not, value of vote

25.s: The population base used for calculating the value of votes in the Presidential election is to remain frozen until
o: a constitutional amendment made after every Census
25.x: The 1971 Census base remains frozen until the first Census conducted after 2026, as provided through the constitutional arrangement referred to in the 84th Amendment.
25.tq: Use the end-point of a constitutional freeze instead of substituting a recent census year.
25.sec: Electoral college - who votes, who does not, value of vote

25.s: Which one of the following correctly describes the constitutional position regarding disputes connected with the election of the President?
o: They are decided by the Election Commission of India alone.
They are decided by Parliament through a joint sitting.
They are decided by the Council of Ministers.
They are decided only by the Supreme Court.
25.x: Under Article 71, disputes relating to the election of the President are decided only by the Supreme Court.
25.tq: Match the constitutional dispute with the authority expressly entrusted to decide it.
25.sec: Electoral college - who votes, who does not, value of vote

25.s: If the election of the President is subsequently declared void, which one of the following is the effect on acts performed by the President before such declaration?
o: All such acts automatically become void.
Their validity is decided by the outgoing President.
Only financial acts remain valid; all other acts become void.
25.x: Article 71 protects acts done by the President in the performance of duties before the election is declared void; those acts do not become invalid merely because of the declaration.
25.tq: Separate the validity of past official acts from the validity of the election itself.
25.sec: Electoral college - who votes, who does not, value of vote

25.s: A vacancy in the electoral college for the election of the President
o: does not by itself constitute a ground for challenging the election
can be challenged only if caused by resignation of an MP
requires postponement of the election until the vacancy is filled
25.x: Article 71(4) provides that the election of the President cannot be called in question on the ground of any vacancy in the electoral college.

25.x: Article 61 lays down the procedure for impeachment of the President.

25.s: Which one of the following pairs is correctly matched?
o: Article 65 — Vice-President to act as President
Article 72 — Council of Ministers to aid and advise the President
25.x: Article 65 provides for the Vice-President acting as President in specified circumstances. Article 72 concerns pardon, Article 74 concerns aid and advice by the Council of Ministers, and Article 76 concerns the Attorney General.
25.tq: Use neighbouring constitutional provisions as distractors and identify the exact article-subject pairing.
25.sec: Articles 52-62 number game

25.s: Articles 52 to 78 of the Constitution of India constitute
o: Part V, Chapter I dealing with the Union Executive
Part VI, Chapter I dealing with the State Executive
Part III dealing with Fundamental Rights
Part V, Chapter II dealing with Parliament
25.x: Articles 52 to 78 fall under Part V, Chapter I, which deals with the Union Executive.
25.tq: Distinguish the Part and Chapter classification from the adjacent chapter on Parliament.
25.sec: Articles 52-62 number game

25.s:
Which of the following are legislative functions of the President of India?
1. Summoning and proroguing both Houses of Parliament
