3. It democratised access to courts.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
44.x: PIL developed through judicial activism and helped democratise access to courts. It was not an outcome of judicial restraint.
44.tq: Reject the reversed conceptual pair and retain the two positively stated consequences.
44.sec: PIL - other name, pioneering judges, origin, landmark PILs  [APPSC]

44.s: Who filed the first Public Interest Litigation case, Hussainara Khatoon v. State of Bihar, in 1979?
44.x: Kapila Hingorani filed Hussainara Khatoon v. State of Bihar, the first major PIL case, concerning the rights of undertrial prisoners.
44.tq: Match the landmark case with the person who initiated it.
44.sec: PIL - other name, pioneering judges, origin, landmark PILs  [APPSC]

44.s: The expression ‘Mother of PILs’ is associated with
44.x: Kapila Hingorani is known as the ‘Mother of PILs’ because she filed the Hussainara Khatoon case on behalf of undertrial prisoners.
44.tq: Distinguish the petitioner, judges and litigant in the same landmark case.
44.sec: PIL - other name, pioneering judges, origin, landmark PILs  [APPSC]

44.s: Hussainara Khatoon v. State of Bihar, decided in 1979, primarily concerned the
o: right to speedy trial of undertrial prisoners
44.x: The Hussainara Khatoon case focused on the right of undertrial prisoners to a speedy trial.
44.tq: Link the landmark case to its distinctive constitutional issue.
44.sec: PIL - other name, pioneering judges, origin, landmark PILs  [APPSC]

44.s: Which one of the following pairs is NOT correctly matched?
o: Hussainara Khatoon case — disclosure of candidates’ assets and education
44.x: The disclosure of candidates’ assets and education was dealt with in the affidavit case. Hussainara Khatoon concerned speedy trial for undertrial prisoners.
44.tq: Find the swapped subject associated with a landmark case.
44.sec: PIL - other name, pioneering judges, origin, landmark PILs  [APPSC]

44.s:
Arrange the following in chronological order:
A. Hussainara Khatoon case
B. S.P. Gupta case
C. Vishaka case
D. M.C. Mehta environmental cases
44.x: Hussainara Khatoon was decided in 1979, S.P. Gupta in 1981, M.C. Mehta environmental cases followed, and Vishaka was decided in 1997.
44.tq: Fix the dated endpoints first and place the intervening PIL developments between them.
44.sec: PIL - other name, pioneering judges, origin, landmark PILs  [APPSC]

44.s: The expression ‘epistolary jurisdiction’ in the context of PIL refers to the practice of treating which of the following as petitions?
o: Only affidavits filed by government departments
Police charge sheets and audit reports
44.x: Under epistolary jurisdiction, courts treated letters and postcards as writ petitions and also acted on newspaper reports indicating violations of rights.
44.tq: Identify the exact forms of informal communication accepted by courts.
44.sec: PIL - other name, pioneering judges, origin, landmark PILs  [APPSC]

44.s:
With reference to Public Interest Litigation, consider the following statements:
1. It may be filed under Article 32 before the Supreme Court.
2. It may be filed under Article 226 before a High Court.
3. It can be initiated only by the person whose fundamental right has been directly violated.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
44.x: PIL may be filed under Articles 32 and 226. The third statement is false because locus standi is relaxed and a public-spirited citizen may approach the court for others.
44.tq: Separate the constitutional remedies from the deliberately narrow description of standing.
44.sec: PIL - other name, pioneering judges, origin, landmark PILs  [APPSC]

44.s: Which of the following judges, apart from Justices V.R. Krishna Iyer and P.N. Bhagwati, helped lay the foundation for judicial activism?
o: O. Chinnappa Reddy and D.A. Desai
44.x: Justices O. Chinnappa Reddy and D.A. Desai are identified as having laid the base of judicial activism along with the better-known PIL pioneers.
44.tq: Distinguish judicial contributors from cases and litigants.
44.sec: PIL - other name, pioneering judges, origin, landmark PILs  [APPSC]

44.s: Which of the following is a major negative consequence associated with the increasing misuse of Public Interest Litigation?
o: Removal of locus standi from constitutional law
Transfer of all cases to Lok Adalats
44.x: Although PIL democratised access to courts, its misuse has also contributed to the overburdening of courts.
44.tq: Balance the stated positive and negative consequences instead of choosing an extreme institutional effect.
44.sec: PIL - other name, pioneering judges, origin, landmark PILs  [APPSC]

44.s: Which Article declares that laws inconsistent with Fundamental Rights are void?
44.x: Article 13 provides that laws inconsistent with Fundamental Rights are void, including pre-Constitution laws to the extent of inconsistency.
44.tq: Associate the constitutional provision with the precise consequence it creates.
44.sec: Judicial review - Articles 13, 32, 137, 226; polity it symbolises; source country  [APPSC]

44.s: The power of the Supreme Court to review its own judgments is provided under
44.x: Article 137 empowers the Supreme Court to review judgments or orders made by it, subject to constitutional and statutory provisions.
44.tq: Discriminate among nearby Articles by matching the specific judicial function.
44.sec: Judicial review - Articles 13, 32, 137, 226; polity it symbolises; source country  [APPSC]

44.s: Article 226 differs from Article 32 principally because the High Courts may issue writs under Article 226 for
o: Fundamental Rights and any other purpose
44.x: The writ jurisdiction of High Courts under Article 226 extends to enforcement of Fundamental Rights and for any other purpose, making it wider in scope than Article 32.
44.tq: Compare the scope of two similar writ jurisdictions by identifying the additional phrase.
44.sec: Judicial review - Articles 13, 32, 137, 226; polity it symbolises; source country  [APPSC]

44.s: Article 32 enables the Supreme Court to protect Fundamental Rights primarily through
44.x: Article 32 empowers the Supreme Court to issue writs for the enforcement of Fundamental Rights.
44.tq: Identify the constitutional remedy linked to the enforcement function.
44.sec: Judicial review - Articles 13, 32, 137, 226; polity it symbolises; source country  [APPSC]

44.s:
Consider the following statements regarding the constitutional basis of judicial review:
1. The expression ‘judicial review’ is expressly defined in the Constitution.
2. The power flows from several constitutional provisions.
3. It is regarded as part of the basic structure of the Constitution.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
44.x: The term ‘judicial review’ is not used in the Constitution, but the power flows from several Articles and is part of the basic structure.
44.tq: Distinguish an express constitutional label from a power inferred from several provisions.
44.sec: Judicial review - Articles 13, 32, 137, 226; polity it symbolises; source country  [APPSC]

44.s: Judicial review in India is based on which combination of constitutional features?
o: Collective responsibility, adult suffrage and emergency powers
A written Constitution, federalism and Fundamental Rights
An unwritten constitution, unitary government and parliamentary privilege
44.x: Judicial review follows from India’s written Constitution, federal structure and protection of Fundamental Rights.
44.tq: Select the combination of structural features that supports the power under examination.
44.sec: Judicial review - Articles 13, 32, 137, 226; polity it symbolises; source country  [APPSC]

44.s: The concept of judicial review in India was borrowed primarily from the Constitution of
44.x: The United States is the principal constitutional source of the concept of judicial review adopted in India.
44.tq: Separate the source of judicial review from other borrowed parliamentary and federal features.
44.sec: Judicial review - Articles 13, 32, 137, 226; polity it symbolises; source country  [APPSC]

44.s: Which statement best explains the difference between the Indian and American approaches to judicial review mentioned in the constitutional comparison?
o: India uses procedure established by law, whereas the United States uses due process
India uses due process, whereas the United States uses procedure established by law
Both systems use identical constitutional language and scope
Neither system permits review of legislative action
44.x: India follows ‘procedure established by law’ under Article 21, while the United States employs the broader expression ‘due process’; consequently, Indian review is narrower in this respect.
44.tq: Discriminate between two look-alike constitutional phrases.
44.sec: Judicial review - Articles 13, 32, 137, 226; polity it symbolises; source country  [APPSC]

44.s: The Indian system of judicial review is described as blending
o: American judicial supremacy with British parliamentary sovereignty
French administrative supremacy with British federalism
Canadian judicial restraint with Australian parliamentary sovereignty
British judicial supremacy with American parliamentary sovereignty
44.x: India combines the American idea of judicial supremacy with the British tradition of parliamentary sovereignty.
44.tq: Match each constitutional characteristic with its correct comparative source.
44.sec: Judicial review - Articles 13, 32, 137, 226; polity it symbolises; source country  [APPSC]

44.s: What was the effect of the 42nd and 43rd Constitutional Amendments on the judicial review power of High Courts?
o: The 42nd Amendment restored the power and the 43rd abolished it
The 42nd Amendment barred review of Central laws by High Courts and the 43rd restored that power
Both Amendments abolished judicial review by High Courts
The 42nd Amendment transferred the power to State Legislatures and the 43rd returned it to Parliament
44.x: The 42nd Amendment, 1976, restricted High Courts from reviewing Central laws; the 43rd Amendment, 1977, restored that power.
44.tq: Track the reversal by pairing each Amendment with its distinct effect.
44.sec: Judicial review - Articles 13, 32, 137, 226; polity it symbolises; source country  [APPSC]

44.s: Which one of the following Articles confers original jurisdiction on the Supreme Court in disputes between the Union and the States?
44.x: Article 131 provides the Supreme Court’s original jurisdiction in specified disputes involving the Union and States.
44.tq: Identify the jurisdiction by its constitutional Article rather than by the court exercising it.
44.sec: Judicial review - Articles 13, 32, 137, 226; polity it symbolises; source country  [APPSC]

44.s: Special Leave to Appeal jurisdiction of the Supreme Court is associated with
44.x: Article 136 confers the Supreme Court’s special leave jurisdiction, while Articles 132 to 135 deal with specified appellate matters.
44.tq: Use the distinctive phrase ‘Special Leave’ to locate the correct Article.
44.sec: Judicial review - Articles 13, 32, 137, 226; polity it symbolises; source country  [APPSC]

44.s: A Presidential reference seeking the advisory opinion of the Supreme Court is dealt with under
44.x: Article 143 provides for the advisory jurisdiction of the Supreme Court on matters referred by the President.
44.tq: Match the advisory function with the constitutional authority that initiates it.
44.sec: Judicial review - Articles 13, 32, 137, 226; polity it symbolises; source country  [APPSC]

44.s: The power of superintendence of a High Court over subordinate courts is provided under
44.x: Article 227 confers on High Courts the power of superintendence over all courts and tribunals within their territorial jurisdiction, subject to constitutional limitations.
44.tq: Distinguish High Court writ jurisdiction from its supervisory jurisdiction.
44.sec: Judicial review - Articles 13, 32, 137, 226; polity it symbolises; source country  [APPSC]

44.s:
Consider the following statements:
1. Article 245 makes legislative power subject to the Constitution.
2. Article 246(3) gives the States exclusive power over matters in the State List, subject to the Constitution.
3. Articles 251 and 254 deal with repugnancy between certain laws.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
44.x: All three statements are correct. Articles 245 and 246 govern legislative competence, while Articles 251 and 254 address inconsistency or repugnancy between laws.
44.tq: Test several related Articles as a constitutional-competence cluster.
44.sec: Judicial review - Articles 13, 32, 137, 226; polity it symbolises; source country  [APPSC]

44.s: Under Article 254, a State law that is repugnant to a law made by Parliament is generally
o: void to the extent of the inconsistency
44.x: Article 254 embodies the rule of repugnancy: the State law is void to the extent that it is inconsistent with the applicable Parliamentary law.
44.tq: Apply the consequence of repugnancy rather than confusing it with legislative privilege.
44.sec: Judicial review - Articles 13, 32, 137, 226; polity it symbolises; source country  [APPSC]

44.s: Article 372(1) is relevant to judicial review because it concerns
o: the appointment of High Court judges
the advisory jurisdiction of the Supreme Court
44.x: Article 372(1) provides the constitutional basis for continuing pre-Constitution laws subject to their consistency with the Constitution and judicial review.
44.tq: Identify the historical category of laws linked to the Article.
44.sec: Judicial review - Articles 13, 32, 137, 226; polity it symbolises; source country  [APPSC]

44.s: Which one of the following is NOT a recognised ground of judicial review in India?
o: Contravention of constitutional provisions or the basic structure
Disagreement with the policy preference of the majority party
44.x: The recognised grounds include violation of Fundamental Rights, lack of legislative competence and contravention of constitutional provisions or the basic structure. Mere disagreement with political policy is not by itself a ground.
44.tq: Exclude a political preference that is not a constitutional ground of review.
44.sec: Judicial review - Articles 13, 32, 137, 226; polity it symbolises; source country  [APPSC]

44.s: The Supreme Court’s recognition of judicial review as part of the basic structure is associated particularly with
o: Kesavananda Bharati, 1973, and L. Chandra Kumar, 1997
44.x: The basic-structure status of judicial review is associated with Kesavananda Bharati, 1973, and was reaffirmed in the context of judicial review of tribunals in L. Chandra Kumar, 1997.
44.tq: Match the constitutional doctrine with its landmark cases and years.
44.sec: Judicial review - Articles 13, 32, 137, 226; polity it symbolises; source country  [APPSC]

44.s: The concept of judicial activism originated and developed in which country?
44.x: Judicial activism originated and developed in the United States of America. It later influenced judicial approaches in other jurisdictions, including India.
44.tq: Use the direct origin-country recall approach.
44.sec: Judicial activism - origin, activism vs overreach

44.s: Who coined the term ‘judicial activism’ in 1947?
44.x: The term ‘judicial activism’ was coined in 1947 by Arthur Schlesinger Jr., an American historian.
44.tq: Distinguish the person associated with coining a term from later theorists.
44.sec: Judicial activism - origin, activism vs overreach

44.s:
Consider the following statements:
1. Judicial review tests laws against the Constitution.
2. Judicial activism involves a wider form of judicial intervention that may shape public policy.
3. Judicial overreach refers to judicial intervention that remains entirely within the executive domain.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
44.x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct. Statement 3 is incorrect because judicial overreach occurs when courts enter the executive or legislative domain, thereby straining separation of powers.
44.tq: Find the statement that reverses the meaning of a closely related concept.
44.sec: Judicial activism - origin, activism vs overreach

44.s: Which one of the following most appropriately distinguishes judicial activism from judicial review?
o: Judicial review and judicial activism are identical expressions for striking down legislation.
Judicial review is political, whereas judicial activism is exclusively administrative.
Judicial review examines constitutional validity, whereas judicial activism involves proactive and creative intervention in public policy.
Judicial review is available only to subordinate courts, whereas judicial activism is available only to legislatures.
44.x: Judicial review primarily asks whether a law is constitutionally valid. Judicial activism is a broader, proactive and reform-oriented form of judicial intervention that may shape public policy.
44.tq: Separate a legal validity test from a broader policy-oriented intervention.
44.sec: Judicial activism - origin, activism vs overreach

44.s:
With reference to judicial review and judicial activism, consider the following statements:
1. Judicial review is generally interpretative and legalistic.
2. Judicial activism is generally creative, proactive and reform-oriented.
3. In judicial review, the judge’s role is to declare what the law is while following the framers’ original intent.
4. Judicial activism may require the legislature or executive to perform duties.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
44.x: All four statements correctly describe the distinction between judicial review or restraint and judicial activism.
44.tq: Confirm each row of a comparison before selecting the inclusive option.
44.sec: Judicial activism - origin, activism vs overreach

44.s: Judicial restraint, like judicial activism, was developed in which country, while judicial activism took root in India mainly after which period?
o: Canada; the liberalisation period of the 1990s
United States of America; the Emergency of the mid-1970s
United Kingdom; the First World War
44.x: Judicial restraint was also developed in the United States. In India, judicial activism took root after the Emergency, particularly from the mid-1970s.
44.tq: Pair the correct country with the correct Indian historical period.
44.sec: Judicial activism - origin, activism vs overreach

44.s: Which of the following is NOT commonly identified as a concern associated with judicial activism?
o: Weak enforcement of orders passed in public interest litigation
Reduction of delays in all other pending cases as an automatic consequence
44.x: Judicial activism has been associated with concerns such as violation of separation of powers, courts doing executive work, weak enforcement of PIL orders, letter petitions and delays in other cases. Reduction of all other delays is not such a concern.
44.tq: Locate the option that does not fit the established list of concerns.
44.sec: Judicial activism - origin, activism vs overreach

44.s: The expression ‘judicial adventurism’ in the debate on judicial activism primarily conveys which concern?
o: Legislatures refusing to enact ordinary laws
Subordinate courts exercising appellate jurisdiction over the Supreme Court
The executive appointing judges without consultation
Courts adopting an excessively interventionist approach beyond their proper constitutional role
44.x: ‘Judicial adventurism’ refers to an excessively interventionist judicial approach that may go beyond the proper constitutional role of courts.
44.tq: Interpret the precise meaning of a debate-related expression.
44.sec: Judicial activism - origin, activism vs overreach

44.s: Which of the following may constitute misuse of Public Interest Litigation?
o: Seeking relief for a genuinely disadvantaged group
Enforcing a constitutional right of a vulnerable class
Requesting judicial protection against an unlawful public action
Filing petitions solely for publicity or political motives
44.x: PIL may be misused for publicity or political or personal motives. Genuine protection of disadvantaged groups is the intended purpose of PIL.
44.tq: Apply the purpose of PIL to distinguish genuine public interest from private or political motives.
44.sec: Judicial activism - origin, activism vs overreach

44.s: The concern relating to Article 142 in the context of judicial activism arises mainly because of which combination?
o: Its undefined expression ‘complete justice’ and the possibility of bypassing democratic scrutiny
Its complete prohibition of judicial remedies and legislative review
Its exclusive application to criminal appeals and election disputes
Its transfer of all executive powers to the Supreme Court
44.x: The broad and undefined expression ‘complete justice’ under Article 142 is viewed as capable of bypassing democratic scrutiny when used expansively.
44.tq: Link a constitutional provision with the specific institutional concern attached to it.
44.sec: Judicial activism - origin, activism vs overreach

44.s: According to Upendra Baxi’s view, the proper role of courts in a democratic system is to:
o: Exercise executive power whenever a PIL is filed
Avoid intervention even where constitutional rights are violated
Replace democratic institutions whenever they act slowly
Fill a constitutional or institutional vacuum without replacing democratic institutions
44.x: Upendra Baxi argued that courts should fill a vacuum rather than replace democratic institutions. Judicial prudence represents the ideal approach.
44.tq: Identify the middle position between judicial passivity and judicial substitution.
44.sec: Judicial activism - origin, activism vs overreach

44.s: In which case did the Supreme Court caution judges against encroaching upon legislative and executive functions?
o: State of Rajasthan v. Union of India
M.C. Mehta v. Union of India
Divisional Manager, Aravali Golf Club v. Chander Hass
Madras Bar Association v. Union of India
44.x: In Divisional Manager, Aravali Golf Club v. Chander Hass (2007), the Supreme Court cautioned judges not to encroach upon legislative and executive functions.
44.tq: Match the judicial caution with the correct case name.
44.sec: Judicial activism - origin, activism vs overreach

44.s: The Supreme Court’s approach in State of Rajasthan v. Union of India (1977) is generally regarded as an example of:
o: Judicial review of a validating Act
Judicial abolition of the collegium system
Judicial restraint in relation to a political question
44.x: In State of Rajasthan v. Union of India (1977), the Supreme Court declined to intervene in a political question, illustrating judicial restraint.
44.tq: Associate the case with its distinctive judicial approach rather than its subject alone.
44.sec: Judicial activism - origin, activism vs overreach

44.s: In March 2026, the Supreme Court’s action concerning an NCERT chapter on judicial delay and corruption was criticised by opponents as:
o: Delegated legislation by the Election Commission
A violation of Article 32 by Parliament
44.x: The Supreme Court’s ban on the NCERT chapter was criticised as censorship under Article 19. The criticism formed part of the debate on judicial overreach.
44.tq: Identify the constitutional criticism associated with a contemporary judicial action.
44.sec: Judicial activism - origin, activism vs overreach

44.s: More than how many cases are pending in the lower courts?
44.x: More than four crore cases are pending in the lower courts.
44.tq: Retain the approximate magnitude rather than confusing crore-based figures.
44.sec: Judicial pendency - cases pending, vacancies, reform tools

44.s: In May 2026, the number of vacancies reported in the Supreme Court was:
44.x: There were two vacancies in the Supreme Court in May 2026. Three further retirements were due in 2026.
44.tq: Distinguish existing vacancies from anticipated retirements.
44.sec: Judicial pendency - cases pending, vacancies, reform tools

44.s:
Consider the following statements regarding vacancies in the higher judiciary:
1. Two Supreme Court vacancies were reported in May 2026.
2. Three more Supreme Court retirements were due in 2026.
3. On 8 August 2026, 30 judges were appointed to four High Courts.
4. The 30 appointments were distributed among the Madras, Calcutta, Karnataka and Madhya Pradesh High Courts.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
44.x: All four statements are correct. The 30 High Court appointments comprised 15 for Madras, 8 for Calcutta, 6 for Karnataka and 1 for Madhya Pradesh.
44.tq: Use the total and distribution together to verify all statements.
44.sec: Judicial pendency - cases pending, vacancies, reform tools

44.s: Which institution tracks vacancies in the district judiciary on a monthly basis?
44.x: The Department of Justice web portal tracks vacancies in the district judiciary every month.
44.tq: Identify the responsible administrative portal rather than a judicial body with a similar function.
44.sec: Judicial pendency - cases pending, vacancies, reform tools

44.s: Which of the following correctly describes e-Courts Phase III?
o: It is limited to Gram Nyayalayas and excludes district courts.
It is a scheme for appointing judges to the Supreme Court.
It covers only the period 2014–2019 and replaces all High Courts.
It covers the period 2023–2027 and functions alongside the National Judicial Data Grid as a reform tool.
44.x: e-Courts Phase III covers 2023–2027 and, together with the National Judicial Data Grid, is intended to improve judicial administration and access to case information.
44.tq: Combine the duration of a programme with its institutional purpose.
44.sec: Judicial pendency - cases pending, vacancies, reform tools

44.s: Which State has the first fully paperless district court?
44.x: Kerala has the first fully paperless district court.
44.tq: Use the distinctive achievement-state association.
44.sec: Judicial pendency - cases pending, vacancies, reform tools

44.s: Fast-track courts were cited as a reform tool particularly for cases relating to:
o: Constitutional amendment disputes under the Basic Structure doctrine
Appointment of members of the Finance Commission
Paper leaks under the Public Examinations (Prevention of Unfair Means) Act, 2024
44.x: Fast-track courts may be used for paper-leak cases under the Public Examinations (Prevention of Unfair Means) Act, 2024.
44.tq: Connect a reform mechanism with the specific category of cases for which it was cited.
44.sec: Judicial pendency - cases pending, vacancies, reform tools

44.s: Under the Centrally Sponsored Scheme for court infrastructure, the normal sharing pattern between the Centre and the States is:
44.x: The normal Centre-State sharing pattern is 60:40. The pattern is 90:10 for North-Eastern and Himalayan States and 100% for Union Territories.
44.tq: Remember the normal ratio separately from special-category funding ratios.
44.sec: Judicial pendency - cases pending, vacancies, reform tools

44.s:
Consider the following statements regarding the Centrally Sponsored Scheme for court infrastructure:
1. The scheme provides 90:10 funding for North-Eastern and Himalayan States.
2. Union Territories receive 100 per cent funding under the scheme.
3. ₹5,357 crore was allocated for the period 2021–2026.
4. The allocation included ₹50 crore for Gram Nyayalayas.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
44.x: All four statements are correct. The scheme provides special funding ratios for specified regions and includes the stated overall and Gram Nyayalaya allocations.
44.tq: Check special ratios and embedded allocation figures before choosing the complete combination.
44.sec: Judicial pendency - cases pending, vacancies, reform tools

44.s: The court-infrastructure scheme is monitored through which portal?
44.x: The Centrally Sponsored Scheme for court infrastructure is monitored on the Nyaya Vikas Portal.
44.tq: Distinguish the monitoring portal from the case-data grid and legal-aid platforms.
44.sec: Judicial pendency - cases pending, vacancies, reform tools

44.s: The amount specified for Phase I of the Andhra Pradesh Judicial Academy was:
44.x: Phase I of the Andhra Pradesh Judicial Academy was associated with an amount of ₹130.38 crore.
44.tq: Recall the exact project allocation and reject nearby rounded figures.
44.sec: Judicial pendency - cases pending, vacancies, reform tools

44.s: When a legislature responds to a judicial judgment, which of the following is constitutionally permissible?
o: Overruling the Constitution through an ordinary statute
Removing the basis of the judgment through an amendment to law, including retrospectively where valid, or amending the Constitution subject to the basic structure
Directing the judiciary to reconsider every concluded case through an executive order
Simply declaring the judgment void without changing the legal basis
44.x: The legislature cannot simply overrule a judgment. It may remove the legal basis through a valid amendment, including a retrospective validating Act where appropriate, or amend the Constitution subject to the basic structure doctrine.
44.tq: Distinguish changing the legal basis of a judgment from directly nullifying judicial power.
44.sec: Legislative response to judgments - ordinary law vs amendment

44.s: The First Amendment to the Constitution in 1951 was associated with the legislative response to early rulings concerning:
o: Emergency powers and preventive detention only
44.x: The First Amendment, enacted in 1951, followed early judicial rulings relating to land reform and reservation.
44.tq: Link a constitutional amendment with the subjects that prompted it.
44.sec: Legislative response to judgments - ordinary law vs amendment

44.s: Which constitutional amendment sought to replace the collegium system but was struck down in 2015?
44.x: The 99th Constitutional Amendment sought to replace the collegium system. It was struck down by the Supreme Court in 2015.
44.tq: Discriminate among nearby amendment numbers using the subject associated with each.
44.sec: Legislative response to judgments - ordinary law vs amendment

44.s:
Consider the following statements regarding the Tribunals Reforms Act, 2021:
1. It re-enacted conditions that had earlier been struck down by the Court.
2. The re-enacted provisions were struck down again in Madras Bar Association in 2025.
3. It replaced the Constitution’s basic structure doctrine with ordinary statutory law.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
44.x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct. Statement 3 is false because an ordinary Act cannot replace the basic structure doctrine of the Constitution.
44.tq: Reject the extreme claim that an ordinary statute can alter a constitutional limitation.
44.sec: Legislative response to judgments - ordinary law vs amendment

44.s:
Under Article 217 of the Constitution, a Judge of a High Court is appointed by the President after consultation with which of the following?
1. Chief Justice of India
2. Governor of the State
3. Chief Justice of the concerned High Court in the case of a puisne Judge
Which of the statements given above are correct?
44.x: The President appoints High Court Judges after consulting the CJI and the Governor; in the case of a puisne Judge, the Chief Justice of the concerned High Court is also consulted.
44.tq: Identify all constitutionally prescribed consultees and avoid confusing appointment with transfer.
44.sec: High Court judges - appointment, transfer, resignation, removal instances, writ and supervisory powers, contempt

44.s: In the present collegium procedure, the initial proposal for appointment of a High Court Judge is made by the Chief Justice of the High Court along with the High Court collegium consisting of the Chief Justice and:
o: All serving Judges of that High Court
44.x: The High Court collegium for initiating proposals consists of the Chief Justice and the two senior-most Judges of that High Court.
44.tq: Use the composition of the relevant collegium rather than the larger Supreme Court collegium.
44.sec: High Court judges - appointment, transfer, resignation, removal instances, writ and supervisory powers, contempt

44.s: The collegium at the Supreme Court level that examines proposals for appointment of High Court Judges comprises the Chief Justice of India and:
o: The two senior-most Judges of the concerned High Court
The four senior-most Judges of the Supreme Court
The two senior-most Judges of the Supreme Court
The Law Minister and two senior-most Judges of the Supreme Court
44.x: The Supreme Court collegium mentioned for these proposals consists of the CJI and the two senior-most Judges of the Supreme Court.
44.tq: Distinguish the Supreme Court collegium from the High Court collegium and from executive consultation.
44.sec: High Court judges - appointment, transfer, resignation, removal instances, writ and supervisory powers, contempt

44.s: Who has the constitutional power to transfer a Judge from one High Court to another under Article 222?
o: The Governor after consulting the Chief Justice of India
The Union Law Minister after consulting the High Court collegium
The Chief Justice of India acting alone
The President after consulting the Chief Justice of India
44.x: A High Court Judge is transferred by the President after consultation with the Chief Justice of India.
44.tq: Ask who would perform the constitutional action and separate transfer from appointment.
44.sec: High Court judges - appointment, transfer, resignation, removal instances, writ and supervisory powers, contempt

44.s:
Consider the following statements regarding removal of a High Court Judge:
1. Article 218 applies the Supreme Court Judge removal procedure to High Court Judges.
2. The procedure is governed by the Judges (Inquiry) Act, 1968.
3. A High Court Judge may be removed by the Governor through an executive order.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
44.x: Articles 218 and the Judges (Inquiry) Act, 1968 provide the applicable removal framework. A Governor cannot remove a High Court Judge by executive order.
44.tq: Reject the wrong-authority trap and match the High Court procedure with the Supreme Court procedure.
44.sec: High Court judges - appointment, transfer, resignation, removal instances, writ and supervisory powers, contempt

44.s: Justice Soumitra Sen was associated with which of the following events?
o: He became the first Chief Justice of the Andhra Pradesh High Court
He resigned in 2011 after the Rajya Sabha voted for his removal
He was removed by the Governor of West Bengal
He was transferred from the Madras High Court to the Calcutta High Court
44.x: Justice Soumitra Sen of the Calcutta High Court resigned in 2011 after the Rajya Sabha voted for his removal.
44.tq: Match the judge with the specific removal-related event rather than the formal general procedure.
44.sec: High Court judges - appointment, transfer, resignation, removal instances, writ and supervisory powers, contempt

44.s:
With reference to recent proceedings concerning High Court Judges, consider the following statements:
1. A motion against Justice G.R. Swaminathan of the Madras High Court was noticed by 107 Members of Parliament in December 2025.
2. An inquiry report on Yashwant Varma was to be tabled despite his resignation.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
44.x: Both statements are correct. The motion against Justice G.R. Swaminathan involved 107 MPs, and the inquiry report concerning Yashwant Varma was to be tabled despite his resignation.
44.tq: Check each recent factual detail independently before selecting the combined option.
44.sec: High Court judges - appointment, transfer, resignation, removal instances, writ and supervisory powers, contempt

44.s: Which one of the following best describes the scope of writ jurisdiction of a High Court under Article 226?
o: It extends only to disputes arising within the physical territory of the High Court
It is confined exclusively to enforcement of Fundamental Rights
It extends to Fundamental Rights and other legal rights, including where the cause of action arises within its territory
It can be exercised only on a reference from the Supreme Court
44.x: Article 226 enables High Courts to issue writs for Fundamental Rights and for any other purpose. A High Court may act even when the respondent is outside its territory if the cause of action arises within it.
44.tq: Contrast the wider wording of Article 226 with the narrower purpose traditionally associated with Article 32.
44.sec: High Court judges - appointment, transfer, resignation, removal instances, writ and supervisory powers, contempt

44.s: The inclusion of the power of High Courts to issue writs for ‘any other purpose’ makes Article 226 wider than Article 32 in respect of:
o: The power to amend the Constitution
The number of judges required to hear a petition
The range of rights that may be enforced
The power to remove constitutional authorities
44.x: Article 226 covers Fundamental Rights as well as other legal rights, whereas Article 32 is principally a remedy for enforcement of Fundamental Rights.
44.tq: Discriminate between the purposes of Articles 226 and 32 by focusing on the phrase ‘any other purpose’.
44.sec: High Court judges - appointment, transfer, resignation, removal instances, writ and supervisory powers, contempt

44.s:
Arrange the following in chronological order:
A. 42nd Constitutional Amendment
B. 43rd Constitutional Amendment
C. 44th Constitutional Amendment
D. Contempt of Courts Act
44.x: The 42nd Amendment was enacted in 1976, the 43rd in 1977, the Contempt of Courts Act in 1971, and the 44th Amendment in 1978. Therefore, strictly by year the correct order is D, A, B, C.
44.tq: Check the dates of every item rather than relying on the apparent constitutional sequence.
44.sec: High Court judges - appointment, transfer, resignation, removal instances, writ and supervisory powers, contempt

44.s: The statement that High Courts exercise superintendence over all courts and tribunals within their territory, except military tribunals, refers to:
44.x: Article 227 confers on High Courts the power of superintendence over courts and tribunals within their territory, excluding military tribunals.
44.tq: Match the constitutional Article with its distinctive institutional power.
44.sec: High Court judges - appointment, transfer, resignation, removal instances, writ and supervisory powers, contempt

44.s:
Consider the following statements regarding Article 227:
1. It covers both administrative and judicial matters.
2. The High Court may exercise the power suo motu.
3. The Supreme Court possesses an identical power under Article 227.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
44.x: Article 227 covers administrative and judicial superintendence and may be exercised suo motu. Article 227 is a High Court provision; the Supreme Court has no identical Article 227 power.
44.tq: Spot the institutional-body swap in the third statement.
44.sec: High Court judges - appointment, transfer, resignation, removal instances, writ and supervisory powers, contempt

44.s: Which of the following is correctly matched?
o: Article 215 — High Courts as courts of record
Article 226 — Salaries of High Court Judges
Article 218 — Contempt jurisdiction of High Courts
44.x: Article 215 declares every High Court to be a court of record. Article 226 concerns writs, Article 227 superintendence, and Article 233 appointment of district judges.
44.tq: Start with the sure Article–subject pair and eliminate nearby constitutional provisions.
44.sec: High Court judges - appointment, transfer, resignation, removal instances, writ and supervisory powers, contempt

44.s: Which one of the following is NOT a feature of the appellate jurisdiction of a High Court mentioned in the constitutional scheme?
o: The High Court is primarily a court of appeal
A death sentence awarded by a Sessions Court requires High Court confirmation
Second civil appeals are confined to questions of law
Every factual finding of a subordinate court must be reconsidered in every second appeal
44.x: A second civil appeal is limited to a substantial question of law; there is no requirement that every factual finding be reconsidered. The other three describe features of High Court appellate work.
44.tq: Find the statement that exaggerates a limited appellate power into an absolute one.
44.sec: High Court judges - appointment, transfer, resignation, removal instances, writ and supervisory powers, contempt

44.s: The requirement that a death sentence awarded by a Sessions Court must be confirmed by the High Court is presently governed in the criminal procedural framework by the:
44.x: The Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 replaced the Code of Criminal Procedure from 1 July 2024 and contains the relevant criminal procedure framework.
44.tq: Use the current statutory replacement rather than the repealed procedural code.
44.sec: High Court judges - appointment, transfer, resignation, removal instances, writ and supervisory powers, contempt

44.s: The Contempt of Courts Act, 1971 was enacted pursuant to the recommendations of the:
44.x: The Contempt of Courts Act, 1971 followed the report of the H.N. Sanyal Committee.
44.tq: Associate the statute with the committee that directly preceded it.
44.sec: High Court judges - appointment, transfer, resignation, removal instances, writ and supervisory powers, contempt

44.s: Which one of the following correctly distinguishes civil contempt from criminal contempt?
o: Civil contempt is confined to inaccurate reporting, while criminal contempt covers fair criticism
Civil contempt is punishable only by the Governor, while criminal contempt is punishable only by Parliament
Civil contempt concerns only contempt of the Supreme Court, while criminal contempt concerns only High Courts
Civil contempt involves wilful disobedience, while criminal contempt includes scandalising or obstructing the administration of justice
44.x: Civil contempt includes wilful disobedience of a judgment, order or undertaking. Criminal contempt includes acts such as scandalising the court or obstructing the administration of justice.
44.tq: Compare the operative definitions instead of confusing the two categories by the court involved.
44.sec: High Court judges - appointment, transfer, resignation, removal instances, writ and supervisory powers, contempt

44.s: Which of the following is recognised as an exception or safeguard in contempt jurisdiction?
o: Wilful disobedience of a court order
Obstruction of the administration of justice
44.x: Fair criticism and accurate reporting are recognised exceptions or safeguards; wilful disobedience, obstruction and scandalising conduct may constitute contempt.
44.tq: Identify the legally protected expression among acts that can constitute contempt.
44.sec: High Court judges - appointment, transfer, resignation, removal instances, writ and supervisory powers, contempt

44.s: The Restatement of Values of Judicial Life adopted in 1997 consists of:
44.x: The 1997 Restatement of Values of Judicial Life contains 16 points.
44.tq: Use the exact numerical figure rather than the nearby constitutional and statutory dates.
44.sec: High Court judges - appointment, transfer, resignation, removal instances, writ and supervisory powers, contempt

44.s: The in-house procedure relating to judicial ethics was formulated in:
44.x: The in-house procedure referred to in the judicial ethics framework was formulated in 1999.
44.tq: Distinguish the year of the ethics values document from the later in-house procedure.
44.sec: High Court judges - appointment, transfer, resignation, removal instances, writ and supervisory powers, contempt

44.s: In September 2026, the Supreme Court refused to stay contempt proceedings of the Bombay High Court relating to:
o: A dispute over the appointment of a district judge
A disagreement over the transfer of a High Court Judge
A challenge to the Gram Nyayalayas Act
A Maharashtra judicial officer’s courtroom outburst
44.x: The proceedings concerned a courtroom outburst by a Maharashtra judicial officer, and the Supreme Court refused to stay the Bombay High Court contempt proceedings.
44.tq: Link the recent judicial event with the conduct that triggered the proceeding.
44.sec: High Court judges - appointment, transfer, resignation, removal instances, writ and supervisory powers, contempt

44.s: Under Article 233, a person seeking appointment as a District Judge from outside the judicial service must have been an advocate or pleader for at least:
44.x: Article 233 requires at least seven years’ standing as an advocate or pleader for such appointment.
44.tq: Recall the statutory threshold and distinguish it from longer judicial-service experience requirements.
44.sec: Subordinate judiciary - Article 233, AIJS, Lok Adalats, Gram Nyayalayas, mobile courts

44.s:
Consider the following statements regarding appointment of District Judges under Article 233:
1. The Governor appoints District Judges in consultation with the High Court.
2. A person already in the service of the Union or the State is eligible for direct appointment under Article 233 merely on completing seven years as an advocate.
3. The provision requires seven years’ standing as an advocate or pleader for a person appointed from outside the judicial service.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
44.x: The Governor appoints District Judges in consultation with the High Court, and the seven-year advocacy requirement applies to a person from outside the judicial service. Mere completion of seven years as an advocate does not make a serving government employee eligible under this route.
44.tq: Use the eligibility exception to detect the overbroad statement.
44.sec: Subordinate judiciary - Article 233, AIJS, Lok Adalats, Gram Nyayalayas, mobile courts

44.s: Which one of the following constitutional provisions deals with the appointment of judicial officers other than District Judges?
44.x: Article 234 concerns recruitment of persons other than District Judges to the judicial service of a State.
44.tq: Separate the provision for District Judges from the provision for other judicial officers.
44.sec: Subordinate judiciary - Article 233, AIJS, Lok Adalats, Gram Nyayalayas, mobile courts

44.s: For appointment of judicial officers other than District Judges under Article 234, the Governor makes rules after consultation with the:
o: State Election Commission and Legislative Council
High Court collegium and Union Law Commission
State Public Service Commission and High Court
Union Public Service Commission and Supreme Court
44.x: Article 234 requires consultation with the State Public Service Commission and the High Court.
44.tq: Identify the correct combination of State-level recruiting authority and constitutional judicial authority.
44.sec: Subordinate judiciary - Article 233, AIJS, Lok Adalats, Gram Nyayalayas, mobile courts

44.s: The control over district courts and courts subordinate thereto, including postings, promotions and leave, is vested in the High Court under:
44.x: Article 235 vests control over district and subordinate courts in the High Court, including matters such as postings, promotions and leave.
44.tq: Match the administrative control function with its constitutional Article.
44.sec: Subordinate judiciary - Article 233, AIJS, Lok Adalats, Gram Nyayalayas, mobile courts

44.s: Which of the following is included within the constitutional meaning of ‘District Judge’ under Article 236?
o: City civil court judges and additional, joint and assistant district judges
All members of the Supreme Court
44.x: Article 236 includes judges of a city civil court and additional, joint and assistant district judges within the expression ‘District Judge’.
44.tq: Test the inclusive constitutional definition rather than the ordinary administrative meaning.
44.sec: Subordinate judiciary - Article 233, AIJS, Lok Adalats, Gram Nyayalayas, mobile courts

44.s: Under Article 237, the Governor may direct that the provisions relating to subordinate judiciary shall apply to:
44.x: Article 237 enables the Governor to apply the relevant provisions to magistrates in the State.
44.tq: Associate the enabling provision with the specific category of officers named in it.
44.sec: Subordinate judiciary - Article 233, AIJS, Lok Adalats, Gram Nyayalayas, mobile courts

44.s: Which one of the following correctly describes the position of a District Judge in the district judicial hierarchy?
o: The District Judge is subordinate to the District Magistrate in judicial matters
The District Judge hears only constitutional writ petitions
The District Judge is the highest civil court of the district and also functions as Sessions Judge in criminal matters
The District Judge is the lowest criminal court of the district
44.x: The District Judge is the highest civil court in the district and also exercises the powers of a Sessions Judge in criminal matters.
44.tq: Combine the civil and criminal roles instead of treating the District Judge as belonging to only one jurisdiction.
44.sec: Subordinate judiciary - Article 233, AIJS, Lok Adalats, Gram Nyayalayas, mobile courts

44.s: An appeal from the District Court ordinarily lies to the:
44.x: The ordinary appellate chain mentioned is District Court to High Court.
44.tq: Trace the appellate hierarchy from the subordinate court to the constitutional court above it.
44.sec: Subordinate judiciary - Article 233, AIJS, Lok Adalats, Gram Nyayalayas, mobile courts

44.s: The All India Judicial Service is constitutionally enabled by:
o: Article 312, as amended by the 42nd Amendment
Article 233, as amended by the 44th Amendment
Article 235, as amended by the 20th Amendment
Article 368, as amended by the 43rd Amendment
44.x: Article 312, as amended by the 42nd Constitutional Amendment, enables the creation of an All India Judicial Service. It has not yet been created.
44.tq: Match the service with both its enabling Article and the relevant constitutional amendment.
44.sec: Subordinate judiciary - Article 233, AIJS, Lok Adalats, Gram Nyayalayas, mobile courts

44.s: Which of the following is a principal issue in the debate over the All India Judicial Service?
o: Uniform merit-based recruitment versus State and High Court control and local-language needs
Replacement of civil courts by Lok Adalats in every case
Appointment of Governors versus election of Governors
Abolition of the Supreme Court versus creation of military tribunals
44.x: The debate balances uniform merit-based recruitment against concerns relating to State and High Court control and the importance of local languages.
44.tq: Identify the two competing institutional considerations rather than an unrelated judicial reform.
44.sec: Subordinate judiciary - Article 233, AIJS, Lok Adalats, Gram Nyayalayas, mobile courts

44.s: Which one of the following correctly describes the present status of the All India Judicial Service?
o: It is constitutionally enabled but has not yet been created
It functions only in Union Territories
It was abolished by the 44th Amendment
It was created by the 42nd Amendment and is fully operational
44.x: The Constitution enables the All India Judicial Service through Article 312, but the service has not yet been created.
44.tq: Distinguish constitutional authorisation from actual implementation.
44.sec: Subordinate judiciary - Article 233, AIJS, Lok Adalats, Gram Nyayalayas, mobile courts

44.s: Lok Adalats derive their statutory basis primarily from the:
44.x: Lok Adalats are established under the Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987.
44.tq: Match the institution with its specific parent statute.
44.sec: Subordinate judiciary - Article 233, AIJS, Lok Adalats, Gram Nyayalayas, mobile courts

44.s: Which one of the following bodies is also stated to hold Lok Adalats?

44.sec: Subordinate judiciary - Article 233, AIJS, Lok Adalats, Gram Nyayalayas, mobile courts

44.x: Gram Nyayalayas are established under the Gram Nyayalayas Act, 2008.
44.tq: Separate the year of the Gram Nyayalayas statute from the year in which it came into force.
44.sec: Subordinate judiciary - Article 233, AIJS, Lok Adalats, Gram Nyayalayas, mobile courts
