1. It has laws mandating time-bound delivery of notified services.
2. These laws provide for appeal in cases of delay.
3. These laws provide for penalty on the responsible official.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
89.x: Andhra Pradesh has laws providing for time-bound delivery of notified services, appeal and penalties for responsible officials in cases of delay.
89.tq: Check whether the State-level law contains all three standard service-guarantee features.
89.sec: Right to Services Acts - origin, order of enactment, first state

89.s: The word “Sevottam” is formed from which combination?
89.x: Sevottam is derived from “Seva” and “Uttam”, conveying excellence in service.
89.tq: Use the exact word derivation rather than translating the general objective alone.

89.s: The Sevottam model was suggested in which report of the Second Administrative Reforms Commission?
o: The 2nd report on Right to Information
89.x: The Sevottam model was suggested in the Second Administrative Reforms Commission's 12th report, titled Citizen Centric Administration.
89.tq: Match the model with the exact ARC report number and title.

89.s: Implementation of the Sevottam model in departments began in:
89.x: Implementation of the Sevottam model in departments began in 2009.
89.tq: Distinguish the implementation year from the dates of Citizens' Charter adoption and MGNREGA.

89.s:
Match List-I with List-II:

List-I (Module)
A. Citizens' Charter
B. Public Grievance Redress
C. Service Delivery Capability

List-II (Focus)
1. Build organisational capacity
2. Receive, track and resolve complaints
3. Publish service standards

Select the correct answer using the code given below.
89.x: The Citizens' Charter module publishes service standards; Public Grievance Redress receives, tracks and resolves complaints; Service Delivery Capability builds organisational capacity.
89.tq: Start with the direct service-standards pair and complete the remaining two functional matches.

89.s: Sevottam-compliant certification follows which standard?
89.x: Sevottam-compliant certification follows Indian Standard IS 15700:2005.
89.tq: Identify the exact standard number rather than substituting a familiar quality or information-security standard.

89.s: Which institution designs and promotes the Sevottam framework?
89.x: DARPG designs and promotes the Sevottam framework.
89.tq: Apply the “who performs this governance-reform function?” method to distinguish the responsible body.

89.s: CPGRAMS is administered by which department and Ministry?
o: Department of Administrative Reforms and Public Grievances, Ministry of Personnel, Public Grievances and Pensions
Department of Expenditure, Ministry of Finance
Department of Legal Affairs, Ministry of Law and Justice
Department of Rural Development, Ministry of Rural Development
89.x: CPGRAMS is administered by DARPG under the Ministry of Personnel, Public Grievances and Pensions.
89.tq: Match the grievance platform with its department and parent ministry, avoiding neighbouring ministries.

89.s: CPGRAMS was launched in:
89.x: The Centralised Public Grievance Redress and Monitoring System was launched in 2007 by DARPG.
89.tq: Separate the CPGRAMS launch year from the 2009 start of Sevottam implementation.

89.s: Which of the following correctly describes the access modes of CPGRAMS?
o: It is available only through physical applications at District Collectorates.
It is available only to pensioners through CPENGRAMS.
It is accessible only during designated government office hours through email.
It is available 24x7 through the web, app and UMANG.
89.x: CPGRAMS is a 24x7 grievance platform accessible through the web, a mobile application and UMANG. CPENGRAMS is the separate pensioners' grievance system.
89.tq: Use the complete access description and reject options that narrow the platform's users or channels.

89.s: A circular of DARPG dated 23 August 2024 reduced the maximum disposal time for CPGRAMS grievances from:
89.x: The DARPG circular dated 23 August 2024 reduced the maximum disposal time from 30 days to 21 days.
89.tq: Retain both the original and revised limits; the reduction pair is the tested fact.

89.s:
Consider the following statements about CPGRAMS:
1. CPGRAMS 7.0 is available in many Indian languages.
2. IGMS uses artificial intelligence and machine learning and is associated with IIT Kanpur.
3. Grievances can be submitted through 5.1 lakh Common Service Centres.
4. The system is associated with the idea “One Nation - One Portal”.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
89.x: All four statements describe features associated with CPGRAMS: multilingual CPGRAMS 7.0, AI/ML-based IGMS with IIT Kanpur, access through 5.1 lakh CSCs and the “One Nation - One Portal” approach.
89.tq: Test the complete set of platform features, including the exact CSC figure and associated slogan.

89.s: Samadhan Didi is associated with CPGRAMS as a:
89.x: Samadhan Didi is an artificial-intelligence voice chatbot in CPGRAMS.
89.tq: Discriminate between a technology feature and the institutional mechanisms listed alongside it.

89.s: The Grievance Redressal Assessment and Index (GRAI) ranks ministries on:
89.x: GRAI ranks ministries on 11 indicators grouped into four dimensions: efficiency, feedback, domain and organisational commitment.
89.tq: Keep the indicator count separate from the number and names of dimensions.

89.s: Which one of the following is NOT a dimension of GRAI?
89.x: The four GRAI dimensions are efficiency, feedback, domain and organisational commitment. Transparency is not listed as a GRAI dimension here.
89.tq: Find the term outside the exact four-dimension classification.

89.s: Which of the following pairs is correctly matched?
o: Samadhan Didi — Meghalaya social audit law
IGMS — statutory Right to Services Act
89.x: CPENGRAMS is the CPGRAMS-related grievance system for pensioners. The other pairs confuse separate grievance, audit, assessment and legislative mechanisms.
89.tq: Use the user group as the sure matching clue and reject cross-domain substitutions.

89.s: The title of the Second Administrative Reforms Commission's 12th report is:
o: Citizen Centric Administration - The Heart of Governance
Promoting e-Governance - The Smart Way Forward
89.x: The 12th report was titled “Citizen Centric Administration - The Heart of Governance” and was published in 2009.
89.tq: Match the exact report title with the report number and citizen-centric theme.
89.sec: Second ARC 12th report 'Citizen Centric Administration' - key recommendations

89.s: Who chaired the Second Administrative Reforms Commission when it produced the 12th report on Citizen Centric Administration?
o: M. Veerappa Moily's predecessor, P. C. Hota
89.x: Veerappa Moily chaired the Second Administrative Reforms Commission associated with the 12th report on Citizen Centric Administration.
89.tq: Test the report-chairman association directly while keeping the alternatives within the administrative-reform domain.
89.sec: Second ARC 12th report 'Citizen Centric Administration' - key recommendations

89.s:
Which of the following recommendations were made in the Second Administrative Reforms Commission's 12th report?
1. Adoption of the Sevottam model
2. Statutory backing for Citizens' Charters
3. Strong grievance redress mechanisms
4. Social audits and e-governance
5. Legislation on the right to public services
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
89.x: The report recommended Sevottam, statutory Citizens' Charters, strong grievance redress, social audits, e-governance and right-to-public-services legislation.
89.tq: Check whether each recommendation belongs to the report's citizen-centric governance package before selecting the complete combination.
89.sec: Second ARC 12th report 'Citizen Centric Administration' - key recommendations

89.s: The Second Administrative Reforms Commission recommended training for which purpose?
o: Replacing all departmental grievance officers with elected representatives
Developing a citizen-centric mindset among public officials
89.x: The Commission recommended training public officials to develop a citizen-centric mindset.
89.tq: Translate the recommendation into its administrative objective rather than selecting an institutional replacement.
89.sec: Second ARC 12th report 'Citizen Centric Administration' - key recommendations

89.s: Which one of the following correctly links the Second ARC recommendation on social audit with its intended scope?
o: Transfer all social audits to the Election Commission
Abolish community participation in welfare monitoring
Institutionalise social audits in all major welfare schemes
Limit social audits exclusively to MGNREGA
89.x: The Second ARC recommended institutionalising social audits in all major welfare schemes, extending the practice beyond MGNREGA alone.
89.tq: Watch for the restrictive word “exclusively” and apply the recommendation to its broader intended scope.
89.sec: Social audit - MGNREGA, first law, AP society

89.s: The institution of the Ombudsman originated in which country and in which year?
89.x: The institution of the Ombudsman originated in Sweden in 1809.
89.tq: Directly link the institution with its country of origin and year.

89.s:
Consider the following statements regarding the recommendation for Lokpal and Lokayukta:
1. The First Administrative Reforms Commission functioned during 1966–70.
2. Morarji Desai was associated with the First Administrative Reforms Commission.
3. The Commission recommended a Lokpal at the Union level and Lokayuktas at the State level.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
89.x: All three statements are correct. The First Administrative Reforms Commission, associated with Morarji Desai and functioning during 1966–70, recommended Lokpal for the Union and Lokayukta for the States.
89.tq: Check the institutional period, associated person and recommendation together.

89.s: Who coined the term ‘Lokayukta’?
89.x: The term ‘Lokayukta’ was coined by L. M. Singhvi.
89.tq: Use the person-term association rather than confusing the term’s originator with a reform commission member.

89.s:
Match List-I with List-II:

List-I (Mechanism)

a. CPGRAMS and State portals
b. Lokpal and Lokayukta
c. Classic Ombudsman

List-II (Primary character)

i. Independent officer of the legislature
 ii. Corruption allegations against public functionaries
 iii. Service-delivery grievances

Select the correct answer using the code given below:
89.x: CPGRAMS and State portals deal with service-delivery grievances; Lokpal and Lokayukta deal with corruption allegations against public functionaries; and the classic Ombudsman is an independent officer of the legislature.
89.tq: Start from the sure pair and eliminate codes that reverse the mechanism and its function.

89.s: Which one of the following correctly describes the nature of disposal under CPGRAMS and State grievance portals?
o: Legislative and indefinite examination of corruption cases
Judicial and unrestricted disposal of criminal cases
Executive and time-bound disposal of service-delivery grievances
Private and voluntary settlement of constitutional disputes
89.x: CPGRAMS and State portals are executive mechanisms intended for time-bound disposal of service-delivery grievances.
89.tq: Identify the mechanism by matching its function with the nature of authority and disposal.

89.s:
With reference to the Lokpal, consider the following statements:
1. It consists of a Chairperson and up to eight members.
2. Fifty per cent of its members are required to be judicial members.
3. Not less than fifty per cent of its members are required to be from SCs, STs, OBCs, minorities and women.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
89.x: The Lokpal consists of a Chairperson and up to eight members. Fifty per cent are judicial members, and not less than fifty per cent are from SCs, STs, OBCs, minorities and women.
89.tq: Separate the numerical composition requirement from the social-representation requirement.

89.s: A citizen complains that a government office has failed to deliver a public service within the prescribed time. Which mechanism is primarily suited to deal with such a complaint?
o: Classic Ombudsman as an officer of the legislature
Lokpal under the Lokpal and Lokayuktas Act, 2013
CPGRAMS or an appropriate State grievance portal
89.x: CPGRAMS and State portals are designed for service-delivery grievances and provide for executive, time-bound disposal. Lokpal and Lokayukta primarily deal with corruption allegations against public functionaries.
89.tq: Apply the subject-matter test: service delivery points to grievance portals, while corruption points to Lokpal or Lokayukta.

89.s: The statutory status of the Lokpal and Lokayukta is associated with which legislation?
89.x: Lokpal and Lokayukta are statutory institutions under the Lokpal and Lokayuktas Act, 2013.
89.tq: Match the institution with its exact statutory basis and year.

89.s: Which of the following is NOT correctly matched?
o: Classic Ombudsman — Independent officer of the legislature
Lokpal and Lokayukta — Corruption allegations against public functionaries
CPGRAMS and State portals — Service-delivery grievances
Lokpal and Lokayukta — Non-statutory voluntary mediation mechanism
89.x: Lokpal and Lokayukta are statutory institutions under the Lokpal and Lokayuktas Act, 2013; they are not non-statutory voluntary mediation mechanisms.
89.tq: Find the one option that reverses the statutory nature of the institution.

89.s: Which of the following is a criticism commonly associated with Citizens’ Charters?
o: They deal exclusively with corruption allegations
They possess excessive judicial enforceability in every case
They are independent officers of the legislature
89.x: A major criticism of Citizens’ Charters is that they lack legal force, which can limit enforceability of their commitments.
89.tq: Distinguish a governance limitation from the functions of grievance and anti-corruption institutions.

89.s:
Consider the following statements:
1. The 50th CPGRAMS report was associated with DARPG.
2. The report included GRAI and was dated 9 August 2026.
3. Meekosam was upgraded with data analytics in January 2026.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
89.x: All three statements are correct. DARPG’s 50th CPGRAMS report included GRAI and was dated 9 August 2026, while Meekosam was upgraded with data analytics in January 2026.
89.tq: Verify the reporting institution, report detail and date-based portal development separately.

89.s:
Arrange the following Andhra Pradesh grievance and social-audit references in the sequence in which they are presented as part of the State’s grievance-platform progression:
A. Spandana
B. Prajavani
C. SSAAT
D. Meekosam

Select the correct answer using the code given below:
89.x: The grievance-platform progression is Prajavani, followed by Meekosam and then Spandana. SSAAT is associated with social audit in Andhra Pradesh.
89.tq: Separate the three grievance platforms from SSAAT and preserve the stated progression.

89.s: In the context of Andhra Pradesh, SSAAT is associated with which of the following?
89.x: SSAAT is associated with social audit in Andhra Pradesh.
89.tq: Identify the State-specific institutional acronym by its governance function.

89.s: According to the cited figure, the number of grievances pending on CPGRAMS in September 2025 was:
89.x: The cited figure records more than 71,000 grievances pending on CPGRAMS in September 2025.
89.tq: Treat the month, year and magnitude as a single quantitative fact.

90.s: Which one of the following is included in the definition of “information” under Section 2(f) of the Right to Information Act, 2005?
o: Records, documents, e-mails, opinions, samples and electronic data
Only opinions expressed by public officials
90.x: Section 2(f) includes records, documents, e-mails, opinions, advice, press releases, circulars, orders, logbooks, contracts, reports, papers, samples, models and electronic data.
90.tq: Use the exact statutory definition instead of narrowing the term to paper records.
90.sec: RTI Act sections and Section 8 exemptions

90.s:
With reference to the Right to Information Act, 2005, consider the following statements:
1. A body substantially financed or controlled by the government may be a public authority.
2. A body established by a government notification may be a public authority.
3. Only bodies created directly by the Constitution can be public authorities.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
90.x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct under Section 2(h). Statement 3 is false because public authorities also include bodies established by law or government notification and substantially financed or controlled by government.
90.tq: Split the definition into its alternative categories and reject the word “only”.
90.sec: RTI Act sections and Section 8 exemptions

90.s: Which of the following is NOT a component of the right to information under Section 2(j) of the Right to Information Act, 2005?
o: Inspection of work, documents and records
Compelling a public authority to create new information
90.x: Section 2(j) permits inspection, taking notes or extracts, obtaining certified copies and taking certified samples. It does not require a public authority to create information that it does not hold.
90.tq: Distinguish access to existing records from a demand to generate new information.
90.sec: RTI Act sections and Section 8 exemptions

90.s: Which Section of the Right to Information Act, 2005 provides that every citizen shall have the right to information?
90.x: Section 3 declares that all citizens shall have the right to information, subject to the provisions of the Act.
90.tq: Test the precise section number rather than the broader subject of the provision.
90.sec: RTI Act sections and Section 8 exemptions

90.s:
Under Section 6 of the Right to Information Act, 2005, an application for information may be made in which of the following ways and languages?
1. By post, in person or through e-mail
2. In Hindi, English or the official language of the area
3. Only after stating the reasons for seeking the information
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
90.x: Applications may be submitted by post, in person or electronically and may be made in Hindi, English or the local official language. Under Section 6(2), the applicant need not give reasons for seeking information, so statement 3 is false.
90.tq: Catch the reversed requirement that an applicant must disclose reasons.
90.sec: RTI Act sections and Section 8 exemptions

90.s:
Match List-I with List-II relating to provisions of the Right to Information Act, 2005:

List-I (Section)
A. Section 5
B. Section 9
C. Section 12
D. Section 15

List-II (Subject)
1. Constitution of the Central Information Commission
2. Constitution of the State Information Commission
3. Designation of Public Information Officers and Assistant Public Information Officers
4. Rejection where disclosure would infringe copyright of a person other than the State

Select the correct answer using the code given below.
90.x: Section 5 concerns PIOs and APIOs; Section 9 concerns copyright belonging to a person other than the State; Sections 12 and 15 concern the CIC and SIC respectively.
90.tq: Start with the sure statutory pair and eliminate codes that disturb it.
90.sec: RTI Act sections and Section 8 exemptions

90.s: Which of the following is correctly matched with Section 8(1) of the Right to Information Act, 2005?
o: Commercial confidence and trade secrets — Section 8(1)(a)
Information held in a fiduciary relationship — Section 8(1)(e)
Information from a foreign government in confidence — Section 8(1)(j)
90.x: Section 8(1)(e) covers information available to a person in his fiduciary relationship. Commercial confidence and trade secrets fall under clause (d), foreign-government information under clause (f), and personal information under clause (j).
90.tq: Discriminate between neighbouring clauses by matching each exemption with its exact letter.
90.sec: RTI Act sections and Section 8 exemptions

90.s: Under Section 8(2) of the Right to Information Act, 2005, information covered by an exemption may be disclosed when
o: the information is more than five years old
the public interest in disclosure outweighs the harm to the protected interests
the applicant is a citizen for more than five years
the information is requested through an APIO
90.x: Section 8(2) permits disclosure where the public interest in disclosure outweighs the harm to the protected interests, including in cases involving the Official Secrets Act.
90.tq: Apply the public-interest override rather than treating exemptions as absolute.
90.sec: RTI Act sections and Section 8 exemptions

90.s:
Consider the following statements regarding Section 8(3) of the Right to Information Act, 2005:
1. Exempt information is generally disclosable after twenty years.
2. Cabinet deliberations are excluded from the twenty-year disclosure rule.
3. Information concerning foreign relations is excluded from the twenty-year disclosure rule.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
90.x: All three statements are correct. The twenty-year rule does not apply to cabinet deliberations, information affecting security, strategic or economic interests, foreign relations and incitement to an offence.
90.tq: Look for statutory exceptions to a general time rule instead of assuming it is universal.
90.sec: RTI Act sections and Section 8 exemptions

90.s: Disclosure of information may be rejected under Section 9 of the Right to Information Act, 2005 when such disclosure would
o: disclose information older than twenty years
reveal any information held by a public authority
infringe the copyright of a person other than the State
90.x: Section 9 permits rejection where access would involve infringement of copyright subsisting in a person other than the State.
90.tq: Separate the copyright-based ground under Section 9 from the security and privacy exemptions under Section 8.
90.sec: RTI Act sections and Section 8 exemptions

90.s: Which one of the following is NOT included among the organisations generally covered by the exemption under Section 24 and the Second Schedule of the Right to Information Act, 2005?
90.x: The IB, R&AW and CRPF are among the intelligence and security organisations covered by Section 24. The Central Information Commission is the appellate information body and is not a Section 24 exempt organisation.
90.tq: Identify the odd institutional category instead of confusing an exempt security body with the appellate authority.
90.sec: RTI Act sections and Section 8 exemptions

90.s: Which of the following statements regarding Section 24 of the Right to Information Act, 2005 is correct?
o: Information relating to corruption and human-rights violations is not excluded from disclosure merely because it is held by a listed organisation.
It applies only to organisations created after 2005.
It excludes all information held by intelligence and security organisations without exception.
It removes the jurisdiction of the Information Commission in every case involving a security organisation.
90.x: Section 24 generally excludes listed intelligence and security organisations, but information concerning corruption and human-rights violations remains subject to disclosure under the specified conditions.
90.tq: Test the exception to a broad exclusion and reject absolute wording such as “all” and “without exception”.
90.sec: RTI Act sections and Section 8 exemptions

90.s: The Central Bureau of Investigation was added to the exempt organisations under the Second Schedule of the Right to Information Act in
90.x: The Central Bureau of Investigation was added to the Second Schedule in 2011, subject to the statutory exceptions relating to corruption and human-rights violations.
90.tq: Use the distinctive amendment year rather than the year of enactment of the Act.
90.sec: RTI Act sections and Section 8 exemptions

90.s:
Which of the following pairs is correctly matched?

1. Section 11 — Third-party information
2. Section 19 — Appeals
3. Section 20 — Penalties on Public Information Officers
4. Section 22 — Overriding effect over the Official Secrets Act, 1923

Select the correct answer using the code given below.
90.x: All four pairs are correct. Sections 11, 19, 20 and 22 respectively deal with third-party information, appeals, penalties and the overriding effect of the RTI Act.
90.tq: Check each section–subject pair and use the comprehensive option only when every pair is accurate.
90.sec: RTI Act sections and Section 8 exemptions

90.s:
Arrange the following stages of an RTI appeal process in the correct chronological order:
A. Second appeal to the Central or State Information Commission
B. Application for information to the Public Information Officer
C. First appeal to the First Appellate Authority
D. Decision or expiry of the period prescribed for the first application

Select the correct answer using the code given below.
90.x: The applicant first approaches the PIO, waits for the decision or expiry of the prescribed period, files the first appeal, and may thereafter file a second appeal before the Information Commission.
90.tq: Fix the initial application and final second appeal, then place the first appeal between them.
90.sec: Time limits - reply, life and liberty, third party, appeals

90.s: An application for information is submitted through an Assistant Public Information Officer. Within what maximum period should the normal response ordinarily be provided?
90.x: An application routed through an APIO carries an additional five days over the normal thirty-day period, making the period thirty-five days.
90.tq: Add the APIO forwarding period to the ordinary thirty-day limit.
90.sec: Time limits - reply, life and liberty, third party, appeals

90.s: Where the information sought concerns the life or liberty of a person, the Public Information Officer is required to provide it within
90.x: Requests concerning the life or liberty of a person must be answered within forty-eight hours.
90.tq: Distinguish the special urgent limit from the normal thirty-day period.
90.sec: Time limits - reply, life and liberty, third party, appeals

90.s: The time limit for dealing with information relating to a third party under Section 11 of the Right to Information Act is generally
90.x: Third-party information cases carry a period of forty days because the third party must be given an opportunity to make a representation.
90.tq: Do not substitute the ordinary PIO period for the special third-party period.
90.sec: Time limits - reply, life and liberty, third party, appeals

90.s:
Consider the following statements regarding appeals under the Right to Information Act, 2005:
1. The first appeal is ordinarily filed within thirty days.
2. The First Appellate Authority may decide the first appeal within thirty days or, for recorded reasons, within an extended period not exceeding forty-five days.
3. A second appeal to the Central or State Information Commission is ordinarily filed within ninety days.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
90.x: All three statements are correct. The first appeal is due within thirty days, its decision period may extend to forty-five days with reasons, and the second appeal is ordinarily filed within ninety days.
90.tq: Separate the filing period from the decision period and then identify the longer second-appeal limit.
90.sec: Time limits - reply, life and liberty, third party, appeals

90.s: In a case involving a human-rights allegation against an organisation exempt under Section 24, information is to be provided within
o: 45 days, with the approval of the Information Commission
40 days, after approval of the Public Information Officer
90 days, after approval of the Central Government
90.x: For human-rights allegations involving a Section 24 exempt organisation, disclosure may be made within forty-five days and requires the approval of the Information Commission.
90.tq: Match the special case with both its exceptional time limit and approving authority.
90.sec: Time limits - reply, life and liberty, third party, appeals

90.s: Which enactment is associated with Sweden's pioneering recognition of freedom of information in 1766?
90.x: Sweden enacted the Freedom of the Press Act in 1766, regarded as the world's first freedom-of-information law.
90.tq: Identify the exact title associated with the landmark year.
90.sec: Background - Sweden, FOI Act, MKSS, first states - chronology  [APPSC]

90.s: Article 19 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights is significant in the context of the right to information because it recognises the right to
o: free legal aid in all civil disputes
access confidential state records without restriction
90.x: UDHR Article 19, adopted in 1948, recognises the right to seek and receive information.
90.tq: Match the international instrument with the precise right it recognises.
90.sec: Background - Sweden, FOI Act, MKSS, first states - chronology  [APPSC]

90.s: The public hearings known as ‘jan sunwais’, involving muster rolls and bills, were central to the activities of which organisation?
o: National Campaign for People's Right to Information
90.x: The Mazdoor Kisan Shakti Sangathan conducted jan sunwais in Rajasthan to demand access to muster rolls and bills, helping initiate the RTI movement.
90.tq: Link the distinctive activity with the organisation that conducted it.
90.sec: Background - Sweden, FOI Act, MKSS, first states - chronology  [APPSC]

90.s: Which one of the following sets contains the principal leaders associated with the MKSS-led public hearings in Rajasthan?
o: Aruna Roy, Medha Patkar and Shankar Singh
Aruna Roy, Nikhil Dey and Shankar Singh
Shankar Singh, Jayaprakash Narayan and Nikhil Dey
Nikhil Dey, Anna Hazare and Aruna Roy
90.x: The Rajasthan movement was associated with Aruna Roy, Nikhil Dey and Shankar Singh.
90.tq: Discriminate between closely associated public-activism names.
90.sec: Background - Sweden, FOI Act, MKSS, first states - chronology  [APPSC]

90.s:
Arrange the following earlier State-level right-to-information laws in chronological order:
A. Delhi
B. Rajasthan and Karnataka
C. Maharashtra and Assam
D. Tamil Nadu and Goa
90.x: Tamil Nadu and Goa enacted laws in 1997, Rajasthan and Karnataka in 2000, Delhi in 2001, and Maharashtra and Assam in 2002.
90.tq: Use the years attached to the state-level laws to fix the sequence.
90.sec: Background - Sweden, FOI Act, MKSS, first states - chronology  [APPSC]

90.s:
Consider the following statements regarding the judicial basis of the right to information:
1. The right to know has been read into Article 19(1)(a).
2. Article 21 has also been associated with the judicial protection of the right to know.
3. State of U.P. v. Raj Narain and S.P. Gupta v. Union of India are important cases in this context.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
90.x: The right to know has been judicially linked with Articles 19(1)(a) and 21. State of U.P. v. Raj Narain and S.P. Gupta v. Union of India are important decisions supporting this principle.
90.tq: Check the constitutional provisions and case-law references together.
90.sec: Background - Sweden, FOI Act, MKSS, first states - chronology  [APPSC]

90.s: Which of the following correctly describes the nature of the right created by the Right to Information Act, 2005?
o: It is merely an administrative privilege available at the discretion of each public authority.
It is a Fundamental Right expressly created by a separate constitutional article.
It is a statutory right, while the Supreme Court has read the right to know into Article 19(1)(a).
It is a constitutional right confined to citizens holding public office.
90.x: The Act creates a statutory right. Separately, the Supreme Court has treated the right to know as implicit in Article 19(1)(a).
90.tq: Separate the statutory source of the Act from its constitutional interpretation.
90.sec: Act milestones and nature  [APPSC]

90.s: Under the Right to Information framework, information is provided free of cost to applicants belonging to which category?
o: All applicants below 25 years of age
All applicants belonging to rural areas
90.x: Applicants belonging to the below-poverty-line category are entitled to information without payment of the prescribed fee.
90.tq: Recall the specific beneficiary category attached to fee exemption.
90.sec: Act milestones and nature  [APPSC]

90.s: The Preamble of the Right to Information Act seeks to promote an informed citizenry and transparency primarily in order to
o: contain corruption and hold governments accountable, while harmonising these objectives with other public interests
transfer all information-related functions from public authorities to courts
make every government document automatically public without exception
replace the parliamentary system with direct democracy
90.x: The Preamble connects informed citizenship and transparency with containing corruption and ensuring accountability, subject to harmonisation with other public interests.
90.tq: Choose the option that retains the complete purpose without an absolute claim.
90.sec: Act milestones and nature  [APPSC]

90.s:
Consider the following statements about the Central and State Information Commissions:
1. Both are statutory bodies created under the Right to Information Act.
2. Both have powers of a civil court.
3. Both hear second appeals and complaints under the Act.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
90.x: The Central and State Information Commissions are statutory bodies. They exercise civil-court powers and deal with second appeals and complaints under the Act.
90.tq: Verify the common features before considering the Central-State distinction.
90.sec: Central/State Information Commission - composition, appointment, removal, penalty  [APPSC]

90.s: With reference to the composition of the Information Commissions, which one of the following is correct?
o: The Central and State Commissions may each consist of a Chief Information Commissioner and up to ten Information Commissioners.
The State Commission has a Chief Information Commissioner and a maximum of five Information Commissioners.
Each Commission must consist of exactly ten Information Commissioners besides its Chief.
The Central Commission consists only of the Chief Information Commissioner, whereas the State Commission has up to ten members.
90.x: At both levels, the structure consists of a Chief Information Commissioner and up to ten Information Commissioners.
90.tq: Watch the difference between ‘up to’ and a compulsory fixed number.
90.sec: Central/State Information Commission - composition, appointment, removal, penalty  [APPSC]

90.s: Which one of the following is NOT a ground mentioned for removal of an Information Commissioner?
o: Disagreement with the decision of a Public Information Officer
Holding paid employment outside the office
Conviction for an offence involving moral turpitude
90.x: Removal may be connected with insolvency, conviction involving moral turpitude, paid employment and other specified grounds. Mere disagreement with a PIO's decision is not a ground for removal.
90.tq: Find the option that is unrelated to the statutory removal grounds.
90.sec: Central/State Information Commission - composition, appointment, removal, penalty  [APPSC]

90.s: In the ordinary procedure for removal of a Central Information Commissioner on the ground of proved misbehaviour or incapacity, which combination is correct?
o: The Chief Justice of India orders removal after an inquiry by the President.
The Prime Minister orders removal after an inquiry by Parliament.
The Governor orders removal after an inquiry by the High Court.
The President orders removal after an inquiry by the Supreme Court.
90.x: For proved misbehaviour or incapacity, the President may remove a Central Information Commissioner after the Supreme Court conducts the required inquiry.
90.tq: Use the ‘who would do this job?’ method for authority and inquiry.
90.sec: Central/State Information Commission - composition, appointment, removal, penalty  [APPSC]

90.s: Which of the following statements regarding eligibility for appointment as an Information Commissioner is correct?
o: Only serving Members of Parliament and Members of Legislative Assemblies are eligible.
A person holding an office of profit is automatically eligible because the post is statutory.
A person connected with a political party is expressly preferred for appointment.
A person of eminence in public life with experience in fields such as law, science and technology, social service, management, journalism, mass media or administration may be appointed.
90.x: Eligibility requires eminence in public life and experience in specified fields. MPs and MLAs, persons holding an office of profit, and persons connected with political parties or business are ineligible.
90.tq: Select the inclusive eligibility statement while rejecting disqualifying conditions.
90.sec: Central/State Information Commission - composition, appointment, removal, penalty  [APPSC]

90.s: Which one of the following is correctly matched with the post-2019 position regarding the tenure of Information Commissioners?
o: The Act continues to prescribe five years or the age of 65 years in all cases.
The Constitution fixes a uniform tenure of six years.
The concerned High Court fixes the tenure separately for each Commissioner.
The Central Government notifies the term; under the RTI Rules, 2019, it is three years.
90.x: After the 2019 amendment, the Central Government is empowered to notify the term. The RTI Rules, 2019 provide a three-year term.
90.tq: Distinguish the original tenure provision from the post-2019 rule-based position.
90.sec: Central/State Information Commission - composition, appointment, removal, penalty  [APPSC]

90.s: Who was the first Central Information Commissioner of India?
90.x: Wajahat Habibullah was the first Central Information Commissioner. Aruna Roy, Nikhil Dey and Shankar Singh were associated with the MKSS movement.
90.tq: Separate the first office-holder from activists associated with the RTI movement.
90.sec: Central/State Information Commission - composition, appointment, removal, penalty  [APPSC]

90.s:
Match List-I with List-II:

List-I (Case)
a. CBSE v. Aditya Bandopadhyay
b. Girish Ramchandra Deshpande v. CIC
c. CPIO, Supreme Court v. Subhash Chandra Agarwal
d. Zee Telefilms v. Union of India

List-II (Decision)
i. BCCI is not ‘State’ under Article 12
 ii. Service records and tax returns of a public servant are personal information
 iii. Evaluated answer sheets are information accessible to examinees
 iv. Office of the Chief Justice of India is a public authority under the RTI Act

Which of the following is the correct match?
90.x: CBSE v. Aditya Bandopadhyay recognised evaluated answer sheets as information; Girish Deshpande treated service records and tax returns as personal information; Subhash Chandra Agarwal covered the CJI’s office; and Zee Telefilms held that BCCI was not State under Article 12.
90.tq: Start from the sure case–holding pairs and eliminate codes with swapped judicial decisions.
90.sec: Landmark RTI judgements - issue decided

90.s:
With reference to CBSE v. Aditya Bandopadhyay (2011), consider the following statements:
1. Evaluated answer sheets are information under the RTI Act.
2. Examinees can inspect their evaluated answer sheets.
3. An examining body holds evaluated answer sheets in a fiduciary capacity in every case.
4. Indiscriminate and impractical demands may clog administration.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
90.x: Statements 1, 2 and 4 are correct. Statement 3 is false because the Supreme Court held that the examining body does not hold the evaluated answer sheets in a fiduciary capacity.
90.tq: Find the single overbroad statement containing ‘in every case’.
90.sec: Landmark RTI judgements - issue decided

90.s: In Girish Ramchandra Deshpande v. Central Information Commission (2012), which of the following was treated as personal information under Section 8(1)(j) of the RTI Act?
o: Only the public servant’s official designation and office address
A public servant’s service record, disciplinary action, assets and tax returns
Only information concerning recruitment to public employment
All information relating to the functioning of the concerned department
90.x: The judgment treated the public servant’s service record, disciplinary proceedings, assets and tax returns as personal information protected under Section 8(1)(j).
90.tq: Test the exact scope of the privacy-related exemption rather than the person’s official identity.
90.sec: Landmark RTI judgements - issue decided

90.s:
Consider the following statements regarding the office of the Chief Justice of India under the RTI Act:
1. The office of the Chief Justice of India was held to be a public authority.
2. The decision was delivered in CPIO, Supreme Court v. Subhash Chandra Agarwal.
3. Disclosure was held to be entirely unconditional, irrespective of privacy and judicial independence.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
90.x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct. Statement 3 is false because disclosure must be balanced against privacy and judicial independence.
90.tq: Reject the absolute claim created by the word ‘entirely’.
90.sec: Landmark RTI judgements - issue decided

90.s: Which one of the following correctly distinguishes the decisions concerning BCCI under the RTI Act and Article 12?
o: BCCI was held to be State under Article 12 but exempt from the RTI Act because it is a sports body.
BCCI was held to be a public authority under Section 2(h) and State under Article 12.
BCCI performs public functions but was held not to be State under Article 12 and was also ruled not to be a public authority under Section 2(h).
BCCI performs no public functions and is outside all forms of public accountability.
90.x: Zee Telefilms held that BCCI performs public functions but is not State under Article 12. A later CIC ruling also held that BCCI is not a public authority under Section 2(h) of the RTI Act.
90.tq: Separate the Article 12 question from the distinct Section 2(h) public-authority question.
90.sec: Landmark RTI judgements - issue decided

90.s:
The judicial basis of the right to information is associated with which of the following pairs?

1. State of Uttar Pradesh v. Raj Narain — right to know how the Government functions
2. S.P. Gupta case — transparency is essential to democracy

Select the correct answer using the code given below.
90.x: Both propositions are correct. Raj Narain recognised the citizen’s right to know how the Government functions, while S.P. Gupta linked transparency with democracy.
90.tq: Use paired landmark cases and distinguish their closely related constitutional principles.
90.sec: Landmark RTI judgements - issue decided

90.s: A Madras High Court observation in 2014 regarding an RTI application was later withdrawn. Which of the following correctly describes the issue?
o: An applicant could seek information only after exhausting departmental remedies.
An applicant could seek information only through a lawyer, as required by Section 6(2).
An applicant had to state the reason for seeking information, contrary to Section 6(2).
An applicant had to pay a special fee for information concerning public authorities.
90.x: The 2014 observation said that an applicant should state the reason for seeking information. It was later withdrawn because Section 6(2) provides that an applicant need not give any reason for requesting information.
90.tq: Identify the judicial observation that conflicts with the express statutory safeguard in Section 6(2).
90.sec: Landmark RTI judgements - issue decided

90.s:
Arrange the following developments in chronological order:
A. CIC declares six national political parties to be public authorities
B. CIC holds that the office of the CJI is a public authority
C. Delhi High Court rules that a husband’s income-tax return details are personal information exempt from disclosure to his estranged wife
D. Supreme Court agrees to examine whether the DPDP Act’s ‘en bloc embargo’ is repugnant to the RTI Act
90.x: The political-party decision was in 2013, the CJI-office decision in 2019, the Delhi High Court ruling was in May 2026, and the Supreme Court agreed to examine the DPDP issue in August 2026.
90.tq: Fix the dated 2013 and 2019 events first, then place the two 2026 developments.
90.sec: Landmark RTI judgements - issue decided

90.s: In May 2026, the Delhi High Court held that disclosure of a husband’s income-tax return details to his estranged wife was not required because the details were
o: personal information and no larger public interest was shown
information permanently exempted by the Official Secrets Act
information held exclusively by the Central Information Commission
90.x: The Delhi High Court treated the income-tax return details as personal information and found no larger public interest justifying disclosure to the estranged wife.
90.tq: Match the privacy exemption with the absence of a larger public-interest justification.
90.sec: Landmark RTI judgements - issue decided

90.s: Which one of the following statements regarding recent RTI-related decisions is NOT correct?
o: The CIC held that BCCI was a public authority under Section 2(h) in May 2026.
The CIC had held in 2010 that the Rajiv Gandhi Foundation was not a public authority.
The Delhi High Court dismissed the 2011 plea to bring the Rajiv Gandhi Foundation under RTI because of non-appearance.
The CIC directed CBSE to disclose answer-book tender and procurement data that had been withheld under Section 8(1)(e).
90.x: Statement d is incorrect. The CIC ruled in May 2026 that BCCI was not a public authority under Section 2(h); the other statements correctly describe the reported decisions.
90.tq: Find the reversed public-authority conclusion among otherwise precise case descriptions.
90.sec: Landmark RTI judgements - issue decided

90.s:
Which of the following correctly describes the position after the RTI (Amendment) Act, 2019?
1. The term of CICs and ICs is as prescribed by the Central Government.
2. Their salaries are as prescribed by the Central Government.
3. The term of State Information Commissioners continues to be fixed independently in the RTI Act.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
90.x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct. Statement 3 is false because the amendment also placed the determination of the term of State Information Commissioners with the Central Government.
90.tq: Spot the unchanged-provision trap in the statement about State Information Commissioners.
90.sec: RTI (Amendment) Act 2019 and DPDP Act 2023 - provisions changed

90.s: Which of the following pairs correctly compares the salaries of information commissioners before and after the RTI (Amendment) Act, 2019?
o: Before: equal for all commissioners; After: fixed by the Supreme Court
Before: determined by the Finance Commission; After: determined by the Election Commission
Before: linked to the CEC, Election Commissioner, or Chief Secretary as applicable; After: fixed by the Central Government
Before: fixed by each State legislature; After: fixed by the President
90.x: At the central level, the CIC’s salary was equated with that of the Chief Election Commissioner and an IC’s with that of an Election Commissioner. At the State level, the State CIC and State IC were linked to the Election Commissioner and Chief Secretary respectively; after 2019, the Central Government fixes the salaries.
90.tq: Compare the authority and benchmark before and after the amendment instead of confusing tenure with salary.
90.sec: RTI (Amendment) Act 2019 and DPDP Act 2023 - provisions changed

90.s: The principal criticism of the 2019 changes relating to the tenure and salaries of Information Commissions is that they
o: removed the power of the Commissions to impose penalties
weakened the autonomy of the Commissions by placing tenure and pay in executive hands
made all decisions of the Commissions subject to approval by political parties
90.x: The criticism is that executive control over tenure and remuneration may weaken the institutional autonomy of the Information Commissions.
90.tq: Connect the institutional design change with its governance consequence.
90.sec: RTI (Amendment) Act 2019 and DPDP Act 2023 - provisions changed

90.s: Section 44(3) of the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 altered Section 8(1)(j) of the RTI Act by
o: making personal information a blanket exemption and dropping the earlier public-interest override
transferring all RTI appeals to the Data Protection Board
requiring every applicant to disclose the reason for seeking personal information
removing all exemptions relating to personal information
90.x: Section 44(3) rewrote Section 8(1)(j) to exempt personal information outright, dropping the earlier test concerning relationship to public activity, unwarranted invasion of privacy and the public-interest override.
90.tq: Contrast the original conditional privacy exemption with the amended blanket exemption.
90.sec: RTI (Amendment) Act 2019 and DPDP Act 2023 - provisions changed

90.s: Under the original Section 8(1)(j) of the RTI Act, personal information could be withheld when it was unrelated to public activity or involved an unwarranted invasion of privacy, subject to
o: approval by the concerned political party
a mandatory order of the Election Commission
90.x: The original provision contained a public-interest override, allowing disclosure where the larger public interest justified it. The DPDP amendment removed this safeguard by creating a blanket exemption for personal information.
90.tq: Distinguish the former conditional exemption from the later en-bloc embargo.
90.sec: RTI (Amendment) Act 2019 and DPDP Act 2023 - provisions changed

90.s:
Which of the following statements regarding the challenge to the DPDP amendment is correct?
1. The Centre notified the amendment in November 2025.
2. The Supreme Court referred the challenge to a Constitution Bench in February 2026.
3. On 7 August 2026, the Supreme Court agreed to examine whether the en-bloc embargo was repugnant to the RTI Act.
4. The Attorney-General opined that the amendment diluted the RTI Act.
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
90.x: Statements 1, 2 and 3 are correct. Statement 4 is false: the Attorney-General opined in January 2026 that the amendment did not dilute the RTI Act.
90.tq: Use the dated sequence and reject the statement that reverses the Attorney-General’s opinion.
90.sec: RTI (Amendment) Act 2019 and DPDP Act 2023 - provisions changed

90.s: In 2013, the Central Information Commission declared which of the following to be public authorities under the RTI Act?
o: Only political parties receiving foreign contributions
Only political parties represented in State legislatures
All registered political parties, including every local party
90.x: The CIC declared six national political parties to be public authorities in 2013. The parties did not comply with the direction, and the RTI (Amendment) Bill, 2013 seeking to exclude them later lapsed.
90.tq: Avoid expanding a precise institutional category into the broader class of all political parties.
90.sec: Public authority - political parties, NGOs, courts

90.s:
Consider the following statements about political parties and the RTI framework:
1. The six national parties declared public authorities by the CIC complied with the CIC’s direction.
2. The RTI (Amendment) Bill, 2013 seeking to exclude political parties lapsed.
3. Some accounts incorrectly state that the 2013 Bill had already removed political parties from the RTI framework.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
90.x: Statements 2 and 3 are correct. Statement 1 is false because the political parties did not comply with the CIC’s declaration; the Bill seeking exclusion lapsed, rather than successfully removing them.
90.tq: Separate an enacted legal change from a bill that merely lapsed.
90.sec: Public authority - political parties, NGOs, courts

90.s: An NGO substantially financed by the Government would be treated as a public authority under the RTI Act in accordance with which decision?
90.x: The DAV College Trust decision in 2019 recognised that NGOs substantially financed by the Government can fall within the meaning of public authority under the RTI Act.
90.tq: Match the statutory category of substantial government financing with the relevant case.
90.sec: Public authority - political parties, NGOs, courts

90.s:
Which of the following institutions or activities has been recognised as falling within the RTI framework in the stated manner?
1. Office of the Chief Justice of India — public authority
2. NGO substantially financed by Government — public authority
3. MPLADS works — covered by RTI
4. BCCI — public authority under Section 2(h)
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
90.x: Statements 1, 2 and 3 are correct. Statement 4 is false because the CIC ruled that BCCI is not a public authority under Section 2(h).
90.tq: Find the single reversed institutional classification among three covered categories.
90.sec: Public authority - political parties, NGOs, courts

90.s: As of July 2026, the approximate number of RTI appeals and complaints pending across Information Commissions was reported to be
90.x: More than 4 lakh RTI appeals and complaints were reported to be pending across Information Commissions as of July 2026.
90.tq: Use the exact numerical figure rather than being distracted by nearby order-of-magnitude options.
90.sec: Issues - pendency, vacancies, RTI activists

90.s: Which of the following is identified as a major institutional reason for delays in the disposal of RTI matters?
o: Absence of judicial review over RTI orders
Compulsory prior approval of Parliament for every RTI application
Chronic vacancies in the Central and State Information Commissions
90.x: Chronic vacancies in the Central Information Commission and State Information Commissions, together with a large backlog of appeals, cause long delays.
90.tq: Identify the institutional cause directly linked to the stated administrative consequence.
90.sec: Issues - pendency, vacancies, RTI activists

90.s:
Consider the following statements regarding the contemporary status of RTI institutions:
1. A 2025 report of Satark Nagrik Sangathan flagged significant gaps in Information Commissions.
2. The report was issued as the RTI Act approached its twentieth anniversary.
3. The report stated that all Information Commissions had completely eliminated pendency.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
90.x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct. Statement 3 is false because significant gaps and pendency remained in the Information Commissions.
90.tq: Reject the absolute claim that an institutional problem has been completely eliminated.
90.sec: Issues - pendency, vacancies, RTI activists

90.s: The Economic Survey 2025-26 suggested re-examination of the RTI framework mainly in the context of exempting which of the following categories of information?
o: Only information supplied by private bodies
All information held by local authorities
All records relating to public expenditure and contracts
Confidential service records and draft or exploratory policy discussions
90.x: The Economic Survey suggested considering exemptions for confidential service records and draft or exploratory policy discussions, along with a possible ministerial veto.
90.tq: Match the policy proposal with the specific categories named in it.
90.sec: Issues - pendency, vacancies, RTI activists

90.s: Which one of the following was proposed as a possible feature of the Economic Survey 2025-26's suggested re-examination of the RTI regime?
o: A ministerial veto over disclosure in specified cases
A complete abolition of Section 4 disclosure
Transfer of all Information Commissions to the Supreme Court
A constitutional amendment abolishing the right to know
90.x: The proposal included the possibility of a ministerial veto in relation to certain confidential or draft policy information.
90.tq: Distinguish the specific proposed institutional safeguard from exaggerated alternatives.
90.sec: Issues - pendency, vacancies, RTI activists

90.s: The 2019 amendment to the RTI Act raised concerns about the autonomy of Information Commissions because it empowered the Central Government to determine their
o: appointment of all Public Information Officers
jurisdiction over constitutional disputes and writ petitions
90.x: The 2019 amendment allowed the Central Government to prescribe the tenure and salaries of Information Commissioners, raising autonomy concerns.
90.tq: Apply the ‘who controls the service conditions?’ method to identify the autonomy issue.
90.sec: Issues - pendency, vacancies, RTI activists

90.s:
Arrange the following events in chronological order:
A. Passage of the RTI Bill by the Lok Sabha
B. Passage of the RTI Bill by the Rajya Sabha
C. Presidential assent to the RTI Act
D. Full commencement of the RTI Act
Select the correct sequence.
90.x: The Lok Sabha passed the Bill on 11 May 2005, the Rajya Sabha on 12 May 2005, assent was given on 15 June 2005, and the Act fully came into force on 12 October 2005.
90.tq: Fix the first and last events, then place the two parliamentary stages between them.
90.sec: Commencement - assent, enactment and coming into force

90.s: Which of the following provisions came into force immediately upon enactment of the RTI Act, along with Sections 4(1), 5 and 12?
90.x: Sections 13, 15, 16 and 24 were among the provisions that came into force immediately, along with Sections 4(1), 5 and 12.
90.tq: Test the exception to the general commencement date by recalling the specified section cluster.
90.sec: Commencement - assent, enactment and coming into force

90.s: Under Section 2(f) of the RTI Act, which of the following is included within the meaning of ‘information’?
o: Information personally generated by an applicant after filing a request
Only physical records maintained by public authorities
Material in any form, including records, e-mails, opinions, contracts, samples and electronic data
Only final judicial decisions published in the Gazette
90.x: Section 2(f) covers material in any form, including records, documents, e-mails, opinions, advice, contracts, samples, models and electronic data.
90.tq: Choose the option reflecting the broad statutory wording ‘material in any form’.
90.sec: Meaning of 'information' and 'right to information'

90.s: Information relating to a private body is accessible under Section 2(f) when it is
o: accessible to a public authority under a law
requested only by a government servant
held by any private individual in any circumstances
90.x: Information concerning a private body is covered when it is accessible to a public authority under a law.
90.tq: Apply the statutory limiting condition instead of treating all private information as automatically accessible.
90.sec: Meaning of 'information' and 'right to information'

90.s: Which of the following is NOT a component of the ‘right to information’ under Section 2(j)?
o: Compelling an authority to create a new explanation or opinion
Taking notes, extracts or certified copies
Inspection of works, documents and records
90.x: Section 2(j) includes inspection, notes, extracts, certified copies, certified samples and electronic information. It does not require an authority to create a new explanation or opinion.
90.tq: Find the option that demands creation of information rather than access to existing information.
90.sec: Meaning of 'information' and 'right to information'

90.s: A citizen seeks information from a public authority by e-mail in the local official language and claims the BPL fee waiver. Which of the following is correct?
o: The local official language may be used only before a State Information Commission
The request is invalid because only English applications are permitted
The request is valid in principle, and the fee is waived for a BPL applicant
E-mail requests are valid only when made by a public servant
90.x: An RTI request may be made by post, in person or by e-mail in Hindi, English or the local official language. The application fee is waived for applicants below the poverty line.
90.tq: Combine the rules on mode, language and fee waiver in a practical situation.
90.sec: Meaning of 'information' and 'right to information'

90.s:
With reference to the nature and constitutional basis of the RTI, consider the following statements:
1. The RTI is a statutory right.
2. It gives effect to the fundamental right to know under Article 19(1)(a).
3. It is available to every person, irrespective of citizenship.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
90.x: The RTI is a statutory right giving effect to the fundamental right to know under Article 19(1)(a). Under the Act, only citizens can apply, so statement 3 is false.
90.tq: Separate the constitutional rationale from the statutory eligibility condition.
90.sec: Meaning of 'information' and 'right to information'

90.s: Which of the following is NOT among the stated objectives of the RTI Act?
o: Promoting transparency and an informed citizenry
Harmonising disclosure with legitimate confidentiality needs
Replacing the entire system of representative government with direct administration
Containing corruption and holding governments accountable
90.x: The Act seeks transparency, accountability, reduced corruption and an informed citizenry while recognising confidentiality needs. It does not seek to replace representative government.
90.tq: Identify the option unrelated to the stated purposes of the legislation.
90.sec: Meaning of 'information' and 'right to information'

90.s: Who is empowered to impose the penalty under Section 20 of the RTI Act?
o: The Central or State Information Commission
The applicant through a private complaint
90.x: The Central Information Commission or State Information Commission may impose the Section 20 penalty on the concerned Public Information Officer.
90.tq: Use the ‘who would do this job?’ method to identify the statutory authority imposing the penalty.
90.sec: Penalties on PIOs and compensation

90.s: The penalty under Section 20 of the RTI Act is imposed at the rate of
o: ₹500 per day, subject to a maximum of ₹50,000
₹100 per day, subject to a maximum of ₹10,000
₹1,000 per day, without any maximum limit
₹250 per day, subject to a maximum of ₹25,000
90.x: The penalty is ₹250 per day until the application is received or information is furnished, subject to a maximum of ₹25,000.
90.tq: Recall both parts of the penalty formula: daily rate and statutory ceiling.
90.sec: Penalties on PIOs and compensation

90.s: Which one of the following is NOT a stated ground for imposing a penalty on a Public Information Officer?
o: Disclosing information within the prescribed time
Knowingly giving incorrect or misleading information
Refusing to receive an RTI application
Destroying information or obstructing its disclosure
90.x: Penalty grounds include refusal to receive an application, delay, mala fide denial, knowingly incorrect or misleading information, destruction of information and obstruction. Timely disclosure is not a ground for penalty.
90.tq: Find the conduct that is compliant rather than penal in nature.
90.sec: Penalties on PIOs and compensation

90.s: Before imposing a penalty under Section 20, the Public Information Officer
o: must be removed from service immediately
must obtain permission from the applicant
must be given an opportunity of being heard
must prove the applicant's mala fides
90.x: The PIO must be heard before penalty is imposed. The burden of proof in the penalty proceeding lies on the PIO.
90.tq: Distinguish procedural fairness from the separate rule regarding burden of proof.
90.sec: Penalties on PIOs and compensation

90.s: In proceedings relating to penalty under Section 20, the burden of proof is placed on the
90.x: The burden of proof is on the Public Information Officer in the Section 20 penalty proceeding.
90.tq: Track the statutory burden rather than assuming that the complainant must prove the entire case.
90.sec: Penalties on PIOs and compensation

90.s: Apart from imposing a monetary penalty, the Information Commission may also
o: amend the RTI Act by executive order
recommend disciplinary action against the PIO
90.x: The Commission may recommend disciplinary action against the Public Information Officer in addition to imposing the statutory penalty.
90.tq: Separate the Commission’s disciplinary recommendation from powers belonging to other authorities.
90.sec: Penalties on PIOs and compensation

90.s: Under Section 19(8)(b), the Information Commission may require the public authority to
o: provide lifetime employment to the applicant
compensate the applicant for loss suffered
pay a penalty directly to the Information Commissioner
90.x: Section 19(8)(b) enables the Commission to require the public authority to compensate the applicant for any loss or other detriment suffered.
90.tq: Distinguish compensation for the applicant from the separate penalty imposed on the PIO.
90.sec: Penalties on PIOs and compensation

90.s:
Which of the following is the most appropriate description of the achievements attributed to the RTI Act?
1. It has helped break the culture of secrecy.
2. It has strengthened citizen participation and service delivery.
3. It has reduced corruption and misuse of public funds.
4. It has completely eliminated corruption in public administration.
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
90.x: The Act has helped break secrecy, improve accountability, reduce corruption and misuse of public funds, and strengthen participation and service delivery. It has not completely eliminated corruption.
90.tq: Reject the extreme claim of complete elimination while retaining the qualified achievements.
90.sec: Achievements vs misuse - transparency gains, frivolous and vexatious applications

90.s:
Assertion (A): The RTI Act has generally increased the sense of responsibility in the bureaucracy.
Reason (R): The Act has made access to government information more transparent and has strengthened accountability.
o: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
90.x: Both statements are true. Greater transparency and accountability provide the basis for increased responsibility among officials.
90.tq: Test whether the reason explains the administrative effect stated in the assertion.
90.sec: Achievements vs misuse - transparency gains, frivolous and vexatious applications

90.s: Which of the following is an example of misuse of the RTI Act by applicants?
o: Using information to participate in public affairs
Seeking certified copies of government documents
Using RTI for frivolous or vexatious personal disputes and blackmail
Making a request for inspection of public records
90.x: Frivolous, vexatious or bulk applications, including use of RTI for personal disputes or blackmail, are identified as forms of applicant misuse.
90.tq: Distinguish legitimate access to records from demands made for harassment or private leverage.
90.sec: Achievements vs misuse - transparency gains, frivolous and vexatious applications

90.s: Which one of the following is correctly matched?
o: Applicants — excessive use of Section 8 to deny information
Public authorities — frivolous personal disputes and blackmail
Applicants — clogging offices with indiscriminate demands
Public authorities — use of RTI for private disputes
90.x: C—even offices with indiscriminate demands is attributed to misuse by applicants. Excessive use of Section 8, delays and misleading replies are forms of misuse by public authorities.
90.tq: Separate the two columns by identifying who performs the action rather than focusing only on the action itself.
90.sec: Achievements vs misuse - transparency gains, frivolous and vexatious applications

90.s: Which of the following represents misuse of the RTI Act by public authorities?
o: Making bulk applications for personal disputes
Excessive and bad-faith use of Section 8 exemptions to deny information
90.x: Public-authority misuse includes excessive or bad-faith reliance on Section 8 exemptions, along with delayed, incomplete or misleading replies and weak proactive disclosure.
90.tq: Use the actor-based distinction between applicant misuse and authority misuse.
90.sec: Achievements vs misuse - transparency gains, frivolous and vexatious applications

90.s:
Assertion (A): The RTI Act has been misused by both members of the public and public authorities.
Reason (R): Applicants may file frivolous or bulk requests, while authorities may delay replies or invoke Section 8 in bad faith.
o: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
90.x: Both the assertion and reason are true. The reason identifies the two distinct forms of misuse by applicants and public authorities.
90.tq: Link the general conclusion to concrete examples supplied in the reason.
90.sec: Achievements vs misuse - transparency gains, frivolous and vexatious applications

90.s: The Economic Survey 2025-26 described India's RTI regime as ‘uniquely broad’ and associated it with a possible chilling effect on
90.x: The Economic Survey associated the uniquely broad RTI regime with a possible chilling effect on honest decision-making and proposed re-examination of the framework.
90.tq: Match the distinctive quoted description with the precise effect linked to it.
90.sec: Achievements vs misuse - transparency gains, frivolous and vexatious applications

90.s: Which of the following correctly describes the risks faced by RTI activists and whistle-blowers?
o: They are automatically protected from prosecution under the RTI Act
They may face harassment, legal intimidation and physical attacks
They are prohibited from seeking information about public authorities
They face only civil liability for filing applications
90.x: RTI activists and whistle-blowers face harassment, legal intimidation and physical attacks in connection with their disclosures and applications.
90.tq: Select the option that captures the complete range of risks rather than a single form of pressure.
90.sec: RTI activists' safety - attacks and whistle-blower protection

90.s: More than how many RTI activists were reported to have been killed by July 2026?
90.x: Reports cited that more than 100 RTI activists had been killed by July 2026.
90.tq: Recall the reported threshold and avoid confusing it with lower estimates.
90.sec: Issues - pendency, vacancies, RTI activists

90.s: The Second Administrative Reforms Commission recommended that the RTI framework should be linked firmly with
90.x: The Second Administrative Reforms Commission recommended firmly linking RTI with whistle-blower protection to prevent victimisation of those who disclose information.
90.tq: Identify the protection mechanism that directly addresses victimisation of information-seekers.
90.sec: RTI activists' safety - attacks and whistle-blower protection

90.s:
Consider the following statements about whistle-blower protection in India:
1. The Whistle Blowers Protection Act was enacted in 2014.
2. The Act has not been operationalised.
3. A 2015 amendment Bill sought to dilute the Act.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
90.x: All three statements are correct: the Whistle Blowers Protection Act, 2014 exists, has not been operationalised, and a 2015 amendment Bill sought to dilute it.
90.tq: Use the complete sequence of enactment, non-operationalisation and proposed dilution.
90.sec: RTI activists' safety - attacks and whistle-blower protection

90.s: Which one of the following best explains the recommendation to protect RTI activists through whistle-blower legislation?
o: To exempt activists from all criminal laws
To allow activists to impose penalties on Public Information Officers
To enable activists to appoint Information Commissioners
To prevent victimisation for exposing information in the public interest
90.x: The recommendation seeks to prevent victimisation, harassment and attacks against persons who disclose information in the public interest.
90.tq: Connect the institutional recommendation with the harm it is intended to prevent.
90.sec: RTI activists' safety - attacks and whistle-blower protection

90.s: Which one of the following was NOT among the six national political parties declared public authorities by the Central Information Commission in June 2013?
90.x: The six parties were INC, BJP, CPI, CPI(M), NCP and BSP. The Aam Aadmi Party was not included in that CIC order.
90.tq: Find the odd name by recalling the complete six-party list.
90.sec: Political parties under RTI - CIC order and compliance

90.s:
Consider the following statements regarding the demand to bring political parties under the Right to Information Act:
1. It is intended to help check corruption and crony capitalism.
2. It seeks greater scrutiny of illegal foreign contributions.
3. It is linked with the state privileges enjoyed by political parties, including free airtime on Doordarshan.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
90.x: All three statements describe the reasons advanced by activists for bringing political parties under RTI.
90.tq: Test the cumulative rationale by checking each policy objective separately.
90.sec: Political parties under RTI - CIC order and compliance

90.s:
With reference to political parties and the Right to Information Act, consider the following statements:
1. The RTI Act expressly named political parties as public authorities when it was enacted in 2005.
2. The six parties declared public authorities by the CIC did not comply with the order.
3. The issue was pending before the Supreme Court in the position described.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
90.x: Statement 1 is false because the 2005 Act did not expressly name political parties. Statements 2 and 3 are correct in the stated position.
90.tq: Spot the wrong historical premise concerning the original wording of the Act.
90.sec: Political parties under RTI - CIC order and compliance

90.s: The 2026 demand concerning recognised national political parties under the Right to Information framework primarily seeks which of the following?
o: A transparent and auditable electoral-funding system
Abolition of all public funding of elections
Transfer of election expenditure to the Supreme Court
Removal of political parties from Section 2(h)
90.x: The 2026 demand was to bring recognised national parties under RTI along with a transparent and auditable electoral-funding system.
90.tq: Identify the precise institutional reform rather than an extreme alternative.
90.sec: Political parties under RTI - CIC order and compliance

90.s: Section 4 of the Right to Information Act, 2005 is primarily associated with which of the following?
o: Imposition of penalty on every delayed applicant
Compulsory adjudication of all RTI appeals by courts
Exemption of personal information from disclosure
Suo motu disclosure by public authorities
90.x: Section 4 mandates proactive or suo motu disclosure by public authorities, reducing the need for citizens to file separate applications.
90.tq: Match the statutory section with its distinctive function.
90.sec: Proactive disclosure compliance - Section 4 audits

90.s:
The Second Administrative Reforms Commission recommended, in the context of RTI, that:
1. Maximum information should automatically be placed in the public domain.
2. Section 8 exemptions should be interpreted narrowly.
3. Citizens should be required to file applications even for routinely publishable information.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
90.x: Statements 1 and 2 reflect the recommendation. Statement 3 is contrary to proactive disclosure because routinely publishable information should be available without an application.
90.tq: Reject the statement that reverses the purpose of proactive disclosure.
90.sec: Proactive disclosure compliance - Section 4 audits

90.s: The Andhra Pradesh Information Commission inspected how many offices in how many districts while examining compliance with Section 4(1)(b)?
90.x: The inspection covered 258 offices across 18 districts and found violations of Section 4(1)(b).
90.tq: Separate the two linked figures and reject reversed or altered numerical pairs.
90.sec: Proactive disclosure compliance - Section 4 audits

90.s: Which of the following correctly describes the Action Taken Reports published by the Andhra Pradesh Secretariat from 22 June 2026?
o: They concerned only District Mineral Foundation expenditure.
They concerned six constitutional amendments and were issued by the CIC.
They concerned seven sector white papers and reflected proactive disclosure under Section 4.
They concerned RTI penalties imposed on political parties.
90.x: From 22 June 2026, the AP Secretariat published Action Taken Reports on seven sector white papers as an example of disclosure in the spirit of Section 4.
90.tq: Use the who-what-when combination to distinguish a current-affairs fact from nearby RTI issues.
90.sec: Proactive disclosure compliance - Section 4 audits

90.s: Which of the following pairs is correctly matched?
o: MPLADS works — tracked through the eSAKSHI portal
District Mineral Foundations — exempt from online publication of plans
Section 4(1)(b) — prohibition on suo motu disclosure
Seven sector white papers — disclosure beginning in 2013 through the central RTI portal
90.x: MPLADS works are subject to RTI and are tracked through the eSAKSHI portal. The other pairs incorrectly describe the relevant disclosure requirements or dates.
90.tq: Start with the sure scheme-portal pair and eliminate mismatched statutory functions and dates.
90.sec: Proactive disclosure compliance - Section 4 audits

90.s: The RTI Online portal of the Department of Personnel and Training was launched in which year?
90.x: The central RTI Online portal, rtionline.gov.in, was launched in 2013 by the Department of Personnel and Training.
90.tq: Test the launch year directly against nearby RTI milestone years.
90.sec: Online RTI portals - central and Andhra Pradesh

90.s: The central RTI Online portal primarily facilitates which of the following?
o: Applications exclusively concerning Andhra Pradesh public authorities
Applications and first appeals concerning central public authorities, with online fee payment
Only appeals against orders of State Information Commissions
Filing of criminal complaints against public servants
90.x: The portal at rtionline.gov.in enables filing of RTI applications and first appeals to central public authorities and provides online fee payment.
90.tq: Identify the correct jurisdiction and function of the digital platform.
90.sec: Online RTI portals - central and Andhra Pradesh

90.s: Which one of the following statements best expresses the e-governance approach associated with RTI?
o: Digital disclosure should be mandated so that information is easy to reach.
Only information specifically requested by a citizen should be placed online.
Digital systems should replace every statutory appeal under the RTI Act.
Online disclosure should be restricted to Union public authorities.
