The CBI is a statutory body established directly by the Central Vigilance Commission Act, 2003.
The CBI derives its powers from the Delhi Special Police Establishment Act, 1946 and is associated with the Department of Personnel and Training.
The CBI derives its powers exclusively from the Lokpal and Lokayuktas Act, 2013.
98.x: The CBI is non-statutory in itself and draws its powers from the DSPE Act, 1946. It is associated with the Department of Personnel and Training.
98.tq: Distinguish an organisation's operational source of power from its own constitutional or statutory status.
98.sec: Statutory bodies → parent Act and ministry  [APPSC]

98.s: The Director of the Central Bureau of Investigation is chosen by a committee consisting of the Prime Minister, the Chief Justice of India or nominee, and the:
o: Leader of the Opposition in the Lok Sabha
98.x: The CBI Director is selected by a committee comprising the Prime Minister, the Chief Justice of India or a nominee, and the Leader of the Opposition.
98.tq: Identify the correct appointing or selection authority by separating it from nearby constitutional offices.
98.sec: Statutory bodies → parent Act and ministry  [APPSC]

98.s: Under Section 6 of the Delhi Special Police Establishment Act, the Central Bureau of Investigation generally requires which of the following?
o: Prior consent of the concerned State Government
Consent of the Supreme Court in every case
Approval of the Election Commission of India
98.x: Section 6 of the DSPE Act requires the consent of the concerned State Government for exercising CBI powers in that State. Several States have withdrawn general consent.
98.tq: Ask which authority must consent when a central investigative agency operates within a State.
98.sec: Statutory bodies → parent Act and ministry  [APPSC]

98.s: The origin of the Central Bureau of Investigation is associated with which committee and period?
98.x: The origin of the CBI is associated with the Santhanam Committee of 1962–63.
98.tq: Match the institution with the committee and period specifically linked to its origin.
98.sec: Statutory bodies → parent Act and ministry  [APPSC]

98.s:
Which of the following pairs is correctly matched with the method of creation and nature of the body?

1. Planning Commission — Government resolution — Advisory body
2. National Development Council — Executive resolution — Executive coordinating body
3. NITI Aayog — Cabinet resolution — Think tank
4. Law Commission — Department of Legal Affairs notification — Advisory research body
98.x: All four pairs are correct. These bodies are not created as constitutional bodies by the Constitution; they arise through resolutions or executive notifications and perform advisory or coordinating functions.
98.tq: Test creation mechanism and institutional nature together instead of treating all non-constitutional bodies alike.
98.sec: Executive/non-statutory bodies - resolution-based, advisory (NITI Aayog, Planning Commission, NDC, Law Commission)  [APPSC]

98.s: The Planning Commission was created by a Government resolution in:
98.x: The Planning Commission was created by a Government resolution in March 1950. The Advisory Planning Board associated with K.C. Neogi preceded it in 1946.
98.tq: Use the year and month to distinguish the Planning Commission from other resolution-based bodies.
98.sec: Executive/non-statutory bodies - resolution-based, advisory (NITI Aayog, Planning Commission, NDC, Law Commission)  [APPSC]

98.s: Which one of the following statements about the Planning Commission is correct?
o: It was a constitutional body under Article 263.
It was chaired by the President and included all Chief Ministers as members.
It was a statutory body chaired by the Union Finance Minister.
It was an advisory body chaired by the Prime Minister, and the States were not represented in it.
98.x: The Planning Commission was an advisory body created by Government resolution, chaired by the Prime Minister; the States were not represented in its composition.
98.tq: Separate chairperson, nature and representation from the arrangements of the NDC and NITI Aayog.
98.sec: Executive/non-statutory bodies - resolution-based, advisory (NITI Aayog, Planning Commission, NDC, Law Commission)  [APPSC]

98.s:
Consider the following statements regarding the National Development Council:
1. It includes the Prime Minister, all Union Cabinet Ministers, all Chief Ministers and Union Territory Administrators.
2. All Union Cabinet Ministers became members of it from 1967.
3. It was created by an executive resolution.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
98.x: All three statements are correct. The NDC was created by executive resolution and includes the listed Union and State-level leadership, with all Union Cabinet Ministers included from 1967.
98.tq: Combine original creation, later composition and membership categories in a coded statement question.
98.sec: Executive/non-statutory bodies - resolution-based, advisory (NITI Aayog, Planning Commission, NDC, Law Commission)  [APPSC]

98.s: Which one of the following correctly describes the Governing Council of NITI Aayog?
o: It consists only of Union Cabinet Ministers and Governors of States.
It consists of the President, Vice-President and all Governors of States.
It consists of all Chief Ministers and Lieutenant Governors of Union Territories, with the Prime Minister as Chairperson of NITI Aayog.
It consists of Members of Parliament nominated by the Speaker of the Lok Sabha.
98.x: NITI Aayog is a think tank with the Prime Minister as Chairperson, and its Governing Council includes all Chief Ministers and Lieutenant Governors of Union Territories.
98.tq: Identify the correct membership pattern by contrasting it with constitutional bodies and the former Planning Commission.
98.sec: Executive/non-statutory bodies - resolution-based, advisory (NITI Aayog, Planning Commission, NDC, Law Commission)  [APPSC]

98.s: The Sarkaria Commission recommended that the National Development Council should be given constitutional status under Article 263 and renamed as the:
98.x: The Sarkaria Commission recommended constitutional status for the NDC under Article 263 and proposed the name National Economic and Development Council.
98.tq: Match a commission recommendation with the precise proposed institutional name and Article.
98.sec: Executive/non-statutory bodies - resolution-based, advisory (NITI Aayog, Planning Commission, NDC, Law Commission)  [APPSC]

98.s:
Consider the following statements about the Law Commission of India:
1. It is a constitutional body.
2. It is a quasi-judicial body that advises the President.
3. It is an advisory research body that makes recommendations to the Government.
4. It reports to the Ministry of Law and Justice.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
98.x: Statements 1 and 2 are false. The Law Commission is neither constitutional nor statutory nor quasi-judicial, and it advises the Government rather than the President; statements 3 and 4 are correct.
98.tq: Reject familiar but incorrect labels by distinguishing advisory research from constitutional and quasi-judicial functions.
98.sec: Executive/non-statutory bodies - resolution-based, advisory (NITI Aayog, Planning Commission, NDC, Law Commission)  [APPSC]

98.s: The Law Commission is constituted through a notification issued by the:
98.x: The Law Commission is constituted through a notification of the Department of Legal Affairs and is constituted every three years.
98.tq: Identify the issuing department rather than the broader ministry commonly associated with the subject.
98.sec: Executive/non-statutory bodies - resolution-based, advisory (NITI Aayog, Planning Commission, NDC, Law Commission)  [APPSC]

98.s: The 23rd Law Commission of India covers which period?
98.x: The 23rd Law Commission operates from 1 September 2024 to 31 August 2027.
98.tq: Read both the starting and ending dates carefully; close periods are used as distractors.
98.sec: Executive/non-statutory bodies - resolution-based, advisory (NITI Aayog, Planning Commission, NDC, Law Commission)  [APPSC]

98.s: Who chaired the first Law Commission of India constituted in 1834?
98.x: The first Law Commission, constituted in 1834, was chaired by Lord Macaulay.
98.tq: Associate the earliest commission with its chairperson and distinguish it from the first post-Independence commission.
98.sec: Executive/non-statutory bodies - resolution-based, advisory (NITI Aayog, Planning Commission, NDC, Law Commission)  [APPSC]

98.s: The first Law Commission constituted after Independence in 1955 was chaired by:
98.x: The first Law Commission after Independence was constituted in 1955 under the chairmanship of M.C. Setalvad.
98.tq: Use the qualifying phrase ‘after Independence’ to avoid confusing two different first commissions.
98.sec: Executive/non-statutory bodies - resolution-based, advisory (NITI Aayog, Planning Commission, NDC, Law Commission)

98.s: Which one of the following bodies was established first?
o: Public Service Commission at the central level
98.x: The predecessor of the UPSC, the Public Service Commission, was established in 1926. The Federal Public Service Commission followed under the Government of India Act, 1935, and the UPSC came into existence in 1950.
98.tq: Use the earliest date to eliminate the later constitutional bodies.
98.sec: Bodies → year of establishment

98.s:
Consider the following pairs:
1. Election Commission of India — 1950
2. First Finance Commission — 1951
3. National Development Council — 1952
4. Inter-State Council — 1990
Which of the pairs given above are correctly matched?
98.x: All four pairs are correctly matched. The Election Commission was established in 1950, the first Finance Commission in 1951, the National Development Council in 1952 and the Inter-State Council in 1990.
98.tq: Check each year independently before selecting the coded combination.
98.sec: Bodies → year of establishment

98.s: Which one of the following sequences correctly represents the establishment years of the Inter-State Council, NCM and NHRC?
98.x: The Inter-State Council was established in 1990, the NCM in 1992 and the NHRC in 1993.
98.tq: Arrange the institutions by their establishment years.
98.sec: Bodies → year of establishment

98.s:
With reference to the Securities and Exchange Board of India, consider the following statements:
1. SEBI was initially set up by a resolution in 1988.
2. SEBI acquired statutory status under the SEBI Act, 1992.
3. SEBI was a constitutional body before becoming statutory.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
98.x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct. SEBI was initially established through a 1988 resolution and became a statutory body under the SEBI Act, 1992; it was not a constitutional body.
98.tq: Reject the wrong-status statement by distinguishing non-statutory, statutory and constitutional bodies.
98.sec: Bodies whose status changed (NCBC, SEBI, NCSC/NCST) → amendment or Act

98.s: Which of the following pairs is NOT correctly matched?
98.x: The NCBC acquired constitutional status under the 102nd Constitutional Amendment Act, 2018, and Article 338B. The 89th Amendment Act, 2003, relates to the separation of the NCSC and NCST.
98.tq: Find the institution-amendment mismatch rather than the correctly matched statutory bodies.
98.sec: Bodies whose status changed (NCBC, SEBI, NCSC/NCST) → amendment or Act

98.s: Which one of the following best describes a quasi-judicial body?
o: A constitutional court exercising the complete jurisdiction of the Supreme Court
A purely advisory body with no authority to apply law
An executive department that can make laws without statutory authority
A non-judicial body empowered to interpret and apply law, examine matters, summon persons and impose sanctions under statutory authority
98.x: A quasi-judicial body is not a court, but it can interpret and apply law, examine matters, summon persons and impose sanctions under authority granted by a statute.
98.tq: Identify the defining combination of statutory authority and non-court adjudicatory functions.
98.sec: Quasi-judicial bodies - defining features, civil court powers

98.s: Which one of the following is NOT generally regarded as a quasi-judicial body in the context described?
o: Securities and Exchange Board of India
98.x: NITI Aayog is an advisory body and is not quasi-judicial. NHRC, SEBI and CIC are examples of bodies having quasi-judicial features.
98.tq: Remove the advisory institution from the group of bodies that apply law or adjudicate statutory matters.
98.sec: Quasi-judicial bodies - defining features, civil court powers

98.s: Which of the following bodies has civil court powers such as summoning witnesses and requisitioning records?
98.x: The NCBC has powers of a civil court, including summoning witnesses and requisitioning records, particularly after it received constitutional status in 2018.
98.tq: Use the ‘civil court powers’ clue to distinguish commissions from advisory bodies.
98.sec: Quasi-judicial bodies - defining features, civil court powers

98.s:
Consider the following statements:
1. NHRC has powers of a civil court in specified matters.
2. NCM has powers of a civil court in specified matters.
3. CIC exercises such powers under the Right to Information Act.
4. The Law Commission is a quasi-judicial body with civil court powers.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
98.x: Statements 1, 2 and 3 are correct. The Law Commission is advisory and is not a quasi-judicial body with civil court powers.
98.tq: Test the exception by separating advisory bodies from statutory quasi-judicial bodies.
98.sec: Quasi-judicial bodies - defining features, civil court powers

98.s: The State Election Commission derives its constitutional basis for conducting elections to Panchayats and municipalities respectively from:
98.x: Article 243K relates to elections to Panchayats and Article 243ZA relates to elections to municipalities. Both fall within the constitutional framework of the State Election Commission.
98.tq: Match each state-level election function with its specific constitutional article.
98.sec: State counterparts → Article/Act

98.s: The State Finance Commission is constituted under Articles 243I and 243Y to review finances of:
o: State Public Service Commissions and Joint Public Service Commissions
98.x: Article 243I concerns the finances of Panchayats, while Article 243Y extends the corresponding framework to municipalities. The State Finance Commission is constituted every five years.
98.tq: Link the Finance Commission articles with the two levels of local government.
98.sec: State counterparts → Article/Act

98.s:
With reference to State Commissions for Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes, consider the following statements:
1. They are established under State laws.
2. Article 338(9) and Article 338A(9) make consultation with the national commissions mandatory on major policy matters.
3. They are directly created as constitutional bodies under Article 338 and Article 338A.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
98.x: State SC and ST Commissions are established under State laws. Articles 338(9) and 338A(9) require consultation with the national commissions on major policy matters; the State commissions themselves are not directly created by Articles 338 and 338A.
98.tq: Distinguish the constitutional national commissions from state commissions created by state law.
98.sec: State counterparts → Article/Act

98.s: Which one of the following correctly describes the procedure for the UPSC annual report?
o: It is submitted to the Prime Minister and laid before the Rajya Sabha only.
It is submitted directly to the Speaker of the Lok Sabha without any memorandum.
It is submitted to the President and laid before Parliament with a memorandum explaining non-acceptance of advice, if any.
It is submitted to the Governor and laid before the State Legislature.
98.x: Under Article 323, the UPSC submits its annual report to the President. It is laid before Parliament along with a memorandum explaining cases where its advice was not accepted.
98.tq: Use the constitutional recipient and the accompanying memorandum as the decisive clues.
98.sec: Reports of constitutional bodies → to whom submitted and where laid

98.s:
Consider the following pairs:
1. Finance Commission — President; Parliament with an explanatory memorandum
2. SPSC — Governor; State Legislature
3. Joint SPSC — Each Governor concerned; Each State Legislature
4. NCSC, NCST and NCBC — President; Parliament
Which of the pairs given above are correctly matched?
98.x: All four pairs are correctly matched. The Finance Commission report is laid with an explanatory memorandum, while the other listed commissions follow the recipients and legislatures specified in the pairs.
98.tq: Verify both columns—recipient and legislature—rather than matching only the institution.
98.sec: Reports of constitutional bodies → to whom submitted and where laid

98.s: The report of the Special Officer for Linguistic Minorities is submitted to the President and:
o: submitted to the Inter-State Council for approval
laid only before the Lok Sabha
laid before Parliament and sent to the States
laid only before the concerned State Legislatures
98.x: Under Article 350B, the report of the Special Officer for Linguistic Minorities is submitted to the President, laid before Parliament and also sent to the concerned States.
98.tq: Remember the additional transmission to the States as the distinguishing feature.
98.sec: Reports of constitutional bodies → to whom submitted and where laid

98.s: Which one of the following statements regarding the consideration of annual reports of constitutional bodies is correct?
o: Only the Lok Sabha considers them because financial accountability is involved.
Only the Rajya Sabha considers them because constitutional bodies are appointed by the Union.
They are considered only by the President and not by Parliament.
Both Houses consider them, and the Rajya Sabha has equal status with the Lok Sabha in this matter.
98.x: Both Houses of Parliament consider the annual reports of bodies such as the CAG, Finance Commission and UPSC. The Rajya Sabha has equal status with the Lok Sabha in this regard.
98.tq: Reject the common trap that financial or constitutional reports belong exclusively to the Lok Sabha.
98.sec: Reports of constitutional bodies → to whom submitted and where laid

98.s: In the order of precedence, which of the following groups is placed at rank 9A?
o: Chairperson of UPSC, Chief Election Commissioner and Comptroller and Auditor General
Chairpersons of NCM, NCSC and NCST
Chairperson of the Finance Commission, Attorney General and Cabinet Secretary
Chairpersons of the State Election Commission and State Finance Commission
98.x: The Chairperson of the UPSC, the Chief Election Commissioner and the CAG are placed at rank 9A in the order of precedence. The Chairpersons of NCM, NCSC and NCST are placed at rank 17.
98.tq: Compare the two stated rank groups instead of relying on the constitutional status of the bodies.
98.sec: Universal angles

98.s: Which one of the following pairs is correctly matched with rank in the order of precedence?
98.x: The Chairpersons of NCM, NCSC and NCST are placed at rank 17. The UPSC Chairperson, CEC and CAG are placed at rank 9A.
98.tq: Detect the reversed rank by comparing the three commission chairpersons with the constitutional office-holders.
98.sec: Universal angles

98.s: Which one of the following current developments is associated with the Andhra Pradesh State Commission for Scheduled Castes?
o: It acquired constitutional status under the 102nd Amendment in August 2026.
It submitted the Union CAG report to Parliament in August 2026.
It reviewed SC/ST welfare schemes in Nellore district in August 2026.
It replaced the National Commission for Minorities in August 2026.
98.x: The Andhra Pradesh State SC Commission, chaired by K.S. Jawahar, reviewed SC/ST welfare schemes in Nellore district in August 2026.
98.tq: Match the current event with the correct state commission, place and activity.
98.sec: Universal angles

98.s: The withdrawal of general consent by States for the Central Bureau of Investigation is described as a continuing issue of:
98.x: Withdrawals of general consent for CBI investigations remain a federal flashpoint because they concern the relationship between the Union investigative agency and State governments.
98.tq: Identify the federal dimension of a dispute involving Union and State executive authority.
98.sec: Universal angles

99.s: Which one of the following correctly describes the Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority of India (IRDAI)?
o: A statutory body under the IRDA Act, 1999, regulating insurance and reinsurance companies
A constitutional body regulating only life insurance
A statutory body under the SEBI Act, 1992, regulating pension funds
A non-statutory body under the Companies Act, 2013, regulating banks
99.x: IRDAI is a statutory body constituted under the IRDA Act, 1999. It is the apex regulator of insurance and reinsurance companies.
99.tq: Use the establishing Act and regulated sector to eliminate swapped-body options.
99.sec: IRDAI - statutory basis, recommending committee, year, sector regulated, expert panels

99.s: The opening of the insurance sector to private participation was associated with which legislation?
o: Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority Act, 1999
Pension Fund Regulatory and Development Authority Act, 2013
Securities and Exchange Board of India Act, 1992
99.x: The IRDA Act, 1999 opened the insurance sector to private participation and provided the statutory basis for IRDAI.
99.tq: Match the reform outcome with the correct establishing legislation.
99.sec: IRDAI - statutory basis, recommending committee, year, sector regulated, expert panels

99.s: The establishment of IRDAI was recommended by the:
99.x: The Malhotra Committee recommended insurance-sector reforms that led to the establishment of IRDAI. The Gadgil Committee is the confusable but incorrect option here.
99.tq: Discriminate between similarly placed committees by linking the Malhotra Committee with insurance reforms.
99.sec: IRDAI - statutory basis, recommending committee, year, sector regulated, expert panels

99.s: IRDAI was set up in:
99.x: IRDAI was set up in April 2000 under the statutory framework created by the IRDA Act, 1999.
99.tq: Use the year sequence carefully: the Act preceded the setting up of the regulator.
99.sec: IRDAI - statutory basis, recommending committee, year, sector regulated, expert panels

99.s: Under which provision does IRDAI frame regulations for the insurance industry?
99.x: IRDAI frames regulations for the insurance industry under Section 114A of the Insurance Act, 1938. Section 16A of the IRDA Act concerns the Policyholders' Education and Protection Fund.
99.tq: Separate provisions by matching each section with its statute and subject.
99.sec: IRDAI - statutory basis, recommending committee, year, sector regulated, expert panels

99.s: The IRDAI panel on a standard cyber liability insurance product was chaired by:
99.x: The IRDAI expert panel on a standard cyber liability insurance product was chaired by P. Umesh.
99.tq: Identify the person directly associated with the specialised expert panel.
99.sec: IRDAI - statutory basis, recommending committee, year, sector regulated, expert panels

99.s:
With reference to the Sabka Bima Sabki Raksha (Amendment of Insurance Laws) Act, 2025, consider the following statements:
1. It allows up to 100% foreign direct investment in insurance companies.
2. It amends the Insurance Act, 1938, the LIC Act, 1956 and the IRDA Act, 1999.
3. It was passed on 17 December 2025.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
99.x: All three statements are correct. The Act passed on 17 December 2025 permits up to 100% FDI in insurance companies and amends the three specified laws.
99.tq: Check the date, FDI limit and complete set of amended Acts together.
99.sec: IRDAI - statutory basis, recommending committee, year, sector regulated, expert panels

99.s: IRDAI operationalised the Policyholders' Education and Protection Fund in:
99.x: IRDAI operationalised the Policyholders' Education and Protection Fund in July 2026.
99.tq: Distinguish the enactment date from the later operationalisation date.
99.sec: IRDAI - statutory basis, recommending committee, year, sector regulated, expert panels

99.s: Which one of the following was NOT a measure included in the package associated with operationalisation of the Policyholders' Education and Protection Fund?
o: Revision of actuarial and investment rules
Mandatory tagging of an authorised salesperson to each policy
Perpetual licensing of intermediaries with an annual fee
Abolition of licensing requirements for intermediaries
99.x: The package made an authorised salesperson mandatory for each policy, introduced perpetual licensing with an annual fee for intermediaries, and revised actuarial and investment rules. It did not abolish licensing requirements.
99.tq: Find the option that reverses the stated regulatory reform.
99.sec: IRDAI - statutory basis, recommending committee, year, sector regulated, expert panels

99.s: Which accounting standards replaced IGAAP for insurers?
99.x: Ind AS 117 and Ind AS 109 replaced IGAAP for insurers, and IRDAI enforces their adoption.
99.tq: Pair the exact accounting standards with the insurance-sector transition.
99.sec: IRDAI - statutory basis, recommending committee, year, sector regulated, expert panels

99.s: Which of the following is NOT included among the Domestic Systemically Important Insurers for FY 2025–26?
o: General Insurance Corporation of India Re
99.x: The Domestic Systemically Important Insurers for FY 2025–26 are LIC, GIC Re and New India Assurance. HDFC Bank is listed among the D-SIBs, not the D-SIIs.
99.tq: Separate systemically important insurers from systemically important banks.
99.sec: IRDAI - statutory basis, recommending committee, year, sector regulated, expert panels

99.s:
Match List-I with List-II:

List-I (Regulator)
 a. RBI
 b. IRDAI
 c. IBBI
 d. IFSCA

List-II (Establishing Act)
 i. Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016
 ii. IRDA Act, 1999
 iii. RBI Act, 1934
 iv. IFSCA Act, 2019

Select the correct answer using the code given below:
99.x: RBI is established under the RBI Act, 1934; IRDAI under the IRDA Act, 1999; IBBI under the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016; and IFSCA under the IFSCA Act, 2019.
99.tq: Start from the sure Act–regulator pairs and eliminate codes containing a mismatch.
99.sec: Regulator → establishing Act and date set up

99.s: Which one of the following pairs is correctly matched?
99.x: The RBI was set up on 1 April 1935 and was nationalised in 1949. PFRDA became statutory from 2014, IBBI was set up on 1 October 2016, and IFSCA on 27 April 2020.
99.tq: Use the date and status together; the distractors swap dates among regulators.
99.sec: Regulator → establishing Act and date set up

99.s:
Consider the following statements:
1. SEBI was set up as a non-statutory body on 12 April 1988.
2. SEBI received statutory powers on 30 January 1992.
3. SEBI became autonomous or statutory from 12 April 1992.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
99.x: All three statements are correct for the chronology of SEBI's institutional development. The dates distinguish its initial non-statutory existence, statutory powers and later autonomous or statutory status.
99.tq: Arrange institutional milestones by reading each date and status precisely.
99.sec: Regulator → establishing Act and date set up

99.s: PFRDA was initially constituted as an interim body by resolution in 2003 and became statutory from:
99.x: PFRDA was constituted as an interim body by resolution in 2003 and became statutory from 2014 under the PFRDA Act, 2013.
99.tq: Distinguish the interim-body year from the year in which statutory status began.
99.sec: Regulator → establishing Act and date set up

99.s:
Which of the following chronological sequences is correct?
A. RBI is set up
B. SEBI is set up as a non-statutory body
C. IBBI is set up
D. IFSCA is set up
99.x: The correct sequence is RBI in 1935, SEBI as a non-statutory body in 1988, IBBI in 2016 and IFSCA in 2020.
99.tq: Fix the earliest and latest events first, then place the intermediate regulator.
99.sec: Regulator → establishing Act and date set up

99.s: Which one of the following pairs is NOT correctly matched?
o: IBBI — New Delhi — Ministry of Finance
PFRDA — New Delhi — Ministry of Finance
99.x: IBBI is headquartered in New Delhi but comes under the Ministry of Corporate Affairs, not the Ministry of Finance. The other pairs are correctly matched.
99.tq: Check the parent ministry rather than relying only on the headquarters.
99.sec: Regulator → headquarters and parent ministry

99.s: The headquarters of the International Financial Services Centres Authority (IFSCA) is located at:
99.x: IFSCA is headquartered at GIFT City, Gandhinagar. It functions under the Ministry of Finance.
99.tq: Use the distinctive headquarters location to separate IFSCA from the Mumbai- and Delhi-based regulators.
99.sec: Regulator → headquarters and parent ministry

99.s: Which regulator has regional offices in New Delhi, Kolkata, Chennai and Ahmedabad in addition to its headquarters?
99.x: SEBI is headquartered in Mumbai and has regional offices in New Delhi, Kolkata, Chennai and Ahmedabad.
99.tq: Match the complete regional-office pattern with the correct regulator.
99.sec: Regulator → headquarters and parent ministry

99.s:
Consider the following statements:
1. The Ministry of Finance nominates representatives to the boards of SEBI, IRDAI and RBI.
2. IBBI is under the Ministry of Corporate Affairs.
3. IFSCA is under the Ministry of Finance.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
99.x: All three statements are correct. The Ministry of Finance nominates representatives to the boards of SEBI, IRDAI and RBI; IBBI belongs to Corporate Affairs, while IFSCA belongs to Finance.
99.tq: Compare parent ministries and board-nomination authority without reversing institutional relationships.
99.sec: Regulator → headquarters and parent ministry

99.s: Which of the following is associated with IFSCA?
o: Promotion of FinTech and regulatory and innovation sandboxes
Issue of the one-rupee currency note
Management of the Public Debt Office
99.x: IFSCA promotes FinTech as well as regulatory and innovation sandboxes. The other functions belong to RBI or IRDAI-related domains.
99.tq: Identify the regulator from the function rather than from its location alone.
99.sec: Regulator → headquarters and parent ministry

99.s: The Monetary Policy Committee of the RBI is a statutory body consisting of:
o: Six members, all external members appointed by the Centre
Seven members, including four from the RBI and three from the Finance Ministry
Six members, including three from the RBI and three external members appointed by the Centre
Five members, all appointed by the RBI Governor
99.x: The MPC is a statutory six-member body under the RBI Act, 1934. It has three RBI members and three external members appointed by the Centre.
99.tq: Use the composition split to reject wrong strength and appointing-authority claims.
99.sec: RBI - Monetary Policy Committee, banker/regulator functions, inflation-targeting mandate

99.s: Which one of the following correctly describes the RBI Governor's position in the Monetary Policy Committee?
o: The Governor is a member without voting rights
The Governor is the chair and has a casting vote
The Governor appoints all three external members and has no casting vote
The Governor is nominated by the Ministry of Corporate Affairs
99.x: The RBI Governor chairs the MPC and has a casting vote. The three external members are appointed by the Centre.
99.tq: Ask who performs the role and who holds the deciding power.
99.sec: RBI - Monetary Policy Committee, banker/regulator functions, inflation-targeting mandate

99.s: The external members of the Monetary Policy Committee are appointed by the Centre for a period of:
99.x: The three external members of the MPC are appointed by the Centre for four years.
99.tq: Distinguish the four-year tenure from the five-year inflation-target cycle.
99.sec: RBI - Monetary Policy Committee, banker/regulator functions, inflation-targeting mandate

99.s: Under the inflation-targeting framework, the inflation target is set by the Centre in consultation with the RBI once every:
99.x: Under Section 45ZA, the Centre, in consultation with the RBI, sets the inflation target every five years.
99.tq: Separate the five-year target-setting cycle from the four-year MPC external-member tenure.
99.sec: RBI - Monetary Policy Committee, banker/regulator functions, inflation-targeting mandate

99.s: The inflation target under India's flexible inflation-targeting framework is:
o: 6% headline CPI with no tolerance band

103.s: Which one of the following best describes a pressure group?

103.s: Since which year has NABARD been fully owned by the Government of India?
103.x: NABARD has been fully owned by the Government of India since 2019.
103.tq: Distinguish the ownership date from the establishment and SHG-pilot dates.
103.sec: SHG-Bank Linkage Programme - NABARD role, DAY-NRLM

103.s: The SHG-Bank Linkage Programme, for which NABARD is known, was piloted in:
103.x: The SHG-Bank Linkage Programme was piloted in 1992 and encourages banks to lend to SHGs of poor women.
103.tq: Use the sequence of NABARD-related dates to separate the 1992 pilot from its 1982 establishment.
103.sec: SHG-Bank Linkage Programme - NABARD role, DAY-NRLM

103.s: The principal purpose of the SHG-Bank Linkage Programme is to encourage banks to lend to:
o: Political parties registered under the Representation of the People Act
103.x: The programme encourages banks to provide credit to Self-Help Groups of poor women.
103.tq: Apply the programme's target-group feature to the lending scenario.
103.sec: SHG-Bank Linkage Programme - NABARD role, DAY-NRLM

103.s: DAY-NRLM is best characterised as a:
103.x: DAY-NRLM is community-driven and develops SHG members as community resource persons.
103.tq: Identify the defining institutional character of the programme.
103.sec: SHG-Bank Linkage Programme - NABARD role, DAY-NRLM

103.s: Which of the following is NOT included among the community resource-person roles associated with DAY-NRLM?
103.x: The listed roles are Pashu Sakhi, Krishi Sakhi, Bank Sakhi, Bima Sakhi and Poshan Sakhi. Nyaya Sakhi is not included in the stated list.
103.tq: Identify the odd term by recalling the complete set of community resource-person roles.
103.sec: SHG-Bank Linkage Programme - NABARD role, DAY-NRLM

103.s: Which umbrella initiative is run under DAY-NRLM for village enterprises?
103.x: DAY-NRLM runs the SVEP umbrella for village enterprises.
103.tq: Match the programme with its specific enterprise-support initiative.
103.sec: SHG-Bank Linkage Programme - NABARD role, DAY-NRLM

103.s: The national DAY-NRLM campaign launched in 2026 focused on:
o: SHG non-farm enterprises and rural women's entrepreneurship
Foreign-fund regulation and NGO asset takeover
103.x: The national campaign focused on SHG non-farm enterprises and rural women's entrepreneurship.
103.tq: Identify the precise thematic focus rather than the broader objectives of DAY-NRLM.
103.sec: SHG-Bank Linkage Programme - NABARD role, DAY-NRLM

103.s:
Consider the following statements regarding the role of civil society organisations:
1. They have helped secure rights relating to work, education, food and information.
2. Their role has remained confined to service delivery.
3. They increasingly undertake advocacy, policy formulation and watchdog functions.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
103.x: Statements 1 and 3 are correct. Civil society organisations have moved beyond service delivery to advocacy, policy formulation and watchdog functions; statement 2 is false.
103.tq: Separate the continuing role from the expanded functions of civil society organisations.
103.sec: Civil society role → examples

103.s:
Civil society is commonly described as the sector that exists alongside which of the following?
1. The State
2. The market
3. The judiciary
4. The military
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
103.x: Civil society is called the third sector, alongside the State as the first sector and the market as the second sector.
103.tq: Use the sector-number relationship to eliminate unrelated institutions.
103.sec: Civil society role → examples

103.s: Which one of the following is NOT included among the groups covered by the World Bank's broad understanding of civil society?
103.x: The broad definition includes NGOs, unions, faith-based groups, professional associations and foundations. Central banks are not included in this classification.
103.tq: Find the institution outside the recognised civil-society grouping.
103.sec: Civil society role → examples

103.s: The Mazdoor Kisan Shakti Sangathan (MKSS) is associated with which one of the following combinations?
103.x: MKSS emerged in Rajasthan in 1990 and is associated with Aruna Roy. Its campaign contributed to the enactment of the Right to Information Act, 2005.
103.tq: Match the organisation with its year, location and associated personality.
103.sec: Civil society role → examples

103.s: The campaign of the Mazdoor Kisan Shakti Sangathan contributed significantly to which legislation?
o: Mahatma Gandhi National Rural Employment Guarantee Act, 2005
103.x: The MKSS campaign for transparency and public hearings contributed to the Right to Information Act, 2005.
103.tq: Link a movement's distinctive campaign with the legislation it influenced.
103.sec: Civil society role → examples

103.s: The Anti-arrack movement of 1992 began at which place?
103.x: The Anti-arrack movement began in 1992 at Dubagunta village in Nellore. It resulted in an arrack ban and later prohibition in Andhra Pradesh.
103.tq: Test the exact place associated with a regional movement.
103.sec: Civil society role → examples

103.s:
Arrange the following civil society movements in chronological order:
A. Narmada Bachao Andolan
B. Anti-arrack movement
C. Chipko Movement
D. Mazdoor Kisan Shakti Sangathan
103.x: The correct sequence is Chipko (1973), Narmada Bachao Andolan (1985), Anti-arrack movement (1992), and MKSS (1990). Wait: because MKSS occurred in 1990, the correct chronological order is Chipko, Narmada Bachao Andolan, MKSS, Anti-arrack movement; therefore option c is correct.
103.tq: Place movements by their stated years before comparing the middle entries.
103.sec: Civil society role → examples

103.s: Which one of the following correctly describes the outcome associated with the Narmada Bachao Andolan?
o: Campaign for an arrack ban in Andhra Pradesh
Campaign for minimum wages in Rajasthan
Campaign for a three-capitals plan in Andhra Pradesh
103.x: The Narmada Bachao Andolan brought the displacement caused by large dams, particularly the Sardar Sarovar project, into public debate.
103.tq: Distinguish the outcome of one movement from those of similarly prominent movements.
103.sec: Civil society role → examples

103.s: The National Policy on the Voluntary Sector was adopted in which year by the Planning Commission?
103.x: The National Policy on the Voluntary Sector was adopted in 2007 by the Planning Commission.
103.tq: Test the policy year against nearby legislation and policy years.
103.sec: National Policy on the Voluntary Sector 2007 - objectives, NGO accountability

103.s:
Which of the following are objectives of the National Policy on the Voluntary Sector, 2007?
1. Creation of an enabling environment for voluntary organisations
2. Easier mobilisation of resources
3. Partnership between voluntary organisations and government
4. Complete subordination of voluntary organisations to government departments
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
103.x: The policy seeks an enabling environment, easier resource mobilisation and partnership with government. It does not seek complete subordination of voluntary organisations to government departments.
103.tq: Reject the extreme control-based statement and retain the partnership objectives.
103.sec: National Policy on the Voluntary Sector 2007 - objectives, NGO accountability

103.s: With regard to accountability of voluntary organisations, the National Policy on the Voluntary Sector, 2007 gives preference to:
o: Transparency, self-regulation and codes of conduct
Direct management by the Planning Commission
Confidentiality and exemption from public scrutiny
103.x: The policy favours transparency, self-regulation and codes of conduct rather than tight government control.
103.tq: Identify the policy approach by contrasting self-regulation with state control.
103.sec: National Policy on the Voluntary Sector 2007 - objectives, NGO accountability

103.s:
Consider the following statements about media in a democracy:
1. Press freedom is read into Article 19(1)(a) of the Constitution.
2. A free press is necessary for a vibrant democracy.
3. New media technologies have made communication more participatory.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
103.x: All three statements are correct. Freedom of speech and expression under Article 19(1)(a) includes press freedom, while new media has increased participatory communication.
103.tq: Use the constitutional provision and the two stated democratic functions together.
103.sec: Media's role - fourth estate, free press, new media, image-building, paid and fake news

103.s: Which of the following best explains the manner in which mass media build the image of political personalities?
o: The ideology and treatment of news by the media outlet influence the image
The Election Commission directly prepares all media images
Image-building is unrelated to public opinion
Only the personal wealth of the politician determines the image
103.x: Mass media shape political images through the ideology of the outlet and the manner in which news is selected and presented.
103.tq: Apply the relationship between media treatment and political image-building.
103.sec: Media's role - fourth estate, free press, new media, image-building, paid and fake news

103.s: Which of the following is NOT identified as a problem associated with the contemporary media environment?
103.x: Dependence on government advertisements is identified as a problem. Universal independence from government advertising is not a characteristic of the media environment described.
103.tq: Identify the reversed statement that converts a reported problem into its opposite.
103.sec: Media's role - fourth estate, free press, new media, image-building, paid and fake news

103.s: Which one of the following combinations correctly represents issues that may be associated with misuse against media or journalists?
o: FCRA, Census Act and Finance Act
RTI Act, RTE Act and MGNREGA
UAPA, IT Rules and defamation law
Forest Rights Act, Motor Vehicles Act and GST Act
103.x: The misuse of UAPA, IT Rules and defamation law is identified as a concern affecting media freedom.
103.tq: Match the relevant legal instruments with the issue of media regulation and misuse.
103.sec: Media's role - fourth estate, free press, new media, image-building, paid and fake news

103.s: India is placed in which category in the Reporters Without Borders classification of press freedom?
103.x: India is placed in the 'very serious' category in the Reporters Without Borders classification mentioned here.
103.tq: Distinguish the exact category from adjacent press-freedom classifications.
103.sec: Media's role - fourth estate, free press, new media, image-building, paid and fake news

103.s: Written demands or memoranda submitted to authorities constitute which technique of influencing public policy?
103.x: Petitioning involves submitting written demands or memoranda to authorities.
103.tq: Distinguish written representation from lobbying, litigation and direct action.
103.sec: Techniques - definitions  [APPSC, GROUP-II]

103.s: Which one of the following is correctly matched?
o: Dharna — Written memorandum to an authority
Litigation — Public Interest Litigations and court cases
Petitioning — Direct action to disrupt public life
Media campaign — Filing electoral cases in courts
103.x: Litigation includes PILs and court cases, such as electoral cases filed by ADR. Direct disruption is associated with strikes, bandhs and dharnas, while written memoranda constitute petitioning.
103.tq: Find the correctly matched technique after separating legal, written and direct-action methods.
103.sec: Techniques - definitions  [APPSC, GROUP-II]

103.s: Strikes, bandhs and dharnas are examples of:
o: Direct action to disrupt and force attention
103.x: Strikes, bandhs and dharnas are forms of direct action intended to disrupt normal activity and force public or governmental attention.
103.tq: Identify the common purpose shared by the listed forms of protest.
103.sec: Techniques - definitions  [APPSC, GROUP-II]

103.s: The Press Council of India was first set up in 1966 under which legislation?
o: Press and Registration of Books Act, 1867
103.x: The Press Council was first set up in 1966 under the Press Council Act, 1965. Its present statutory framework is associated with the Press Council Act, 1978.
103.tq: Separate the original establishment year and Act from the later statutory framework.
103.sec: Press Council of India - legal nature, composition, powers

103.s: The Press Council of India consists of:
103.x: The composition of the Press Council of India is a Chairman plus 28 members.
103.tq: Test the exact statutory composition using nearby numerical distractors.
103.sec: Press Council of India - legal nature, composition, powers

103.s:
Consider the following statements regarding the Press Council of India:
1. It can warn newspapers and journalists.
2. It can admonish or censure newspapers and journalists.
3. It possesses punitive powers to impose criminal punishment.
4. Its jurisdiction covers print media only.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
103.x: The Press Council can warn, admonish or censure newspapers and journalists and covers print media only. It lacks punitive powers, so statement 3 is false.
103.tq: Separate moral or regulatory sanctions from punitive powers.
103.sec: Press Council of India - legal nature, composition, powers

103.s: Which one of the following is NOT a power or characteristic of the Press Council of India?
103.x: The Press Council may warn, admonish or censure, but it lacks punitive powers to impose criminal penalties.
103.tq: Find the sanction that exceeds the body's stated authority.
103.sec: Press Council of India - legal nature, composition, powers

103.s: Which one of the following correctly distinguishes a political party from a pressure group?
o: A political party seeks to capture power and govern, whereas a pressure group seeks to influence those in power.
A political party never contests elections, whereas a pressure group contests all elections.
A pressure group seeks to govern the entire country, whereas a political party represents only one sectional interest.
Both are answerable only to government departments.
103.x: Political parties seek to capture power and govern. Pressure groups seek to influence those in power without seeking governmental office.
103.tq: Compare the central aim of each organisation rather than its methods alone.
103.sec: Pressure groups vs political parties

103.s:
Consider the following statements about pressure groups:
1. They generally do not contest elections.
2. They are answerable primarily to their members.
3. They usually represent a specific sectional interest.
4. They necessarily seek to form the government.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
103.x: Pressure groups generally do not contest elections, are answerable to their members and represent sectional interests. Seeking to form the government is the characteristic of a political party, not a pressure group.
103.tq: Use the election, accountability and scope distinctions to reject the party-related statement.
103.sec: Pressure groups vs political parties

103.s: Pressure groups are also referred to as the:
103.x: Pressure groups are described as the 'Anonymous Empire' because they influence public policy without directly seeking governmental office.
103.tq: Recall the distinctive descriptive phrase associated with pressure groups.
103.sec: Pressure groups vs political parties

103.s: Which one of the following pairs is correctly matched?
o: India Against Corruption — Anna Hazare — Jan Lokpal
MKSS — Medha Patkar — Sardar Sarovar dam
Narmada Bachao Andolan — Anna Hazare — Right to Information
103.x: India Against Corruption was led by Anna Hazare and demanded a Jan Lokpal. MKSS is associated with Aruna Roy and Nikhil Dey, while the Narmada movement is associated with Medha Patkar and Baba Amte.
103.tq: Match each movement with its own leader and demand before eliminating swapped pairs.
103.sec: Civil society movements - leader and demand  [GROUP-II]

103.s: The principal demand associated with the Chipko Movement was:
o: A ban on arrack in Nellore
103.x: The Chipko Movement demanded that tree-felling be stopped in the Uttarakhand Himalayas.
103.tq: Separate an environmental demand from the governance and prohibition demands of other movements.
103.sec: Civil society movements - leader and demand  [GROUP-II]

103.s: The Narmada Bachao Andolan was primarily associated with opposition to:
o: The use of information technology in elections
The Sardar Sarovar dam and displacement
103.x: The Narmada Bachao Andolan opposed the Sardar Sarovar dam and the displacement associated with it.
103.tq: Link the movement to its specific project and affected issue.
103.sec: Civil society movements - leader and demand  [GROUP-II]

103.s: Which of the following demands is associated with the MKSS movement?
o: Minimum wages and the right to information through jan sunwai
Immediate formation of a political party
103.x: MKSS raised issues of minimum wages and the right to information, using the public hearing or jan sunwai process.
103.tq: Identify the distinctive demand and method associated with MKSS.
103.sec: Civil society movements - leader and demand  [GROUP-II]

103.s: The Lokpal and Lokayuktas Act followed the India Against Corruption movement in:
103.x: The Lokpal and Lokayuktas Act followed the India Against Corruption movement in 2013.
103.tq: Distinguish the movement year from the year of the resulting legislation.
103.sec: Civil society movements - leader and demand  [GROUP-II]

103.s: The Amaravati farmers' agitation began in December 2019 primarily in opposition to:
o: The introduction of the Right to Information Act
The construction of the Sardar Sarovar dam
The establishment of the Press Council of India
103.x: Farmers involved in land pooling in Amaravati protested from December 2019 against the three-capitals plan.
103.tq: Link the regional agitation with its immediate policy trigger and date.
103.sec: Andhra Pradesh examples  [GROUP-II]

103.s:
Which of the following are examples of pressure groups in Andhra Pradesh?
1. AP NGOs' Association
2. Rythu sanghams
3. Election Commission of India
4. Farmers' associations
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
103.x: The AP NGOs' Association and farmers' associations, including rythu sanghams, are examples of pressure groups. The Election Commission is a constitutional authority, not a pressure group.
103.tq: Identify civil-society associations while excluding a constitutional body.
103.sec: Andhra Pradesh examples  [GROUP-II]

103.s: In July 2026, the Andhra Pradesh Cabinet asked the police to constitute a task force against:
o: Fake news and defamatory social-media content
Displacement caused by the Sardar Sarovar dam
Irregularities in the appointment of Press Council members
103.x: The Andhra Pradesh Cabinet asked the police for a task force to address fake news and defamatory content on social media.
103.tq: Match the state-level administrative response with the specific contemporary media problem.
103.sec: Andhra Pradesh examples  [GROUP-II]

103.s: The FCRA Amendment Rules, 2026, which drew opposition letters seeking their withdrawal, were notified in which month and year?
103.x: The FCRA Amendment Rules, 2026, drew opposition in June 2026.
103.tq: Use the precise date instead of being distracted by nearby current-affairs months.
103.sec: Universal angles

103.s: Who among the following wrote opposition letters seeking withdrawal of the FCRA Amendment Rules, 2026?
103.x: The opposition letters were written by K.C. Venugopal and John Brittas, seeking withdrawal of the FCRA Amendment Rules, 2026.
103.tq: Discriminate between closely associated political names rather than relying on general familiarity.
103.sec: Universal angles

103.s:
Consider the following statements regarding the debate over the Foreign Contribution Regulation Act (FCRA):
1. Critics argue that the FCRA has shifted from regulating foreign funds towards State control of civil society.
2. The government justifies its position on the grounds of transparency and national security.
3. The debate is unrelated to the civic space available to non-governmental organisations.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
103.x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct. Statement 3 is false because FCRA curbs and NGO funding regulations are specifically debated in relation to shrinking civic space.
103.tq: Find the statement that reverses the central criticism before selecting the coded combination.
103.sec: Universal angles

103.s:
With reference to Self-Help Group (SHG)-Bank Linkage, consider the following statements:
1. Andhra Pradesh leads India in SHG-Bank Linkage.
2. The relevant performance reference is APSES 2024-25.
3. Andhra Pradesh is described as lagging behind all other Indian States in this linkage.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
103.x: Andhra Pradesh leads India in SHG-Bank Linkage, with APSES 2024-25 serving as the stated reference. Statement 3 is false because it reverses Andhra Pradesh's position.
103.tq: Check the direction of the comparison and separate the true performance claim from its reversal.
103.sec: Universal angles

103.s: Which one of the following developments was associated with civil-society activity in July 2026?
o: The notification of the FCRA Amendment Rules, 2025
The introduction of the Lokpal Bill, 2011
The launch of an AP social-media task force
The establishment of the Press Council of India
103.x: An AP social-media task force was associated with civil-society and governance developments in July 2026.
103.tq: Match the event with its correct month and jurisdiction while rejecting unrelated institutional events.
103.sec: Universal angles

103.s: The NEET paper-leak protests received solidarity from civil society in which country, as reported in July 2026?
103.x: The NEET paper-leak protests drew solidarity from Sri Lankan civil society in July 2026.
103.tq: Identify the cross-border civil-society connection rather than the location of the domestic protest.
103.sec: Universal angles

103.s: Press-freedom concerns were highlighted in which month and year in the cited current-affairs context?
103.x: Press-freedom concerns were highlighted in May 2026.
103.tq: Distinguish between closely placed months and years in current-affairs chronology.
103.sec: Universal angles

103.s: Which of the following statements best describes a criticism of pressure groups in governance?
o: They can capture policy-making for narrow interests.
They are constitutionally empowered to exercise judicial review.
They are required to represent every social group equally.
They eliminate the need for civil-society participation in governance.
103.x: A recognised criticism is that pressure groups may capture policy for narrow interests. The other statements assign them powers or obligations not stated in the context.
103.tq: Apply the concept to a governance situation and distinguish criticism from an institutional power.
103.sec: Universal angles

104.s: Which one of the following best describes acculturation?
o: Absorption of a minority culture into the dominant culture with loss of its identity
Convergence of all cultures towards a single global pattern
Mixing of global and local elements into a new blended form
Exchange of cultural traits between two cultures in contact, with both changing while remaining distinct
104.x: Acculturation involves mutual exchange of traits between cultures in contact. Both cultures change, but each retains its distinct identity.
104.tq: Distinguish closely related cultural-change terms by checking whether identities are retained.
104.sec: Cultural change terms → meaning

104.s: A minority culture is absorbed into the dominant culture and loses its distinct identity. This process is known as:
104.x: Assimilation occurs when a minority culture is absorbed into the dominant culture and loses its distinct identity.
104.tq: Use the identity-loss clue to distinguish assimilation from acculturation.
104.sec: Cultural change terms → meaning

104.s:
Consider the following statements:
1. Glocalisation involves adapting global products and ideas to local tastes.
2. Homogenisation refers to cultures converging towards one global, often Western, pattern.
3. Hybridisation involves the mixing of global and local elements to create blended forms.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
104.x: All three statements are correct. Glocalisation adapts global influences locally, homogenisation produces cultural convergence, and hybridisation creates blended global-local forms.
104.tq: Separate adaptation, convergence and mixing before selecting the coded combination.
104.sec: Cultural change terms → meaning

104.s: The spread of the principles of efficiency, calculability, predictability and control from fast-food restaurants to wider society is termed:
104.x: McDonaldisation refers to the spread of fast-food principles such as efficiency, calculability, predictability and control across society.
104.tq: Match the distinctive four-principle formulation with the exact sociological term.
104.sec: Cultural change terms → meaning

104.s: Which of the following is identified as a criticism of globalisation?
o: It may encourage mindless imitation of Western lifestyles and weaken traditional identity
It prevents the movement of technology between countries
It confines people to local markets
104.x: A major criticism is that globalisation may lead to mindless aping of Western lifestyles and loss of traditional cultural identity.
104.tq: Identify the critical perspective rather than the claimed benefits of global integration.
104.sec: Cultural change terms → meaning

104.s:
Match List-I with List-II:

List-I (Term)
 a. Glocalisation
 b. Homogenisation
 c. Hybridisation
 d. McDonaldisation

List-II (Meaning)
 i. Blending of global and local elements
 ii. Spread of fast-food principles through society
 iii. Adaptation of global ideas to local tastes
 iv. Convergence towards one global cultural pattern

Select the correct answer using the code given below:
104.x: Glocalisation means local adaptation, homogenisation means convergence, hybridisation means blending, and McDonaldisation means the spread of fast-food principles.
104.tq: Start from the sure pair of McDonaldisation with fast-food principles and eliminate codes.
104.sec: Cultural change terms → meaning

104.s: Anthony Giddens associated globalisation with which of the following concepts?
o: Time-space distanciation and the idea of a runaway world
104.x: Anthony Giddens described globalisation through time-space distanciation and referred to the contemporary world as a runaway world.
104.tq: Match the theorist with the distinctive phrase most closely associated with the concept.
104.sec: Globalisation theorists → concept

104.s: The concepts of ‘glocalisation’ and ‘the world as a single place’ are associated with:
104.x: Roland Robertson is associated with glocalisation and the idea of the world as a single place.
104.tq: Use the exact conceptual pairing rather than the general theme of globalisation.
104.sec: Globalisation theorists → concept

104.s: Which one of the following pairs is correctly matched?
104.x: George Ritzer developed the concept of McDonaldisation of society. The five scapes belong to Arjun Appadurai, space of flows to Manuel Castells, and runaway world to Anthony Giddens.
104.tq: Check the scholar-concept pair and reject the swapped theorist names.
104.sec: Globalisation theorists → concept

104.s:
Consider the following statements:
1. Manuel Castells is associated with the idea of a network society.
2. Castells uses the concept of ‘space of flows’ in analysing contemporary society.
3. Arjun Appadurai’s five scapes include ethnoscapes, mediascapes and technoscapes.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
104.x: All three statements are correct. Castells developed the ideas of network society and space of flows, while Appadurai identified five scapes including ethnoscapes, mediascapes and technoscapes.
104.tq: Combine the two theorists only after separating Castells’s network concepts from Appadurai’s scapes.
104.sec: Globalisation theorists → concept

104.s: Which of the following is NOT one of Arjun Appadurai’s five ‘scapes’?
104.x: Appadurai’s five scapes are ethnoscapes, mediascapes, technoscapes, financescapes and ideoscapes. ‘Politiscapes’ is not included in this list.
104.tq: Find the item outside the memorised five-member list.
104.sec: Globalisation theorists → concept

104.s: Immanuel Wallerstein’s world-systems theory classifies the global system into:
o: Developed, developing and least developed regions only
104.x: Wallerstein’s world-systems theory divides the global system into core, semi-periphery and periphery.
104.tq: Recall the exact three-part classification and reject near-synonymous substitutions.
104.sec: Globalisation theorists → concept

104.s: According to the World Migration Report 2026, the estimated number of international migrants worldwide is:
104.x: The World Migration Report 2026 estimates 304 million international migrants, constituting 3.7% of the world’s population.
104.tq: Use the distinctive numerical value and verify it against the accompanying percentage.
104.sec: Migration - international migrants, remittances rank, Gulf migration from AP/Telugu states

104.s: The 304 million international migrants referred to in the World Migration Report 2026 constituted approximately what share of the world population?
104.x: The report places the number of international migrants at 304 million, or approximately 3.7% of the world population.
104.tq: Test the percentage separately from the absolute number to avoid overlooking a paired statistic.
104.sec: Migration - international migrants, remittances rank, Gulf migration from AP/Telugu states

104.s: The World Migration Report is published by the IOM and has been issued biennially since:
104.x: The International Organization for Migration publishes the World Migration Report, which has been issued biennially since 2000.
104.tq: Link the institutional publisher with the starting year of the recurring report.
104.sec: Migration - international migrants, remittances rank, Gulf migration from AP/Telugu states

104.s: Which one of the following correctly describes India’s position in global remittances in 2024?
o: India was the second-largest recipient, with US$97 billion
India was the top recipient, with US$75 billion
India was outside the top five recipients, with US$137 billion
India was the top recipient and the only country receiving more than US$100 billion, with US$137 billion
104.x: India remained the top remittance recipient in 2024, receiving US$137 billion and being the only country to receive more than US$100 billion.
104.tq: Check rank, exclusivity and amount together because each is a possible trap.
104.sec: Migration - international migrants, remittances rank, Gulf migration from AP/Telugu states

104.s: Global remittances in 2024 were estimated at approximately:
104.x: Global remittances were estimated at US$905 billion in 2024.
104.tq: Select the precise figure rather than relying only on the country-level remittance statistic.
104.sec: Migration - international migrants, remittances rank, Gulf migration from AP/Telugu states

104.s:
Consider the following statements:
1. India has the largest diaspora in the world.
2. The India-UAE migration corridor ranks fifth among the top migration corridors.
3. The India-US migration corridor ranks sixth among the top migration corridors.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
104.x: All three statements are correct. India has the world’s largest diaspora, while India-UAE and India-US are ranked fifth and sixth respectively among the stated top migration corridors.
104.tq: Keep the two corridor ranks in sequence while checking the broader diaspora statement.
104.sec: Migration - international migrants, remittances rank, Gulf migration from AP/Telugu states

104.s: The Gulf labour force is described as the backbone of India’s:
104.x: Gulf labour is described as the backbone of India’s remittance economy.
104.tq: Identify the economic channel directly associated with overseas Gulf employment.
104.sec: Migration - international migrants, remittances rank, Gulf migration from AP/Telugu states

104.s: Which institution signs Migration and Mobility Partnerships and conducts Pre-Departure Orientation Training under the Pravasi Kaushal Vikas Yojana?

Separating nation, nationality, ethnicity and citizenship
Classifying Indian tribes exclusively by race

A taboo on killing tigers called iyu-ena

o: It is the largest tribe of Arunachal Pradesh and hosts the Pakke Paga festival.
It follows a taboo called iyu-ena on killing tigers.
It is associated with Longpi pottery in Manipur.
It is a matrilineal community in which the youngest daughter inherits.

112.s: Which one of the following statements about Santhali is correct?
o: It is written in Roman script and was included through the 73rd Amendment of 1992.
It is written in Ol Chiki, created by Raghunath Murmu in 1925, and entered the Eighth Schedule through the 92nd Amendment of 2003.
It is written in Ol Chiki, created in 1950, and is not a Scheduled Language.
It is written in Devanagari and entered the Eighth Schedule through the 42nd Amendment of 1976.
112.x: Santhali is written in Ol Chiki, created by Raghunath Murmu in 1925. It was included in the Eighth Schedule through the 92nd Constitutional Amendment Act, 2003.

112.s:
Which of the following statements regarding the official languages of Meghalaya is correct?

1. Khasi and Garo were made official languages alongside English.
2. Khasi belongs to the Austro-Asiatic Mon-Khmer group.
3. Garo belongs to the Bodo group of the Sino-Tibetan family.
4. Khasi and Garo are included in the Eighth Schedule.

Select the correct answer using the code given below.
112.x: Statements 1, 2 and 3 are correct. Khasi and Garo are official languages of Meghalaya alongside English, but neither is included in the Eighth Schedule.

112.sec: Ethnic groups of India - North-East groups, linguistic groups, ethnic minorities

Consider the following statements:

2. The States Reorganisation Commission was constituted in 1953.
3. The formation of Andhra Pradesh followed the States Reorganisation Act, 1956.

Arrange the following reorganisations in chronological order:

B. Formation of Andhra State

112.sec: Language groups and linguistic identity - linguistic states, Potti Sriramulu, Andhra State

o: Telangana became a Union Territory and Andhra Pradesh was divided into two States.
Jammu and Kashmir and Ladakh became Union Territories.
Sikkim became the 22nd State of India.
Punjab and Haryana were formed and Chandigarh became a Union Territory.

112.s: According to Arnold Rose, a minority is a group that is set apart by
o: economic class alone and is recognised only by the State
race, nationality, religion or language, and is regarded as different by itself and by others
territorial concentration alone, irrespective of identity
112.x: Arnold Rose describes a minority as a group set apart by race, nationality, religion or language that sees itself, and is seen by others, as different, with negative connotations.
112.tq: Select the option containing the complete definition rather than a partial attribute.
112.sec: Ethnic Muslim minority groups and 'national minority' - concept

112.s: Which of the following is NOT included among the features associated with minorities in Giddens' formulation?
112.x: Giddens identifies disadvantage, group solidarity and physical or social isolation as features associated with minorities; constitutional sovereignty is not included.
112.tq: Identify the unrelated constitutional term among the three stated sociological features.
112.sec: Ethnic Muslim minority groups and 'national minority' - concept

112.s: A national minority is best understood as
o: a non-dominant citizen group possessing an ethnic, religious or linguistic identity
a group recognised only on the basis of economic backwardness
a dominant citizen group with no distinct identity
112.x: A national minority is a non-dominant citizen group with its own ethnic, religious or linguistic identity.
112.tq: Discriminate between non-dominant citizenship-based identity and foreign or economic categories.
112.sec: Ethnic Muslim minority groups and 'national minority' - concept

112.s: The expression ‘national minority’ has its conceptual origin in
112.x: The term ‘national minority’ comes from European minority-rights law.

112.s: Which of the following communities is NOT included among the minorities notified under the National Commission for Minorities Act, 1992?
112.x: The notified minorities listed are Muslims, Christians, Sikhs, Buddhists, Parsis and Jains. Hindus are not included in that listed notification.
112.tq: Find the community outside the legally notified list rather than relying on numerical status.
112.sec: Ethnic Muslim minority groups and 'national minority' - concept

112.s: Which of the following was the latest community added to the listed national minorities in 2014?
112.x: Jains were included among the notified national minorities in 2014; the list also contains Muslims, Christians, Sikhs, Buddhists and Parsis.
112.tq: Use the year-linked addition to distinguish Jains from communities already in the list.
112.sec: Ethnic Muslim minority groups and 'national minority' - concept

112.s:
Consider the following statements:

2. Uyghurs, Hui and Tibetans are examples of groups covered by the law.
3. Critics argue that the law strengthens non-Han identity by reducing Han dominance.

Sixth Schedule, Election Commission, peace accords and Finance Commission
MDoNER, Supreme Court, GST Council and State Finance Commission

112.s: Which of the following correctly describes the democratic and political consequences attributed to regionalism?
o: It always produces secessionism and never supports democratic participation.
It is confined exclusively to linguistic state formation.
It eliminates vote-bank politics wherever autonomous councils exist.
It can aid democratisation, as in the Tripura ADC, but can also feed secessionism and vote-bank politics.
112.x: Regionalism may aid democratisation, illustrated by the Tripura ADC, but may also feed secessionism such as Greater Nagalim and vote-bank politics.
112.tq: Select the balanced option containing both the positive and negative consequences.

112.sec: Universal angles

112.s: The Tronglaobi bomb attack referred to in the reported Manipur disturbances occurred in which district?

112.x: The killing of two Tangkhul Nagas was reported in Ukhrul.

B. Formation of Telangana

113.s: Which one of the following pairs is correctly matched?
o: Technology — Industrial Revolution and the inventions of Watt and Hargreaves
Media — migration of nomads in a particular season

113.s:
Consider the following statements regarding factors and sources of social change:
1. The spread of modern education is an example of education as a source of social change.
2. The Untouchability (Offences) Act, 1955, illustrates the role of law.
3. Street plays under Nasha Mukt Bharat illustrate behaviour-change communication through media.
4. Reform and Dalit movements are examples of social movements.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
113.x: All four statements are correct. Modern education, legislation, behaviour-change communication and social movements are all identified as sources or illustrations of social change.
113.tq: Test each statement against the factor-example relationship before selecting the coded combination.
113.sec: Factors and sources of social change

113.s: The Green Revolution is cited as an example of the role of planning in social change under which Five-Year Plan?
113.x: The Green Revolution is associated with the Third Plan in the classification of planning as a factor of social change.
113.tq: Use the plan-number association rather than confusing it with technology-led modernisation under the Seventh Plan.
113.sec: Factors and sources of social change

113.s: Inclusive growth was identified as a goal of planning under which Five-Year Plan?
113.x: Inclusive growth is identified as a goal of the Eleventh Plan.
113.tq: Distinguish the planning example of inclusive growth from the Green Revolution and technology-led modernisation.
113.sec: Factors and sources of social change

113.s: According to the December 2025 LENS reference, the number of internet users illustrating the technological basis of social change was more than:

113.tq: Watch the scale of the numerical figure and reject nearby but altered values.

113.s:
The change among Dalits has been associated with which of the following combination of processes?
1. State policy
2. Reform movements
3. Sanskritisation
4. Westernisation
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
113.x: State policy, reform movements, Sanskritisation and Westernisation are all identified as contributing to change among Dalits.
113.tq: The inclusive option is tested after verifying that each listed process is separately supported.
113.sec: Factors and sources of social change

113.s: A minority community gradually merges into the wider society and loses its distinct identity. This process is known as:
113.x: Assimilation occurs when a minority merges fully into the wider society and loses its distinct identity.
113.tq: Apply the definition to the scenario instead of treating every cultural contact as acculturation.

113.s: Which of the following pairs is NOT correctly matched in relation to diffusionist schools?
o: British school — Elliot Smith and Perry
113.x: Boas and Wissler are associated with the American school, not the British school. Elliot Smith and Perry belong to the British school, while Graebner and Schmidt belong to the German-Austrian school.
113.tq: Find the swapped scholars rather than relying only on the school names.

113.s: Which one of the following correctly represents the central idea associated with the German-Austrian diffusionist school?
o: Egypt as the source of all culture
113.x: The German-Austrian school, associated with Graebner and Schmidt, developed the idea of culture circles.
113.tq: Match the school with its distinctive explanatory concept.

113.s: In the diffusionist interpretation of the Indus civilisation, which scholar is associated with migration from Mesopotamia?
113.x: Mackay is associated with the interpretation that the Indus civilisation involved migration from Mesopotamia. Wheeler represented diffusion of ideas, while Marshall is associated with indigenous evolution.
113.tq: Use the scholar-debate association and distinguish migration from diffusion of ideas.

113.s:
Arrange the following interpretations of the Indus civilisation in the order in which they are presented as positions in the debate:
A. Migration from Mesopotamia — Mackay
B. Diffusion of ideas — Wheeler
C. Indigenous evolution — Marshall

Select the correct answer using the code given below.
113.x: The sequence presented is Mackay's migration interpretation, Wheeler's diffusion-of-ideas interpretation and Marshall's indigenous-evolution position.
113.tq: Track the sequence of positions and scholars as stated, rather than imposing historical chronology.

113.s: M.N. Srinivas originally used which term before adopting the term Sanskritisation?
113.x: Srinivas first called the process Brahminisation before using the broader term Sanskritisation.
113.tq: Distinguish the original label from the later, more inclusive term.
113.sec: Sanskritisation - originator, book, definition, reference groups, de-sanskritisation

113.s: Sanskritisation, in the formulation of M.N. Srinivas, primarily involves:
o: The spread of technology from one society to another
A minority losing its identity through complete assimilation into another society
The state maintaining equal respect for all religions
A low caste or tribe adopting the customs and way of life of a higher caste to claim higher rank
113.x: Sanskritisation is the adoption by a low caste or tribe of the customs, rituals and way of life of a higher, often twice-born, caste to claim higher status.
113.tq: Select the option containing the complete definition rather than a neighbouring sociological process.
113.sec: Sanskritisation - originator, book, definition, reference groups, de-sanskritisation

113.s: Which one of the following correctly describes the type of change produced by Sanskritisation?
o: Structural change in the entire caste system
Constitutional change in the relationship between religion and the state
Only economic change without social change
113.x: Sanskritisation brings positional change for a group within the existing social structure; it does not by itself bring structural change.
113.tq: Separate change in social position from transformation of the social structure.
113.sec: Sanskritisation - originator, book, definition, reference groups, de-sanskritisation

113.s:
Which of the following may function as reference groups in Sanskritisation?
1. Brahmins
2. Kshatriyas
3. Vaishyas
4. The local dominant caste
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
113.x: Reference groups may include Brahmins, Kshatriyas, Vaishyas and the locally dominant caste.
113.tq: Check whether the list includes both the traditionally twice-born groups and the local dominant caste.
113.sec: Sanskritisation - originator, book, definition, reference groups, de-sanskritisation

113.s: De-sanskritisation refers to a process in which groups:
o: Reject Sanskritic norms and assert their own identity
Replace non-material culture with material culture
Adopt only Western technology and institutions
Merge completely with a dominant culture
113.x: De-sanskritisation involves rejecting Sanskritic norms and asserting one's own identity, as illustrated by the non-Brahmin or Dravidian movement.
113.tq: Use the reversal of Sanskritisation carefully; rejection and identity assertion are the key clues.
113.sec: Sanskritisation - originator, book, definition, reference groups, de-sanskritisation

113.s: Which book published in 1952 contained the original formulation of Sanskritisation by M.N. Srinivas?
o: Religion and Society among the Coorgs of South India
113.x: The concept was coined by M.N. Srinivas in Religion and Society among the Coorgs of South India, published in 1952. It was further developed in Social Change in Modern India.
