The SIT was constituted by the Vijayawada court and later transferred to the NHRC.
127.x: The NHRC sought reports in June 2026, and subsequently the Supreme Court gave the SIT seven-day custody of suspended CI Nagaraju.
127.tq: Arrange the connected events by identifying the earliest institutional action and rejecting reversed sequences.
127.sec: Universal angles

127.s: The SIT in the Gade Sai Krishna custodial-death case was headed by:
o: The Chairperson of the State Police Complaints Authority
127.x: The Supreme Court gave the SIT, headed by IGP M. Ravi Prakash, seven-day custody of suspended CI Nagaraju.
127.tq: Separate the investigating authority from the officer whose custody was granted.
127.sec: Universal angles

127.s: On 31 July 2026, the Supreme Court gave the SIT how many days’ custody of suspended CI Nagaraju?
127.x: On 31 July 2026, the Supreme Court granted the SIT seven-day custody of suspended CI Nagaraju.
127.tq: Identify the exact duration and avoid confusing it with the 14-day safeguard in death-penalty cases.
127.sec: Universal angles

127.s: Which development occurred on 11 August 2026 in relation to the Gade Sai Krishna custodial-death case?
o: A Vijayawada court summoned the Tirupati MP to record his statement.
The Supreme Court abolished the SIT.
The State Police Complaints Authority sentenced nine policemen to death.
127.x: On 11 August 2026, a Vijayawada court summoned the Tirupati MP to record his statement.
127.tq: Match the date with the precise procedural development and reject institutional substitutions.
127.sec: Universal angles

127.s: The debate between retributive and reformative justice in the context of custodial violence and the death penalty primarily concerns the choice between:
o: Punishment as retaliation and punishment aimed at reform
127.x: Retributive justice emphasises punishment or retaliation for wrongdoing, whereas reformative justice focuses on rehabilitation and reform of the offender.
127.tq: Separate the two competing purposes of punishment rather than confusing them with procedural or administrative issues.
127.sec: Universal angles

127.s: Which one of the following best reflects the criticism concerning convictions in custodial-death cases?
o: Conviction is automatic whenever a custodial death occurs.
Custodial-death cases are decided only by Police Complaints Authorities.
The conviction rate is near zero.
The conviction rate is consistently above 90%.
127.x: A major criticism is that the conviction rate in custodial-death cases remains near zero, raising concerns about accountability and impunity.
127.tq: Identify the reported trend and reject absolute or institutionally incorrect alternatives.
127.sec: Universal angles

128.s: The judgment in Shah Bano (1985) is associated with which of the following issues?
o: Entry of women aged 10–50 into the Sabarimala temple
Permanent commission for women Army officers
Maintenance of a divorced Muslim woman under Section 125 of the CrPC
128.x: The Shah Bano judgment recognised the entitlement of a divorced Muslim woman to maintenance under Section 125 of the CrPC and also urged the adoption of a Uniform Civil Code.
128.tq: Match the landmark case with its distinctive legal issue.
128.sec: Landmark judgements on women's rights → issue

128.s: Sarla Mudgal v. Union of India (1995) primarily dealt with which of the following?
o: Conversion to Islam to contract a second Hindu marriage
Adultery under Section 497 of the IPC
128.x: Sarla Mudgal held that conversion to Islam cannot be used to validate a second marriage by a Hindu man and stressed the need for a Uniform Civil Code.
128.tq: Use the wrong-person or wrong-issue trap in landmark-judgment questions.
128.sec: Landmark judgements on women's rights → issue

128.s: The guidelines issued in Vishaka (1997) were principally concerned with
o: Sexual harassment of women at the workplace
128.x: The Vishaka judgment laid down guidelines against sexual harassment at the workplace, which were later followed by the POSH Act, 2013.
128.tq: Identify the judgment by linking it to the legislation that followed.
128.sec: Landmark judgements on women's rights → issue

128.s: Which one of the following pairs is NOT correctly matched?
o: Joseph Shine — Entry of women into Sabarimala
Seema v. Ashwani Kumar — Compulsory registration of all marriages
Shayara Bano — Instant triple talaq unconstitutional
Babita Puniya — Permanent commission for women Army officers
128.x: Joseph Shine (2018) struck down adultery under Section 497 of the IPC. Entry of women aged 10–50 into Sabarimala was the issue in the Sabarimala case.
128.tq: Find the swapped issue among closely related landmark judgments.
128.sec: Landmark judgements on women's rights → issue

128.s:
Consider the following pairs:
a. Seema v. Ashwani Kumar — 2006
b. Shayara Bano — August 2017
c. Joseph Shine — 2018
d. Vineeta Sharma — 2020
Which of the pairs given above are correctly matched?
128.x: Seema v. Ashwani Kumar was decided in 2006, Shayara Bano in August 2017, Joseph Shine in 2018 and Vineeta Sharma in 2020.
128.tq: Check dates against the named judgments before selecting the coded combination.
128.sec: Landmark judgements on women's rights → issue

128.s: In which case was the right of a daughter to be a coparcener by birth recognised, irrespective of whether the father was alive on 9 September 2005?
128.x: Vineeta Sharma (2020) recognised that a daughter is a coparcener by birth, whether or not the father was alive on 9 September 2005.
128.tq: Use the precise legal consequence to distinguish similar women’s-rights judgments.
128.sec: Landmark judgements on women's rights → issue

128.s: The Sabarimala judgment concerning women's rights dealt with the entry of women belonging to which age group into the temple?
128.x: The Sabarimala judgment concerned the entry of women aged 10–50 into the temple.
128.tq: Focus on the exact age range rather than the general subject of the case.
128.sec: Landmark judgements on women's rights → issue

128.s:
Consider the following statements regarding the Muslim Women (Protection of Rights on Marriage) Act, 2019:
1. It makes instant triple talaq void.
2. The offence is cognisable and non-bailable.
3. It provides for imprisonment up to three years.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
128.x: The 2019 Act declares instant triple talaq void, makes the offence cognisable and non-bailable, and provides for imprisonment up to three years.
128.tq: Test the legal status, procedural character and punishment together.
128.sec: Landmark judgements on women's rights → issue

128.s: The National Policy for Empowerment of Women, 2001 was associated with which of the following developments?
o: The shift in the Eighth Plan from development to empowerment
The replacement of empowerment by welfare
128.x: The Eighth Plan marked a shift in policy emphasis from development of women to empowerment of women. The year 2001 was also observed as the Year of Women’s Empowerment.
128.tq: Identify the policy milestone by its distinctive planning-period shift.
128.sec: National Policy for Empowerment of Women 2001 and draft 2016 policy - objectives

128.s: Which of the following is NOT an objective of the National Policy for Empowerment of Women, 2001?
o: Promoting commercial surrogacy as an employment opportunity
Ending discrimination and violence against women
Ensuring equal access to health, education and employment
128.x: The policy objectives included advancement and empowerment, equal access to health, education and employment, ending discrimination and violence, and gender mainstreaming. Commercial surrogacy is not a policy objective listed here.
128.tq: Find the unrelated legal concept inserted among genuine policy objectives.
128.sec: National Policy for Empowerment of Women 2001 and draft 2016 policy - objectives

128.s: Which of the following was NOT identified as a priority area in the Draft National Policy for Women, 2016?
128.x: The 2016 draft policy identified health, food security and nutrition, education, economy, governance and decision-making, violence against women, enabling environment, and environment and climate change as priority areas.
128.tq: Separate the listed policy priorities from an invented institutional measure.
128.sec: National Policy for Empowerment of Women 2001 and draft 2016 policy - objectives

128.s:
Consider the following statements:
1. The Draft National Policy for Women, 2016 included food security and nutrition under health.
2. It included governance and decision-making as a priority area.
3. It excluded environmental and climate-change concerns.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
128.x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct. Statement 3 is false because environment and climate change were expressly included as priority areas.
128.tq: Detect the negative reversal of a listed policy priority.
128.sec: National Policy for Empowerment of Women 2001 and draft 2016 policy - objectives

128.s: Under the Surrogacy (Regulation) Act, 2021, which form of surrogacy is permitted?
o: Altruistic surrogacy limited to medical costs and insurance
128.x: The Act permits altruistic surrogacy, under which medical costs and insurance are allowed. Commercial surrogacy is prohibited, and certificates of essentiality and eligibility are required.
128.tq: Distinguish the permitted form from the prohibited commercial form.
128.sec: Reproductive rights laws - Surrogacy Act 2021, ART Act 2021, MTP (Amendment) Act 2021

128.s:
Consider the following statements regarding surrogacy under the Surrogacy (Regulation) Act, 2021:
1. Commercial surrogacy is prohibited.
2. A woman can be a surrogate only once.
3. Sex selection is permitted if the surrogate gives written consent.
4. The couple requires certificates of essentiality and eligibility.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
128.x: Statements 1, 2 and 4 are correct. Sex selection is prohibited and cannot be permitted merely through the surrogate’s consent.
128.tq: Use one reversed prohibition to eliminate an otherwise attractive combination.
128.sec: Reproductive rights laws - Surrogacy Act 2021, ART Act 2021, MTP (Amendment) Act 2021

128.s: A foetus carried through surrogacy may be aborted under the applicable law only when
o: the intending couple alone gives consent
the ART clinic recommends it without further approval
the surrogate gives written consent and authorisation is obtained under the MTP Act
the surrogate’s consent is specifically excluded
128.x: Abortion of a surrogate foetus is not prohibited outright. It requires the surrogate’s written consent and authorisation under the MTP Act.
128.tq: Apply the exception to a general prohibition instead of treating abortion as absolutely banned.
128.sec: Reproductive rights laws - Surrogacy Act 2021, ART Act 2021, MTP (Amendment) Act 2021

128.s: The ART (Regulation) Act, 2021 provides for which of the following?
o: Registered ART clinics and banks along with a national registry
Unregistered ART clinics and unrestricted sale of embryos
Sale of gametes without regulatory control
128.x: The ART Act provides for registered ART clinics and banks and establishes a national registry. Sex-selective ART and the sale of gametes or embryos are prohibited.
128.tq: Identify the regulatory framework by its institutional components.
128.sec: Reproductive rights laws - Surrogacy Act 2021, ART Act 2021, MTP (Amendment) Act 2021

128.s: Which one of the following is NOT correctly matched under the ART (Regulation) Act, 2021?
o: National registry — Regulatory record of ART institutions
Sale of gametes or embryos — Prohibited
128.x: Sex-selective ART is prohibited under the ART Act, 2021. Registered clinics and banks and a national registry are permitted regulatory arrangements.
128.tq: Locate the option that reverses a statutory prohibition.
128.sec: Reproductive rights laws - Surrogacy Act 2021, ART Act 2021, MTP (Amendment) Act 2021

128.s: Under the MTP (Amendment) Act, 2021, termination of pregnancy up to 20 weeks is permitted on the opinion of
o: A State Medical Board in every case
Two judges of a Family Court
128.x: The Act permits termination up to 20 weeks on the opinion of one doctor. A period of up to 24 weeks is available for specified special categories.
128.tq: Separate the one-doctor, special-category and Medical Board thresholds.
128.sec: Reproductive rights laws - Surrogacy Act 2021, ART Act 2021, MTP (Amendment) Act 2021

128.s:
Consider the following statements regarding the MTP (Amendment) Act, 2021:
1. Termination up to 20 weeks may be undertaken on one doctor’s opinion.
2. Termination up to 24 weeks is available for special categories.
3. Beyond 24 weeks, a State Medical Board may permit termination for substantial foetal abnormality.
4. The woman’s identity may be disclosed without restriction.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
128.x: Statements 1, 2 and 3 are correct. The Act prohibits disclosure of the woman’s identity, so statement 4 is false.
128.tq: Combine statutory limits with the confidentiality safeguard and reject the reversed statement.
128.sec: Reproductive rights laws - Surrogacy Act 2021, ART Act 2021, MTP (Amendment) Act 2021

128.s: In cases of substantial foetal abnormality, termination beyond 24 weeks under the MTP framework is decided by the
128.x: A State Medical Board decides cases involving substantial foetal abnormality beyond 24 weeks; in such cases no gestational limit applies.
128.tq: Ask which institution performs the specific statutory function.
128.sec: Reproductive rights laws - Surrogacy Act 2021, ART Act 2021, MTP (Amendment) Act 2021

128.s: The PCPNDT Act, 1994 prohibits
o: Sex selection and prenatal sex determination
Termination of pregnancy up to 20 weeks
128.x: The PCPNDT Act bans sex selection and prenatal sex determination. Tests are allowed for detecting genetic abnormalities.
128.tq: Distinguish the prohibited diagnostic purpose from permitted testing for genetic abnormality.
128.sec: Reproductive rights laws - Surrogacy Act 2021, ART Act 2021, MTP (Amendment) Act 2021

128.s: The Supreme Court’s 2022 ruling on abortion access removed distinctions based on
o: The State in which the woman resides
128.x: The Supreme Court in 2022 removed marital-status distinctions in access to abortion, invoking Article 14.
128.tq: Identify the exact discriminatory distinction removed by the judgment.
128.sec: Reproductive rights laws - Surrogacy Act 2021, ART Act 2021, MTP (Amendment) Act 2021

128.s:
Consider the following statements regarding the National Commission for Women:
1. It reviews safeguards and laws relating to women.
2. It can take suo motu notice of complaints and matters.
3. It may inspect jails and remand homes.
4. The Centre must consult it on policy matters affecting women.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
128.x: All four statements correctly describe functions or responsibilities associated with the NCW, including review, suo motu action, inspection and consultation on relevant policy matters.
128.tq: Recognise the comprehensive option when all listed institutional functions are supported.
128.sec: Institutions for women's justice - NCW, AP State Commission for Women, Family Courts, first women's court

128.s: Who nominates the Chairperson, members and Member-Secretary of the National Commission for Women?
128.x: The Chairperson, five members and Member-Secretary of the NCW are nominated by the Centre.
128.tq: Use the ‘who appoints or nominates?’ method for institutional questions.
128.sec: Institutions for women's justice - NCW, AP State Commission for Women, Family Courts, first women's court

128.s: Which one of the following best describes gender discrimination?
o: Male dominance in family and society
Equal treatment of men and women in public employment
Unequal treatment by society of men and women
Biological differences between men and women
128.x: Gender discrimination means unequal treatment by society of men and women. Biological differences relate to sex, while male dominance describes patriarchy.
128.tq: Distinguish the exact definition from closely related gender concepts.
128.sec: Gender concepts → meaning

128.s:
Consider the following statements:
1. Sex refers primarily to biological characteristics.
2. Gender refers to socially constructed roles.
3. Gender and sex are identical concepts.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
128.x: Sex is biological, whereas gender consists of socially constructed roles. Therefore, statement 3 is incorrect.
128.tq: Split the options by identifying the statement that reverses a confusable pair.
128.sec: Gender concepts → meaning

128.s: Patriarchy is best understood as a system in which
o: men hold primary power and status in family and society
women hold primary power in family and society
descent is traced only through the female line
all family decisions are taken collectively
128.x: Patriarchy denotes male dominance and the primary holding of power and status by men in family and society.
128.tq: Match the sociological term with its precise meaning.
128.sec: Gender concepts → meaning

128.s: Which of the following is regarded as an exception to the general pattern of patriarchy mentioned in the context of family and society?
128.x: Matrilineal tribes are identified as an exception to the general pattern in which men hold primary power and status.
128.tq: Test the exception rather than the general rule.
128.sec: Gender concepts → meaning

128.s: The term ‘Missing women’ was coined by
128.x: Amartya Sen coined the term ‘missing women’ to refer to the consequences of discrimination against women, including intra-household discrimination.
128.tq: Use the person–concept association without confusing it with other gender scholars.
128.sec: Gender concepts → meaning

128.s: Which one of the following pairs is correctly matched?
o: Uma Chakravarti — A Field of One’s Own
Gail Omvedt — Seeing Like a Feminist
Bina Agarwal — Land rights and A Field of One’s Own
128.x: Bina Agarwal is associated with land rights and authored A Field of One’s Own. Seeing Like a Feminist is associated with Nivedita Menon, while ‘missing women’ was coined by Amartya Sen.
128.tq: Start from the sure author–work pair and eliminate swapped scholars.
128.sec: Gender concepts → meaning

128.s: Gender mainstreaming refers to
o: measuring only women’s participation in elections
restricting welfare policies to women alone
assessing the impact of every policy on women and men
replacing all gender-specific laws with personal laws
128.x: Gender mainstreaming builds a gender perspective into policy-making by assessing the impact of policies on women and men.
128.tq: Apply the concept to a policy-making situation rather than relying on a keyword.
128.sec: Gender concepts → meaning

128.s: Which of the following statements correctly distinguishes gender mainstreaming from a gender audit?
o: Mainstreaming concerns only biological differences, whereas auditing concerns only employment.
Mainstreaming is limited to personal law, whereas auditing is limited to criminal law.
There is no conceptual distinction between the two.
Mainstreaming is a Beijing strategy, whereas a gender audit checks whether policies and budgets affect women and men equally.
128.x: Gender mainstreaming involves building a gender lens into every policy and was adopted as a Beijing strategy. A gender audit examines whether policies and budgets affect women and men equally.
128.tq: Compare two closely related concepts by their function and scope.
128.sec: Gender concepts → meaning

128.s: CEDAW was adopted by the United Nations General Assembly in
128.x: The UN General Assembly adopted CEDAW in 1979. India signed it in 1980 and ratified it in 1993.
128.tq: Separate the international adoption year from India’s signature and ratification years.
128.sec: International commitments - CEDAW, Beijing Declaration and Platform for Action

128.s:
Consider the following statements regarding India and CEDAW:
1. India signed CEDAW in 1980.
2. India ratified CEDAW in 1993.
3. India adopted CEDAW only after the Beijing Conference of 1995.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
128.x: India signed CEDAW in 1980 and ratified it in 1993. Statement 3 is false because both events preceded the Beijing Conference of 1995.
128.tq: Use the chronological relationship among signature, ratification and conference dates.
128.sec: International commitments - CEDAW, Beijing Declaration and Platform for Action

128.s: India’s reservation under CEDAW relates to
o: Article 29(1) concerning arbitration or the International Court of Justice
128.x: India made a reservation regarding Article 29(1), which concerns arbitration or reference of disputes to the International Court of Justice.
128.tq: Distinguish the reservation article from the articles carrying declarations.
128.sec: International commitments - CEDAW, Beijing Declaration and Platform for Action

128.s: Which of the following Articles of CEDAW were the subject of India’s declarations mentioned in the international commitments?
128.x: India made declarations concerning Articles 5(a), 16(1) and 16(2). Article 29(1) was associated with a reservation.
128.tq: Discriminate between a declaration and a reservation by checking the exact article numbers.
128.sec: International commitments - CEDAW, Beijing Declaration and Platform for Action

128.s: The Beijing Declaration and Platform for Action was adopted at the
o: First World Conference on Women, Mexico City, 1975
128.x: The Beijing Declaration and Platform for Action emerged from the Fourth World Conference on Women held in 1995.
128.tq: Match the declaration with the correct conference and year.
128.sec: International commitments - CEDAW, Beijing Declaration and Platform for Action

128.s: How many critical areas of concern are identified in the Beijing Platform for Action?
128.x: The Beijing Platform for Action identifies 12 critical areas, including poverty, education, health, violence, economy, decision-making, media, environment and the girl child.
128.tq: Recall the precise number in a named international framework.
128.sec: International commitments - CEDAW, Beijing Declaration and Platform for Action

128.s: Which one of the following is NOT identified as a critical area in the Beijing Platform for Action?
128.x: The Beijing Platform for Action covers areas such as violence, economy and decision-making. Expansion of nuclear weapons is not one of its 12 critical areas.
128.tq: Find the unrelated item among a list of recognised agenda areas.
128.sec: International commitments - CEDAW, Beijing Declaration and Platform for Action

128.s: Which Article of the Constitution provides for special provisions for women and children?
128.x: Article 15(3) enables the State to make special provisions for women and children.
128.tq: Identify the specific sub-clause rather than the broader equality provision.
128.sec: Constitutional provisions for women → content

128.s:
Consider the following statements:
1. Article 14 embodies equality.
2. Article 15(1) prohibits discrimination on the ground of sex.
3. Article 16(2) prohibits discrimination on the ground of sex in public employment.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
128.x: Articles 14, 15(1) and 16(2) respectively provide equality, prohibit sex discrimination and prohibit such discrimination in public employment.
128.tq: Combine related constitutional provisions while checking the scope of each Article.
128.sec: Constitutional provisions for women → content

128.s: Article 39(d) of the Constitution relates to
o: renunciation of practices derogatory to women’s dignity
128.x: Article 39(d) directs the State towards equal pay for equal work. Article 39(a) concerns an adequate means of livelihood.
128.tq: Distinguish neighbouring Directive Principles by their exact wording.
128.sec: Constitutional provisions for women → content

128.s: Which constitutional provision directs the State to secure just and humane conditions of work and maternity relief?
128.x: Article 42 directs the State to make provisions for securing just and humane conditions of work and maternity relief.
128.tq: Match the constitutional Article with the specific welfare objective.
128.sec: Constitutional provisions for women → content

128.s: Renouncing practices derogatory to the dignity of women is a fundamental duty under
128.x: Article 51A(e) includes the duty to renounce practices derogatory to the dignity of women.
128.tq: Separate a Fundamental Duty from Directive Principles and reservation provisions.
128.sec: Constitutional provisions for women → content

128.s: Which one of the following pairs is correctly matched?
o: Article 243D — reservation of seats and chairperson offices in Panchayats
Article 42 — reservation of seats in State Assemblies
128.x: Article 243D provides for at least one-third reservation of seats and chairperson offices in Panchayats. Article 243T relates to Municipalities.
128.tq: Use the local-body distinction between Panchayats and Municipalities.
128.sec: Constitutional provisions for women → content

128.s: Under the constitutional provisions described, Article 243T concerns reservation for women in
128.x: Article 243T provides for reservation in Municipalities, including at least one-third of seats and chairperson posts for women.
128.tq: Discriminate between Articles 243D and 243T by the institution concerned.
128.sec: Constitutional provisions for women → content

128.s: According to the stated implementation detail, the 33 per cent quota under the Nari Shakti Vandan Adhiniyam came into effect in the Jammu and Kashmir and Puducherry Assemblies on
128.x: The stated implementation date for the 33 per cent quota in the Jammu and Kashmir and Puducherry Assemblies is 17 April 2026.
128.tq: Separate the implementation date from dates belonging to personal-law and labour-law reforms.
128.sec: Constitutional provisions for women → content

128.s: The Hindu Succession Act, 1956 is associated with which of the following reforms?
o: Abolition of the female heir’s limited estate and equal inheritance for women
Mandatory registration of every inter-faith marriage under one uniform law
128.x: The Hindu Succession Act, 1956 gave women equal inheritance and abolished the female heir’s limited estate. Civil marriage irrespective of religion is associated with the Special Marriage Act.
128.tq: Distinguish personal-law reform from marriage and labour legislation.
128.sec: Personal law reforms - Hindu Succession (Amendment) 2005 and AP amendment, Special Marriage Act, Hindu Marriage Act

128.s: The principal effect of the Hindu Succession (Amendment) Act, 2005 was that daughters became
128.x: The 2005 amendment made daughters coparceners by birth and gave them rights equal to those of sons in coparcenary property.
128.tq: Test the operative legal change using the exact phrase ‘by birth’.
128.sec: Personal law reforms - Hindu Succession (Amendment) 2005 and AP amendment, Special Marriage Act, Hindu Marriage Act

128.s: Which State had already made unmarried daughters coparceners through its amendment before the national Hindu Succession (Amendment) Act, 2005?
128.x: Andhra Pradesh made unmarried daughters coparceners through an earlier amendment. The Andhra Pradesh Assembly passed the relevant Act on 24 September 1985 under NTR.
128.tq: Identify the State-level precursor to the later central reform.
128.sec: Personal law reforms - Hindu Succession (Amendment) 2005 and AP amendment, Special Marriage Act, Hindu Marriage Act

128.s: The Andhra Pradesh Assembly passed its Hindu Succession (Amendment) Act on
128.x: The Andhra Pradesh Assembly passed its Hindu Succession (Amendment) Act on 24 September 1985 under NTR.
128.tq: Distinguish the date of passage from the later year of the national amendment.
128.sec: Personal law reforms - Hindu Succession (Amendment) 2005 and AP amendment, Special Marriage Act, Hindu Marriage Act

128.s: The Hindu Succession Act does not apply to
o: all persons belonging to Scheduled Castes
all women belonging to Scheduled Tribes notified under the Act’s exclusion
128.x: Section 2(2) excludes notified Scheduled Tribes from the application of the Hindu Succession Act. The Supreme Court held that this exclusion cannot be extended to tribals merely on the basis of their religion.
128.tq: Test the statutory exception and avoid replacing Scheduled Tribes with Scheduled Castes.
128.sec: Personal law reforms - Hindu Succession (Amendment) 2005 and AP amendment, Special Marriage Act, Hindu Marriage Act

128.s: In Vineeta Sharma v. Rakesh Sharma (2020), the daughter’s coparcenary right was held to exist
o: whether or not the father was alive on 9 September 2005
only if the father was alive on 9 September 2005
only if the daughter was married after 2005
128.x: Vineeta Sharma held that the daughter’s coparcenary right is by birth and does not depend on whether the father was alive on 9 September 2005.
128.tq: Reject the tempting but incorrect condition concerning the father’s survival on the cut-off date.
128.sec: Personal law reforms - Hindu Succession (Amendment) 2005 and AP amendment, Special Marriage Act, Hindu Marriage Act

128.s: The Supreme Court upheld the exclusion of Scheduled Tribes from the Hindu Succession Act on
128.x: The stated date of the Supreme Court decision upholding the exclusion of Scheduled Tribes is 8 October 2025.
128.tq: Match the judicial development with its precise date rather than the amendment date.
128.sec: Personal law reforms - Hindu Succession (Amendment) 2005 and AP amendment, Special Marriage Act, Hindu Marriage Act

128.s: Which one of the following is correctly matched?
o: Special Marriage Act, 1954 — civil marriage irrespective of religion
Hindu Marriage Act, 1955 — equal pay for equal work
Hindu Succession Act, 1956 — regulation of night shifts
Equal Remuneration Act, 1976 — grounds of divorce under Hindu law
128.x: The Special Marriage Act, 1954 provides a civil marriage framework irrespective of religion. The Hindu Marriage Act, 1955 deals with monogamy and grounds of divorce.
128.tq: Match each law with its subject and reject cross-subject substitutions.
128.sec: Personal law reforms - Hindu Succession (Amendment) 2005 and AP amendment, Special Marriage Act, Hindu Marriage Act

128.s: The Hindu Marriage Act, 1955 is primarily associated with
128.x: The Hindu Marriage Act, 1955 provides for monogamy and specifies grounds of divorce under Hindu personal law.
128.tq: Identify the subject matter of the personal law statute without confusing it with succession law.
128.sec: Personal law reforms - Hindu Succession (Amendment) 2005 and AP amendment, Special Marriage Act, Hindu Marriage Act

128.s: The Equal Remuneration Act, 1976 was enacted to provide for
o: equal pay for equal work and absence of sex bias in recruitment and promotion
128.x: The Equal Remuneration Act, 1976 addressed equal pay for equal work and prohibited gender bias in recruitment and promotion.
128.tq: Separate the employment-equality statute from maternity and marriage laws.
128.sec: Equal pay and work rights - Equal Remuneration Act 1976, Code on Wages, night shifts

128.s: The Equal Remuneration Act, 1976 was subsumed into the
128.x: The Equal Remuneration Act, 1976 was subsumed into the Code on Wages, 2019, along with specified wage-related enactments.
128.tq: Match the earlier statute with the labour code that absorbed it.
128.sec: Equal pay and work rights - Equal Remuneration Act 1976, Code on Wages, night shifts

128.s: Which of the following enactments was NOT absorbed into the Code on Wages, 2019?
128.x: The Code on Wages, 2019 absorbed the Equal Remuneration Act, Minimum Wages Act, Payment of Wages Act and Payment of Bonus Act. The Maternity Benefit (Amendment) Act, 2017 was not among these four enactments.
128.tq: Find the statute outside the specific group of laws subsumed by the Code.
128.sec: Equal pay and work rights - Equal Remuneration Act 1976, Code on Wages, night shifts

128.s: The Code on Wages, 2019 prohibits wage discrimination on the ground of gender, including discrimination against
128.x: The Code on Wages prohibits gender-based wage discrimination and includes transgender persons within its protection. It also provides for a statutory floor wage.
128.tq: Apply the scope of an anti-discrimination provision to the protected category specified.
128.sec: Equal pay and work rights - Equal Remuneration Act 1976, Code on Wages, night shifts

128.s: The Code on Wages, 2019 also provides for a
o: reservation of one-third seats in Municipalities
128.x: Apart from prohibiting gender discrimination in wages and recruitment, the Code on Wages provides for a statutory floor wage.
128.tq: Test an additional feature of the statute rather than its principal prohibition alone.
128.sec: Equal pay and work rights - Equal Remuneration Act 1976, Code on Wages, night shifts

129.s: Under Section 2 of the Dowry Prohibition Act, 1961, the term ‘dowry’ refers to:
o: Only property demanded by the bride’s family before marriage
Property or valuable security given or agreed to be given, directly or indirectly, in connection with a marriage
Any gift exchanged between the spouses after marriage, including mahr
Only cash or movable property given after marriage
129.x: Dowry includes property or valuable security given or agreed to be given directly or indirectly, before, at or any time after marriage, in connection with the marriage. Dower or mahr under Muslim personal law is excluded.
129.tq: Test the exact statutory definition and distinguish the excluded term.
129.sec: Dowry Prohibition Act 1961 - commencement, definition, penalties, Dowry Prohibition Officers, IPC/BNS sections

129.tq: Find the wrong authority attached to a statutory power.
129.sec: Dowry Prohibition Act 1961 - commencement, definition, penalties, Dowry Prohibition Officers, IPC/BNS sections

129.s: The minimum punishment prescribed for giving, taking or abetting the giving or taking of dowry under Section 3 of the Dowry Prohibition Act is:
o: Imprisonment of six months and fine up to ₹10,000
Imprisonment of not less than five years and fine of not less than ₹15,000 or the value of the dowry, whichever is more
Imprisonment up to five years and fine up to ₹15,000
Imprisonment of two years and fine equal to the value of the dowry
129.x: Section 3 prescribes imprisonment of not less than five years and a fine of not less than ₹15,000 or the value of the dowry, whichever is more. Five years is the minimum, not the maximum.
129.tq: Distinguish a statutory minimum from an apparent maximum.
129.sec: Dowry Prohibition Act 1961 - commencement, definition, penalties, Dowry Prohibition Officers, IPC/BNS sections

Imprisonment from two to five years without any fine
Imprisonment of not less than five years and fine of ₹15,000
Imprisonment up to six months and fine equal to the dowry value
129.x: Section 4 deals with demanding dowry and prescribes imprisonment from six months to two years, along with a fine up to ₹10,000.
129.tq: Separate the punishment for demanding dowry from the more severe punishment under Section 3.
129.sec: Dowry Prohibition Act 1961 - commencement, definition, penalties, Dowry Prohibition Officers, IPC/BNS sections

o: Only the Dowry Prohibition Officer appointed by the State Government
Only the aggrieved woman’s immediate relatives
Only the police officer investigating the case
A recognised welfare body, among other permissible sources

129.sec: Dowry Prohibition Act 1961 - commencement, definition, penalties, Dowry Prohibition Officers, IPC/BNS sections

Cruelty — BNS Section 80; corresponding IPC Section 498A
Presumption of dowry death — BNS Section 85; corresponding Evidence Act Section 113B
Dowry death — BNS Section 86; corresponding IPC Section 304B
129.x: Dowry death is covered by BNS Section 80, corresponding to IPC Section 304B. Cruelty is covered by BNS Sections 85 and 86, corresponding to IPC Section 498A, while the presumption is under BSA Section 118, corresponding to Evidence Act Section 113B.
